Ibn 'Atiyya said: The more evident view is that it is the customary greeting, and the honour lies in God's greeting him and bestowing peace upon him in the situations in which a person is in utmost weakness, need, lack of resource, and poverty before God. Al-Tabari mentions from al-Hasan that 'Isa and Yahya, peace be upon them both, met, and they were cousins, and Yahya said to 'Isa: "Pray for me, for you are better than I," and 'Isa said to him: "Rather you pray for me, for you are better than I. God has greeted you with peace, and I have greeted myself with peace."

Abu 'Abdullah al-Razi said: ﴿On the day he was born﴾, that is, safety for him from the Devil reaching him; ﴿and the day he dies﴾, that is, safety from the punishment of the grave; ﴿and the day he is raised alive﴾ from God's punishment on the Day of Resurrection. In His saying ﴿and the day he is raised alive﴾ there is an indication that he is among the martyrs, due to His saying ﴿Rather, they are alive with their Lord, provided for﴾ [Al 'Imran: 169]. This greeting may come from God or from the angels. End of quotation. The more evident view is that it is from God, because it is in the context of ﴿And We gave him wisdom﴾.

**[p. 170]** Surah Maryam: ninety-eight verses, Meccan.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Kaf, Ha, Ya, 'Ayn, Sad.﴾ ﴿A mention of the mercy of your Lord to His servant Zakariya,﴾ ﴿when he called to his Lord in a secret supplication.﴾ ﴿He said, "My Lord, indeed my bones have weakened, and my head has filled with gray, and I have never been unsuccessful in my supplication to You, my Lord.﴾ ﴿And indeed I fear the successors after me, and my wife has been barren, so give me from Yourself an heir,﴾ ﴿who will inherit me and inherit from the family of Ya'qub. And make him, my Lord, pleasing [to You]."﴾ ﴿"O Zakariya, indeed We give you good tidings of a boy whose name is Yahya; We have not assigned to anyone before [this] name."﴾ ﴿He said, "My Lord, how can I have a boy when my wife has been barren and I have reached extreme old age?"﴾ ﴿He said, "So it will be. Your Lord says, 'It is easy for Me, and I had already created you before, when you were nothing.'"﴾ ﴿He said, "My Lord, appoint for me a sign." He said, "Your sign is that you will not speak to the people for three nights, although sound."﴾ ﴿So he came out to his people from the prayer niche and conveyed to them, "Exalt [Allah] in the morning and the afternoon."﴾ ﴿"O Yahya, take the Scripture with determination." And We gave him judgment while still a child,﴾ ﴿and compassion from Us and purity. And he was fearful [of Allah],﴾ ﴿and dutiful to his parents, and he was not a tyrant or disobedient.﴾ ﴿And peace is upon him the day he was born, and the day he dies, and the day he is raised alive.﴾

﴿And mention in the Scripture Maryam, when she withdrew from her family to an eastern place.﴾ [Maryam: 16] ﴿And she took a screen [to conceal herself] from them. Then We sent to her Our Spirit, and it took for her the form of a man in all respects.﴾ [Maryam: 17] ﴿She said, "Indeed, I seek refuge in the Most Merciful from you, if you should be fearing [Allah]."﴾ [Maryam: 18] ﴿He said, "I am only the messenger of your Lord, to give you a pure boy."﴾ [Maryam: 19] ﴿She said, "How can I have a boy when no man has touched me and I have not been unchaste?"﴾ [Maryam: 20] ﴿He said, "So it will be. Your Lord says, 'It is easy for Me, and We will make him a sign for the people and a mercy from Us, and it is a matter already decreed.'"﴾ [Maryam: 21] ﴿So she conceived him, and she withdrew with him to a remote place.﴾ [Maryam: 22] ﴿Then the pains of childbirth drove her to the trunk of a palm tree. She said, "Oh, I wish I had died before this and had been forgotten and out of mind."﴾ [Maryam: 23] ﴿But he called to her from beneath her, "Do not grieve; your Lord has provided beneath you a stream.﴾ [Maryam: 24] ﴿And shake toward yourself the trunk of the palm tree; it will drop upon you ripe, fresh dates.﴾ [Maryam: 25] ﴿So eat and drink and be contented. And if you see anyone of the human being, say, 'Indeed, I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast, so I will not speak today to any person.'"﴾ [Maryam: 26] ﴿Then she brought him to her people, carrying him. They said, "O Maryam, you have certainly come with a thing unprecedented.﴾ [Maryam: 27] ﴿O sister of Harun, your father was not a man of evil, nor was your mother unchaste."﴾ [Maryam: 28] ﴿So she pointed to him. They said, "How can we speak to one who is in the cradle, a child?"﴾ [Maryam: 29].

**[p. 170]** (Ishtiʿal al-nar), the kindling of the fire: its scattering as it blazes, so that it becomes flames (shuʿal). It is also said that the shuʿaʿ (sparks) of the fire. Al-shayb (gray hair) is well known. (Shaba sha'ruhu) means his hair turned white after it had been of another color. (Al-makhad) is the intensification of the pain of labor, the pangs of delivery. (Al-jidh, trunk) is the part between the ground where the tree is rooted and the point where its branches divide. The word is also applied to a branch, and its plural is ajdhaʿ for the few and judhudh for the many. (Al-sarriy) means one of high rank; it is said sarawa yasruw, and its plural is sarawa with a fatḥa on the sin, and surawaʾ. These two plural forms are irregular for it; the regular pattern would be afʿilaʾ. Al-sarriy also means a small stream, because water flows in it; its final radical is yāʾ, as the final radical of that root is wāw. Labid said:

*So they both crossed the width of the stream, and it split, its banks well-watered, its edges neighboring.*

That is, a rivulet. (Al-hazz) means shaking. (Al-rutab) is well known; its singular is rutbah, and it is irregularly pluralized as arṭāb, like rubʿ and arbāʿ. It is what is cut before it hardens and dries. Al-janiyy is what is ripe and suitable for picking. Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala said: it has not dried or withered. It is also said that al-janiyy is what has become soft from the unripe dates. Al-Farra' said: al-janiyy and al-majniyy are the same, and it is also said that al-janiyy is what has been cut off. (Qurrat al-ʿayn), the coolness of the eye, derives from qarr (coolness). It is said: tears of joy are cool to the touch, and tears of grief are hot to the touch. Abu Tammam said:

*As for the eyes of the lovers, they have grown hot, but the eyes of the gloaters have grown cool.*

The Quraysh say qararTu bihi ʿaynan, and qararTu bi-l-makan aqarru. The people of Najd say qirtu bihi ʿaynan with kasra. Al-fariyy means a great matter, used both for good and for evil. From it comes the description of ʿUmar: "I have not seen a genius who performs his great deed." Al-fariyy also means cutting. In the proverb: "He came doing great things," meaning he did something great, in word or deed. Al-Zamakhshari said: al-fariyy means wondrous, and it derives from fary al-jild (flaying the hide). Al-ishara (gesture) is well known; it is made with the hand, the eye, the garment, the head, or the mouth. Ashāra's alif is converted from yāʾ. It is said tashayarna al-hilal, for the reciprocal form. Kathir said:

*I said, while within the entrails there is an insidious ailment: "Oh, how sweet, O ʿAzz, is that gesturing!"*

**[p. 171]** In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿Kaf, Ha, Ya, 'Ayn, Sad.﴾ [The rest of the passage repeats the verses 1–50 of the surah as above, with the reciting of verses as cited.]

**[p. 172]** This surah is Meccan, like the surah before it. Muqatil said: except for the prostration verse, which is Medinan, revealed after the emigration of the believers to Abyssinia. Its connection with what precedes it is that Allah, exalted is He, included in the surah before it wondrous narratives, such as the story of the People of the Cave, the story of Musa with al-Khidr, and the story of Dhu al-Qarnayn. This surah includes wondrous narratives: the birth of Yahya to an aged, decrepit man and a barren woman, and the birth of ʿIsa without a father. Since both share this astonishing matter, it fits to mention this surah after that one. The discussion of the disjointed letters at the beginnings of surahs was already covered at the beginning of al-Baqara, and what is to be pausing on is there.

(Dhikr) is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: this recited part of this Qur'an is a mention. It is also said that dhikr is the predicate of the statement "Kaf, Ha, Ya, 'Ayn, Sad," which is the subject; al-Farra' mentioned this. It is said there is remoteness in this, because the predicate is in meaning the subject, and the disjointed letters do not contain a mention of mercy, nor is their meaning the mention of mercy. It is also said that dhikr is the subject and the predicate is omitted, its estimate being: in what is recited is dhikr.

The majority read kāf with sukūn on the fāʾ. It is reported from al-Hasan that it is read with ḍamma. Nafi' inclined the hāʾ and the yāʾ between the two pronunciations, and made the dāl of ṣād clear at that point. (Dhikr): al-Hasan read the hāʾ with ḍamma, and also from him the yāʾ with ḍamma and the hāʾ with kasra. From ʿĀṣim, the yāʾ with ḍamma, and also both with kasra. From Hamza, the hāʾ with fatḥa and the yāʾ with kasra. Abu 'Amr al-Dani said: the meaning of ḍamma on the hāʾ and yāʾ is the completion of emphatic pronunciation, not the pure ḍamma that requires conversion. Abu al-Fadl ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Ahmad ibn al-Hasan al-Muqri al-Razi said in his book al-Lawāmiḥ fi Shawādhdh al-Qirāʾāt: Kharija from al-Hasan: kāf with ḍamma on the kāf; Nasr ibn ʿAsim from him with ḍamma on the hāʾ; and Harun ibn Musa al-ʿAtaki from Isma'il from him with ḍamma. These three are classed under ḍamma, but in reality the letters are not vowelled with ḍamma, for if they were, the alifs following them would have to be converted to wāws. Rather, these alifs were moved toward the wāw according to the dialect of the people of the Hijaz, and these are called the alif of emphasis, the opposite of the inclined alif. They resemble the fatḥas from which the ḍammas were produced. This rendering is like what they rendered for the inclined fatḥa close to kasra, with a kasra, due to the alif after it moving toward the yāʾ. End of quotation.

Abu Ja'far read these letters separately, distinguishing each from the others, to differentiate them from the letters that combine, so that they become parts of words; this requires the final letter of each to be vowelled with sukūn. Most readers made the dāl of ṣād clear before the dhāl of (dhikr), and Abu 'Amr assimilated it. Hafs from ʿAsim and a group read the nūn of (ʿayn) with clear pronunciation; the majority pronounced it with concealment (ikhfa').

Al-Hasan and Ibn Ya'mur read (dhakara) as a past verb, with (raḥmata) in the accusative, which Abu al-Fath reported and al-Zamakhshari mentioned from al-Hasan: meaning, this recited part of the Qur'an: "a mention of the mercy of your Lord." Al-Dani mentioned from Ibn Ya'mur (dhakkir) as an imperative verb from tadhkir (reminding), with (raḥmata) in the accusative, and (ʿabdahu) in the accusative governed by the mercy: that is, remind that the mercy of your Lord [was shown to] His servant. The author of al-Lawāmiḥ mentioned that (dhakkara), with shadda, in the past tense, from al-Hasan with variation, and it is authentic from Ibn Ya'mur. Its meaning: the recited part, that is the Qur'an, reminded [people] of the mercy of your Lord. When the preposition is removed, it takes the accusative. It is also possible that its meaning is: the Qur'an reminded the people with a reminder that Allah had shown mercy to His servant; the verbal noun then governs (ʿabdahu Zakariyya), because it reminded them of what they had forgotten of Allah's mercy, and so by the Qur'an and its revelation upon the Prophet (ﷺ) it was renewed for them. It is also possible that (dhakkara) is in the past tense with Allah, exalted is He, as its subject.

Al-Kalbi read (dhakara), in the past tense, lightened, from dhikr, (raḥmata rabbika) with the tā' in the accusative, and (ʿabduhu) in the nominative, attributing the verb to him. Ibn Khalawayh said: (dhakara raḥmata rabbika ʿabduhu), Yahya ibn Ya'mur; and (dhakkir) as an imperative from him also. End of quotation.

(Idh) is an adverb whose governing element al-Hawfi said is (dhikr). Abu al-Baqa' said: (idh) is an adverb of (raḥma) or of (dhikr). End of quotation.

The calling is described as hidden. Ibn Juraij said: so that it would not be mixed with show-off. Muqatil said: so that he would not be blamed for seeking a child in old age. Qatada said: because secret and public are equal before Him, exalted is He. It is also said: he kept it secret from his clients whom he feared. It is also said: because it was a worldly matter, so he hid it, for if it was answered, that was his goal, and if not, no one would know of it. It is also said: because it was in the depth of night. It is also said: because of his sincerity in it, so that no one knows it except Allah. It is also said: because of the weakness of his voice due to his old age, as it is said: "The elder's voice is faint, and his hearing is failing." It is also said: because concealment is the practice of the prophets, and loud calling is considered transgression. In revelation: ﴿Call upon your Lord humbly and secretly; indeed, He does not like transgressors.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 55]. In a hadith: "Indeed, you do not call upon one who is deaf or absent."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 19, verse 1–15 (part 2 of 3):

﴿He said, "My Lord, indeed my bones have weakened, and my head has ignited with white hair."﴾ This is the manner of his supplication and the explanation of his calling out. The majority (al-Jumhur) read (wahana) with a fatha on the ha'. Al-A'mash read it with a kasra. It is also read with a damma; there are three dialects (lughat thalath), and its meaning is weakness. The weakness is attributed to the bone because it is the pillar of the body (amud al-badan), upon which its stability rests, and it is the foundation of its structure. When it weakens, what is behind it collapses and its strength falls away. Also, it is the hardest and most solid part of it, so when it weakens, what is beneath it is even weaker. He used the singular "the bone" (al-'azm) because it denotes the genus (al-jins), intending that this genus, which is the pillar and the support, and the hardest of what the body is composed of, has been struck by weakness. Were it put in the plural, it would have been a different purpose, namely that not some of his bones had weakened, but all of them. Qatada said: he complained of the falling out of his molars. Al-Karmani said: he was seventy years old. It was said: seventy-five. It was said: eighty-five. It was said: sixty. It was said: sixty-five.

The white hair was likened to the flame of fire in its whiteness, its spreading through the hair, its pervading it, and its taking hold of it in every direction, to the kindling of fire. Then he brought it out as a metaphor (isti'ara). Then he attributed the kindling to the place of the hair and its growth, which is the head. He brought out the white hair as a specification (tamyiz) and did not add "the head" (to the noun), being satisfied with the addressee's knowledge that it is the head of Zakariyya. For this reason the sentence is sound and is attested to be eloquent, as al-Zamakhshari said. To this Ibn Duraid also looked, when he said:

"The whitened one ignited in its blackness, like the kindling of fire in dry ghada wood."

Some grammarians parsed (shaybан) as a verbal noun (masdar), saying: because the meaning of "and the head ignited" is "it turned white," so it is a masdar derived from the meaning. It was also said: it is a masdar in the accusative position as a circumstantial state (hal). The kindling of the head is a metaphor of the sensible for the sensible, since the borrowed-from is fire and the borrowed-for is white hair, and what unites them is spreading and dispersion.

﴿And I have never been﴾: a negation regarding the past, i.e., I have never been "with Your supplication, my Lord, unfortunate" (shaqiyan), but rather I was happy and successful, since You used to answer my supplication, so I was made happy by that. On this reading the kaf is the object (maf'ul). It was also said: the meaning is "with Your calling" to faith, "unfortunate": rather, I was among those who obeyed You and worshipped You sincerely. On this reading the kaf is the subject (fa'il). The first is more apparent, out of thankfulness to God the Exalted for what He had previously bestowed upon him, i.e., You have been good to me before, and I was made happy by my supplication to You, so Your favor requires that You answer me in the end as You answered me at the beginning.

It is related that Hatim al-Ta'i was approached by a seeker of a need, who said: "I did you a kindness at such-and-such a time." Hatim said: "Welcome to the one who made us a means to himself and fulfilled his need."

﴿And indeed I fear the mawali after me﴾. The mawali are the paternal cousins and the relatives who are close by lineage. The poet said:

"Gently, sons of our paternal uncle, gently, our mawali; do not dig up between us what has been buried."

And Labid said:

"And a mawla whom I have repelled the wrong from, while he has become in the state of one who is wronged."

Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada and Abu Salih said: the mawali here are the kalala (collateral heirs); he feared that they would inherit his wealth, and that the kalala would inherit from him. Qatada and al-Hasan related from the Prophet ﷺ: "May God have mercy on my brother Zakariyya; what was upon him was that he inherited his wealth." Another group said: his mawali were neglecting the religion, so he feared that upon his death the religion would be lost, so he sought a guardian who would uphold the religion after him. This is not sound from him, since he (peace be upon him) said: "We, the company of prophets, are not inherited; what we leave behind is charity." The apparent and fitting interpretation for Zakariyya, peace be upon him, given that he is infallible (ma'sum), is that he did not seek a child for the sake of what he would leave of the trappings of this world. Likewise is the statement of one who said: he feared that prophethood would be cut off from his offspring and return to his agnates, because that is something God places wherever He wills, and one does not object to God regarding whom He wills and chooses from among His servants. Al-Zamakhshari said: his mawali, who were his agnates (his brothers and paternal cousins), were the worst of the Children of Israel, so he feared for the religion that they would change it and would not handle the succession over his community well; so he sought a righteous offspring from his own loins who would follow him in reviving the religion.

The majority read (khiftu) from fear (al-khawf). Uthman ibn Affan, Zayd ibn Thabit, Ibn Abbas, Sa'id ibn al-As, Ibn Ya'mur, Ibn Jubayr, Ali ibn al-Husayn and his son Muhammad, Zayd, Shubayl ibn 'Azra, and al-Walid ibn Muslim, according to Abu 'Amir, read (khaffat) with a fatha on the kha' and fa' with shadda, and a kasra on the ta' of feminine marking, with (al-mawali) having a sukun on the ya'. The meaning is: my mawali have ceased and died, so I seek only a guardian who will uphold the religion. Al-Zuhri read (khiftu) from fear, with (al-mawali) having a sukun on the ya'; on the reading (khiftu) from fear, (min warai) means after my death. On the reading (khaffat), (min warai) may be connected to (khaffat), which is the more apparent, so the meaning is that they passed away before him, i.e., they departed, and none of them remained who had strength or support; or it may be connected to (al-mawali), i.e., they became few and were unable to establish the religion. (Warai) means behind me and after me, so he asked his Lord to strengthen them and support them with a guardian whom He would provide. It is related from Ibn Kathir (min waraya), with a maqsur like (asaya).

The explanation of (al-'aqir) has been given in Al 'Imran, and His saying (min ladunka) is an emphasis on his being a guardian who is pleasing, by being attributed to God and proceeding from His presence; or he intended origination from You without a cause, since I and my wife are not fit for childbearing.

The apparent meaning is that he asked God the Exalted to grant him a guardian, and he did not state explicitly that it should be a son, because that was far-fetched in his view given his old age and his wife being barren. It was said: he only asked for a son.

The majority read: (yaritheni wa yarithu), with both verbs in the nominative as descriptions of the guardian. If he asked for a son, then describing him as one who would inherit from him means that the answer should come during his lifetime so that he may inherit from him, lest the answer come in the form of a son who is withheld from him, and so what he intended would not be achieved. Al-Nahwiyyan, al-Zuhri, al-A'mash, Talha, al-Yazidi, Ibn 'Isa al-Isfahani, Ibn Muhaysin and Qatada read both with jazm, as an answer to the imperative. Ali, Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Ibn Ya'mur, al-Jahdari, Qatada, Abu Harb ibn Abi al-Aswad, Ja'far ibn Muhammad and Abu Nahik read (yaritheni) with raf' and ya', and (arith) they made a present verb from waritha. The author of al-Lawami' said: there is a transposition (taqdim) in it, so its meaning is: "Grant me from Yourself a guardian, from the family of Ya'qub, who will inherit me, if I die before him", i.e., my prophethood; and I will inherit him if he dies before me, i.e., his wealth. This is the meaning of al-Hasan's statement. Ali, Ibn Abbas and al-Jahdari read (yaritheni) and (arith) (min ali Ya'qub). Abu al-Fath said: this is tajrid (abstraction), the estimate being (yaritheni) from him and (arith). Al-Zamakhshari said: (arith), i.e., (yaritheni) by him and (arith), and this is called tajrid in the science of rhetoric (bayan). The inheritance intended is the inheritance of knowledge, since prophets do not bequeath wealth. It was said: (yaritheni) refers to the ruling-bodyship (al-hubura), he being a scholar (hibr); and (yarith min ali Ya'qub) refers to kingship (al-mulk). One says: wartuhu and waritu minhu, both being dialects.

It was said: (min) is partitive, not for transitivity, because the family of Ya'qub were not all prophets or scholars. Mujahid read (uwayrith) from the family of Ya'qub with diminutive form; its original is (wuwayrith), then the waw was changed to a hamza obligatorily because of the coming together of two waws. It is the diminutive of (warith), i.e., a small young boy. From al-Jahdari (warith) with a kasra on the waw, meaning by it the pure imala, not the pure kasra. The apparent meaning is that Ya'qub is the son of Ishaq son of Ibrahim. It was said: he is Ya'qub son of Matan, brother of Zakariyya. It was said: this Ya'qub and 'Imran, father of Maryam, were two brothers from the offspring of Sulayman son of Dawud. (Radiyyan) means in the sense of (mardiyy), pleasing.

﴿O Zakariyya﴾, i.e., he was addressed right after the supplication. It was said: He granted him after forty years of his supplication. It was said: after sixty. The one calling out and giving the glad tidings to Zakariyya were the angels, by revelation from God the Exalted, as He said: ﴿So the angels called out to him﴾ [Al 'Imran: 39], and so on. The ghulam is the male child, and it may be said of a female ghulama, as the poet said:

"Ghulama is humiliated by it, and so is the ghulam."

The apparent meaning is that (Yahya) is not Arabic, because their custom was not to name with Arabic words; so its being unassignable (mamnu' al-sarf) is due to proper-name status and foreignness. If it is Arabic, then it is named by the verb, like (ya'mur) and (ya'ish); and they named someone (yamut), and Yamut ibn al-Muzarra' was the nephew of al-Jahiz. And on the assumption that it is Arabic: it was said he was named so because he would be made to live (yahya) by wisdom and chastity. It was said: many people would live by his guidance and direction. It was said: because he would be martyred, and martyrs are alive. It was said: because he would live a long time. It was said: because he came to life between an old man and a barren mother. It was said: because his mother's barrenness was revived through him, as she had not borne. Ibn Abbas, Qatada, al-Suddi and Ibn Aslam said: we had not named anyone before him as Yahya. Al-Zamakhshari said: this is evidence that unusual names are worthy of preference, and it is these that the Arabs used to favor in naming, because they are more distinguished, more lofty, and further removed from commonness; so much so that a poet said in praising a people:

"Strange names, wearing long-trailing waist-wrappers, red, sweeping the ground with their fringes."

Ru'ba said to the Bakri genealogist, who had asked him about his lineage: "I am the son of al-'Ajjaj." He said: "You have shortened and made it known." It was said to al-Salt ibn 'Ata: "How did you come to advance among the Barmakids when among them was one more refined than you?" He said: "I was a stranger in the house, a stranger in name, light in judgment, and stingy with the dearest things." Among what he mentioned as having advanced him was that he was a stranger in name, since his name was al-Salt. Mujahid and others said: (samiyyan) means a like and an equal, and it seems to be from (musama) and (sumuww). Ibn 'Atiyya said: this is far-fetched, since he is not preferred over Ibrahim and Musa. Ibn Abbas also said: no barren women bore one like him.

Al-Zamakhshari said: the word (samiyy) was used for an equal only because each of two alike is called by the name of the like, the similar, the shape, and the counterpart, so each of them is a (samiyy) to his companion. It was said: he had no like in that he never disobeyed and never intended disobedience at all, and that he was born between an aged, decrepit old man and a barren old woman, and that he was a (hasur), a man who does not have intercourse. Ended.

(Anna) means "how": its discussion has already been given in His saying ﴿He said, "My Lord, how will I have a boy when old age has overtaken me and my wife is barren?"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 40] in Al 'Imran. (Al-'Itiyy) is intensive in old age and dryness of a stalk. Abu Bahriyya, Ibn Abi Layla, al-A'mash, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read (itiyyan) with a kasra on the ayn; the rest of the seven read it with a damma; and Abdullah read it with a fatha on the ayn. Both (suliyyan) and (sali) with a damma and kasra, as masdars like (ajij) and (rahil); and with a damma they are likewise, except they are on the pattern fu'ul. From Abdullah and Mujahid (usiyyan), with a damma on the ayn and sin, like (musawwara). It is related by al-Dani from Ibn Abbas, and al-Zamakhshari related it from Ubayy and Mujahid. It is said: 'ata al-'ud and 'asa, meaning it dried, and jasa.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 19, verses 1–15 (part 3 of 3):

﴿He said: "Thus"﴾, that is: the matter is thus, confirming him. Then he began: ﴿Your Lord said﴾. The kaf in "thus" is either in the nominative or the accusative, governed by "said". "Thus" (dhalika) refers to something vague that is explained by ﴿It is easy for Me﴾ and similar statements, such as ﴿And We conveyed to him that decree: that the last remnant of these would be cut off by morning﴾ [al-Hijr: 66]. Al-Hasan read ﴿It is easy for Me﴾, and this reading can only be understood according to the first interpretation, that is: the matter is as I said, and it is easy for Me to do that. Another interpretation is that "that" refers to what preceded of God's promise, not to the words of Zakariyya. He said: the verb "said" is omitted in both readings, meaning: He said ﴿It is easy for Me﴾. If you wish, you need not mark it with a pause, because God is the one addressing him, and the meaning is that He said that and promised him. This is the statement of al-Zamakhshari, and it is the correct one. Ibn 'Atiyya said: As for His saying ﴿He said: "Thus"﴾, it has been said that the meaning is: the angel said to him, "Thus, let it be as you were told." ﴿Your Lord said﴾: the creation of the boy ﴿is easy for Me﴾, that is, it is not something unprecedented, and just as I created you before and brought you from non-existence into existence, so I do now. Al-Tabari said: The meaning of His saying "thus", that is, the matter is that what you mentioned about the barren wife and old age is so, but ﴿Your Lord said﴾; and the meaning, in My view, is that the angel said "thus", that is, in this condition ﴿Your Lord said: It is easy for Me﴾. End of quotation. Al-Hasan read ﴿It is easy for Me﴾ with a kasra on the ya. They have recited the verse of al-Nabigha:

"Upon me is a favour for 'Amr, after favour,
for his father, it is not of the kind with stings."

with a kasra on the ya of the first person. This kasra is similar to the reading of Hamza, ﴿And you are not one to help me [bi-musrikhiyya]﴾ [Ibrahim: 22], with a kasra on the ya. The majority read ﴿And I had created you﴾ with the first-person ta. Al-A'mash, Talha, Ibn Thabbat and Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "We created you" (khalaqnaka) with the royal plural nun. ﴿And you were not a thing﴾, that is, a thing existing. Al-Zamakhshari said: "a thing", because the non-existent is not a thing; or "a thing that is counted," like the saying: "I wonder at the nothing that, when it sees something other than a thing, thinks it a man." (p-176)

﴿He said﴾, that is, Zakariyya: ﴿My Lord, make for me a sign﴾, that is, a token by which I may know the occurrence of what I was given good news of. He asked for this so that he might increase in certainty, as Abraham, peace be upon him, said: ﴿But [I ask] so that my heart may be at rest﴾ [al-Baqarah: 260]. This was not because he doubted the truth of what he had been promised, nor because he suspected that it came from someone other than God, since the prophets are protected from such things. Al-Zajjaj said: The good news came in an unrestricted form, so he did not know the time, and so he asked for a sign so that he would know the time of its occurrence.

﴿He said: "Your sign"﴾. It is narrated from Ibn Zayd that when his wife became pregnant with Yahya, he could not speak to anyone, yet he would recite the Torah and remember God, but when he wanted to call out to someone, he could not. "Sound" (sawiyyan) is a circumstantial accusative (hal) from a pronoun, meaning: do not speak while you are in good health, with no muteness or illness in you. This is the statement of the majority. According to Ibn 'Abbas, it refers to the nights, meaning: complete, even nights. In that case it is an attribute of "three". The mention of nights here, and of days in Al 'Imran, indicates that the restriction on speech lasted for him three days with their nights.

Ibn Abi 'Abla and Zayd ibn 'Ali read ﴿that you do not speak﴾ with a raised mim, treating "an" as the light form of the heavy one, with the sense: "that he does not speak." The majority read it with the mim in the accusative, treating "an" as the one that governs the imperfect (an al-nasiba). ﴿So he came out to his people from the prayer niche (mihrab)﴾, that is, while he was in that state of being unable to speak to people. His mihrab is the place of his prayer. The mihrab has already been discussed in Al 'Imran. ﴿So he signalled to them﴾, that is, he gestured. Qatada, Ibn Munabbih, al-Kalbi and al-Qurtubi said: "He signalled to them" means he gestured. Al-Zamakhshari mentions it from Mujahid, who said: Supporting this is "except by gesture" (ramzan). From Ibn 'Abbas: he wrote for them on the ground. Ibn 'Atiyya said: Mujahid said: Rather he wrote for them in the dust, and both views are a form of revelation (wahy). End of quotation. Ikrima said: He wrote on a leaf, and revelation (wahy) in the speech of the Arabs means writing. From this is the saying of Dhu al-Rumma:

"Except the four dark ones, which seem like
the remnant of revelation within the pages of scrolls."

And 'Antara said:

"Like the revelation of scrolls from the era of Kisra,
which he gave to a non-Arab, a stammerer."

And Jarir said:

"As if a Jew were writing revelation
with a kaf and a lam in its dwellings."

The majority hold that the meaning of ﴿that glorify [Him]﴾ is: pray. It has also been said: he commanded them to remember God and to glorify Him. The commentators said: He used to go out to his people in the morning and evening and command them to pray by gesture. The author of al-Tahrir wa al-Tahbir said: In my view there is a subtle meaning here: that he was specifically commanded to glorify with remembrance, because the custom is that whoever sees something that amazes him, or sees in it wondrous craftsmanship or strange wisdom, says: "Glory be to God, glory to the Creator." When he saw a child born to an old man and a barren woman, he was amazed by that, so he glorified, and he commanded glorification. End of quotation.

Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya said: the "an" is explanatory (mufassira). Al-Hawfi said: ﴿that glorify﴾, the "an" is governed by "revealed" (awha). Abu al-Baqa' said: It may be a verbal "an" (masdariyya), and it may be in the sense of "i.e." (ay). End of quotation. Talha read "that glorify Him" with a pronoun for God, the Exalted. Ibn Ghazwan narrated from Talha: "that glorify" with a doubled nun, without a waw; he attached the emphatic heavy nun to the imperative verb.

﴿O Yahya, take the Book with strength﴾. There is an omission in the speech, and the sense is: when Yahya was born and grew up and reached the age at which he was commanded, God said to him through the angel. Al-Tibrizi was wrong in his view that the one calling him was his father when he grew up and matured; the correct view is what came before, due to His saying ﴿And We gave him wisdom while still a boy﴾. The Book is the Torah. Ibn 'Atiyya said: Without disagreement, because he was born before 'Isa, and the Gospel did not yet exist. End of quotation. This is not as he said; rather it was said that he had a book specifically given to him, just as many of the prophets were given something similar. It has also been said: "the Book" here is a generic noun, meaning: recite the books of God. It has been said: "the Book" is the scrolls of Abraham. Al-Hasan said: He taught him the Torah and the Gospel and sent him to the Children of Israel, and in his childhood he used to fast and pray and call to God (p-177) ﴿with strength﴾: with determination, perseverance and acting upon what is in it. "Wisdom" (hukm) means prophethood, or the judgment of the Book, or wisdom, or knowledge of the rulings, or intellect, which is reason, or the etiquette of service, or sound insight (firasa). These are the views. ﴿While still a boy﴾ (sabiyyan), that is, a youth who had not reached the age of maturity. It has been said he was two years old. It has been said he was three years old. From Ibn 'Abbas, in a raised (marfu') hadith: "seven years old." ﴿And tenderness﴾ is coordinated with "wisdom". Hanan means mercy. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas in one report, and by al-Hasan, Ikrima, Qatada, al-Dahhak, Abu 'Ubayda and al-Farra'. Abu 'Ubayda recited:

"Show tenderness to me; may the King guide you,
for every station has its own speech."

He said: It is most often used in the dual, as in the saying:

"Hanānayka, the lesser of two evils is better than the greater."

Ibn al-Anbari said: the meaning is that We made him "hanan" for the people of his time. Mujahid said: and a kindness from his Lord towards him. From Ibn Jubayr: gentle. From Ikrima and Ibn Zayd: affection. From 'Ata': honour.

His saying ﴿and purity﴾: according to al-Dahhak and Qatada, righteous deeds. From Ibn al-Sa'ib: charity given on behalf of his parents. From al-Zajjaj: purification. From Ibn al-Anbari: increase in good. It has been said: praise, as witnesses are declared upright (yuzakka).

﴿And he was God-fearing (taqiyyan)﴾. Qatada said: He never intended a major sin or a minor sin, nor did he ever desire a woman. Ibn 'Abbas said: He made him one who fears God, and he did not put anything else on a par with Him. Mujahid said: His food was permissible plants, and there were clear channels of tears on his cheeks. ﴿And dutiful to his parents﴾, that is, abundant in goodness, honour and reverence. Al-Hasan, Abu Ja'far in one report, Abu Nahik and Abu Mijlaz read "and dutiful" (wa-barran) in both places with a kasra on the ba', meaning: and one who has dutifulness. ﴿And he was not a tyrant﴾, that is, arrogant. ﴿Disobedient﴾, that is, a disobeyer, abundant in disobedience. Its original form is 'asawiy, an intensive form (fa'ul), and it is possible that it is a fa'il, which is also one of the intensive patterns.

﴿And peace be upon him﴾. Al-Tabari said: that is, safety (aman). Ibn 'Atiyya said: The more evident view is that it is the customary greeting, and the honour lies in God's greeting him and bestowing peace upon him in the situations in which a person is in utmost weakness, need, lack of resource, and poverty before God. Al-Tabari mentions from al-Hasan that 'Isa and Yahya, peace be upon them both, met, and they were cousins, and Yahya said to 'Isa: "Pray for me, for you are better than I," and 'Isa said to him: "Rather you pray for me, for you are better than I. God has greeted you with peace, and I have greeted myself with peace."

Abu 'Abdullah al-Razi said: ﴿On the day he was born﴾, that is, safety for him from the Devil reaching him; ﴿and the day he dies﴾, that is, safety from the punishment of the grave; ﴿and the day he is raised alive﴾ from God's punishment on the Day of Resurrection. In His saying ﴿and the day he is raised alive﴾ there is an indication that he is among the martyrs, due to His saying ﴿Rather, they are alive with their Lord, provided for﴾ [Al 'Imran: 169]. This greeting may come from God or from the angels. End of quotation. The more evident view is that it is from God, because it is in the context of ﴿And We gave him wisdom﴾.

**[p. 170]** Surah Maryam: ninety-eight verses, Meccan.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Kaf, Ha, Ya, 'Ayn, Sad.﴾ ﴿A mention of the mercy of your Lord to His servant Zakariya,﴾ ﴿when he called to his Lord in a secret supplication.﴾ ﴿He said, "My Lord, indeed my bones have weakened, and my head has filled with gray, and I have never been unsuccessful in my supplication to You, my Lord.﴾ ﴿And indeed I fear the successors after me, and my wife has been barren, so give me from Yourself an heir,﴾ ﴿who will inherit me and inherit from the family of Ya'qub. And make him, my Lord, pleasing [to You]."﴾ ﴿"O Zakariya, indeed We give you good tidings of a boy whose name is Yahya; We have not assigned to anyone before [this] name."﴾ ﴿He said, "My Lord, how can I have a boy when my wife has been barren and I have reached extreme old age?"﴾ ﴿He said, "So it will be. Your Lord says, 'It is easy for Me, and I had already created you before, when you were nothing.'"﴾ ﴿He said, "My Lord, appoint for me a sign." He said, "Your sign is that you will not speak to the people for three nights, although sound."﴾ ﴿So he came out to his people from the prayer niche and conveyed to them, "Exalt [Allah] in the morning and the afternoon."﴾ ﴿"O Yahya, take the Scripture with determination." And We gave him judgment while still a child,﴾ ﴿and compassion from Us and purity. And he was fearful [of Allah],﴾ ﴿and dutiful to his parents, and he was not a tyrant or disobedient.﴾ ﴿And peace is upon him the day he was born, and the day he dies, and the day he is raised alive.﴾

﴿And mention in the Scripture Maryam, when she withdrew from her family to an eastern place.﴾ [Maryam: 16] ﴿And she took a screen [to conceal herself] from them. Then We sent to her Our Spirit, and it took for her the form of a man in all respects.﴾ [Maryam: 17] ﴿She said, "Indeed, I seek refuge in the Most Merciful from you, if you should be fearing [Allah]."﴾ [Maryam: 18] ﴿He said, "I am only the messenger of your Lord, to give you a pure boy."﴾ [Maryam: 19] ﴿She said, "How can I have a boy when no man has touched me and I have not been unchaste?"﴾ [Maryam: 20] ﴿He said, "So it will be. Your Lord says, 'It is easy for Me, and We will make him a sign for the people and a mercy from Us, and it is a matter already decreed.'"﴾ [Maryam: 21] ﴿So she conceived him, and she withdrew with him to a remote place.﴾ [Maryam: 22] ﴿Then the pains of childbirth drove her to the trunk of a palm tree. She said, "Oh, I wish I had died before this and had been forgotten and out of mind."﴾ [Maryam: 23] ﴿But he called to her from beneath her, "Do not grieve; your Lord has provided beneath you a stream.﴾ [Maryam: 24] ﴿And shake toward yourself the trunk of the palm tree; it will drop upon you ripe, fresh dates.﴾ [Maryam: 25] ﴿So eat and drink and be contented. And if you see anyone of the human being, say, 'Indeed, I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast, so I will not speak today to any person.'"﴾ [Maryam: 26] ﴿Then she brought him to her people, carrying him. They said, "O Maryam, you have certainly come with a thing unprecedented.﴾ [Maryam: 27] ﴿O sister of Harun, your father was not a man of evil, nor was your mother unchaste."﴾ [Maryam: 28] ﴿So she pointed to him. They said, "How can we speak to one who is in the cradle, a child?"﴾ [Maryam: 29].

**[p. 170]** (Ishtiʿal al-nar), the kindling of the fire: its scattering as it blazes, so that it becomes flames (shuʿal). It is also said that the shuʿaʿ (sparks) of the fire. Al-shayb (gray hair) is well known. (Shaba sha'ruhu) means his hair turned white after it had been of another color. (Al-makhad) is the intensification of the pain of labor, the pangs of delivery. (Al-jidh, trunk) is the part between the ground where the tree is rooted and the point where its branches divide. The word is also applied to a branch, and its plural is ajdhaʿ for the few and judhudh for the many. (Al-sarriy) means one of high rank; it is said sarawa yasruw, and its plural is sarawa with a fatḥa on the sin, and surawaʾ. These two plural forms are irregular for it; the regular pattern would be afʿilaʾ. Al-sarriy also means a small stream, because water flows in it; its final radical is yāʾ, as the final radical of that root is wāw. Labid said:

*So they both crossed the width of the stream, and it split, its banks well-watered, its edges neighboring.*

That is, a rivulet. (Al-hazz) means shaking. (Al-rutab) is well known; its singular is rutbah, and it is irregularly pluralized as arṭāb, like rubʿ and arbāʿ. It is what is cut before it hardens and dries. Al-janiyy is what is ripe and suitable for picking. Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala said: it has not dried or withered. It is also said that al-janiyy is what has become soft from the unripe dates. Al-Farra' said: al-janiyy and al-majniyy are the same, and it is also said that al-janiyy is what has been cut off. (Qurrat al-ʿayn), the coolness of the eye, derives from qarr (coolness). It is said: tears of joy are cool to the touch, and tears of grief are hot to the touch. Abu Tammam said:

*As for the eyes of the lovers, they have grown hot, but the eyes of the gloaters have grown cool.*

The Quraysh say qararTu bihi ʿaynan, and qararTu bi-l-makan aqarru. The people of Najd say qirtu bihi ʿaynan with kasra. Al-fariyy means a great matter, used both for good and for evil. From it comes the description of ʿUmar: "I have not seen a genius who performs his great deed." Al-fariyy also means cutting. In the proverb: "He came doing great things," meaning he did something great, in word or deed. Al-Zamakhshari said: al-fariyy means wondrous, and it derives from fary al-jild (flaying the hide). Al-ishara (gesture) is well known; it is made with the hand, the eye, the garment, the head, or the mouth. Ashāra's alif is converted from yāʾ. It is said tashayarna al-hilal, for the reciprocal form. Kathir said:

*I said, while within the entrails there is an insidious ailment: "Oh, how sweet, O ʿAzz, is that gesturing!"*

**[p. 171]** In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿Kaf, Ha, Ya, 'Ayn, Sad.﴾ [The rest of the passage repeats the verses 1–50 of the surah as above, with the reciting of verses as cited.]

**[p. 172]** This surah is Meccan, like the surah before it. Muqatil said: except for the prostration verse, which is Medinan, revealed after the emigration of the believers to Abyssinia. Its connection with what precedes it is that Allah, exalted is He, included in the surah before it wondrous narratives, such as the story of the People of the Cave, the story of Musa with al-Khidr, and the story of Dhu al-Qarnayn. This surah includes wondrous narratives: the birth of Yahya to an aged, decrepit man and a barren woman, and the birth of ʿIsa without a father. Since both share this astonishing matter, it fits to mention this surah after that one. The discussion of the disjointed letters at the beginnings of surahs was already covered at the beginning of al-Baqara, and what is to be pausing on is there.

(Dhikr) is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: this recited part of this Qur'an is a mention. It is also said that dhikr is the predicate of the statement "Kaf, Ha, Ya, 'Ayn, Sad," which is the subject; al-Farra' mentioned this. It is said there is remoteness in this, because the predicate is in meaning the subject, and the disjointed letters do not contain a mention of mercy, nor is their meaning the mention of mercy. It is also said that dhikr is the subject and the predicate is omitted, its estimate being: in what is recited is dhikr.

The majority read kāf with sukūn on the fāʾ. It is reported from al-Hasan that it is read with ḍamma. Nafi' inclined the hāʾ and the yāʾ between the two pronunciations, and made the dāl of ṣād clear at that point. (Dhikr): al-Hasan read the hāʾ with ḍamma, and also from him the yāʾ with ḍamma and the hāʾ with kasra. From ʿĀṣim, the yāʾ with ḍamma, and also both with kasra. From Hamza, the hāʾ with fatḥa and the yāʾ with kasra. Abu 'Amr al-Dani said: the meaning of ḍamma on the hāʾ and yāʾ is the completion of emphatic pronunciation, not the pure ḍamma that requires conversion. Abu al-Fadl ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Ahmad ibn al-Hasan al-Muqri al-Razi said in his book al-Lawāmiḥ fi Shawādhdh al-Qirāʾāt: Kharija from al-Hasan: kāf with ḍamma on the kāf; Nasr ibn ʿAsim from him with ḍamma on the hāʾ; and Harun ibn Musa al-ʿAtaki from Isma'il from him with ḍamma. These three are classed under ḍamma, but in reality the letters are not vowelled with ḍamma, for if they were, the alifs following them would have to be converted to wāws. Rather, these alifs were moved toward the wāw according to the dialect of the people of the Hijaz, and these are called the alif of emphasis, the opposite of the inclined alif. They resemble the fatḥas from which the ḍammas were produced. This rendering is like what they rendered for the inclined fatḥa close to kasra, with a kasra, due to the alif after it moving toward the yāʾ. End of quotation.

Abu Ja'far read these letters separately, distinguishing each from the others, to differentiate them from the letters that combine, so that they become parts of words; this requires the final letter of each to be vowelled with sukūn. Most readers made the dāl of ṣād clear before the dhāl of (dhikr), and Abu 'Amr assimilated it. Hafs from ʿAsim and a group read the nūn of (ʿayn) with clear pronunciation; the majority pronounced it with concealment (ikhfa').

Al-Hasan and Ibn Ya'mur read (dhakara) as a past verb, with (raḥmata) in the accusative, which Abu al-Fath reported and al-Zamakhshari mentioned from al-Hasan: meaning, this recited part of the Qur'an: "a mention of the mercy of your Lord." Al-Dani mentioned from Ibn Ya'mur (dhakkir) as an imperative verb from tadhkir (reminding), with (raḥmata) in the accusative, and (ʿabdahu) in the accusative governed by the mercy: that is, remind that the mercy of your Lord [was shown to] His servant. The author of al-Lawāmiḥ mentioned that (dhakkara), with shadda, in the past tense, from al-Hasan with variation, and it is authentic from Ibn Ya'mur. Its meaning: the recited part, that is the Qur'an, reminded [people] of the mercy of your Lord. When the preposition is removed, it takes the accusative. It is also possible that its meaning is: the Qur'an reminded the people with a reminder that Allah had shown mercy to His servant; the verbal noun then governs (ʿabdahu Zakariyya), because it reminded them of what they had forgotten of Allah's mercy, and so by the Qur'an and its revelation upon the Prophet (ﷺ) it was renewed for them. It is also possible that (dhakkara) is in the past tense with Allah, exalted is He, as its subject.

Al-Kalbi read (dhakara), in the past tense, lightened, from dhikr, (raḥmata rabbika) with the tā' in the accusative, and (ʿabduhu) in the nominative, attributing the verb to him. Ibn Khalawayh said: (dhakara raḥmata rabbika ʿabduhu), Yahya ibn Ya'mur; and (dhakkir) as an imperative from him also. End of quotation.

(Idh) is an adverb whose governing element al-Hawfi said is (dhikr). Abu al-Baqa' said: (idh) is an adverb of (raḥma) or of (dhikr). End of quotation.

The calling is described as hidden. Ibn Juraij said: so that it would not be mixed with show-off. Muqatil said: so that he would not be blamed for seeking a child in old age. Qatada said: because secret and public are equal before Him, exalted is He. It is also said: he kept it secret from his clients whom he feared. It is also said: because it was a worldly matter, so he hid it, for if it was answered, that was his goal, and if not, no one would know of it. It is also said: because it was in the depth of night. It is also said: because of his sincerity in it, so that no one knows it except Allah. It is also said: because of the weakness of his voice due to his old age, as it is said: "The elder's voice is faint, and his hearing is failing." It is also said: because concealment is the practice of the prophets, and loud calling is considered transgression. In revelation: ﴿Call upon your Lord humbly and secretly; indeed, He does not like transgressors.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 55]. In a hadith: "Indeed, you do not call upon one who is deaf or absent."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 19, verse 1–15 (part 2 of 3):

﴿He said, "My Lord, indeed my bones have weakened, and my head has ignited with white hair."﴾ This is the manner of his supplication and the explanation of his calling out. The majority (al-Jumhur) read (wahana) with a fatha on the ha'. Al-A'mash read it with a kasra. It is also read with a damma; there are three dialects (lughat thalath), and its meaning is weakness. The weakness is attributed to the bone because it is the pillar of the body (amud al-badan), upon which its stability rests, and it is the foundation of its structure. When it weakens, what is behind it collapses and its strength falls away. Also, it is the hardest and most solid part of it, so when it weakens, what is beneath it is even weaker. He used the singular "the bone" (al-'azm) because it denotes the genus (al-jins), intending that this genus, which is the pillar and the support, and the hardest of what the body is composed of, has been struck by weakness. Were it put in the plural, it would have been a different purpose, namely that not some of his bones had weakened, but all of them. Qatada said: he complained of the falling out of his molars. Al-Karmani said: he was seventy years old. It was said: seventy-five. It was said: eighty-five. It was said: sixty. It was said: sixty-five.

The white hair was likened to the flame of fire in its whiteness, its spreading through the hair, its pervading it, and its taking hold of it in every direction, to the kindling of fire. Then he brought it out as a metaphor (isti'ara). Then he attributed the kindling to the place of the hair and its growth, which is the head. He brought out the white hair as a specification (tamyiz) and did not add "the head" (to the noun), being satisfied with the addressee's knowledge that it is the head of Zakariyya. For this reason the sentence is sound and is attested to be eloquent, as al-Zamakhshari said. To this Ibn Duraid also looked, when he said:

"The whitened one ignited in its blackness, like the kindling of fire in dry ghada wood."

Some grammarians parsed (shaybан) as a verbal noun (masdar), saying: because the meaning of "and the head ignited" is "it turned white," so it is a masdar derived from the meaning. It was also said: it is a masdar in the accusative position as a circumstantial state (hal). The kindling of the head is a metaphor of the sensible for the sensible, since the borrowed-from is fire and the borrowed-for is white hair, and what unites them is spreading and dispersion.

﴿And I have never been﴾: a negation regarding the past, i.e., I have never been "with Your supplication, my Lord, unfortunate" (shaqiyan), but rather I was happy and successful, since You used to answer my supplication, so I was made happy by that. On this reading the kaf is the object (maf'ul). It was also said: the meaning is "with Your calling" to faith, "unfortunate": rather, I was among those who obeyed You and worshipped You sincerely. On this reading the kaf is the subject (fa'il). The first is more apparent, out of thankfulness to God the Exalted for what He had previously bestowed upon him, i.e., You have been good to me before, and I was made happy by my supplication to You, so Your favor requires that You answer me in the end as You answered me at the beginning.

It is related that Hatim al-Ta'i was approached by a seeker of a need, who said: "I did you a kindness at such-and-such a time." Hatim said: "Welcome to the one who made us a means to himself and fulfilled his need."

﴿And indeed I fear the mawali after me﴾. The mawali are the paternal cousins and the relatives who are close by lineage. The poet said:

"Gently, sons of our paternal uncle, gently, our mawali; do not dig up between us what has been buried."

And Labid said:

"And a mawla whom I have repelled the wrong from, while he has become in the state of one who is wronged."

Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada and Abu Salih said: the mawali here are the kalala (collateral heirs); he feared that they would inherit his wealth, and that the kalala would inherit from him. Qatada and al-Hasan related from the Prophet ﷺ: "May God have mercy on my brother Zakariyya; what was upon him was that he inherited his wealth." Another group said: his mawali were neglecting the religion, so he feared that upon his death the religion would be lost, so he sought a guardian who would uphold the religion after him. This is not sound from him, since he (peace be upon him) said: "We, the company of prophets, are not inherited; what we leave behind is charity." The apparent and fitting interpretation for Zakariyya, peace be upon him, given that he is infallible (ma'sum), is that he did not seek a child for the sake of what he would leave of the trappings of this world. Likewise is the statement of one who said: he feared that prophethood would be cut off from his offspring and return to his agnates, because that is something God places wherever He wills, and one does not object to God regarding whom He wills and chooses from among His servants. Al-Zamakhshari said: his mawali, who were his agnates (his brothers and paternal cousins), were the worst of the Children of Israel, so he feared for the religion that they would change it and would not handle the succession over his community well; so he sought a righteous offspring from his own loins who would follow him in reviving the religion.

The majority read (khiftu) from fear (al-khawf). Uthman ibn Affan, Zayd ibn Thabit, Ibn Abbas, Sa'id ibn al-As, Ibn Ya'mur, Ibn Jubayr, Ali ibn al-Husayn and his son Muhammad, Zayd, Shubayl ibn 'Azra, and al-Walid ibn Muslim, according to Abu 'Amir, read (khaffat) with a fatha on the kha' and fa' with shadda, and a kasra on the ta' of feminine marking, with (al-mawali) having a sukun on the ya'. The meaning is: my mawali have ceased and died, so I seek only a guardian who will uphold the religion. Al-Zuhri read (khiftu) from fear, with (al-mawali) having a sukun on the ya'; on the reading (khiftu) from fear, (min warai) means after my death. On the reading (khaffat), (min warai) may be connected to (khaffat), which is the more apparent, so the meaning is that they passed away before him, i.e., they departed, and none of them remained who had strength or support; or it may be connected to (al-mawali), i.e., they became few and were unable to establish the religion. (Warai) means behind me and after me, so he asked his Lord to strengthen them and support them with a guardian whom He would provide. It is related from Ibn Kathir (min waraya), with a maqsur like (asaya).

The explanation of (al-'aqir) has been given in Al 'Imran, and His saying (min ladunka) is an emphasis on his being a guardian who is pleasing, by being attributed to God and proceeding from His presence; or he intended origination from You without a cause, since I and my wife are not fit for childbearing.

The apparent meaning is that he asked God the Exalted to grant him a guardian, and he did not state explicitly that it should be a son, because that was far-fetched in his view given his old age and his wife being barren. It was said: he only asked for a son.

The majority read: (yaritheni wa yarithu), with both verbs in the nominative as descriptions of the guardian. If he asked for a son, then describing him as one who would inherit from him means that the answer should come during his lifetime so that he may inherit from him, lest the answer come in the form of a son who is withheld from him, and so what he intended would not be achieved. Al-Nahwiyyan, al-Zuhri, al-A'mash, Talha, al-Yazidi, Ibn 'Isa al-Isfahani, Ibn Muhaysin and Qatada read both with jazm, as an answer to the imperative. Ali, Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Ibn Ya'mur, al-Jahdari, Qatada, Abu Harb ibn Abi al-Aswad, Ja'far ibn Muhammad and Abu Nahik read (yaritheni) with raf' and ya', and (arith) they made a present verb from waritha. The author of al-Lawami' said: there is a transposition (taqdim) in it, so its meaning is: "Grant me from Yourself a guardian, from the family of Ya'qub, who will inherit me, if I die before him", i.e., my prophethood; and I will inherit him if he dies before me, i.e., his wealth. This is the meaning of al-Hasan's statement. Ali, Ibn Abbas and al-Jahdari read (yaritheni) and (arith) (min ali Ya'qub). Abu al-Fath said: this is tajrid (abstraction), the estimate being (yaritheni) from him and (arith). Al-Zamakhshari said: (arith), i.e., (yaritheni) by him and (arith), and this is called tajrid in the science of rhetoric (bayan). The inheritance intended is the inheritance of knowledge, since prophets do not bequeath wealth. It was said: (yaritheni) refers to the ruling-bodyship (al-hubura), he being a scholar (hibr); and (yarith min ali Ya'qub) refers to kingship (al-mulk). One says: wartuhu and waritu minhu, both being dialects.

It was said: (min) is partitive, not for transitivity, because the family of Ya'qub were not all prophets or scholars. Mujahid read (uwayrith) from the family of Ya'qub with diminutive form; its original is (wuwayrith), then the waw was changed to a hamza obligatorily because of the coming together of two waws. It is the diminutive of (warith), i.e., a small young boy. From al-Jahdari (warith) with a kasra on the waw, meaning by it the pure imala, not the pure kasra. The apparent meaning is that Ya'qub is the son of Ishaq son of Ibrahim. It was said: he is Ya'qub son of Matan, brother of Zakariyya. It was said: this Ya'qub and 'Imran, father of Maryam, were two brothers from the offspring of Sulayman son of Dawud. (Radiyyan) means in the sense of (mardiyy), pleasing.

﴿O Zakariyya﴾, i.e., he was addressed right after the supplication. It was said: He granted him after forty years of his supplication. It was said: after sixty. The one calling out and giving the glad tidings to Zakariyya were the angels, by revelation from God the Exalted, as He said: ﴿So the angels called out to him﴾ [Al 'Imran: 39], and so on. The ghulam is the male child, and it may be said of a female ghulama, as the poet said:

"Ghulama is humiliated by it, and so is the ghulam."

The apparent meaning is that (Yahya) is not Arabic, because their custom was not to name with Arabic words; so its being unassignable (mamnu' al-sarf) is due to proper-name status and foreignness. If it is Arabic, then it is named by the verb, like (ya'mur) and (ya'ish); and they named someone (yamut), and Yamut ibn al-Muzarra' was the nephew of al-Jahiz. And on the assumption that it is Arabic: it was said he was named so because he would be made to live (yahya) by wisdom and chastity. It was said: many people would live by his guidance and direction. It was said: because he would be martyred, and martyrs are alive. It was said: because he would live a long time. It was said: because he came to life between an old man and a barren mother. It was said: because his mother's barrenness was revived through him, as she had not borne. Ibn Abbas, Qatada, al-Suddi and Ibn Aslam said: we had not named anyone before him as Yahya. Al-Zamakhshari said: this is evidence that unusual names are worthy of preference, and it is these that the Arabs used to favor in naming, because they are more distinguished, more lofty, and further removed from commonness; so much so that a poet said in praising a people:

"Strange names, wearing long-trailing waist-wrappers, red, sweeping the ground with their fringes."

Ru'ba said to the Bakri genealogist, who had asked him about his lineage: "I am the son of al-'Ajjaj." He said: "You have shortened and made it known." It was said to al-Salt ibn 'Ata: "How did you come to advance among the Barmakids when among them was one more refined than you?" He said: "I was a stranger in the house, a stranger in name, light in judgment, and stingy with the dearest things." Among what he mentioned as having advanced him was that he was a stranger in name, since his name was al-Salt. Mujahid and others said: (samiyyan) means a like and an equal, and it seems to be from (musama) and (sumuww). Ibn 'Atiyya said: this is far-fetched, since he is not preferred over Ibrahim and Musa. Ibn Abbas also said: no barren women bore one like him.

Al-Zamakhshari said: the word (samiyy) was used for an equal only because each of two alike is called by the name of the like, the similar, the shape, and the counterpart, so each of them is a (samiyy) to his companion. It was said: he had no like in that he never disobeyed and never intended disobedience at all, and that he was born between an aged, decrepit old man and a barren old woman, and that he was a (hasur), a man who does not have intercourse. Ended.

(Anna) means "how": its discussion has already been given in His saying ﴿He said, "My Lord, how will I have a boy when old age has overtaken me and my wife is barren?"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 40] in Al 'Imran. (Al-'Itiyy) is intensive in old age and dryness of a stalk. Abu Bahriyya, Ibn Abi Layla, al-A'mash, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read (itiyyan) with a kasra on the ayn; the rest of the seven read it with a damma; and Abdullah read it with a fatha on the ayn. Both (suliyyan) and (sali) with a damma and kasra, as masdars like (ajij) and (rahil); and with a damma they are likewise, except they are on the pattern fu'ul. From Abdullah and Mujahid (usiyyan), with a damma on the ayn and sin, like (musawwara). It is related by al-Dani from Ibn Abbas, and al-Zamakhshari related it from Ubayy and Mujahid. It is said: 'ata al-'ud and 'asa, meaning it dried, and jasa.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 19, verses 1–15 (part 3 of 3):

﴿He said: "Thus"﴾, that is: the matter is thus, confirming him. Then he began: ﴿Your Lord said﴾. The kaf in "thus" is either in the nominative or the accusative, governed by "said". "Thus" (dhalika) refers to something vague that is explained by ﴿It is easy for Me﴾ and similar statements, such as ﴿And We conveyed to him that decree: that the last remnant of these would be cut off by morning﴾ [al-Hijr: 66]. Al-Hasan read ﴿It is easy for Me﴾, and this reading can only be understood according to the first interpretation, that is: the matter is as I said, and it is easy for Me to do that. Another interpretation is that "that" refers to what preceded of God's promise, not to the words of Zakariyya. He said: the verb "said" is omitted in both readings, meaning: He said ﴿It is easy for Me﴾. If you wish, you need not mark it with a pause, because God is the one addressing him, and the meaning is that He said that and promised him. This is the statement of al-Zamakhshari, and it is the correct one. Ibn 'Atiyya said: As for His saying ﴿He said: "Thus"﴾, it has been said that the meaning is: the angel said to him, "Thus, let it be as you were told." ﴿Your Lord said﴾: the creation of the boy ﴿is easy for Me﴾, that is, it is not something unprecedented, and just as I created you before and brought you from non-existence into existence, so I do now. Al-Tabari said: The meaning of His saying "thus", that is, the matter is that what you mentioned about the barren wife and old age is so, but ﴿Your Lord said﴾; and the meaning, in My view, is that the angel said "thus", that is, in this condition ﴿Your Lord said: It is easy for Me﴾. End of quotation. Al-Hasan read ﴿It is easy for Me﴾ with a kasra on the ya. They have recited the verse of al-Nabigha:

"Upon me is a favour for 'Amr, after favour,
for his father, it is not of the kind with stings."

with a kasra on the ya of the first person. This kasra is similar to the reading of Hamza, ﴿And you are not one to help me [bi-musrikhiyya]﴾ [Ibrahim: 22], with a kasra on the ya. The majority read ﴿And I had created you﴾ with the first-person ta. Al-A'mash, Talha, Ibn Thabbat and Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "We created you" (khalaqnaka) with the royal plural nun. ﴿And you were not a thing﴾, that is, a thing existing. Al-Zamakhshari said: "a thing", because the non-existent is not a thing; or "a thing that is counted," like the saying: "I wonder at the nothing that, when it sees something other than a thing, thinks it a man." (p-176)

﴿He said﴾, that is, Zakariyya: ﴿My Lord, make for me a sign﴾, that is, a token by which I may know the occurrence of what I was given good news of. He asked for this so that he might increase in certainty, as Abraham, peace be upon him, said: ﴿But [I ask] so that my heart may be at rest﴾ [al-Baqarah: 260]. This was not because he doubted the truth of what he had been promised, nor because he suspected that it came from someone other than God, since the prophets are protected from such things. Al-Zajjaj said: The good news came in an unrestricted form, so he did not know the time, and so he asked for a sign so that he would know the time of its occurrence.

﴿He said: "Your sign"﴾. It is narrated from Ibn Zayd that when his wife became pregnant with Yahya, he could not speak to anyone, yet he would recite the Torah and remember God, but when he wanted to call out to someone, he could not. "Sound" (sawiyyan) is a circumstantial accusative (hal) from a pronoun, meaning: do not speak while you are in good health, with no muteness or illness in you. This is the statement of the majority. According to Ibn 'Abbas, it refers to the nights, meaning: complete, even nights. In that case it is an attribute of "three". The mention of nights here, and of days in Al 'Imran, indicates that the restriction on speech lasted for him three days with their nights.

Ibn Abi 'Abla and Zayd ibn 'Ali read ﴿that you do not speak﴾ with a raised mim, treating "an" as the light form of the heavy one, with the sense: "that he does not speak." The majority read it with the mim in the accusative, treating "an" as the one that governs the imperfect (an al-nasiba). ﴿So he came out to his people from the prayer niche (mihrab)﴾, that is, while he was in that state of being unable to speak to people. His mihrab is the place of his prayer. The mihrab has already been discussed in Al 'Imran. ﴿So he signalled to them﴾, that is, he gestured. Qatada, Ibn Munabbih, al-Kalbi and al-Qurtubi said: "He signalled to them" means he gestured. Al-Zamakhshari mentions it from Mujahid, who said: Supporting this is "except by gesture" (ramzan). From Ibn 'Abbas: he wrote for them on the ground. Ibn 'Atiyya said: Mujahid said: Rather he wrote for them in the dust, and both views are a form of revelation (wahy). End of quotation. Ikrima said: He wrote on a leaf, and revelation (wahy) in the speech of the Arabs means writing. From this is the saying of Dhu al-Rumma:

"Except the four dark ones, which seem like
the remnant of revelation within the pages of scrolls."

And 'Antara said:

"Like the revelation of scrolls from the era of Kisra,
which he gave to a non-Arab, a stammerer."

And Jarir said:

"As if a Jew were writing revelation
with a kaf and a lam in its dwellings."

The majority hold that the meaning of ﴿that glorify [Him]﴾ is: pray. It has also been said: he commanded them to remember God and to glorify Him. The commentators said: He used to go out to his people in the morning and evening and command them to pray by gesture. The author of al-Tahrir wa al-Tahbir said: In my view there is a subtle meaning here: that he was specifically commanded to glorify with remembrance, because the custom is that whoever sees something that amazes him, or sees in it wondrous craftsmanship or strange wisdom, says: "Glory be to God, glory to the Creator." When he saw a child born to an old man and a barren woman, he was amazed by that, so he glorified, and he commanded glorification. End of quotation.

Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya said: the "an" is explanatory (mufassira). Al-Hawfi said: ﴿that glorify﴾, the "an" is governed by "revealed" (awha). Abu al-Baqa' said: It may be a verbal "an" (masdariyya), and it may be in the sense of "i.e." (ay). End of quotation. Talha read "that glorify Him" with a pronoun for God, the Exalted. Ibn Ghazwan narrated from Talha: "that glorify" with a doubled nun, without a waw; he attached the emphatic heavy nun to the imperative verb.

﴿O Yahya, take the Book with strength﴾. There is an omission in the speech, and the sense is: when Yahya was born and grew up and reached the age at which he was commanded, God said to him through the angel. Al-Tibrizi was wrong in his view that the one calling him was his father when he grew up and matured; the correct view is what came before, due to His saying ﴿And We gave him wisdom while still a boy﴾. The Book is the Torah. Ibn 'Atiyya said: Without disagreement, because he was born before 'Isa, and the Gospel did not yet exist. End of quotation. This is not as he said; rather it was said that he had a book specifically given to him, just as many of the prophets were given something similar. It has also been said: "the Book" here is a generic noun, meaning: recite the books of God. It has been said: "the Book" is the scrolls of Abraham. Al-Hasan said: He taught him the Torah and the Gospel and sent him to the Children of Israel, and in his childhood he used to fast and pray and call to God (p-177) ﴿with strength﴾: with determination, perseverance and acting upon what is in it. "Wisdom" (hukm) means prophethood, or the judgment of the Book, or wisdom, or knowledge of the rulings, or intellect, which is reason, or the etiquette of service, or sound insight (firasa). These are the views. ﴿While still a boy﴾ (sabiyyan), that is, a youth who had not reached the age of maturity. It has been said he was two years old. It has been said he was three years old. From Ibn 'Abbas, in a raised (marfu') hadith: "seven years old." ﴿And tenderness﴾ is coordinated with "wisdom". Hanan means mercy. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas in one report, and by al-Hasan, Ikrima, Qatada, al-Dahhak, Abu 'Ubayda and al-Farra'. Abu 'Ubayda recited:

"Show tenderness to me; may the King guide you,
for every station has its own speech."

He said: It is most often used in the dual, as in the saying:

"Hanānayka, the lesser of two evils is better than the greater."

Ibn al-Anbari said: the meaning is that We made him "hanan" for the people of his time. Mujahid said: and a kindness from his Lord towards him. From Ibn Jubayr: gentle. From Ikrima and Ibn Zayd: affection. From 'Ata': honour.

His saying ﴿and purity﴾: according to al-Dahhak and Qatada, righteous deeds. From Ibn al-Sa'ib: charity given on behalf of his parents. From al-Zajjaj: purification. From Ibn al-Anbari: increase in good. It has been said: praise, as witnesses are declared upright (yuzakka).

﴿And he was God-fearing (taqiyyan)﴾. Qatada said: He never intended a major sin or a minor sin, nor did he ever desire a woman. Ibn 'Abbas said: He made him one who fears God, and he did not put anything else on a par with Him. Mujahid said: His food was permissible plants, and there were clear channels of tears on his cheeks. ﴿And dutiful to his parents﴾, that is, abundant in goodness, honour and reverence. Al-Hasan, Abu Ja'far in one report, Abu Nahik and Abu Mijlaz read "and dutiful" (wa-barran) in both places with a kasra on the ba', meaning: and one who has dutifulness. ﴿And he was not a tyrant﴾, that is, arrogant. ﴿Disobedient﴾, that is, a disobeyer, abundant in disobedience. Its original form is 'asawiy, an intensive form (fa'ul), and it is possible that it is a fa'il, which is also one of the intensive patterns.

﴿And peace be upon him﴾. Al-Tabari said: that is, safety (aman). Ibn 'Atiyya said: The more evident view is that it is the customary greeting, and the honour lies in God's greeting him and bestowing peace upon him in the situations in which a person is in utmost weakness, need, lack of resource, and poverty before God. Al-Tabari mentions from al-Hasan that 'Isa and Yahya, peace be upon them both, met, and they were cousins, and Yahya said to 'Isa: "Pray for me, for you are better than I," and 'Isa said to him: "Rather you pray for me, for you are better than I. God has greeted you with peace, and I have greeted myself with peace."

Abu 'Abdullah al-Razi said: ﴿On the day he was born﴾, that is, safety for him from the Devil reaching him; ﴿and the day he dies﴾, that is, safety from the punishment of the grave; ﴿and the day he is raised alive﴾ from God's punishment on the Day of Resurrection. In His saying ﴿and the day he is raised alive﴾ there is an indication that he is among the martyrs, due to His saying ﴿Rather, they are alive with their Lord, provided for﴾ [Al 'Imran: 169]. This greeting may come from God or from the angels. End of quotation. The more evident view is that it is from God, because it is in the context of ﴿And We gave him wisdom﴾.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 19, verse 16–26 (part 1 of 3):

﴿And mention in the Book Maryam, when she withdrew from her family to an eastern place.﴾ ﴿And she took a screen apart from them; then We sent to her Our Spirit, and it presented itself to her as a well-formed man.﴾ ﴿She said, "Indeed, I seek refuge in the Most Merciful from you, if you should be fearing of Allah."﴾ ﴿He said, "I am only the messenger of your Lord, to give you a pure boy."﴾ ﴿She said, "How can I have a boy when no man has touched me and I have not been unchaste?"﴾ ﴿He said, "So it will be. Your Lord said, 'It is easy for Me. And so We will make him a sign for the people and a mercy from Us; and it is a matter decreed.'"﴾ ﴿So she conceived him, and she withdrew with him to a remote place.﴾ ﴿And the pains of childbirth drove her to the trunk of a palm tree. She said, "Oh, I wish I had died before this and had been a thing forgotten and out of sight."﴾ ﴿But he called to her from below her, "Do not grieve; your Lord has provided beneath you a stream.﴾ ﴿And shake toward you the trunk of the palm tree; it will drop upon you ripe, fresh dates.﴾ ﴿So eat and drink and be cool of eye. And if you see any human, say, 'Indeed, I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast, so I will not speak today to any human being.'"﴾.

(p-١٧٨)(p-١٧٩)The connection of this verse with what precedes it: when Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the story of Zakariyya, his request for a child, and Allah's answer to him, so that a child was born to him from an aged old man and a barren wife, and that was among the things that cause wonder, He followed it with what is even greater in strangeness and wonder, which is the existence of a child without a male. This indicates the greatness of Allah's power and wisdom. Also, He related to them what they had asked about, the story of the People of the Cave, and followed that with the story of al-Khidr and Musa. Then He related to them what they had also asked, which is the story of Dhu al-Qarnayn. So He mentioned in this surah stories they had not asked about, and in them is strangeness. Then He followed that with the story of Ibrahim, Musa and Harun in brief, then with the story of Isma'il and Idris, so that it would settle in their minds that He informed His Prophet about what they had asked and what they had not asked, and that the Messenger—upon him be prayer and peace—received revelation about that in a single manner, which indicates his truthfulness and the soundness of his message, from an unlettered man who did not read books, did not travel, did not mix with anyone learned, and did not concern himself with gathering biographies.

And "al-Kitab" (the Book) is the Qur'an. Maryam is the daughter of 'Imran, mother of 'Isa. "Idh" (when) has been said to be an adverb of time governed by "udhkur" (mention). This is not possible while it remains in its adverbial sense, because the future does not occur in the past. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Idh" is a substitute (badal) for "Maryam," a substitute of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal), because times include what occurs in them, as the intended purpose of mentioning Maryam is mentioning her time, for the occurrence of this strange story in it, end. The governing of "idh" by "udhkur" by way of substitution requires treating "idh" as something other than what it is, for it is one of the adverbs which are not treated in such a way except by adding a time-adverb to it. So it is preferable to posit an omitted conjunctive element, indicated by the meaning, which would govern "idh," and keep it in its adverbial status and its non-variation: that is, to estimate "Maryam and what happened to her, when she withdrew [idh antabadhat]." Abu al-Baqa' disputed al-Zamakhshari's view, saying: because time, if it is not a state of the body, nor a predicate about it, nor a description of it, cannot be a substitute for it, end. His disputing is nothing, for there is no necessary connection. He said: It has been said the estimate is the predicate of Maryam, so "idh" is governed by a predicate. It has been said: it is a state (hal) from this omitted genitive construction. It has been said: "idh" has the meaning of "an" (that) as a verbal noun, as in your saying: "I honour you idh you do not honour me," meaning "in case you do not honour me." Abu al-Baqa' said: according to this, substitution of inclusion is valid, that is: "mention Maryam's withdrawal," end.

"Antabadhat" is the form ifta'ala from nabadha, and its meaning is she threw herself, withdrew, and isolated herself. Al-Suddi said: "antabadhat" means she withdrew to purify herself from her menstruation. Others said: to worship Allah; she was dedicated to the service and ministry of the worship-place, and so she withdrew from people in this way.
