Or because of her grief over the people, or because the people would be sinning because of her. It is related that she heard a call: "Come out, O you who are worshipped besides Allah!" So she grieved and said, ﴿Oh, would that I had died﴾. Wahb said: the distress of childbirth made her forget, and what she had heard from the people, the good news of the angels concerning ʿIsa.

Zirr and ʿAlqama read ﴿so she addressed him﴾ (fa-khāṭabahā) instead of ﴿so he called to her﴾ (fa-nādāhā). This should be taken as an explanation rather than a recitation, because it contradicts the consonantal text of the Mushaf, on which there is consensus. The one who called, apparently, was ʿIsa, meaning that she gave birth to him, and Allah made him speak and he called to her, that is, at the moment of delivery. It was said: it was Jibril, who was in a spot of the earth lower than the place where she was, and al-Hasan said this and swore to it. It was said: he used to receive the child like a midwife. Ibn ʿAbbas read ﴿a angel called to her from beneath her﴾ (malakun min taḥtihā). Al-Bara' ibn ʿAzib, Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, Zayd ibn ʿAli, al-Dahhak, ʿAmr ibn Maymun, Nafiʿ, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Hafs read min as a preposition. Ibn ʿĀmir, the two Ibn Kathirs, Abu ʿAmr (the two Abus), ʿAsim, Zirr, Mujahid, al-Jahdari, al-Hasan, and Ibn ʿAbbas in one transmission from him read man with a fatha on the mim, meaning "the one who," and taḥtahā is an adverbial accusative in the position of a relative complement to man, which is ʿIsa. That is, "the newborn called to her." This was said by Ubayy, al-Hasan, Ibn Jubayr and Mujahid. The an here is an explanatory particle, meaning ﴿do not grieve﴾. The sarī, according to the majority, is the stream. Al-Hasan, Ibn Zayd and Qatada said it means a great man of rank and standing. It is related that al-Hasan explained the verse and said: "Indeed, Allah made him a ﴿sarī﴾, noble." Humayd ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman said: "O Abu Saʿid, he only means by the sarī the stream." Al-Hasan said to this and similar things: "I love your nearness, but the rulers have overcome us."

Then He commanded her to shake the dry trunk of the palm tree, so that she might see another sign in the revival of the dead trunk. (p-184) Another group said: rather, the palm tree was grafted and bore ripe dates. As-Suddi said: the trunk had been cut down, and a river was made to flow beneath it at its side. The apparent meaning is that the one speaking was Jesus, and that the trunk was dry. On this basis, signs appeared to her that gave her comfort, and her sorrow was not due to the lack of food and drink, so that she might be consoled by eating and drinking, but rather because of the breach of custom that appeared in that matter, so that it would become clear to her people that her giving birth without a male was not a novelty in her case. Ibn 'Abbas said: it was a decayed trunk. When she shook it, the palm fronds had already sprouted; then she looked and saw the spathe emerging from between the fronds, then it turned green and became unripe dates, then it reddened and became ripe-yellow dates (zahw), then ripe dates (rutab), all of this in the twinkling of an eye, so that the ripe dates began to fall before her, and none of them was lost.

(Ila) is a particle without any disagreement, and it is connected to His words ﴿And shake﴾. This came contrary to what is established in the science of grammar, that the verb does not transitively reach an attached pronoun, and here it has put an attached pronoun in the nominative. It is not of the category of "zanna," "faqada," or "alima," and these (two) are for one meaning. One does not say: "darabtuka" (I struck you), nor "Zayd darabahu" (Zayd struck him), meaning he struck himself, nor "daraba-ni" (he struck me). In such constructions, one uses the reflexive noun: you say "darabta nafsaka" (you struck yourself), "Zayd daraba nafsahu" (Zayd struck himself), and "darabtu nafsi" (I struck myself). And the pronoun in the genitive, in their view, is like the pronoun in the accusative, so you do not say "hazaztu ilayka" (I shook toward you), nor "Zayd hazza ilayhi" (Zayd shook toward him), nor "hazazta ilayya" (you shook toward me). For this reason they claimed in the verse of the poet:

"So leave aside the plunder that was cried out about in its enclosures, but rather a tale of the riding-camels."

And in the verse of the other:

"Make light for yourself, for the affairs, the measures of them are in the hand of God."

'An and 'ala are not two particles; rather they are two adverbial nouns. This is not far-fetched, because 'an and 'ala have been established as nouns in the verse:

"From 'an the right of the wine-cup, a glance before..."

And in the verse:

"It went from 'alayhi after its thirst had been completed."

Some grammarians claimed that 'ala is never a particle at all, and that it is a noun in all its uses, and this was attributed to Sibawayh. But it cannot be claimed that (ila) is a noun, because of the consensus of the grammarians on its being a particle, as we have said. The parallel to His words, Exalted is He, ﴿And shake toward you﴾ is His words, Exalted is He, ﴿And draw your arm toward you﴾ [al-Qasas: 32]. On the basis of that rule, these two should be interpreted, and their interpretation is that His words "ilayki" are not connected to "hizzi" nor to "udmum," but rather that this is by way of explanation, and the sense is "I mean, toward you," so it is connected to an omitted element, as they said regarding His words ﴿Indeed, I am for you both among the sincere advisers﴾ [al-A'raf: 21] and what resembles it according to some interpretations. The "ba'" in ﴿bi-jidh'﴾ is extra, for emphasis, like His words ﴿And do not cast yourselves with your own hands into destruction﴾ [al-Baqarah: 195]. Abu 'Ali said: just as it is said "alqa bi-yadihi," meaning "alqa yadahu" (he cast his hand). And like the verse:

"Black-eyed, they do not recite with the suras."

That is, they do not recite the suras. Al-Tabari recited:

"In a valley of Yemen whose upper part grows the thorn-tree, and its lower part with the markh and shaban."

Al-Zamakhshari said: or the sense is "command her to shake with it," like the verse:

"It comes out in its hamstrings, my blade."

They said: dates for women in childbirth is a custom from that time, and likewise the tahnik (rubbing the newborn's palate). They said: it was from 'ajwa (a type of date), as said by Muhammad ibn Ka'b. It was said: nothing is better for women in childbirth than ripe dates. It was said: if her delivery is difficult, there is nothing better for her than ripe dates.

The majority read ﴿tusaqit﴾ with a fatha on the ta' and sin, and a shadda after an alif, with a fatha on the qaf. Al-A'mash, Talha, Ibn Thabit, Masruq and Hamza read it likewise, except that they lightened the sin. Hafs read ﴿tusaqit﴾ as the present tense of "saqatat." Abu as-Sammal read "tatasaqatu" with two ta's. Al-Bara' ibn 'Azib and al-A'mash in one narration read "yassaqat" with a ya' from below, present of "as-saqata." Abu Haywa and Masruq read "tusqit" with a ta' from above, with damma and a kasra on the qaf. And from (p-185) Abu Haywa likewise, except with a ya' from below. From him also "tasqut" with a ta' from above, with a fatha and a damma on the qaf, and from him likewise except with a ya' from below. Some said regarding this reading of Abu Haywa that he read "rutabun janiyyun" with the nominative as subject. As for the accusative, if he read it with a transitive verb, he put it in the accusative as object, or with an intransitive verb, then its accusative is as a specification (tamyiz). Whoever reads with a ya' from below, the verb is attributed to the trunk; whoever reads with a ta', it is attributed to the palm tree. It is permissible for it to be attributed to the trunk, in the manner of ﴿some of the travelers will pick him up﴾ [Yusuf: 10] according to the reading of whoever reads "yaltaqit-hu" with a ta' from above.

Al-Mubarrad permitted that in His words ﴿rutaban﴾ it be accusative governed by His words ﴿And shake﴾, meaning: ﴿And shake toward you with the trunk of the palm tree﴾ ripe dates that will fall upon you. According to what he permitted, the matter is of the type of "al-i'mal" (government of two verbs over one object), so the object of "tusaqit" is omitted. Whoever reads with a ya' from below, it is clear. Whoever reads with a ta' from above: if the verb is transitive, it may be of the type of "al-i'mal"; but if it is intransitive, then no, because of the difference in what "hizzi" is connected to at that point and the intransitive verb.

Talha ibn Sulayman read ﴿janiyyan﴾ with a kasra on the jim, following the vowel of the nun. As for provision: if it is already determined, then the son of Adam has been entrusted to striving for what is in it. For this reason Maryam was commanded to shake the trunk, and on this the Law came, and that is not contrary to trust in God.

From Ibn Zayd: Jesus said to her, "Do not grieve." She said: "How could I not grieve, when you are with me, neither possessing a husband nor a slave-woman? What excuse will I have before the people?" ﴿Would that I had died before this﴾, the verse. Then Jesus said to her: "I will take care of the speaking for you." ﴿So eat and drink and be comforted﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: that is, We have gathered for you in the stream and the ripe dates two benefits: one is eating and drinking, and the second is solace of heart, since both are miracles. This is the meaning of His words ﴿So eat and drink and be comforted﴾, that is: be content of soul, do not be distressed, and put away from you what has grieved and worried you, end of quote. And since the custom is to precede eating before drinking, it came first in the verse, and because of the proximity of His words ﴿it will drop upon you ripe dates, fresh﴾. And since the grieving person may also eat and drink, He said: ﴿and be comforted﴾, that is, do not grieve. Then He conveyed to her what she should say if she saw anyone. "Qur'a" was read with a kasra on the qaf, and that is a Najdi dialect, and its mention has already passed.

Abu 'Amr, in what Ibn Rumi narrated from him, read "tara'innna" with replacement of the ya' by a hamza, and it is narrated from him "latara'unna" with hamza also in place of the waw. Ibn Khalawayh said: this is, according to most grammarians, a solecism. Al-Zamakhshari said: this is from the dialect of those who say "labba'tu bi-l-hajj" and "halva'tu al-sawiq," because of the affinity between the hamza and the vowel letters in substitution, end of quote. Talha, Abu Ja'far and Shayba read "taraynna" with a sukun on the ya' and a fatha on the nun, light. Ibn Jinni said: this is irregular, meaning because the jussive did not affect it so as to delete the nun, as al-Afwah al-Awdi said:

"Do you not see my head, which has been humiliated by the troubles of a time of reversal and despair?"

The one commanding her to eat and drink and that statement is, apparently, her son. It was said it was Gabriel, according to the disagreement that preceded. The apparent meaning is that she was permitted to say what she was commanded to say, and this is the view of the majority. A group said: the meaning of ﴿fa-qulli﴾ is, by gesture and not by speech, otherwise contradiction would undermine her statement, end of quote. There is no contradiction, because the meaning is ﴿So I will not speak today to any human being﴾ after "qulli" this, and between the condition and its answer there is an omitted clause indicated by the sense, that is: ﴿If you see any human being﴾ and he asks you or converses with you, ﴿then say﴾.

Zayd ibn 'Ali read "siyaman" and explained "sawman" as abstaining from speech. In the Codex of 'Abdullah it is "samtan." It is narrated from Anas ibn Malik the same. As-Suddi and Ibn Zayd said: the custom of fasting among them was abstaining from food and speech, end of quote. Silence is forbidden, and its vow is not valid. In the hadith: "Order him to speak." Ibn Mas'ud ordered one who did that to speak. And she was commanded to vow the fast, because Jesus, through what God reveals to him, would suffice her in the matter of argument and disputing with fools. His words ﴿human﴾ because she used to speak with the angels (p-186) not with humankind.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 19, verse 16–26 (part 1 of 3):

﴿And mention in the Book Maryam, when she withdrew from her family to an eastern place.﴾ ﴿And she took a screen apart from them; then We sent to her Our Spirit, and it presented itself to her as a well-formed man.﴾ ﴿She said, "Indeed, I seek refuge in the Most Merciful from you, if you should be fearing of Allah."﴾ ﴿He said, "I am only the messenger of your Lord, to give you a pure boy."﴾ ﴿She said, "How can I have a boy when no man has touched me and I have not been unchaste?"﴾ ﴿He said, "So it will be. Your Lord said, 'It is easy for Me. And so We will make him a sign for the people and a mercy from Us; and it is a matter decreed.'"﴾ ﴿So she conceived him, and she withdrew with him to a remote place.﴾ ﴿And the pains of childbirth drove her to the trunk of a palm tree. She said, "Oh, I wish I had died before this and had been a thing forgotten and out of sight."﴾ ﴿But he called to her from below her, "Do not grieve; your Lord has provided beneath you a stream.﴾ ﴿And shake toward you the trunk of the palm tree; it will drop upon you ripe, fresh dates.﴾ ﴿So eat and drink and be cool of eye. And if you see any human, say, 'Indeed, I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast, so I will not speak today to any human being.'"﴾.

(p-١٧٨)(p-١٧٩)The connection of this verse with what precedes it: when Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the story of Zakariyya, his request for a child, and Allah's answer to him, so that a child was born to him from an aged old man and a barren wife, and that was among the things that cause wonder, He followed it with what is even greater in strangeness and wonder, which is the existence of a child without a male. This indicates the greatness of Allah's power and wisdom. Also, He related to them what they had asked about, the story of the People of the Cave, and followed that with the story of al-Khidr and Musa. Then He related to them what they had also asked, which is the story of Dhu al-Qarnayn. So He mentioned in this surah stories they had not asked about, and in them is strangeness. Then He followed that with the story of Ibrahim, Musa and Harun in brief, then with the story of Isma'il and Idris, so that it would settle in their minds that He informed His Prophet about what they had asked and what they had not asked, and that the Messenger—upon him be prayer and peace—received revelation about that in a single manner, which indicates his truthfulness and the soundness of his message, from an unlettered man who did not read books, did not travel, did not mix with anyone learned, and did not concern himself with gathering biographies.

And "al-Kitab" (the Book) is the Qur'an. Maryam is the daughter of 'Imran, mother of 'Isa. "Idh" (when) has been said to be an adverb of time governed by "udhkur" (mention). This is not possible while it remains in its adverbial sense, because the future does not occur in the past. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Idh" is a substitute (badal) for "Maryam," a substitute of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal), because times include what occurs in them, as the intended purpose of mentioning Maryam is mentioning her time, for the occurrence of this strange story in it, end. The governing of "idh" by "udhkur" by way of substitution requires treating "idh" as something other than what it is, for it is one of the adverbs which are not treated in such a way except by adding a time-adverb to it. So it is preferable to posit an omitted conjunctive element, indicated by the meaning, which would govern "idh," and keep it in its adverbial status and its non-variation: that is, to estimate "Maryam and what happened to her, when she withdrew [idh antabadhat]." Abu al-Baqa' disputed al-Zamakhshari's view, saying: because time, if it is not a state of the body, nor a predicate about it, nor a description of it, cannot be a substitute for it, end. His disputing is nothing, for there is no necessary connection. He said: It has been said the estimate is the predicate of Maryam, so "idh" is governed by a predicate. It has been said: it is a state (hal) from this omitted genitive construction. It has been said: "idh" has the meaning of "an" (that) as a verbal noun, as in your saying: "I honour you idh you do not honour me," meaning "in case you do not honour me." Abu al-Baqa' said: according to this, substitution of inclusion is valid, that is: "mention Maryam's withdrawal," end.

"Antabadhat" is the form ifta'ala from nabadha, and its meaning is she threw herself, withdrew, and isolated herself. Al-Suddi said: "antabadhat" means she withdrew to purify herself from her menstruation. Others said: to worship Allah; she was dedicated to the service and ministry of the worship-place, and so she withdrew from people in this way. "Makanan" (a place) is in the accusative as an adverb of place, meaning "in a place," and it was described as "sharqiyyan" (eastern) because it was on the side adjoining Bayt al-Maqdis, or from her house. The reason it was in the east is that they used to venerate the direction of the east, from where the sun rises. From Ibn 'Abbas: the Christians took the east as a direction of prayer for the birth of 'Isa, upon him be peace. It has been said: she sat in a place for bathing from menstruation, screened by a wall, meaning something that covers her, and its place was the mosque; while she was in her bathing place, the angel came to her in the form of a young, beardless human man, of handsome face, curly-haired, of well-formed build, who lacked nothing of the human form, or of beautiful form and well-proportioned build. Qatada said: "sharqiyyan" means far away, distant, end.

The screen she took to conceal herself from people for worshipping her Lord. Al-Suddi said: it was of walls. It has been said: of garments. From Ibn 'Abbas: she placed the mountain between herself and the people as a "hijab" (screen). The apparent sense of "the sending" is from Allah to her, and the conversation of the angel indicates that she was a prophetess. It has been said: she was not made a prophet, but he spoke to her in the likeness of a human, and her seeing the angel was like the seeing of Jibril, upon him be peace, in the form of Dihya, and in his asking about faith and Islam. The apparent meaning is that "al-Ruh" (the Spirit) is Jibril, because religion lives by him and by his revelation, or he called him "His spirit" metaphorically out of love and closeness, as you say to your beloved: "You are my spirit." It has been said: 'Isa, as in "and a spirit from Him," and on this view "fa-tamaththala" (it presented itself) would refer to the angel. Abu Haywa and Sahl read "ruhana" with a fatha on the ra', because he is a cause of what in it is the rest (rawh) of the servants, and attaining rest with Allah, which is the provision of the near ones, in His saying: "And as for if he was of those brought near, then rest and provision" [al-Waqi'a: 88], or because he is among the near ones, and they are the ones promised rest, meaning "our near one" and "possessor of our rest." Al-Naqqash mentioned that it was read "Ruhunna" with the nun doubled, the name of one of the angels. "Bashaamong sawiyyan" is in the accusative as a state (hal) relative to his saying: "Sometimes the angel appears to me as a man." It has been said: he was presented to her in human form only so that she would be at ease with his speech and not shrink from him; had he appeared to her in the angelic form, she would have shrunk away and not been able to listen to his speech. What indicates her chastity and piety is that she sought refuge with Him from that beautiful, surpassingly handsome form, and his presenting himself in that attribute was a trial for her and a test of her chastity.

It has been said: she was in the house of her sister's husband, Zakariyya, and she had a separate sanctuary which she inhabited; when Zakariyya went out, he locked her in. She wished to find a solitary place in the mountain to delouse her head, so the roof split open for her, she went out, and sat in the eastern place behind the mountain, and the angel came to her. It has been said: he stood before her in the form of a companion of hers named Yusuf, one of the servants of Bayt al-Maqdis. Her making seeking refuge conditional on his piety is because seeking refuge is of no benefit and yields nothing except with one who fears Allah; meaning: if it is hoped from you that you fear Allah, revere Him, and attend to seeking refuge in Him, then I am seeking refuge in Him from you. The answer of the condition is omitted, meaning: "then I seek refuge." Al-Zajjaj said: "so you will be admonished by my seeking refuge in Allah from you." It has been said: "then withdraw from me." It has been said: "then do not approach me." The saying of one who said "taqiyy" is the name of a righteous man, or a corrupt man, is not sound. It has been said: "in" is negative, meaning "you are not pious," i.e., by your entering upon me and your looking at me, and her seeking refuge in Allah and her taking refuge in Him at the time of the appearance is evidence that, when he first presented himself to her, she sought refuge without any speech passing between them.

(He said), i.e., Jibril, upon him be peace: ﴿"I am only the messenger of your Lord"﴾, the one watching over your welfare and the owner of your affair, and He is the one you sought refuge in. His saying this to her is reassurance for her, and that I am not one who may be suspected of doubt; He sent me to you ﴿"to give you"﴾. Shayba, Abu al-Hasan, Abu Bahriyya, al-Zuhri, Ibn Munadhir, Ya'qub and al-Yazidi, and among the seven Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read "liyahaba" (that He may give), i.e., that your Lord may give. The majority and the rest of the seven read "li-ahaba" with the hamza of the first person, and attributed the giving to himself because the announcement of it was from him.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "li-ahaba laka" (I may give you): so that I may be a cause of the giving of a boy by breathing into the sleeve/breath. In some codices: "He commanded me that I give you." It may be that this is reported by an omitted verb of saying, meaning: he said "li-ahaba" (that I may give). "Ghulam" (boy) is the name for a child from the time of birth until he reaches the age of middle adulthood. "Zakiyyan" has been interpreted here as righteousness and as prophethood. Maryam marveled and knew, by what was cast into her spirit, that it was from Allah. The discussion of her question about the manner has already preceded in Al 'Imran in her story. And in her saying ﴿"and I have not been unchaste"﴾ there is specification after generalization, because the touching of a human occurs through marriage or through fornication.

Al-Zamakhshari said: The touching was made an expression for lawful marriage, because it is a metaphor for it, as in His saying: "before you touch them" [al-Baqara: 237] or "you have touched women" [al-Nisa: 43]; and fornication is not like that; one only says: "he committed fornication with her," "he defiled himself with her," and similar; it is not fitting that metaphors and courtesies be observed in it, end. "Baghiyy" is the one who openly and notoriously commits fornication. Its pattern is fa'ul according to al-Mubarrad: a waw and a ya' came together, and one of them was preceded by a sukun, so the waw was changed into a ya', and it was assimilated into the ya', and the letter before it was kasra because of the ya', as it is kasred in 'isiyy and dilliyy. It has been said: if it were fa'il, a feminine ta' would be attached to it, so one would say baghiyyah. Ibn Jinni said in Kitab al-Tamam: it is fa'il, and if it were fa'ul, it would be said baghuww, as one says: "fulan nahuww 'an al-munkar" (so-and-so forbids the evil) end. It has been said: since this word was specific to the feminine, it did not need a sign of feminine gender, so it became like ha'id (menstruating) and talia (divorced), and one says of a man only "ba'in." It has been said: baghiyy is fa'il in the sense of maf'ul, like 'ayn kahil, meaning one desired (mabghiyyah), whom her like seek.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 19, verses 16–26 (part 2 of 3):

﴿He said: "So it is. Your Lord said, 'It is easy for Me.'"﴾ [Maryam: 9] The discussion of this is like the earlier discussion in the story of Zakariyya. ﴿And that We may make him﴾ may be coordinated with an omitted reason, whose estimated meaning is "so that We may show by him Our power," ﴿and that We may make him﴾, or with an omitted later element, meaning "We did that." The pronoun in ﴿and that We may make him﴾ refers to the boy, and likewise in His saying ﴿and it was﴾, meaning "and his existence was," ﴿a matter﴾ already decreed, ﴿and his being a mercy from Allah﴾, meaning a path of guidance for a great many people, so that they attain mercy through him.

They mention that Jibril (peace be upon him) blew into the opening of her shift or into it and into her sleeve, and said. That is, the breath that was blown entered through her mouth. The apparent reading is that the one to whom the blowing is attributed is Allah the Exalted, because of His saying ﴿So We blew﴾. It is possible, as they said, that ﴿so she conceived him﴾ means, in her womb, and the meaning is "so she conceived with him." It was said: she was fourteen years old. It was said: she gave birth at fifteen years old, as Wahb and Mujahid said. It was said: thirteen years old. It was said: twelve years old. It was said: ten years old. It was said: after she had menstruated twice. Muhammad ibn al-Haysam related that she had not yet menstruated. It was said: Maryam never menstruated at all, since she was purified from menstruation. So she did not feel anything, and she feared the blame of people, that evil might be attributed to her, so she withdrew with it to a distant place out of shame and flight. It is related that she fled to the land of Egypt or near it, as Wahb said. It was said: to a place known as Bayt Lahm (Bethlehem), four miles between it and Iliya (Jerusalem). It was said: far from her family, behind the mountain. It was said: the farthest part of the house. It was said: she had been betrothed to a paternal cousin of hers named Yusuf. When it was said that she had conceived from fornication, he feared for her the killing of the king, so he fled with her. When they were on part of the road, his soul prompted him to kill her, but Jibril (peace be upon him) came to him and said: "It is from the Holy Spirit, so do not kill her," and he left her. She conceived him in a single hour, and just as she conceived him, she bore him in the same hour, so she gave birth to him without any delay. It was said: the period of pregnancy was three hours. It was said: he was conceived in an hour, formed in an hour, and she delivered him in an hour. It was said: six months. And from ʿAta', Abu al-ʿAliya and al-Dahhak: seven months. It was said: eight months, and no child born at eight months survived except ʿIsa. These are confused and contradictory statements, which should have been set aside entirely, but the exegetes recorded them in their books and filled pages with them.

The preposition in ﴿with it﴾ (bihi) indicates a state, meaning "accompanied by it," that is, she withdrew while he was in her womb, as the poet said:

*"It tramples the skulls and the dust beneath us,"*

meaning, it tramples the skulls while we are on their backs.

The meaning of ﴿so the birth pang drove her﴾ is that it brought her, once, using the preposition bi, and once using the hamza form. Al-Zamakhshari said: "However, its usage may be changed after transitivization to mean compulsion. Do you not see that you do not say, 'I came to the place,' and 'Zayd brought me to it,' as you say, 'I reached it' and 'he made me reach it'? Its counterpart is ātā, which is used only for giving, and one does not say 'I came to the place' or 'so-and-so brought it to me.'" As for his statement, and the statement of others, that usage changed it to the meaning of compulsion, it requires transmission from the linguists who examined the usage of the Arabs. The form with the hamza signifies the general notion, so it is suitable for the meaning of compulsion and also for the meaning of choice, as when you say, "I made Zayd stand," where he may have chosen that, or you may have forced him to stand. As for his saying, "Do you not see that you do not say," to the end, whoever considers transitivization by the hamza to be analogical may permit it even without hearing it, while whoever does not consider it analogical has heard it in jā'a, since they said ajā'a, and so he permits it. As for his comparison of it to ātā, that comparison is not valid, because he based it on the claim that the hamza there is for transitivity and that its root is atā. This is not so. Rather, ātā is formed from afʿala and is not derived from atā with the meaning of jā'a, for if it were derived from atā, which is transitive to one object, then that object would be the second object and the agent the first when made transitive by hamza. You say atā al-māla Zaydan (the wealth came to Zayd), and ātā ʿAmrun Zaydan al-māla (ʿAmr gave Zayd the wealth), so the construction differs by transitivity, since according to the grammarians Zayd is the first object and the wealth is the second. By al-Zamakhshari's account, it would be the reverse, which shows that it is not as he said. Also, ātā is a synonym of aʿṭā (to give), so it differs in meaning. As for his saying, "You do not say ataytu al-makān wa-ātānīhi (I came to the place and he brought me to it)," this is not accepted. Rather, it is said: ataytu al-makān, just as you say ji'tu al-makān (I came to the place). The poet said:

*"They came to my fire, and I said, 'Who are you?' They said, 'Jinn.' I said, 'Be blind to the darkness.'"*

Whoever considers transmission by the hamza to be analogical says ātānīhi (he brought it to me).

The majority read ﴿fa-ajāʾahā﴾, meaning "drove her," that is, drove her toward it. The poet said:

*"And a traveler who went with confidence toward you, fear and hope drove him."*

Al-Aʿmash and Talha pronounced the fatha of the jim with imala (a vowel shift toward i). Hammad ibn Salama related from ʿAsim. Ibn ʿAtiyya said that Shubayl ibn ʿAzra read fājaʾahā, from al-mufājaʾa (suddenness). The author of al-Lawāmih (Abu al-Fath) said that Shubayl ibn ʿAzra read fājaʾahā. It was said: it is from al-mufājaʾa in the pattern fāʿila, and its hamza was replaced by an alif for lightness, contrary to analogy. It is also possible that it is a hamza between two vowels (bayna bayn), not inverted. It is related from Mujahid in the same way as Hammad's reading from ʿAsim. Ibn Kathir (the Qur'an reader), in one transmission, read al-makhāḍ with a kasra on the mim. It is said: makhadat al-ḥāmil makhāḍan wa-mikhāḍan, meaning the pregnant woman went into labour, and the child moved in her womb (tamakhkhada al-walad fī baṭnihā).

The word ﴿to﴾ (ilā) is connected to ﴿fa-ajāʾahā﴾. For the one who reads fājaʾahā from al-mufājaʾa, it is connected to an omitted element, meaning "leaning," that is, while she was leaning against the palm tree.

The widely known and famous report is that the birth of ʿIsa (peace be upon him) took place at Bayt Lahm, and that when she fled and feared for him, she hurried with him and came with him to Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), and she placed him on a rock, and the rock sank down for him and became like a cradle. It still exists today and is visited within the sanctuary of Bayt al-Maqdis. Then, after some days, she set out with him toward the River Jordan and baptized him in it. This is the day that the Christians observe and call the Day of Epiphany (Yawm al-Ghitas), and they think that the waters on that day become holy, which is why they immerse themselves in every water. Whoever claims that she bore him in Egypt says: in the district of Ahnas.

It was said: the palm tree of Maryam still stands to this day. The apparent meaning is that the palm tree existed before Maryam came to it. It was said: Allah caused a palm tree to grow for her, and she clung to it. It is related that she reached a place in which there was a dry, decayed palm trunk, its base rotted by worms, having no top, no fruit, and no greenery. The article al- in ﴿the trunk of the palm tree﴾ is either for the definition of the genus, or it is the one attached to names that are predominant, as if that desert had a well-known palm trunk, so when it is said ﴿the trunk of the palm tree﴾, that is understood from it and no other.

Allah the Exalted guided her to the palm tree so that she might feed herself from it with ripe dates, which are the nourishment of women after childbirth and suitable for her, and so that those signs manifested through it might settle her soul and comfort her eye. Then the matter grew severe for her there, and she embraced (p-183) the trunk because of the intensity of the pain, and she gave birth to ʿIsa (peace be upon him). At the time of her delivery, because of what she saw of the pains, the estrangement, the denial of her people, and the severity of the situation without any apparent cause, she said ﴿Oh, would that I had died before this﴾. Maryam wished for death from a religious standpoint, for she feared that evil would be attributed to her regarding her religion and that she would be reproached, which would harm her. This is permissible, and on this same basis ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab and a group of the righteous wished for death. As for the prohibition against it, it applies only to harm that befalls the body. There has been a disagreement among the readers about the vowel of the mim in mitu (I die), whether kasra or damma, which was discussed in Al ʿImran.

The nisy is a worthless thing that is of the kind that is forgotten and so is not grieved over when lost, like a peg, a rope for the traveler, or a rag used for menstruation. The majority read it with a kasra on the nun, and it is a verb in the sense of a passive object, like dhibh (what is slaughtered), that is, something that is fit to be slaughtered. Ibn Wathhab, Talha, al-Aʿmash, Ibn Abi Layla, Hamza and Hafs read it with a fatha on the nun. Muhammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazi read nisʾan with a kasra on the nun and a hamza in place of the ya', and this is the reading of Nawf al-Aʿrabi. Bakr ibn Habib al-Sahmi and Muhammad ibn Kaʿb also read nasaʾan with a fatha on the nun and a hamza. This is a verbal noun from nasaʾtu al-laban, when you pour water on milk, so the milk is consumed in it because of its small quantity. It is as though she wished she were like that milk which is not seen and is not distinguished from the water.

Ibn ʿAtiyya said: Bakr ibn Habib read nasan with a fatha on the nun and the sin, without hamza, formed on the pattern faʿal, like qabaḍ and nafaḍ. Al-Farra' said: nasy and nisy are two dialects, like al-watr and al-wathr, and the fatha is more beloved to me. Abu ʿAli al-Farisi said: the kasra is the higher of the two dialects. Ibn al-Anbari said: whoever uses the kasra means a noun for what is forgotten, like niqḍ (something that is undone) is a noun for what is unravelled, and whoever uses the fatha, it is a verbal noun standing in for a noun, as one says rajulun danafun and danifun (a sick man). The kasra is the attribute in its proper form, and the fatha is a verbal noun that takes the place of an attribute. It is possible that both have the same meaning, like raṭl and raṭl (a pound). The reference in His saying ﴿this﴾ is to the pregnancy.

It was said: ﴿before this﴾ refers to the day, or to ﴿before this﴾ matter that has happened. Al-Aʿmash and Abu Jaʿfar in one transmission read mansiyyan with a kasra on the mim, following the vowel of the sin, as they say muntin (stinking) with the mim vowel following the vowel of the ta'.

It was said: she wished for that because of the excess of shame that befell her, according to the custom of human nature, not out of aversion to the decree of Allah, or because of the severity of the burden upon her when they accused her while she knew of her innocence, and the opposite of what she was accused of, namely that Allah had singled her out with the utmost honour and generosity, because that is a slippery position on which feet rarely remain firm. Or because of her grief over the people, or because the people would be sinning because of her. It is related that she heard a call: "Come out, O you who are worshipped besides Allah!" So she grieved and said, ﴿Oh, would that I had died﴾. Wahb said: the distress of childbirth made her forget, and what she had heard from the people, the good news of the angels concerning ʿIsa.

Zirr and ʿAlqama read ﴿so she addressed him﴾ (fa-khāṭabahā) instead of ﴿so he called to her﴾ (fa-nādāhā). This should be taken as an explanation rather than a recitation, because it contradicts the consonantal text of the Mushaf, on which there is consensus. The one who called, apparently, was ʿIsa, meaning that she gave birth to him, and Allah made him speak and he called to her, that is, at the moment of delivery. It was said: it was Jibril, who was in a spot of the earth lower than the place where she was, and al-Hasan said this and swore to it. It was said: he used to receive the child like a midwife. Ibn ʿAbbas read ﴿a angel called to her from beneath her﴾ (malakun min taḥtihā). Al-Bara' ibn ʿAzib, Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, Zayd ibn ʿAli, al-Dahhak, ʿAmr ibn Maymun, Nafiʿ, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Hafs read min as a preposition. Ibn ʿĀmir, the two Ibn Kathirs, Abu ʿAmr (the two Abus), ʿAsim, Zirr, Mujahid, al-Jahdari, al-Hasan, and Ibn ʿAbbas in one transmission from him read man with a fatha on the mim, meaning "the one who," and taḥtahā is an adverbial accusative in the position of a relative complement to man, which is ʿIsa. That is, "the newborn called to her." This was said by Ubayy, al-Hasan, Ibn Jubayr and Mujahid. The an here is an explanatory particle, meaning ﴿do not grieve﴾. The sarī, according to the majority, is the stream. Al-Hasan, Ibn Zayd and Qatada said it means a great man of rank and standing. It is related that al-Hasan explained the verse and said: "Indeed, Allah made him a ﴿sarī﴾, noble." Humayd ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman said: "O Abu Saʿid, he only means by the sarī the stream." Al-Hasan said to this and similar things: "I love your nearness, but the rulers have overcome us."

Then He commanded her to shake the dry trunk of the palm tree, so that she might see another sign in the revival of the dead trunk. (p-184) Another group said: rather, the palm tree was grafted and bore ripe dates. As-Suddi said: the trunk had been cut down, and a river was made to flow beneath it at its side. The apparent meaning is that the one speaking was Jesus, and that the trunk was dry. On this basis, signs appeared to her that gave her comfort, and her sorrow was not due to the lack of food and drink, so that she might be consoled by eating and drinking, but rather because of the breach of custom that appeared in that matter, so that it would become clear to her people that her giving birth without a male was not a novelty in her case. Ibn 'Abbas said: it was a decayed trunk. When she shook it, the palm fronds had already sprouted; then she looked and saw the spathe emerging from between the fronds, then it turned green and became unripe dates, then it reddened and became ripe-yellow dates (zahw), then ripe dates (rutab), all of this in the twinkling of an eye, so that the ripe dates began to fall before her, and none of them was lost.

(Ila) is a particle without any disagreement, and it is connected to His words ﴿And shake﴾. This came contrary to what is established in the science of grammar, that the verb does not transitively reach an attached pronoun, and here it has put an attached pronoun in the nominative. It is not of the category of "zanna," "faqada," or "alima," and these (two) are for one meaning. One does not say: "darabtuka" (I struck you), nor "Zayd darabahu" (Zayd struck him), meaning he struck himself, nor "daraba-ni" (he struck me). In such constructions, one uses the reflexive noun: you say "darabta nafsaka" (you struck yourself), "Zayd daraba nafsahu" (Zayd struck himself), and "darabtu nafsi" (I struck myself). And the pronoun in the genitive, in their view, is like the pronoun in the accusative, so you do not say "hazaztu ilayka" (I shook toward you), nor "Zayd hazza ilayhi" (Zayd shook toward him), nor "hazazta ilayya" (you shook toward me). For this reason they claimed in the verse of the poet:

"So leave aside the plunder that was cried out about in its enclosures, but rather a tale of the riding-camels."

And in the verse of the other:

"Make light for yourself, for the affairs, the measures of them are in the hand of God."

'An and 'ala are not two particles; rather they are two adverbial nouns. This is not far-fetched, because 'an and 'ala have been established as nouns in the verse:

"From 'an the right of the wine-cup, a glance before..."

And in the verse:

"It went from 'alayhi after its thirst had been completed."

Some grammarians claimed that 'ala is never a particle at all, and that it is a noun in all its uses, and this was attributed to Sibawayh. But it cannot be claimed that (ila) is a noun, because of the consensus of the grammarians on its being a particle, as we have said. The parallel to His words, Exalted is He, ﴿And shake toward you﴾ is His words, Exalted is He, ﴿And draw your arm toward you﴾ [al-Qasas: 32]. On the basis of that rule, these two should be interpreted, and their interpretation is that His words "ilayki" are not connected to "hizzi" nor to "udmum," but rather that this is by way of explanation, and the sense is "I mean, toward you," so it is connected to an omitted element, as they said regarding His words ﴿Indeed, I am for you both among the sincere advisers﴾ [al-A'raf: 21] and what resembles it according to some interpretations. The "ba'" in ﴿bi-jidh'﴾ is extra, for emphasis, like His words ﴿And do not cast yourselves with your own hands into destruction﴾ [al-Baqarah: 195]. Abu 'Ali said: just as it is said "alqa bi-yadihi," meaning "alqa yadahu" (he cast his hand). And like the verse:

"Black-eyed, they do not recite with the suras."

That is, they do not recite the suras. Al-Tabari recited:

"In a valley of Yemen whose upper part grows the thorn-tree, and its lower part with the markh and shaban."

Al-Zamakhshari said: or the sense is "command her to shake with it," like the verse:

"It comes out in its hamstrings, my blade."

They said: dates for women in childbirth is a custom from that time, and likewise the tahnik (rubbing the newborn's palate). They said: it was from 'ajwa (a type of date), as said by Muhammad ibn Ka'b. It was said: nothing is better for women in childbirth than ripe dates. It was said: if her delivery is difficult, there is nothing better for her than ripe dates.

The majority read ﴿tusaqit﴾ with a fatha on the ta' and sin, and a shadda after an alif, with a fatha on the qaf. Al-A'mash, Talha, Ibn Thabit, Masruq and Hamza read it likewise, except that they lightened the sin. Hafs read ﴿tusaqit﴾ as the present tense of "saqatat." Abu as-Sammal read "tatasaqatu" with two ta's. Al-Bara' ibn 'Azib and al-A'mash in one narration read "yassaqat" with a ya' from below, present of "as-saqata." Abu Haywa and Masruq read "tusqit" with a ta' from above, with damma and a kasra on the qaf. And from (p-185) Abu Haywa likewise, except with a ya' from below. From him also "tasqut" with a ta' from above, with a fatha and a damma on the qaf, and from him likewise except with a ya' from below. Some said regarding this reading of Abu Haywa that he read "rutabun janiyyun" with the nominative as subject. As for the accusative, if he read it with a transitive verb, he put it in the accusative as object, or with an intransitive verb, then its accusative is as a specification (tamyiz). Whoever reads with a ya' from below, the verb is attributed to the trunk; whoever reads with a ta', it is attributed to the palm tree. It is permissible for it to be attributed to the trunk, in the manner of ﴿some of the travelers will pick him up﴾ [Yusuf: 10] according to the reading of whoever reads "yaltaqit-hu" with a ta' from above.

Al-Mubarrad permitted that in His words ﴿rutaban﴾ it be accusative governed by His words ﴿And shake﴾, meaning: ﴿And shake toward you with the trunk of the palm tree﴾ ripe dates that will fall upon you. According to what he permitted, the matter is of the type of "al-i'mal" (government of two verbs over one object), so the object of "tusaqit" is omitted. Whoever reads with a ya' from below, it is clear. Whoever reads with a ta' from above: if the verb is transitive, it may be of the type of "al-i'mal"; but if it is intransitive, then no, because of the difference in what "hizzi" is connected to at that point and the intransitive verb.

Talha ibn Sulayman read ﴿janiyyan﴾ with a kasra on the jim, following the vowel of the nun. As for provision: if it is already determined, then the son of Adam has been entrusted to striving for what is in it. For this reason Maryam was commanded to shake the trunk, and on this the Law came, and that is not contrary to trust in God.

From Ibn Zayd: Jesus said to her, "Do not grieve." She said: "How could I not grieve, when you are with me, neither possessing a husband nor a slave-woman? What excuse will I have before the people?" ﴿Would that I had died before this﴾, the verse. Then Jesus said to her: "I will take care of the speaking for you." ﴿So eat and drink and be comforted﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: that is, We have gathered for you in the stream and the ripe dates two benefits: one is eating and drinking, and the second is solace of heart, since both are miracles. This is the meaning of His words ﴿So eat and drink and be comforted﴾, that is: be content of soul, do not be distressed, and put away from you what has grieved and worried you, end of quote. And since the custom is to precede eating before drinking, it came first in the verse, and because of the proximity of His words ﴿it will drop upon you ripe dates, fresh﴾. And since the grieving person may also eat and drink, He said: ﴿and be comforted﴾, that is, do not grieve. Then He conveyed to her what she should say if she saw anyone. "Qur'a" was read with a kasra on the qaf, and that is a Najdi dialect, and its mention has already passed.

Abu 'Amr, in what Ibn Rumi narrated from him, read "tara'innna" with replacement of the ya' by a hamza, and it is narrated from him "latara'unna" with hamza also in place of the waw. Ibn Khalawayh said: this is, according to most grammarians, a solecism. Al-Zamakhshari said: this is from the dialect of those who say "labba'tu bi-l-hajj" and "halva'tu al-sawiq," because of the affinity between the hamza and the vowel letters in substitution, end of quote. Talha, Abu Ja'far and Shayba read "taraynna" with a sukun on the ya' and a fatha on the nun, light. Ibn Jinni said: this is irregular, meaning because the jussive did not affect it so as to delete the nun, as al-Afwah al-Awdi said:

"Do you not see my head, which has been humiliated by the troubles of a time of reversal and despair?"

The one commanding her to eat and drink and that statement is, apparently, her son. It was said it was Gabriel, according to the disagreement that preceded. The apparent meaning is that she was permitted to say what she was commanded to say, and this is the view of the majority. A group said: the meaning of ﴿fa-qulli﴾ is, by gesture and not by speech, otherwise contradiction would undermine her statement, end of quote. There is no contradiction, because the meaning is ﴿So I will not speak today to any human being﴾ after "qulli" this, and between the condition and its answer there is an omitted clause indicated by the sense, that is: ﴿If you see any human being﴾ and he asks you or converses with you, ﴿then say﴾.

Zayd ibn 'Ali read "siyaman" and explained "sawman" as abstaining from speech. In the Codex of 'Abdullah it is "samtan." It is narrated from Anas ibn Malik the same. As-Suddi and Ibn Zayd said: the custom of fasting among them was abstaining from food and speech, end of quote. Silence is forbidden, and its vow is not valid. In the hadith: "Order him to speak." Ibn Mas'ud ordered one who did that to speak. And she was commanded to vow the fast, because Jesus, through what God reveals to him, would suffice her in the matter of argument and disputing with fools. His words ﴿human﴾ because she used to speak with the angels (p-186) not with humankind.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 19, verse 16–26 (part 1 of 3):

﴿And mention in the Book Maryam, when she withdrew from her family to an eastern place.﴾ ﴿And she took a screen apart from them; then We sent to her Our Spirit, and it presented itself to her as a well-formed man.﴾ ﴿She said, "Indeed, I seek refuge in the Most Merciful from you, if you should be fearing of Allah."﴾ ﴿He said, "I am only the messenger of your Lord, to give you a pure boy."﴾ ﴿She said, "How can I have a boy when no man has touched me and I have not been unchaste?"﴾ ﴿He said, "So it will be. Your Lord said, 'It is easy for Me. And so We will make him a sign for the people and a mercy from Us; and it is a matter decreed.'"﴾ ﴿So she conceived him, and she withdrew with him to a remote place.﴾ ﴿And the pains of childbirth drove her to the trunk of a palm tree. She said, "Oh, I wish I had died before this and had been a thing forgotten and out of sight."﴾ ﴿But he called to her from below her, "Do not grieve; your Lord has provided beneath you a stream.﴾ ﴿And shake toward you the trunk of the palm tree; it will drop upon you ripe, fresh dates.﴾ ﴿So eat and drink and be cool of eye. And if you see any human, say, 'Indeed, I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast, so I will not speak today to any human being.'"﴾.

(p-١٧٨)(p-١٧٩)The connection of this verse with what precedes it: when Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the story of Zakariyya, his request for a child, and Allah's answer to him, so that a child was born to him from an aged old man and a barren wife, and that was among the things that cause wonder, He followed it with what is even greater in strangeness and wonder, which is the existence of a child without a male. This indicates the greatness of Allah's power and wisdom. Also, He related to them what they had asked about, the story of the People of the Cave, and followed that with the story of al-Khidr and Musa. Then He related to them what they had also asked, which is the story of Dhu al-Qarnayn. So He mentioned in this surah stories they had not asked about, and in them is strangeness. Then He followed that with the story of Ibrahim, Musa and Harun in brief, then with the story of Isma'il and Idris, so that it would settle in their minds that He informed His Prophet about what they had asked and what they had not asked, and that the Messenger—upon him be prayer and peace—received revelation about that in a single manner, which indicates his truthfulness and the soundness of his message, from an unlettered man who did not read books, did not travel, did not mix with anyone learned, and did not concern himself with gathering biographies.

And "al-Kitab" (the Book) is the Qur'an. Maryam is the daughter of 'Imran, mother of 'Isa. "Idh" (when) has been said to be an adverb of time governed by "udhkur" (mention). This is not possible while it remains in its adverbial sense, because the future does not occur in the past. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Idh" is a substitute (badal) for "Maryam," a substitute of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal), because times include what occurs in them, as the intended purpose of mentioning Maryam is mentioning her time, for the occurrence of this strange story in it, end. The governing of "idh" by "udhkur" by way of substitution requires treating "idh" as something other than what it is, for it is one of the adverbs which are not treated in such a way except by adding a time-adverb to it. So it is preferable to posit an omitted conjunctive element, indicated by the meaning, which would govern "idh," and keep it in its adverbial status and its non-variation: that is, to estimate "Maryam and what happened to her, when she withdrew [idh antabadhat]." Abu al-Baqa' disputed al-Zamakhshari's view, saying: because time, if it is not a state of the body, nor a predicate about it, nor a description of it, cannot be a substitute for it, end. His disputing is nothing, for there is no necessary connection. He said: It has been said the estimate is the predicate of Maryam, so "idh" is governed by a predicate. It has been said: it is a state (hal) from this omitted genitive construction. It has been said: "idh" has the meaning of "an" (that) as a verbal noun, as in your saying: "I honour you idh you do not honour me," meaning "in case you do not honour me." Abu al-Baqa' said: according to this, substitution of inclusion is valid, that is: "mention Maryam's withdrawal," end.

"Antabadhat" is the form ifta'ala from nabadha, and its meaning is she threw herself, withdrew, and isolated herself. Al-Suddi said: "antabadhat" means she withdrew to purify herself from her menstruation. Others said: to worship Allah; she was dedicated to the service and ministry of the worship-place, and so she withdrew from people in this way. "Makanan" (a place) is in the accusative as an adverb of place, meaning "in a place," and it was described as "sharqiyyan" (eastern) because it was on the side adjoining Bayt al-Maqdis, or from her house. The reason it was in the east is that they used to venerate the direction of the east, from where the sun rises. From Ibn 'Abbas: the Christians took the east as a direction of prayer for the birth of 'Isa, upon him be peace. It has been said: she sat in a place for bathing from menstruation, screened by a wall, meaning something that covers her, and its place was the mosque; while she was in her bathing place, the angel came to her in the form of a young, beardless human man, of handsome face, curly-haired, of well-formed build, who lacked nothing of the human form, or of beautiful form and well-proportioned build. Qatada said: "sharqiyyan" means far away, distant, end.

The screen she took to conceal herself from people for worshipping her Lord. Al-Suddi said: it was of walls. It has been said: of garments. From Ibn 'Abbas: she placed the mountain between herself and the people as a "hijab" (screen). The apparent sense of "the sending" is from Allah to her, and the conversation of the angel indicates that she was a prophetess. It has been said: she was not made a prophet, but he spoke to her in the likeness of a human, and her seeing the angel was like the seeing of Jibril, upon him be peace, in the form of Dihya, and in his asking about faith and Islam. The apparent meaning is that "al-Ruh" (the Spirit) is Jibril, because religion lives by him and by his revelation, or he called him "His spirit" metaphorically out of love and closeness, as you say to your beloved: "You are my spirit." It has been said: 'Isa, as in "and a spirit from Him," and on this view "fa-tamaththala" (it presented itself) would refer to the angel. Abu Haywa and Sahl read "ruhana" with a fatha on the ra', because he is a cause of what in it is the rest (rawh) of the servants, and attaining rest with Allah, which is the provision of the near ones, in His saying: "And as for if he was of those brought near, then rest and provision" [al-Waqi'a: 88], or because he is among the near ones, and they are the ones promised rest, meaning "our near one" and "possessor of our rest." Al-Naqqash mentioned that it was read "Ruhunna" with the nun doubled, the name of one of the angels. "Bashaamong sawiyyan" is in the accusative as a state (hal) relative to his saying: "Sometimes the angel appears to me as a man." It has been said: he was presented to her in human form only so that she would be at ease with his speech and not shrink from him; had he appeared to her in the angelic form, she would have shrunk away and not been able to listen to his speech. What indicates her chastity and piety is that she sought refuge with Him from that beautiful, surpassingly handsome form, and his presenting himself in that attribute was a trial for her and a test of her chastity.

It has been said: she was in the house of her sister's husband, Zakariyya, and she had a separate sanctuary which she inhabited; when Zakariyya went out, he locked her in. She wished to find a solitary place in the mountain to delouse her head, so the roof split open for her, she went out, and sat in the eastern place behind the mountain, and the angel came to her. It has been said: he stood before her in the form of a companion of hers named Yusuf, one of the servants of Bayt al-Maqdis. Her making seeking refuge conditional on his piety is because seeking refuge is of no benefit and yields nothing except with one who fears Allah; meaning: if it is hoped from you that you fear Allah, revere Him, and attend to seeking refuge in Him, then I am seeking refuge in Him from you. The answer of the condition is omitted, meaning: "then I seek refuge." Al-Zajjaj said: "so you will be admonished by my seeking refuge in Allah from you." It has been said: "then withdraw from me." It has been said: "then do not approach me." The saying of one who said "taqiyy" is the name of a righteous man, or a corrupt man, is not sound. It has been said: "in" is negative, meaning "you are not pious," i.e., by your entering upon me and your looking at me, and her seeking refuge in Allah and her taking refuge in Him at the time of the appearance is evidence that, when he first presented himself to her, she sought refuge without any speech passing between them.

(He said), i.e., Jibril, upon him be peace: ﴿"I am only the messenger of your Lord"﴾, the one watching over your welfare and the owner of your affair, and He is the one you sought refuge in. His saying this to her is reassurance for her, and that I am not one who may be suspected of doubt; He sent me to you ﴿"to give you"﴾. Shayba, Abu al-Hasan, Abu Bahriyya, al-Zuhri, Ibn Munadhir, Ya'qub and al-Yazidi, and among the seven Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read "liyahaba" (that He may give), i.e., that your Lord may give. The majority and the rest of the seven read "li-ahaba" with the hamza of the first person, and attributed the giving to himself because the announcement of it was from him.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "li-ahaba laka" (I may give you): so that I may be a cause of the giving of a boy by breathing into the sleeve/breath. In some codices: "He commanded me that I give you." It may be that this is reported by an omitted verb of saying, meaning: he said "li-ahaba" (that I may give). "Ghulam" (boy) is the name for a child from the time of birth until he reaches the age of middle adulthood. "Zakiyyan" has been interpreted here as righteousness and as prophethood. Maryam marveled and knew, by what was cast into her spirit, that it was from Allah. The discussion of her question about the manner has already preceded in Al 'Imran in her story. And in her saying ﴿"and I have not been unchaste"﴾ there is specification after generalization, because the touching of a human occurs through marriage or through fornication.

Al-Zamakhshari said: The touching was made an expression for lawful marriage, because it is a metaphor for it, as in His saying: "before you touch them" [al-Baqara: 237] or "you have touched women" [al-Nisa: 43]; and fornication is not like that; one only says: "he committed fornication with her," "he defiled himself with her," and similar; it is not fitting that metaphors and courtesies be observed in it, end. "Baghiyy" is the one who openly and notoriously commits fornication. Its pattern is fa'ul according to al-Mubarrad: a waw and a ya' came together, and one of them was preceded by a sukun, so the waw was changed into a ya', and it was assimilated into the ya', and the letter before it was kasra because of the ya', as it is kasred in 'isiyy and dilliyy. It has been said: if it were fa'il, a feminine ta' would be attached to it, so one would say baghiyyah. Ibn Jinni said in Kitab al-Tamam: it is fa'il, and if it were fa'ul, it would be said baghuww, as one says: "fulan nahuww 'an al-munkar" (so-and-so forbids the evil) end. It has been said: since this word was specific to the feminine, it did not need a sign of feminine gender, so it became like ha'id (menstruating) and talia (divorced), and one says of a man only "ba'in." It has been said: baghiyy is fa'il in the sense of maf'ul, like 'ayn kahil, meaning one desired (mabghiyyah), whom her like seek.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 19, verses 16–26 (part 2 of 3):

﴿He said: "So it is. Your Lord said, 'It is easy for Me.'"﴾ [Maryam: 9] The discussion of this is like the earlier discussion in the story of Zakariyya. ﴿And that We may make him﴾ may be coordinated with an omitted reason, whose estimated meaning is "so that We may show by him Our power," ﴿and that We may make him﴾, or with an omitted later element, meaning "We did that." The pronoun in ﴿and that We may make him﴾ refers to the boy, and likewise in His saying ﴿and it was﴾, meaning "and his existence was," ﴿a matter﴾ already decreed, ﴿and his being a mercy from Allah﴾, meaning a path of guidance for a great many people, so that they attain mercy through him.

They mention that Jibril (peace be upon him) blew into the opening of her shift or into it and into her sleeve, and said. That is, the breath that was blown entered through her mouth. The apparent reading is that the one to whom the blowing is attributed is Allah the Exalted, because of His saying ﴿So We blew﴾. It is possible, as they said, that ﴿so she conceived him﴾ means, in her womb, and the meaning is "so she conceived with him." It was said: she was fourteen years old. It was said: she gave birth at fifteen years old, as Wahb and Mujahid said. It was said: thirteen years old. It was said: twelve years old. It was said: ten years old. It was said: after she had menstruated twice. Muhammad ibn al-Haysam related that she had not yet menstruated. It was said: Maryam never menstruated at all, since she was purified from menstruation. So she did not feel anything, and she feared the blame of people, that evil might be attributed to her, so she withdrew with it to a distant place out of shame and flight. It is related that she fled to the land of Egypt or near it, as Wahb said. It was said: to a place known as Bayt Lahm (Bethlehem), four miles between it and Iliya (Jerusalem). It was said: far from her family, behind the mountain. It was said: the farthest part of the house. It was said: she had been betrothed to a paternal cousin of hers named Yusuf. When it was said that she had conceived from fornication, he feared for her the killing of the king, so he fled with her. When they were on part of the road, his soul prompted him to kill her, but Jibril (peace be upon him) came to him and said: "It is from the Holy Spirit, so do not kill her," and he left her. She conceived him in a single hour, and just as she conceived him, she bore him in the same hour, so she gave birth to him without any delay. It was said: the period of pregnancy was three hours. It was said: he was conceived in an hour, formed in an hour, and she delivered him in an hour. It was said: six months. And from ʿAta', Abu al-ʿAliya and al-Dahhak: seven months. It was said: eight months, and no child born at eight months survived except ʿIsa. These are confused and contradictory statements, which should have been set aside entirely, but the exegetes recorded them in their books and filled pages with them.

The preposition in ﴿with it﴾ (bihi) indicates a state, meaning "accompanied by it," that is, she withdrew while he was in her womb, as the poet said:

*"It tramples the skulls and the dust beneath us,"*

meaning, it tramples the skulls while we are on their backs.

The meaning of ﴿so the birth pang drove her﴾ is that it brought her, once, using the preposition bi, and once using the hamza form. Al-Zamakhshari said: "However, its usage may be changed after transitivization to mean compulsion. Do you not see that you do not say, 'I came to the place,' and 'Zayd brought me to it,' as you say, 'I reached it' and 'he made me reach it'? Its counterpart is ātā, which is used only for giving, and one does not say 'I came to the place' or 'so-and-so brought it to me.'" As for his statement, and the statement of others, that usage changed it to the meaning of compulsion, it requires transmission from the linguists who examined the usage of the Arabs. The form with the hamza signifies the general notion, so it is suitable for the meaning of compulsion and also for the meaning of choice, as when you say, "I made Zayd stand," where he may have chosen that, or you may have forced him to stand. As for his saying, "Do you not see that you do not say," to the end, whoever considers transitivization by the hamza to be analogical may permit it even without hearing it, while whoever does not consider it analogical has heard it in jā'a, since they said ajā'a, and so he permits it. As for his comparison of it to ātā, that comparison is not valid, because he based it on the claim that the hamza there is for transitivity and that its root is atā. This is not so. Rather, ātā is formed from afʿala and is not derived from atā with the meaning of jā'a, for if it were derived from atā, which is transitive to one object, then that object would be the second object and the agent the first when made transitive by hamza. You say atā al-māla Zaydan (the wealth came to Zayd), and ātā ʿAmrun Zaydan al-māla (ʿAmr gave Zayd the wealth), so the construction differs by transitivity, since according to the grammarians Zayd is the first object and the wealth is the second. By al-Zamakhshari's account, it would be the reverse, which shows that it is not as he said. Also, ātā is a synonym of aʿṭā (to give), so it differs in meaning. As for his saying, "You do not say ataytu al-makān wa-ātānīhi (I came to the place and he brought me to it)," this is not accepted. Rather, it is said: ataytu al-makān, just as you say ji'tu al-makān (I came to the place). The poet said:

*"They came to my fire, and I said, 'Who are you?' They said, 'Jinn.' I said, 'Be blind to the darkness.'"*

Whoever considers transmission by the hamza to be analogical says ātānīhi (he brought it to me).

The majority read ﴿fa-ajāʾahā﴾, meaning "drove her," that is, drove her toward it. The poet said:

*"And a traveler who went with confidence toward you, fear and hope drove him."*

Al-Aʿmash and Talha pronounced the fatha of the jim with imala (a vowel shift toward i). Hammad ibn Salama related from ʿAsim. Ibn ʿAtiyya said that Shubayl ibn ʿAzra read fājaʾahā, from al-mufājaʾa (suddenness). The author of al-Lawāmih (Abu al-Fath) said that Shubayl ibn ʿAzra read fājaʾahā. It was said: it is from al-mufājaʾa in the pattern fāʿila, and its hamza was replaced by an alif for lightness, contrary to analogy. It is also possible that it is a hamza between two vowels (bayna bayn), not inverted. It is related from Mujahid in the same way as Hammad's reading from ʿAsim. Ibn Kathir (the Qur'an reader), in one transmission, read al-makhāḍ with a kasra on the mim. It is said: makhadat al-ḥāmil makhāḍan wa-mikhāḍan, meaning the pregnant woman went into labour, and the child moved in her womb (tamakhkhada al-walad fī baṭnihā).

The word ﴿to﴾ (ilā) is connected to ﴿fa-ajāʾahā﴾. For the one who reads fājaʾahā from al-mufājaʾa, it is connected to an omitted element, meaning "leaning," that is, while she was leaning against the palm tree.

The widely known and famous report is that the birth of ʿIsa (peace be upon him) took place at Bayt Lahm, and that when she fled and feared for him, she hurried with him and came with him to Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), and she placed him on a rock, and the rock sank down for him and became like a cradle. It still exists today and is visited within the sanctuary of Bayt al-Maqdis. Then, after some days, she set out with him toward the River Jordan and baptized him in it. This is the day that the Christians observe and call the Day of Epiphany (Yawm al-Ghitas), and they think that the waters on that day become holy, which is why they immerse themselves in every water. Whoever claims that she bore him in Egypt says: in the district of Ahnas.

It was said: the palm tree of Maryam still stands to this day. The apparent meaning is that the palm tree existed before Maryam came to it. It was said: Allah caused a palm tree to grow for her, and she clung to it. It is related that she reached a place in which there was a dry, decayed palm trunk, its base rotted by worms, having no top, no fruit, and no greenery. The article al- in ﴿the trunk of the palm tree﴾ is either for the definition of the genus, or it is the one attached to names that are predominant, as if that desert had a well-known palm trunk, so when it is said ﴿the trunk of the palm tree﴾, that is understood from it and no other.

Allah the Exalted guided her to the palm tree so that she might feed herself from it with ripe dates, which are the nourishment of women after childbirth and suitable for her, and so that those signs manifested through it might settle her soul and comfort her eye. Then the matter grew severe for her there, and she embraced (p-183) the trunk because of the intensity of the pain, and she gave birth to ʿIsa (peace be upon him). At the time of her delivery, because of what she saw of the pains, the estrangement, the denial of her people, and the severity of the situation without any apparent cause, she said ﴿Oh, would that I had died before this﴾. Maryam wished for death from a religious standpoint, for she feared that evil would be attributed to her regarding her religion and that she would be reproached, which would harm her. This is permissible, and on this same basis ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab and a group of the righteous wished for death. As for the prohibition against it, it applies only to harm that befalls the body. There has been a disagreement among the readers about the vowel of the mim in mitu (I die), whether kasra or damma, which was discussed in Al ʿImran.

The nisy is a worthless thing that is of the kind that is forgotten and so is not grieved over when lost, like a peg, a rope for the traveler, or a rag used for menstruation. The majority read it with a kasra on the nun, and it is a verb in the sense of a passive object, like dhibh (what is slaughtered), that is, something that is fit to be slaughtered. Ibn Wathhab, Talha, al-Aʿmash, Ibn Abi Layla, Hamza and Hafs read it with a fatha on the nun. Muhammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazi read nisʾan with a kasra on the nun and a hamza in place of the ya', and this is the reading of Nawf al-Aʿrabi. Bakr ibn Habib al-Sahmi and Muhammad ibn Kaʿb also read nasaʾan with a fatha on the nun and a hamza. This is a verbal noun from nasaʾtu al-laban, when you pour water on milk, so the milk is consumed in it because of its small quantity. It is as though she wished she were like that milk which is not seen and is not distinguished from the water.

Ibn ʿAtiyya said: Bakr ibn Habib read nasan with a fatha on the nun and the sin, without hamza, formed on the pattern faʿal, like qabaḍ and nafaḍ. Al-Farra' said: nasy and nisy are two dialects, like al-watr and al-wathr, and the fatha is more beloved to me. Abu ʿAli al-Farisi said: the kasra is the higher of the two dialects. Ibn al-Anbari said: whoever uses the kasra means a noun for what is forgotten, like niqḍ (something that is undone) is a noun for what is unravelled, and whoever uses the fatha, it is a verbal noun standing in for a noun, as one says rajulun danafun and danifun (a sick man). The kasra is the attribute in its proper form, and the fatha is a verbal noun that takes the place of an attribute. It is possible that both have the same meaning, like raṭl and raṭl (a pound). The reference in His saying ﴿this﴾ is to the pregnancy.

It was said: ﴿before this﴾ refers to the day, or to ﴿before this﴾ matter that has happened. Al-Aʿmash and Abu Jaʿfar in one transmission read mansiyyan with a kasra on the mim, following the vowel of the sin, as they say muntin (stinking) with the mim vowel following the vowel of the ta'.

It was said: she wished for that because of the excess of shame that befell her, according to the custom of human nature, not out of aversion to the decree of Allah, or because of the severity of the burden upon her when they accused her while she knew of her innocence, and the opposite of what she was accused of, namely that Allah had singled her out with the utmost honour and generosity, because that is a slippery position on which feet rarely remain firm. Or because of her grief over the people, or because the people would be sinning because of her. It is related that she heard a call: "Come out, O you who are worshipped besides Allah!" So she grieved and said, ﴿Oh, would that I had died﴾. Wahb said: the distress of childbirth made her forget, and what she had heard from the people, the good news of the angels concerning ʿIsa.

Zirr and ʿAlqama read ﴿so she addressed him﴾ (fa-khāṭabahā) instead of ﴿so he called to her﴾ (fa-nādāhā). This should be taken as an explanation rather than a recitation, because it contradicts the consonantal text of the Mushaf, on which there is consensus. The one who called, apparently, was ʿIsa, meaning that she gave birth to him, and Allah made him speak and he called to her, that is, at the moment of delivery. It was said: it was Jibril, who was in a spot of the earth lower than the place where she was, and al-Hasan said this and swore to it. It was said: he used to receive the child like a midwife. Ibn ʿAbbas read ﴿a angel called to her from beneath her﴾ (malakun min taḥtihā). Al-Bara' ibn ʿAzib, Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, Zayd ibn ʿAli, al-Dahhak, ʿAmr ibn Maymun, Nafiʿ, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Hafs read min as a preposition. Ibn ʿĀmir, the two Ibn Kathirs, Abu ʿAmr (the two Abus), ʿAsim, Zirr, Mujahid, al-Jahdari, al-Hasan, and Ibn ʿAbbas in one transmission from him read man with a fatha on the mim, meaning "the one who," and taḥtahā is an adverbial accusative in the position of a relative complement to man, which is ʿIsa. That is, "the newborn called to her." This was said by Ubayy, al-Hasan, Ibn Jubayr and Mujahid. The an here is an explanatory particle, meaning ﴿do not grieve﴾. The sarī, according to the majority, is the stream. Al-Hasan, Ibn Zayd and Qatada said it means a great man of rank and standing. It is related that al-Hasan explained the verse and said: "Indeed, Allah made him a ﴿sarī﴾, noble." Humayd ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman said: "O Abu Saʿid, he only means by the sarī the stream." Al-Hasan said to this and similar things: "I love your nearness, but the rulers have overcome us."

Then He commanded her to shake the dry trunk of the palm tree, so that she might see another sign in the revival of the dead trunk. (p-184) Another group said: rather, the palm tree was grafted and bore ripe dates. As-Suddi said: the trunk had been cut down, and a river was made to flow beneath it at its side. The apparent meaning is that the one speaking was Jesus, and that the trunk was dry. On this basis, signs appeared to her that gave her comfort, and her sorrow was not due to the lack of food and drink, so that she might be consoled by eating and drinking, but rather because of the breach of custom that appeared in that matter, so that it would become clear to her people that her giving birth without a male was not a novelty in her case. Ibn 'Abbas said: it was a decayed trunk. When she shook it, the palm fronds had already sprouted; then she looked and saw the spathe emerging from between the fronds, then it turned green and became unripe dates, then it reddened and became ripe-yellow dates (zahw), then ripe dates (rutab), all of this in the twinkling of an eye, so that the ripe dates began to fall before her, and none of them was lost.

(Ila) is a particle without any disagreement, and it is connected to His words ﴿And shake﴾. This came contrary to what is established in the science of grammar, that the verb does not transitively reach an attached pronoun, and here it has put an attached pronoun in the nominative. It is not of the category of "zanna," "faqada," or "alima," and these (two) are for one meaning. One does not say: "darabtuka" (I struck you), nor "Zayd darabahu" (Zayd struck him), meaning he struck himself, nor "daraba-ni" (he struck me). In such constructions, one uses the reflexive noun: you say "darabta nafsaka" (you struck yourself), "Zayd daraba nafsahu" (Zayd struck himself), and "darabtu nafsi" (I struck myself). And the pronoun in the genitive, in their view, is like the pronoun in the accusative, so you do not say "hazaztu ilayka" (I shook toward you), nor "Zayd hazza ilayhi" (Zayd shook toward him), nor "hazazta ilayya" (you shook toward me). For this reason they claimed in the verse of the poet:

"So leave aside the plunder that was cried out about in its enclosures, but rather a tale of the riding-camels."

And in the verse of the other:

"Make light for yourself, for the affairs, the measures of them are in the hand of God."

'An and 'ala are not two particles; rather they are two adverbial nouns. This is not far-fetched, because 'an and 'ala have been established as nouns in the verse:

"From 'an the right of the wine-cup, a glance before..."

And in the verse:

"It went from 'alayhi after its thirst had been completed."

Some grammarians claimed that 'ala is never a particle at all, and that it is a noun in all its uses, and this was attributed to Sibawayh. But it cannot be claimed that (ila) is a noun, because of the consensus of the grammarians on its being a particle, as we have said. The parallel to His words, Exalted is He, ﴿And shake toward you﴾ is His words, Exalted is He, ﴿And draw your arm toward you﴾ [al-Qasas: 32]. On the basis of that rule, these two should be interpreted, and their interpretation is that His words "ilayki" are not connected to "hizzi" nor to "udmum," but rather that this is by way of explanation, and the sense is "I mean, toward you," so it is connected to an omitted element, as they said regarding His words ﴿Indeed, I am for you both among the sincere advisers﴾ [al-A'raf: 21] and what resembles it according to some interpretations. The "ba'" in ﴿bi-jidh'﴾ is extra, for emphasis, like His words ﴿And do not cast yourselves with your own hands into destruction﴾ [al-Baqarah: 195]. Abu 'Ali said: just as it is said "alqa bi-yadihi," meaning "alqa yadahu" (he cast his hand). And like the verse:

"Black-eyed, they do not recite with the suras."

That is, they do not recite the suras. Al-Tabari recited:

"In a valley of Yemen whose upper part grows the thorn-tree, and its lower part with the markh and shaban."

Al-Zamakhshari said: or the sense is "command her to shake with it," like the verse:

"It comes out in its hamstrings, my blade."

They said: dates for women in childbirth is a custom from that time, and likewise the tahnik (rubbing the newborn's palate). They said: it was from 'ajwa (a type of date), as said by Muhammad ibn Ka'b. It was said: nothing is better for women in childbirth than ripe dates.
