He was eloquent in truthfulness, because the essence of the matter of prophethood is truthfulness, and one who confirms Allah's signs and miracles is worthy of being so. This sentence came as a parenthetical insertion between the substituted noun and its substitute, namely (Abraham).

(Idh qāla) is like your saying: "I saw Zayd, an excellent man, your brother." It is permissible for (idh) to be connected to (kāna) or to "ṣiddīqan nabiyyan", meaning: he was combining the attributes of the truthful and the prophets at the time he addressed his father with those addresses. End.

The first analysis requires that (idh) be inflected, and it has previously been established for us that it is not inflected. The second analysis is based on the premise that the defective (kāna) and its sisters govern adverbials of time and place, which is a matter of disagreement. The third analysis is not valid, because government is attributed only to a single word, and it is not attributed to a compound of two words together. It is permissible for it to be an object of "ṣiddīqan" because it is an adjective, except according to the opinion of the Kufans. It may also be an object of "nabiyyan", meaning: he was informed at the time of his saying to his father what he said, and that the informing took place at that time—which is far-fetched.

Abū al-Birr Huthaym recited (innahu kāna ṣādiqan). In His saying "yā abati" there is gentleness and an appeal through kinship. Ibn ʿĀmir, al-Aʿraj and Abū Jaʿfar recited (yā abataa) with a fatḥa on the tāʾ, and Hārūn considered this reading erroneous. The discussion of (yā abati) has preceded in Sūrat Yūsuf, peace be upon him. In the codex of ʿAbdullāh it is "wā abatī" with a waw instead of a yāʾ. Abraham, peace be upon him, inquired about the cause that moved his father to worship the idol, although it lacks hearing, sight, and the ability to avail him anything, as a warning of the monstrousness of the opinion, its ugliness and corruption in worshipping one who lacks these attributes.

Al-Zamakhsharī spoke and said: Observe when he wanted to advise his father and admonish him regarding what he was entangled in of great error and shameful commission, in which he disobeyed the command of reason and departed from the requirement of discernment; how he arranged his speech with him in the finest coherence and presented it in the most graceful manner, while employing courtesy, gentleness, kindness, softness, fine manners, and good character, following in that the counsel of his Lord, majestic and exalted is He. Abū Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, related that he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Allah revealed to Abraham, peace be upon him: You are My friend (khalīl), improve your character even with the disbelievers, you will enter the entrances of the righteous. My word has preceded for the one whose character is good: I will shade him under My Throne and settle him in the enclosure of (p-194) holiness, and bring him close to My neighborhood.'" Al-Zamakhsharī, after this, narrated much speech of the oratorical kind, which we have left out.

Regarding ﴿mā lā yasmaʿu﴾: the apparent reading is that it is a relative pronoun, though they permitted it to be an indefinite qualified noun. The object of (yasmaʿu) and (yubṣiru) is omitted and not intended, meaning: that which has no hearing or sight, because the intent is to negate these two attributes without restriction to an object. (Shayʾan) is either a verbal noun or a direct object. When he asked him about the reason for worshipping the idol and he could not find an answer, he moved with him to inform him that knowledge had come to him which had not come to him, and he did not describe his father as ignorant, since the preceding question sufficed for that. He said "min al-ʿilm" for partitive sense, meaning: some of the knowledge that is not with you. This dialogue indicates that this was after he was made a prophet, since in the expression "jāʾanī" there is the renewal of knowledge. What came to him was either the revelation brought by the angel, or knowledge of the matters of the Hereafter and its reward and punishment, or the oneness of Allah and His being singled out for divinity and worship—three opinions. "Follow me" in the affirmation of Allah's unity in worship, and abandon the idols; "I will guide you to a straight path" which is faith in Allah and singling Him out in worship. He moved from commanding him to follow him to forbidding him from worshipping Satan; his worship of Satan being his obeying him in worshipping idols. Then he made him averse to worshipping Satan by saying that he was disobedient to the Most Merciful, since he disobeyed when commanded to prostrate to Adam and refused; so he is an enemy to you and to your father Adam from before. The word "al-Raḥmān" here serves as a reminder of the vastness of His mercy, and that one with this attribute is the one who deserves to be worshipped and not disobeyed; and it informs of Satan's wretchedness in that he disobeyed one with this attribute and committed what expelled him from this mercy. Even if he was choosing for himself disobedience to his Lord, he does not choose for his offspring anyone whom he disobeys for his sake, except what he chose for himself of their disobedience.

"Yā abati innī akhāfu": al-Farrāʾ and al-Ṭabarī said "akhāfu" means "aʿlamu" (I know), as in His saying: "so We feared that it would overwhelm them" [al-Kahf: 80], meaning: We were certain. The better course is to take "akhāfu" in its original meaning, because he was not despairing of his father's faith; rather he was hopeful for it and fearful that he would not believe and would persist in disbelief so that punishment would touch him. Abraham frightened him of the evil consequence and was courteous with him, since he did not explicitly state that punishment would befall him, but expressed it in the manner of one who fears; he used the word "touch" (masss), which is gentler than "punishment," and he left "punishment" indefinite, and he ordered upon the touch of punishment what is greater than it, namely the guardianship of Satan, just as He said in contrast to that: "and the good pleasure from Allah is greater" [al-Tawbah: 72], meaning: greater than the bliss previously mentioned. He began every piece of counsel with His saying "yā abati," seeking access to him and winning his sympathy.

It was said: guardianship here means being joined with him in the Hereafter, even if they hate each other and disavow one another. It was also said: there is inversion in the speech, and the meaning is: "Indeed I fear that you will be a guardian of Satan in this world, so a punishment from the Most Merciful will touch you in the Hereafter." His saying "an yamassaka ʿadhābun min al-Raḥmān" does not specify that the punishment occurs in the Hereafter; rather it may be understood as abandonment by Allah, so that he becomes a companion of Satan; it may also be that the touch of punishment occurs in this world, by his being tested in his disbelief with a punishment in this world, and that punishment becomes a cause for his persistence in disbelief and his arriving at the guardianship of Satan until he dies upon disbelief, as He said: "And We tested them with good things and bad things, that perhaps they would return" [al-Aʿrāf: 168]. These counsels indicate the intensity of his heart's attachment to treating his father and his eagerness for his guidance, fulfilling the right of fatherhood and guiding to the right path: "that Allah guides a single man through you is better for you than red camels."

(He said), that is, his father: "Do you turn away from my gods, O Abraham?" He asked with a question of denial. Turning away from something (rughbah ʿan al-shayʾ) is abandoning it deliberately; "his gods" are his idols. He was harsh with him in this denial and called him by his name, and did not match "yā abati" with "yā bunayya." Al-Zamakhsharī said: The predicate was placed before the subject in "Do you turn away from my gods," because it was more important to him, and it is what concerns him; and in it is a kind of wonder and denial at his turning away from his gods, and that his gods are not what anyone should turn away from. In this there is consolation and cooling of the chest of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) regarding what he suffered from similar treatment from the disbelievers of his people. End.

The preferred parsing of "a-rāghibun anta" is that "rāghib" is a subject (mubtadaʾ) because it relies on the interrogative particle, and "anta" is an agent that stands in place of the predicate. This is preferred over al-Zamakhsharī's parsing that "rāghib" is the predicate and "anta" the subject, for two reasons:

First: there would be no fronting or postponement, since the rank of the predicate is to come after the subject.

Second: there would be no separation between the operator, which is "rāghib," and its complement, which is "ʿan ālihatī," by something that is not a complement of the operator; because the predicate is not an operator on the subject, unlike "anta" being the agent, which is a complement of "rāghib." So "rāghib" and "ʿan ālihatī" are not separated by an alien element; rather it is separated by a complement of it.

When he denied to him his turning away from his gods, he threatened him, swearing to carry out what he threatened him with if he did not desist. The complement of "tantahi" is omitted; it may be that it means: from addressing me with what you addressed me with and calling me to it; and it may be that "la-in lam tantahi" means from turning away from my gods. "La-arjumannaka" is the answer to the omitted oath preceding "la-in." Al-Ḥasan said: with stones. It was said: "I will surely kill you." Al-Suddī, al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Ibn Jurayj said: "I will surely revile you."

Al-Zamakhsharī said: If you ask: upon what is "wa-ihjurnī" conjoined? I say: upon an omitted conjoined element indicated by "la-arjumannaka," meaning: "beware of me and abandon me," because "la-arjumannaka" is a threat and a rebuke. End. He needed the omission only to make the conjoined clauses and the clause conjoined to correspond; but this is not necessary according to Sībawayh, rather it is permissible to conjoin a declarative clause to an imperative clause. So "wa-ihjurnī" is conjoined to "la-in lam tantahi la-arjumannaka," and both are objects of "qāla."

"Malīyyan" is in the accusative as an adverb of time, meaning: a long period, as said by the majority, al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid and others. From it comes "al-malawān," which are the night and the day. "Al-mulāwah," with the vowel of the mīm in its three forms, is a long age, from the saying: "amlaytu li-fulān fī al-amr" when I prolonged it for him. The poet said:

"We lived in it through youth in a long span, and so the signs of the Messenger, the beloved, prevailed."

Sibawayh said: "A long time passed over him," meaning a lengthy period of time. Ibn Abbas and others said: "*maliyyan*" (﴿مَلِيًّا﴾) means "safe and sound," so it is a circumstantial accusative (*hal*) referring to the subject of ﴿واهْجُرْنِي﴾ ("and leave me"). Ibn Atiyya said: "The summary of this is that it means: relying on your state, independent of me, sufficient unto yourself." Al-Suddi said: "It means forever." From this is the verse of Muhalhil:

*So the solid mountains were split at his death,*
*And the widowed women wept over him long.*

Ibn Jubayr said: "It means a long time." The root meaning of the word is staying, as in the saying: "I stayed (*tamallaytu*) for a while." Al-Zamakhshari said: "Or ﴿maliyyan﴾ means: by going away from me and abandoning me before I wound you with beating so that you cannot move. One says: 'So-and-so is *maliyy* in such-and-such' when he is capable of it and equal to it." End of quote.

﴿قالَ سَلامٌ عَلَيْكَ﴾ ("He said: Peace be upon you"). Abu al-Birr Huthaym recited *salaman* with a fatha (accusative). The majority said: this carries the meaning of *musalama* (peaceful disengagement), not the meaning of greeting; that is, "a safe conduct from me to you." These scholars do not permit initiating the greeting of peace with a disbeliever. Al-Naqqash said: "It is a forbearing man addressing a foolish one, like His saying: ﴿وإذا خاطَبَهُمُ الجاهِلُونَ قالُوا سَلامًا﴾ ("When the ignorant address them, they say, 'Peace'") [al-Furqan: 63]." It was also said: "It is the greeting of one who parts ways." The proponent of this view permitted greeting a disbeliever and beginning with the legislated greeting of peace. This is the view of Sufyan ibn Uyayna, relying on His saying: ﴿لا يَنْهاكُمُ اللَّهُ عَنِ الَّذِينَ لَمْ يُقاتِلُوكُمْ﴾ ("God does not forbid you from those who do not fight you") [al-Mumtahana: 8], up to the end of the verse, and on His saying: ﴿قَدْ كانَتْ لَكم أُسْوَةٌ حَسَنَةٌ في إبْراهِيمَ﴾ ("There has been for you an excellent example in Abraham") [al-Mumtahana: 4], up to the end of the verse.

Abraham *said* to his father ﴿سَلامٌ عَلَيْكَ﴾, and what they cited as evidence is interpreted (*mutawwal*), and their position is refuted by what is established in Sahih Muslim: "Do not begin the Jews and the Christians with the greeting of peace." The nominative *salamun* (سَلامٌ) is the subject of a nominal clause, and the accusative *salaman* (سَلامًا) is a verbal noun, meaning: "I greeted with a greeting," as a supplication for him for safety, in the manner of winning him over. Then he promised him *istighfar* (seeking forgiveness). That is conditional upon the presence of what makes *istighfar* possible, which is faith in God and devoting worship to Him alone. This is like how a command and a prohibition are addressed to a disbeliever, yet compliance is not valid except with the condition of faith. The meaning of ﴿سَأسْتَغْفِرُ لَكَ﴾ ("I will ask forgiveness for you") is: "I will call upon God regarding your guidance, and He will forgive you through faith." It is not to be interpreted about Abraham, peace be upon him, that he did not know that God does not forgive a disbeliever. Ibn Atiyya said: "It is possible that Abraham, peace be upon him, was the first prophet to whom it was revealed that God does not forgive a disbeliever, because this matter is known only through revelation. This statement was made by him to his father before it was revealed to him. That is because it became clear to him regarding his father that he was an enemy of God in one of two ways: either by his dying in disbelief, as has been narrated, or by a decisive revelation to him (about this)."

Al-Zamakhshari said: "One may say: what prevents seeking forgiveness for a disbeliever is only revelation. As for the rational principle, it does not reject it. So it is permissible that the promise of seeking forgiveness, and its fulfillment, occurred before revelation came, based on the rational principle. What indicates its validity is His saying: ﴿إلّا قَوْلَ إبْراهِيمَ لِأبِيهِ لَأسْتَغْفِرَنَّ لَكَ﴾ ("except for the saying of Abraham to his father: 'I will surely ask forgiveness for you'") [al-Mumtahana: 4]. Had it been conditional upon faith, it would not have been something disapproved of and excepted from what was obligatory in it." As for the view of one who said: "He sought forgiveness for him only because he promised him that he would believe," citing His saying: ﴿إلّا عَنْ مَوْعِدَةٍ وعَدَها إيّاهُ﴾ ("except for a promise he had made to him") [al-Tawba: 114], making the promiser Azar and the promised Abraham, peace be upon him, this is not sound, because in this verse the promise of seeking forgiveness comes after that harsh statement of his: ﴿لَئِنْ لَمْ تَنْتَهِ﴾ ("If you do not desist"), up to the end of the verse. So how could his promise be one of faith? Also, the one who promised is Abraham, and this is indicated by the reading of Hammad which narrates: (*wa'adaha iyyahu*) (وعَدَها إيّاهُ) ("he had made to her/it").

*Al-hafiyy* (الحَفِيُّ) means the one who honors, is attentive, and is greatly kind and gentle. Its linguistic explanation was given earlier in His saying: ﴿كَأنَّكَ حَفِيٌّ عَنْها﴾ ("as if you were well-informed about it") [al-A'raf: 187]. Ibn Abbas said: "Merciful." Al-Kalbi said: "Forbearing." Al-Qutaybi said: "Dutiful." Al-Suddi said: "Your *hafiyy* is one whose concern is your affair." Since in His saying ﴿لَأرْجُمَنَّكَ﴾ ("I will surely stone you") there is harshness and hardness of heart, Abraham met it with supplication for his peace and safety, and he promised him forgiveness, fulfilling the right of fatherhood, even though harshness had come from him.

When He commanded him to abandon him for a long time, He informed him that he would carry out His command and withdraw from him, his people, and what they worshipped. So he emigrated to Syria, it was said, or to Harran, and they were in the land of Kawtha. During this emigration he married Sarah and met the tyrant who gave Hajar to serve Sarah. The more apparent view is that His saying ﴿وأدْعُو رَبِّي﴾ ("and I will call upon my Lord") means "and I will worship my Lord," as in the hadith: "Supplication is worship," in accordance with His saying: ﴿فَلَمّا اعْتَزَلَهم وما يَعْبُدُونَ مِن دُونِ اللَّهِ﴾ ("So when he had withdrawn from them and what they worshipped other than God"). It is also permissible that what is meant is the supplication recounted by God in Surat al-Shu'ara': ﴿رَبِّ هَبْ لِي حُكْمًا﴾ ("My Lord, grant me wisdom") [al-Shu'ara': 83], and so on to the end. He hinted at their wretchedness by calling upon their gods in His saying: ﴿عَسى ألّا أكُونَ بِدُعاءِ رَبِّي شَقِيًّا﴾ ("Perhaps I shall not be, in my supplication to my Lord, unfortunate"), together with humility before God in the word *'asa* ("perhaps") and what it contains of self-abasement. In *'asa* there is hope which, within it, contains intense fear.

When he parted from the disbelievers and their land, God replaced them for him with prophetic offspring and the Holy Land, so he dwelt there, and he would travel to Mecca. Then Ishaq was born to him, and his son Ya'qub, as consolation for him and strengthening of his arm. Ishaq was younger than Isma'il. When Hajar bore Isma'il, Sarah became jealous, then she conceived Ishaq.

As for His saying ﴿مِن رَحْمَتِنا﴾ ("from Our mercy") [Maryam: 53]: al-Hasan said: "It is prophethood." al-Kalbi said: "Wealth and children." The best view is that it includes religious and worldly good, such as knowledge, status, and honor in this world, and bliss in the Hereafter.

*Lisan sidq* (لِسانَ صِدْقٍ) is the good and enduring praise upon them until the end of time, as said by Ibn Abbas. He expressed it by "tongue," just as one expresses by "hand" what is meant by "hand," which is giving. In the speech of the Arabs, *lisan* means a fine message, whether it was for good or for evil. A poet said:

*A message (lisan) came to me that does not please me with it.*

And another said:

*I regretted a word (lisan) that came from me.*

*Lisan al-'Arab* is their language and their speech. God answered his supplication: ﴿واجْعَلْ لِي لِسانَ صِدْقٍ في الآخِرِينَ﴾ ("and make for me a tongue of truthfulness among the later generations") [al-Shu'ara': 84], so He made him an exemplar until all the religious communities exalted him and claimed him. He said: ﴿مِلَّةَ أبِيكم إبْراهِيمَ﴾ ("the creed of your father Abraham") [al-Hajj: 78], and ﴿مِلَّةَ إبْراهِيمَ حَنِيفًا﴾ ("the creed of Abraham, a *hanif*") [al-Baqara: 135], and ﴿ثُمَّ أوْحَيْنا إلَيْكَ أنِ اتَّبِعْ مِلَّةَ إبْراهِيمَ حَنِيفًا﴾ ("Then We revealed to you: follow the creed of Abraham, a *hanif*") [al-Nahl: 123]. He gave that to his offspring, so He raised their remembrance and praised them, just as He raised his remembrance and praised him.

(p-196)

(p-192) ﴿And mention in the Book Abraham. Indeed, he was a man of truth, a prophet.﴾ ﴿When he said to his father, "O my father, why do you worship that which hears not, nor sees, nor can avail you anything?"﴾ ﴿"O my father, indeed there has come to me of knowledge that which has not come to you, so follow me; I will guide you to a straight path."﴾ ﴿"O my father, do not worship Satan. Indeed, Satan has been to the Most Merciful a disobedient one."﴾ ﴿"O my father, indeed I fear that a punishment from the Most Merciful will touch you, so you would be a companion to Satan."﴾ ﴿He said, "Do you turn away from my gods, O Abraham? If you do not desist, I will surely stone you, so leave me for a long time."﴾ ﴿He said, "Peace be upon you. I will ask forgiveness for you from my Lord. Indeed, He has been ever gracious to me."﴾ ﴿"And I will separate myself from you and what you invoke other than Allah, and I will call upon my Lord; perhaps I will not be in my supplication to my Lord unfortunate."﴾ ﴿So when he had separated himself from them and what they worshipped other than Allah, We gave him Isaac and Jacob, and each We made a prophet.﴾ ﴿And We gave them of Our mercy, and We made for them a tongue of truthfulness, high and exalted.﴾.

(p-193) "And mention" is an address to the Messenger (ﷺ), and the intended meaning is: recite to them the account of (Abraham). The one who mentions it and conveys it in the revelation is Allah, exalted is He. The connection of this verse with what precedes it is that when Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the story of Mary and her son Jesus, and the disagreement of the factions concerning them and their worship besides Allah, and they were among those whom life had sustained, He mentioned the misguided group who worshipped an inanimate object. The two groups, although they share in misguidance, the group worshipping the inanimate object is more astray. Then He mentioned the story of Abraham with his father, peace be upon him, as a reminder to the Arabs of what Abraham had of the monotheism of Allah, and to make clear that they follow a path other than his. In it is also the truthfulness of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in what he reported, and that this is received through revelation.

"Ṣiddīq" is from the forms of intensification; it is derived from the triliteral for emphasis, meaning one who is abundantly truthful. Truthfulness (ṣidq) in common usage is opposed to lying, and it may be used of actions, character, and inanimate things. It is said: "ṣadaqanī al-ṭaʿām kadhā wa-kadhā qafīzan" (the food gave me so-and-so many qafīz), and "ʿūdun ṣidqun" for a good solid piece of wood. Thus Abraham is described as truthful in general, in his sayings and his deeds. The state of being a ṣiddīq has degrees; do you not see the description of believers with it in His saying: "of the prophets and the truthful (ṣiddīqīn)" [al-Nisāʾ: 69]? Among the strange reports is what some grammarians held: that when fiʿʿīl is derived from a transitive verb, it may govern, so one says "hādhā shirrībun muskirun" (this is a drinker of an intoxicant), just as the Basrans made faʿūl, faʿʿāl and mif'āl govern.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: The intended meaning is the excess of his truthfulness and the abundance of what he affirmed of the unseen matters of Allah, His signs, His books and His messengers, and the predominance and prevalence lay in this affirming of the books and messengers, that is, he was one who confirmed all the prophets and their books. He was a prophet in himself, based on His saying, exalted is He: "Rather, he brought the truth and confirmed the messengers" [al-Ṣāffāt: 37]. He was eloquent in truthfulness, because the essence of the matter of prophethood is truthfulness, and one who confirms Allah's signs and miracles is worthy of being so. This sentence came as a parenthetical insertion between the substituted noun and its substitute, namely (Abraham).

(Idh qāla) is like your saying: "I saw Zayd, an excellent man, your brother." It is permissible for (idh) to be connected to (kāna) or to "ṣiddīqan nabiyyan", meaning: he was combining the attributes of the truthful and the prophets at the time he addressed his father with those addresses. End.

The first analysis requires that (idh) be inflected, and it has previously been established for us that it is not inflected. The second analysis is based on the premise that the defective (kāna) and its sisters govern adverbials of time and place, which is a matter of disagreement. The third analysis is not valid, because government is attributed only to a single word, and it is not attributed to a compound of two words together. It is permissible for it to be an object of "ṣiddīqan" because it is an adjective, except according to the opinion of the Kufans. It may also be an object of "nabiyyan", meaning: he was informed at the time of his saying to his father what he said, and that the informing took place at that time—which is far-fetched.

Abū al-Birr Huthaym recited (innahu kāna ṣādiqan). In His saying "yā abati" there is gentleness and an appeal through kinship. Ibn ʿĀmir, al-Aʿraj and Abū Jaʿfar recited (yā abataa) with a fatḥa on the tāʾ, and Hārūn considered this reading erroneous. The discussion of (yā abati) has preceded in Sūrat Yūsuf, peace be upon him. In the codex of ʿAbdullāh it is "wā abatī" with a waw instead of a yāʾ. Abraham, peace be upon him, inquired about the cause that moved his father to worship the idol, although it lacks hearing, sight, and the ability to avail him anything, as a warning of the monstrousness of the opinion, its ugliness and corruption in worshipping one who lacks these attributes.

Al-Zamakhsharī spoke and said: Observe when he wanted to advise his father and admonish him regarding what he was entangled in of great error and shameful commission, in which he disobeyed the command of reason and departed from the requirement of discernment; how he arranged his speech with him in the finest coherence and presented it in the most graceful manner, while employing courtesy, gentleness, kindness, softness, fine manners, and good character, following in that the counsel of his Lord, majestic and exalted is He. Abū Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, related that he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Allah revealed to Abraham, peace be upon him: You are My friend (khalīl), improve your character even with the disbelievers, you will enter the entrances of the righteous. My word has preceded for the one whose character is good: I will shade him under My Throne and settle him in the enclosure of (p-194) holiness, and bring him close to My neighborhood.'" Al-Zamakhsharī, after this, narrated much speech of the oratorical kind, which we have left out.

Regarding ﴿mā lā yasmaʿu﴾: the apparent reading is that it is a relative pronoun, though they permitted it to be an indefinite qualified noun. The object of (yasmaʿu) and (yubṣiru) is omitted and not intended, meaning: that which has no hearing or sight, because the intent is to negate these two attributes without restriction to an object. (Shayʾan) is either a verbal noun or a direct object. When he asked him about the reason for worshipping the idol and he could not find an answer, he moved with him to inform him that knowledge had come to him which had not come to him, and he did not describe his father as ignorant, since the preceding question sufficed for that. He said "min al-ʿilm" for partitive sense, meaning: some of the knowledge that is not with you. This dialogue indicates that this was after he was made a prophet, since in the expression "jāʾanī" there is the renewal of knowledge. What came to him was either the revelation brought by the angel, or knowledge of the matters of the Hereafter and its reward and punishment, or the oneness of Allah and His being singled out for divinity and worship—three opinions. "Follow me" in the affirmation of Allah's unity in worship, and abandon the idols; "I will guide you to a straight path" which is faith in Allah and singling Him out in worship. He moved from commanding him to follow him to forbidding him from worshipping Satan; his worship of Satan being his obeying him in worshipping idols. Then he made him averse to worshipping Satan by saying that he was disobedient to the Most Merciful, since he disobeyed when commanded to prostrate to Adam and refused; so he is an enemy to you and to your father Adam from before. The word "al-Raḥmān" here serves as a reminder of the vastness of His mercy, and that one with this attribute is the one who deserves to be worshipped and not disobeyed; and it informs of Satan's wretchedness in that he disobeyed one with this attribute and committed what expelled him from this mercy. Even if he was choosing for himself disobedience to his Lord, he does not choose for his offspring anyone whom he disobeys for his sake, except what he chose for himself of their disobedience.

"Yā abati innī akhāfu": al-Farrāʾ and al-Ṭabarī said "akhāfu" means "aʿlamu" (I know), as in His saying: "so We feared that it would overwhelm them" [al-Kahf: 80], meaning: We were certain. The better course is to take "akhāfu" in its original meaning, because he was not despairing of his father's faith; rather he was hopeful for it and fearful that he would not believe and would persist in disbelief so that punishment would touch him. Abraham frightened him of the evil consequence and was courteous with him, since he did not explicitly state that punishment would befall him, but expressed it in the manner of one who fears; he used the word "touch" (masss), which is gentler than "punishment," and he left "punishment" indefinite, and he ordered upon the touch of punishment what is greater than it, namely the guardianship of Satan, just as He said in contrast to that: "and the good pleasure from Allah is greater" [al-Tawbah: 72], meaning: greater than the bliss previously mentioned. He began every piece of counsel with His saying "yā abati," seeking access to him and winning his sympathy.

It was said: guardianship here means being joined with him in the Hereafter, even if they hate each other and disavow one another. It was also said: there is inversion in the speech, and the meaning is: "Indeed I fear that you will be a guardian of Satan in this world, so a punishment from the Most Merciful will touch you in the Hereafter." His saying "an yamassaka ʿadhābun min al-Raḥmān" does not specify that the punishment occurs in the Hereafter; rather it may be understood as abandonment by Allah, so that he becomes a companion of Satan; it may also be that the touch of punishment occurs in this world, by his being tested in his disbelief with a punishment in this world, and that punishment becomes a cause for his persistence in disbelief and his arriving at the guardianship of Satan until he dies upon disbelief, as He said: "And We tested them with good things and bad things, that perhaps they would return" [al-Aʿrāf: 168]. These counsels indicate the intensity of his heart's attachment to treating his father and his eagerness for his guidance, fulfilling the right of fatherhood and guiding to the right path: "that Allah guides a single man through you is better for you than red camels."

(He said), that is, his father: "Do you turn away from my gods, O Abraham?" He asked with a question of denial. Turning away from something (rughbah ʿan al-shayʾ) is abandoning it deliberately; "his gods" are his idols. He was harsh with him in this denial and called him by his name, and did not match "yā abati" with "yā bunayya." Al-Zamakhsharī said: The predicate was placed before the subject in "Do you turn away from my gods," because it was more important to him, and it is what concerns him; and in it is a kind of wonder and denial at his turning away from his gods, and that his gods are not what anyone should turn away from. In this there is consolation and cooling of the chest of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) regarding what he suffered from similar treatment from the disbelievers of his people. End.

The preferred parsing of "a-rāghibun anta" is that "rāghib" is a subject (mubtadaʾ) because it relies on the interrogative particle, and "anta" is an agent that stands in place of the predicate. This is preferred over al-Zamakhsharī's parsing that "rāghib" is the predicate and "anta" the subject, for two reasons:

First: there would be no fronting or postponement, since the rank of the predicate is to come after the subject.

Second: there would be no separation between the operator, which is "rāghib," and its complement, which is "ʿan ālihatī," by something that is not a complement of the operator; because the predicate is not an operator on the subject, unlike "anta" being the agent, which is a complement of "rāghib." So "rāghib" and "ʿan ālihatī" are not separated by an alien element; rather it is separated by a complement of it.

When he denied to him his turning away from his gods, he threatened him, swearing to carry out what he threatened him with if he did not desist. The complement of "tantahi" is omitted; it may be that it means: from addressing me with what you addressed me with and calling me to it; and it may be that "la-in lam tantahi" means from turning away from my gods. "La-arjumannaka" is the answer to the omitted oath preceding "la-in." Al-Ḥasan said: with stones. It was said: "I will surely kill you." Al-Suddī, al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Ibn Jurayj said: "I will surely revile you."

Al-Zamakhsharī said: If you ask: upon what is "wa-ihjurnī" conjoined? I say: upon an omitted conjoined element indicated by "la-arjumannaka," meaning: "beware of me and abandon me," because "la-arjumannaka" is a threat and a rebuke. End. He needed the omission only to make the conjoined clauses and the clause conjoined to correspond; but this is not necessary according to Sībawayh, rather it is permissible to conjoin a declarative clause to an imperative clause. So "wa-ihjurnī" is conjoined to "la-in lam tantahi la-arjumannaka," and both are objects of "qāla."

"Malīyyan" is in the accusative as an adverb of time, meaning: a long period, as said by the majority, al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid and others. From it comes "al-malawān," which are the night and the day. "Al-mulāwah," with the vowel of the mīm in its three forms, is a long age, from the saying: "amlaytu li-fulān fī al-amr" when I prolonged it for him. The poet said:

"We lived in it through youth in a long span, and so the signs of the Messenger, the beloved, prevailed."

Sibawayh said: "A long time passed over him," meaning a lengthy period of time. Ibn Abbas and others said: "*maliyyan*" (﴿مَلِيًّا﴾) means "safe and sound," so it is a circumstantial accusative (*hal*) referring to the subject of ﴿واهْجُرْنِي﴾ ("and leave me"). Ibn Atiyya said: "The summary of this is that it means: relying on your state, independent of me, sufficient unto yourself." Al-Suddi said: "It means forever." From this is the verse of Muhalhil:

*So the solid mountains were split at his death,*
*And the widowed women wept over him long.*

Ibn Jubayr said: "It means a long time." The root meaning of the word is staying, as in the saying: "I stayed (*tamallaytu*) for a while." Al-Zamakhshari said: "Or ﴿maliyyan﴾ means: by going away from me and abandoning me before I wound you with beating so that you cannot move. One says: 'So-and-so is *maliyy* in such-and-such' when he is capable of it and equal to it." End of quote.

﴿قالَ سَلامٌ عَلَيْكَ﴾ ("He said: Peace be upon you"). Abu al-Birr Huthaym recited *salaman* with a fatha (accusative). The majority said: this carries the meaning of *musalama* (peaceful disengagement), not the meaning of greeting; that is, "a safe conduct from me to you." These scholars do not permit initiating the greeting of peace with a disbeliever. Al-Naqqash said: "It is a forbearing man addressing a foolish one, like His saying: ﴿وإذا خاطَبَهُمُ الجاهِلُونَ قالُوا سَلامًا﴾ ("When the ignorant address them, they say, 'Peace'") [al-Furqan: 63]." It was also said: "It is the greeting of one who parts ways." The proponent of this view permitted greeting a disbeliever and beginning with the legislated greeting of peace. This is the view of Sufyan ibn Uyayna, relying on His saying: ﴿لا يَنْهاكُمُ اللَّهُ عَنِ الَّذِينَ لَمْ يُقاتِلُوكُمْ﴾ ("God does not forbid you from those who do not fight you") [al-Mumtahana: 8], up to the end of the verse, and on His saying: ﴿قَدْ كانَتْ لَكم أُسْوَةٌ حَسَنَةٌ في إبْراهِيمَ﴾ ("There has been for you an excellent example in Abraham") [al-Mumtahana: 4], up to the end of the verse.

Abraham *said* to his father ﴿سَلامٌ عَلَيْكَ﴾, and what they cited as evidence is interpreted (*mutawwal*), and their position is refuted by what is established in Sahih Muslim: "Do not begin the Jews and the Christians with the greeting of peace." The nominative *salamun* (سَلامٌ) is the subject of a nominal clause, and the accusative *salaman* (سَلامًا) is a verbal noun, meaning: "I greeted with a greeting," as a supplication for him for safety, in the manner of winning him over. Then he promised him *istighfar* (seeking forgiveness). That is conditional upon the presence of what makes *istighfar* possible, which is faith in God and devoting worship to Him alone. This is like how a command and a prohibition are addressed to a disbeliever, yet compliance is not valid except with the condition of faith. The meaning of ﴿سَأسْتَغْفِرُ لَكَ﴾ ("I will ask forgiveness for you") is: "I will call upon God regarding your guidance, and He will forgive you through faith." It is not to be interpreted about Abraham, peace be upon him, that he did not know that God does not forgive a disbeliever. Ibn Atiyya said: "It is possible that Abraham, peace be upon him, was the first prophet to whom it was revealed that God does not forgive a disbeliever, because this matter is known only through revelation. This statement was made by him to his father before it was revealed to him. That is because it became clear to him regarding his father that he was an enemy of God in one of two ways: either by his dying in disbelief, as has been narrated, or by a decisive revelation to him (about this)."

Al-Zamakhshari said: "One may say: what prevents seeking forgiveness for a disbeliever is only revelation. As for the rational principle, it does not reject it. So it is permissible that the promise of seeking forgiveness, and its fulfillment, occurred before revelation came, based on the rational principle. What indicates its validity is His saying: ﴿إلّا قَوْلَ إبْراهِيمَ لِأبِيهِ لَأسْتَغْفِرَنَّ لَكَ﴾ ("except for the saying of Abraham to his father: 'I will surely ask forgiveness for you'") [al-Mumtahana: 4]. Had it been conditional upon faith, it would not have been something disapproved of and excepted from what was obligatory in it." As for the view of one who said: "He sought forgiveness for him only because he promised him that he would believe," citing His saying: ﴿إلّا عَنْ مَوْعِدَةٍ وعَدَها إيّاهُ﴾ ("except for a promise he had made to him") [al-Tawba: 114], making the promiser Azar and the promised Abraham, peace be upon him, this is not sound, because in this verse the promise of seeking forgiveness comes after that harsh statement of his: ﴿لَئِنْ لَمْ تَنْتَهِ﴾ ("If you do not desist"), up to the end of the verse. So how could his promise be one of faith? Also, the one who promised is Abraham, and this is indicated by the reading of Hammad which narrates: (*wa'adaha iyyahu*) (وعَدَها إيّاهُ) ("he had made to her/it").

*Al-hafiyy* (الحَفِيُّ) means the one who honors, is attentive, and is greatly kind and gentle. Its linguistic explanation was given earlier in His saying: ﴿كَأنَّكَ حَفِيٌّ عَنْها﴾ ("as if you were well-informed about it") [al-A'raf: 187]. Ibn Abbas said: "Merciful." Al-Kalbi said: "Forbearing." Al-Qutaybi said: "Dutiful." Al-Suddi said: "Your *hafiyy* is one whose concern is your affair." Since in His saying ﴿لَأرْجُمَنَّكَ﴾ ("I will surely stone you") there is harshness and hardness of heart, Abraham met it with supplication for his peace and safety, and he promised him forgiveness, fulfilling the right of fatherhood, even though harshness had come from him.

When He commanded him to abandon him for a long time, He informed him that he would carry out His command and withdraw from him, his people, and what they worshipped. So he emigrated to Syria, it was said, or to Harran, and they were in the land of Kawtha. During this emigration he married Sarah and met the tyrant who gave Hajar to serve Sarah. The more apparent view is that His saying ﴿وأدْعُو رَبِّي﴾ ("and I will call upon my Lord") means "and I will worship my Lord," as in the hadith: "Supplication is worship," in accordance with His saying: ﴿فَلَمّا اعْتَزَلَهم وما يَعْبُدُونَ مِن دُونِ اللَّهِ﴾ ("So when he had withdrawn from them and what they worshipped other than God"). It is also permissible that what is meant is the supplication recounted by God in Surat al-Shu'ara': ﴿رَبِّ هَبْ لِي حُكْمًا﴾ ("My Lord, grant me wisdom") [al-Shu'ara': 83], and so on to the end. He hinted at their wretchedness by calling upon their gods in His saying: ﴿عَسى ألّا أكُونَ بِدُعاءِ رَبِّي شَقِيًّا﴾ ("Perhaps I shall not be, in my supplication to my Lord, unfortunate"), together with humility before God in the word *'asa* ("perhaps") and what it contains of self-abasement. In *'asa* there is hope which, within it, contains intense fear.

When he parted from the disbelievers and their land, God replaced them for him with prophetic offspring and the Holy Land, so he dwelt there, and he would travel to Mecca. Then Ishaq was born to him, and his son Ya'qub, as consolation for him and strengthening of his arm. Ishaq was younger than Isma'il. When Hajar bore Isma'il, Sarah became jealous, then she conceived Ishaq.

As for His saying ﴿مِن رَحْمَتِنا﴾ ("from Our mercy") [Maryam: 53]: al-Hasan said: "It is prophethood." al-Kalbi said: "Wealth and children." The best view is that it includes religious and worldly good, such as knowledge, status, and honor in this world, and bliss in the Hereafter.

*Lisan sidq* (لِسانَ صِدْقٍ) is the good and enduring praise upon them until the end of time, as said by Ibn Abbas. He expressed it by "tongue," just as one expresses by "hand" what is meant by "hand," which is giving. In the speech of the Arabs, *lisan* means a fine message, whether it was for good or for evil. A poet said:

*A message (lisan) came to me that does not please me with it.*

And another said:

*I regretted a word (lisan) that came from me.*

*Lisan al-'Arab* is their language and their speech. God answered his supplication: ﴿واجْعَلْ لِي لِسانَ صِدْقٍ في الآخِرِينَ﴾ ("and make for me a tongue of truthfulness among the later generations") [al-Shu'ara': 84], so He made him an exemplar until all the religious communities exalted him and claimed him. He said: ﴿مِلَّةَ أبِيكم إبْراهِيمَ﴾ ("the creed of your father Abraham") [al-Hajj: 78], and ﴿مِلَّةَ إبْراهِيمَ حَنِيفًا﴾ ("the creed of Abraham, a *hanif*") [al-Baqara: 135], and ﴿ثُمَّ أوْحَيْنا إلَيْكَ أنِ اتَّبِعْ مِلَّةَ إبْراهِيمَ حَنِيفًا﴾ ("Then We revealed to you: follow the creed of Abraham, a *hanif*") [al-Nahl: 123]. He gave that to his offspring, so He raised their remembrance and praised them, just as He raised his remembrance and praised him.

(p-196)

(p-192) ﴿And mention in the Book Abraham. Indeed, he was a man of truth, a prophet.﴾ ﴿When he said to his father, "O my father, why do you worship that which hears not, nor sees, nor can avail you anything?"﴾ ﴿"O my father, indeed there has come to me of knowledge that which has not come to you, so follow me; I will guide you to a straight path."﴾ ﴿"O my father, do not worship Satan. Indeed, Satan has been to the Most Merciful a disobedient one."﴾ ﴿"O my father, indeed I fear that a punishment from the Most Merciful will touch you, so you would be a companion to Satan."﴾ ﴿He said, "Do you turn away from my gods, O Abraham? If you do not desist, I will surely stone you, so leave me for a long time."﴾ ﴿He said, "Peace be upon you. I will ask forgiveness for you from my Lord. Indeed, He has been ever gracious to me."﴾ ﴿"And I will separate myself from you and what you invoke other than Allah, and I will call upon my Lord; perhaps I will not be in my supplication to my Lord unfortunate."﴾ ﴿So when he had separated himself from them and what they worshipped other than Allah, We gave him Isaac and Jacob, and each We made a prophet.﴾ ﴿And We gave them of Our mercy, and We made for them a tongue of truthfulness, high and exalted.﴾.

(p-193) "And mention" is an address to the Messenger (ﷺ), and the intended meaning is: recite to them the account of (Abraham). The one who mentions it and conveys it in the revelation is Allah, exalted is He. The connection of this verse with what precedes it is that when Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the story of Mary and her son Jesus, and the disagreement of the factions concerning them and their worship besides Allah, and they were among those whom life had sustained, He mentioned the misguided group who worshipped an inanimate object. The two groups, although they share in misguidance, the group worshipping the inanimate object is more astray. Then He mentioned the story of Abraham with his father, peace be upon him, as a reminder to the Arabs of what Abraham had of the monotheism of Allah, and to make clear that they follow a path other than his. In it is also the truthfulness of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in what he reported, and that this is received through revelation.

"Ṣiddīq" is from the forms of intensification; it is derived from the triliteral for emphasis, meaning one who is abundantly truthful. Truthfulness (ṣidq) in common usage is opposed to lying, and it may be used of actions, character, and inanimate things. It is said: "ṣadaqanī al-ṭaʿām kadhā wa-kadhā qafīzan" (the food gave me so-and-so many qafīz), and "ʿūdun ṣidqun" for a good solid piece of wood. Thus Abraham is described as truthful in general, in his sayings and his deeds. The state of being a ṣiddīq has degrees; do you not see the description of believers with it in His saying: "of the prophets and the truthful (ṣiddīqīn)" [al-Nisāʾ: 69]? Among the strange reports is what some grammarians held: that when fiʿʿīl is derived from a transitive verb, it may govern, so one says "hādhā shirrībun muskirun" (this is a drinker of an intoxicant), just as the Basrans made faʿūl, faʿʿāl and mif'āl govern.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: The intended meaning is the excess of his truthfulness and the abundance of what he affirmed of the unseen matters of Allah, His signs, His books and His messengers, and the predominance and prevalence lay in this affirming of the books and messengers, that is, he was one who confirmed all the prophets and their books. He was a prophet in himself, based on His saying, exalted is He: "Rather, he brought the truth and confirmed the messengers" [al-Ṣāffāt: 37]. He was eloquent in truthfulness, because the essence of the matter of prophethood is truthfulness, and one who confirms Allah's signs and miracles is worthy of being so. This sentence came as a parenthetical insertion between the substituted noun and its substitute, namely (Abraham).

(Idh qāla) is like your saying: "I saw Zayd, an excellent man, your brother." It is permissible for (idh) to be connected to (kāna) or to "ṣiddīqan nabiyyan", meaning: he was combining the attributes of the truthful and the prophets at the time he addressed his father with those addresses. End.

The first analysis requires that (idh) be inflected, and it has previously been established for us that it is not inflected. The second analysis is based on the premise that the defective (kāna) and its sisters govern adverbials of time and place, which is a matter of disagreement. The third analysis is not valid, because government is attributed only to a single word, and it is not attributed to a compound of two words together. It is permissible for it to be an object of "ṣiddīqan" because it is an adjective, except according to the opinion of the Kufans. It may also be an object of "nabiyyan", meaning: he was informed at the time of his saying to his father what he said, and that the informing took place at that time—which is far-fetched.

Abū al-Birr Huthaym recited (innahu kāna ṣādiqan). In His saying "yā abati" there is gentleness and an appeal through kinship. Ibn ʿĀmir, al-Aʿraj and Abū Jaʿfar recited (yā abataa) with a fatḥa on the tāʾ, and Hārūn considered this reading erroneous. The discussion of (yā abati) has preceded in Sūrat Yūsuf, peace be upon him. In the codex of ʿAbdullāh it is "wā abatī" with a waw instead of a yāʾ. Abraham, peace be upon him, inquired about the cause that moved his father to worship the idol, although it lacks hearing, sight, and the ability to avail him anything, as a warning of the monstrousness of the opinion, its ugliness and corruption in worshipping one who lacks these attributes.

Al-Zamakhsharī spoke and said: Observe when he wanted to advise his father and admonish him regarding what he was entangled in of great error and shameful commission, in which he disobeyed the command of reason and departed from the requirement of discernment; how he arranged his speech with him in the finest coherence and presented it in the most graceful manner, while employing courtesy, gentleness, kindness, softness, fine manners, and good character, following in that the counsel of his Lord, majestic and exalted is He. Abū Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, related that he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Allah revealed to Abraham, peace be upon him: You are My friend (khalīl), improve your character even with the disbelievers, you will enter the entrances of the righteous. My word has preceded for the one whose character is good: I will shade him under My Throne and settle him in the enclosure of (p-194) holiness, and bring him close to My neighborhood.'" Al-Zamakhsharī, after this, narrated much speech of the oratorical kind, which we have left out.

Regarding ﴿mā lā yasmaʿu﴾: the apparent reading is that it is a relative pronoun, though they permitted it to be an indefinite qualified noun. The object of (yasmaʿu) and (yubṣiru) is omitted and not intended, meaning: that which has no hearing or sight, because the intent is to negate these two attributes without restriction to an object. (Shayʾan) is either a verbal noun or a direct object. When he asked him about the reason for worshipping the idol and he could not find an answer, he moved with him to inform him that knowledge had come to him which had not come to him, and he did not describe his father as ignorant, since the preceding question sufficed for that. He said "min al-ʿilm" for partitive sense, meaning: some of the knowledge that is not with you. This dialogue indicates that this was after he was made a prophet, since in the expression "jāʾanī" there is the renewal of knowledge. What came to him was either the revelation brought by the angel, or knowledge of the matters of the Hereafter and its reward and punishment, or the oneness of Allah and His being singled out for divinity and worship—three opinions. "Follow me" in the affirmation of Allah's unity in worship, and abandon the idols; "I will guide you to a straight path" which is faith in Allah and singling Him out in worship. He moved from commanding him to follow him to forbidding him from worshipping Satan; his worship of Satan being his obeying him in worshipping idols. Then he made him averse to worshipping Satan by saying that he was disobedient to the Most Merciful, since he disobeyed when commanded to prostrate to Adam and refused; so he is an enemy to you and to your father Adam from before. The word "al-Raḥmān" here serves as a reminder of the vastness of His mercy, and that one with this attribute is the one who deserves to be worshipped and not disobeyed; and it informs of Satan's wretchedness in that he disobeyed one with this attribute and committed what expelled him from this mercy. Even if he was choosing for himself disobedience to his Lord, he does not choose for his offspring anyone whom he disobeys for his sake, except what he chose for himself of their disobedience.

"Yā abati innī akhāfu": al-Farrāʾ and al-Ṭabarī said "akhāfu" means "aʿlamu" (I know), as in His saying: "so We feared that it would overwhelm them" [al-Kahf: 80], meaning: We were certain. The better course is to take "akhāfu" in its original meaning, because he was not despairing of his father's faith; rather he was hopeful for it and fearful that he would not believe and would persist in disbelief so that punishment would touch him. Abraham frightened him of the evil consequence and was courteous with him, since he did not explicitly state that punishment would befall him, but expressed it in the manner of one who fears; he used the word "touch" (masss), which is gentler than "punishment," and he left "punishment" indefinite, and he ordered upon the touch of punishment what is greater than it, namely the guardianship of Satan, just as He said in contrast to that: "and the good pleasure from Allah is greater" [al-Tawbah: 72], meaning: greater than the bliss previously mentioned. He began every piece of counsel with His saying "yā abati," seeking access to him and winning his sympathy.

It was said: guardianship here means being joined with him in the Hereafter, even if they hate each other and disavow one another. It was also said: there is inversion in the speech, and the meaning is: "Indeed I fear that you will be a guardian of Satan in this world, so a punishment from the Most Merciful will touch you in the Hereafter." His saying "an yamassaka ʿadhābun min al-Raḥmān" does not specify that the punishment occurs in the Hereafter; rather it may be understood as abandonment by Allah, so that he becomes a companion of Satan; it may also be that the touch of punishment occurs in this world, by his being tested in his disbelief with a punishment in this world, and that punishment becomes a cause for his persistence in disbelief and his arriving at the guardianship of Satan until he dies upon disbelief, as He said: "And We tested them with good things and bad things, that perhaps they would return" [al-Aʿrāf: 168]. These counsels indicate the intensity of his heart's attachment to treating his father and his eagerness for his guidance, fulfilling the right of fatherhood and guiding to the right path: "that Allah guides a single man through you is better for you than red camels."

(He said), that is, his father: "Do you turn away from my gods, O Abraham?" He asked with a question of denial. Turning away from something (rughbah ʿan al-shayʾ) is abandoning it deliberately; "his gods" are his idols. He was harsh with him in this denial and called him by his name, and did not match "yā abati" with "yā bunayya." Al-Zamakhsharī said: The predicate was placed before the subject in "Do you turn away from my gods," because it was more important to him, and it is what concerns him; and in it is a kind of wonder and denial at his turning away from his gods, and that his gods are not what anyone should turn away from. In this there is consolation and cooling of the chest of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) regarding what he suffered from similar treatment from the disbelievers of his people. End.

The preferred parsing of "a-rāghibun anta" is that "rāghib" is a subject (mubtadaʾ) because it relies on the interrogative particle, and "anta" is an agent that stands in place of the predicate. This is preferred over al-Zamakhsharī's parsing that "rāghib" is the predicate and "anta" the subject, for two reasons:

First: there would be no fronting or postponement, since the rank of the predicate is to come after the subject.

Second: there would be no separation between the operator, which is "rāghib," and its complement, which is "ʿan ālihatī," by something that is not a complement of the operator; because the predicate is not an operator on the subject, unlike "anta" being the agent, which is a complement of "rāghib." So "rāghib" and "ʿan ālihatī" are not separated by an alien element; rather it is separated by a complement of it.

When he denied to him his turning away from his gods, he threatened him, swearing to carry out what he threatened him with if he did not desist. The complement of "tantahi" is omitted; it may be that it means: from addressing me with what you addressed me with and calling me to it; and it may be that "la-in lam tantahi" means from turning away from my gods. "La-arjumannaka" is the answer to the omitted oath preceding "la-in." Al-Ḥasan said: with stones. It was said: "I will surely kill you." Al-Suddī, al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Ibn Jurayj said: "I will surely revile you."

Al-Zamakhsharī said: If you ask: upon what is "wa-ihjurnī" conjoined? I say: upon an omitted conjoined element indicated by "la-arjumannaka," meaning: "beware of me and abandon me," because "la-arjumannaka" is a threat and a rebuke. End. He needed the omission only to make the conjoined clauses and the clause conjoined to correspond; but this is not necessary according to Sībawayh, rather it is permissible to conjoin a declarative clause to an imperative clause. So "wa-ihjurnī" is conjoined to "la-in lam tantahi la-arjumannaka," and both are objects of "qāla."

"Malīyyan" is in the accusative as an adverb of time, meaning: a long period, as said by the majority, al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid and others. From it comes "al-malawān," which are the night and the day. "Al-mulāwah," with the vowel of the mīm in its three forms, is a long age, from the saying: "amlaytu li-fulān fī al-amr" when I prolonged it for him. The poet said:

"We lived in it through youth in a long span, and so the signs of the Messenger, the beloved, prevailed."

Sibawayh said: "A long time passed over him," meaning a lengthy period of time. Ibn Abbas and others said: "*maliyyan*" (﴿مَلِيًّا﴾) means "safe and sound," so it is a circumstantial accusative (*hal*) referring to the subject of ﴿واهْجُرْنِي﴾ ("and leave me"). Ibn Atiyya said: "The summary of this is that it means: relying on your state, independent of me, sufficient unto yourself." Al-Suddi said: "It means forever." From this is the verse of Muhalhil:

*So the solid mountains were split at his death,*
*And the widowed women wept over him long.*

Ibn Jubayr said: "It means a long time." The root meaning of the word is staying, as in the saying: "I stayed (*tamallaytu*) for a while." Al-Zamakhshari said: "Or ﴿maliyyan﴾ means: by going away from me and abandoning me before I wound you with beating so that you cannot move. One says: 'So-and-so is *maliyy* in such-and-such' when he is capable of it and equal to it." End of quote.

﴿قالَ سَلامٌ عَلَيْكَ﴾ ("He said: Peace be upon you"). Abu al-Birr Huthaym recited *salaman* with a fatha (accusative). The majority said: this carries the meaning of *musalama* (peaceful disengagement), not the meaning of greeting; that is, "a safe conduct from me to you." These scholars do not permit initiating the greeting of peace with a disbeliever. Al-Naqqash said: "It is a forbearing man addressing a foolish one, like His saying: ﴿وإذا خاطَبَهُمُ الجاهِلُونَ قالُوا سَلامًا﴾ ("When the ignorant address them, they say, 'Peace'") [al-Furqan: 63]." It was also said: "It is the greeting of one who parts ways." The proponent of this view permitted greeting a disbeliever and beginning with the legislated greeting of peace. This is the view of Sufyan ibn Uyayna, relying on His saying: ﴿لا يَنْهاكُمُ اللَّهُ عَنِ الَّذِينَ لَمْ يُقاتِلُوكُمْ﴾ ("God does not forbid you from those who do not fight you") [al-Mumtahana: 8], up to the end of the verse, and on His saying: ﴿قَدْ كانَتْ لَكم أُسْوَةٌ حَسَنَةٌ في إبْراهِيمَ﴾ ("There has been for you an excellent example in Abraham") [al-Mumtahana: 4], up to the end of the verse.

Abraham *said* to his father ﴿سَلامٌ عَلَيْكَ﴾, and what they cited as evidence is interpreted (*mutawwal*), and their position is refuted by what is established in Sahih Muslim: "Do not begin the Jews and the Christians with the greeting of peace." The nominative *salamun* (سَلامٌ) is the subject of a nominal clause, and the accusative *salaman* (سَلامًا) is a verbal noun, meaning: "I greeted with a greeting," as a supplication for him for safety, in the manner of winning him over. Then he promised him *istighfar* (seeking forgiveness). That is conditional upon the presence of what makes *istighfar* possible, which is faith in God and devoting worship to Him alone. This is like how a command and a prohibition are addressed to a disbeliever, yet compliance is not valid except with the condition of faith. The meaning of ﴿سَأسْتَغْفِرُ لَكَ﴾ ("I will ask forgiveness for you") is: "I will call upon God regarding your guidance, and He will forgive you through faith." It is not to be interpreted about Abraham, peace be upon him, that he did not know that God does not forgive a disbeliever. Ibn Atiyya said: "It is possible that Abraham, peace be upon him, was the first prophet to whom it was revealed that God does not forgive a disbeliever, because this matter is known only through revelation. This statement was made by him to his father before it was revealed to him. That is because it became clear to him regarding his father that he was an enemy of God in one of two ways: either by his dying in disbelief, as has been narrated, or by a decisive revelation to him (about this)."

Al-Zamakhshari said: "One may say: what prevents seeking forgiveness for a disbeliever is only revelation. As for the rational principle, it does not reject it. So it is permissible that the promise of seeking forgiveness, and its fulfillment, occurred before revelation came, based on the rational principle. What indicates its validity is His saying: ﴿إلّا قَوْلَ إبْراهِيمَ لِأبِيهِ لَأسْتَغْفِرَنَّ لَكَ﴾ ("except for the saying of Abraham to his father: 'I will surely ask forgiveness for you'") [al-Mumtahana: 4]. Had it been conditional upon faith, it would not have been something disapproved of and excepted from what was obligatory in it." As for the view of one who said: "He sought forgiveness for him only because he promised him that he would believe," citing His saying: ﴿إلّا عَنْ مَوْعِدَةٍ وعَدَها إيّاهُ﴾ ("except for a promise he had made to him") [al-Tawba: 114], making the promiser Azar and the promised Abraham, peace be upon him, this is not sound, because in this verse the promise of seeking forgiveness comes after that harsh statement of his: ﴿لَئِنْ لَمْ تَنْتَهِ﴾ ("If you do not desist"), up to the end of the verse. So how could his promise be one of faith? Also, the one who promised is Abraham, and this is indicated by the reading of Hammad which narrates: (*wa'adaha iyyahu*) (وعَدَها إيّاهُ) ("he had made to her/it").

*Al-hafiyy* (الحَفِيُّ) means the one who honors, is attentive, and is greatly kind and gentle. Its linguistic explanation was given earlier in His saying: ﴿كَأنَّكَ حَفِيٌّ عَنْها﴾ ("as if you were well-informed about it") [al-A'raf: 187]. Ibn Abbas said: "Merciful." Al-Kalbi said: "Forbearing." Al-Qutaybi said: "Dutiful." Al-Suddi said: "Your *hafiyy* is one whose concern is your affair." Since in His saying ﴿لَأرْجُمَنَّكَ﴾ ("I will surely stone you") there is harshness and hardness of heart, Abraham met it with supplication for his peace and safety, and he promised him forgiveness, fulfilling the right of fatherhood, even though harshness had come from him.

When He commanded him to abandon him for a long time, He informed him that he would carry out His command and withdraw from him, his people, and what they worshipped. So he emigrated to Syria, it was said, or to Harran, and they were in the land of Kawtha. During this emigration he married Sarah and met the tyrant who gave Hajar to serve Sarah. The more apparent view is that His saying ﴿وأدْعُو رَبِّي﴾ ("and I will call upon my Lord") means "and I will worship my Lord," as in the hadith: "Supplication is worship," in accordance with His saying: ﴿فَلَمّا اعْتَزَلَهم وما يَعْبُدُونَ مِن دُونِ اللَّهِ﴾ ("So when he had withdrawn from them and what they worshipped other than God"). It is also permissible that what is meant is the supplication recounted by God in Surat al-Shu'ara': ﴿رَبِّ هَبْ لِي حُكْمًا﴾ ("My Lord, grant me wisdom") [al-Shu'ara': 83], and so on to the end. He hinted at their wretchedness by calling upon their gods in His saying: ﴿عَسى ألّا أكُونَ بِدُعاءِ رَبِّي شَقِيًّا﴾ ("Perhaps I shall not be, in my supplication to my Lord, unfortunate"), together with humility before God in the word *'asa* ("perhaps") and what it contains of self-abasement. In *'asa* there is hope which, within it, contains intense fear.

When he parted from the disbelievers and their land, God replaced them for him with prophetic offspring and the Holy Land, so he dwelt there, and he would travel to Mecca. Then Ishaq was born to him, and his son Ya'qub, as consolation for him and strengthening of his arm. Ishaq was younger than Isma'il. When Hajar bore Isma'il, Sarah became jealous, then she conceived Ishaq.

As for His saying ﴿مِن رَحْمَتِنا﴾ ("from Our mercy") [Maryam: 53]: al-Hasan said: "It is prophethood." al-Kalbi said: "Wealth and children." The best view is that it includes religious and worldly good, such as knowledge, status, and honor in this world, and bliss in the Hereafter.

*Lisan sidq* (لِسانَ صِدْقٍ) is the good and enduring praise upon them until the end of time, as said by Ibn Abbas. He expressed it by "tongue," just as one expresses by "hand" what is meant by "hand," which is giving. In the speech of the Arabs, *lisan* means a fine message, whether it was for good or for evil. A poet said:

*A message (lisan) came to me that does not please me with it.*

And another said:

*I regretted a word (lisan) that came from me.*

*Lisan al-'Arab* is their language and their speech. God answered his supplication: ﴿واجْعَلْ لِي لِسانَ صِدْقٍ في الآخِرِينَ﴾ ("and make for me a tongue of truthfulness among the later generations") [al-Shu'ara': 84], so He made him an exemplar until all the religious communities exalted him and claimed him. He said: ﴿مِلَّةَ أبِيكم إبْراهِيمَ﴾ ("the creed of your father Abraham") [al-Hajj: 78], and ﴿مِلَّةَ إبْراهِيمَ حَنِيفًا﴾ ("the creed of Abraham, a *hanif*") [al-Baqara: 135], and ﴿ثُمَّ أوْحَيْنا إلَيْكَ أنِ اتَّبِعْ مِلَّةَ إبْراهِيمَ حَنِيفًا﴾ ("Then We revealed to you: follow the creed of Abraham, a *hanif*") [al-Nahl: 123]. He gave that to his offspring, so He raised their remembrance and praised them, just as He raised his remembrance and praised him.

(p-196)

(p-192) ﴿And mention in the Book Abraham. Indeed, he was a man of truth, a prophet.﴾ ﴿When he said to his father, "O my father, why do you worship that which hears not, nor sees, nor can avail you anything?"﴾ ﴿"O my father, indeed there has come to me of knowledge that which has not come to you, so follow me; I will guide you to a straight path."﴾ ﴿"O my father, do not worship Satan. Indeed, Satan has been to the Most Merciful a disobedient one."﴾ ﴿"O my father, indeed I fear that a punishment from the Most Merciful will touch you, so you would be a companion to Satan."﴾ ﴿He said, "Do you turn away from my gods, O Abraham? If you do not desist, I will surely stone you, so leave me for a long time."﴾ ﴿He said, "Peace be upon you. I will ask forgiveness for you from my Lord. Indeed, He has been ever gracious to me."﴾ ﴿"And I will separate myself from you and what you invoke other than Allah, and I will call upon my Lord; perhaps I will not be in my supplication to my Lord unfortunate."﴾ ﴿So when he had separated himself from them and what they worshipped other than Allah, We gave him Isaac and Jacob, and each We made a prophet.﴾ ﴿And We gave them of Our mercy, and We made for them a tongue of truthfulness, high and exalted.﴾.

(p-193) "And mention" is an address to the Messenger (ﷺ), and the intended meaning is: recite to them the account of (Abraham). The one who mentions it and conveys it in the revelation is Allah, exalted is He. The connection of this verse with what precedes it is that when Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the story of Mary and her son Jesus, and the disagreement of the factions concerning them and their worship besides Allah, and they were among those whom life had sustained, He mentioned the misguided group who worshipped an inanimate object. The two groups, although they share in misguidance, the group worshipping the inanimate object is more astray. Then He mentioned the story of Abraham with his father, peace be upon him, as a reminder to the Arabs of what Abraham had of the monotheism of Allah, and to make clear that they follow a path other than his. In it is also the truthfulness of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in what he reported, and that this is received through revelation.

"Ṣiddīq" is from the forms of intensification; it is derived from the triliteral for emphasis, meaning one who is abundantly truthful. Truthfulness (ṣidq) in common usage is opposed to lying, and it may be used of actions, character, and inanimate things. It is said: "ṣadaqanī al-ṭaʿām kadhā wa-kadhā qafīzan" (the food gave me so-and-so many qafīz), and "ʿūdun ṣidqun" for a good solid piece of wood. Thus Abraham is described as truthful in general, in his sayings and his deeds. The state of being a ṣiddīq has degrees; do you not see the description of believers with it in His saying: "of the prophets and the truthful (ṣiddīqīn)" [al-Nisāʾ: 69]? Among the strange reports is what some grammarians held: that when fiʿʿīl is derived from a transitive verb, it may govern, so one says "hādhā shirrībun muskirun" (this is a drinker of an intoxicant), just as the Basrans made faʿūl, faʿʿāl and mif'āl govern.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: The intended meaning is the excess of his truthfulness and the abundance of what he affirmed of the unseen matters of Allah, His signs, His books and His messengers, and the predominance and prevalence lay in this affirming of the books and messengers, that is, he was one who confirmed all the prophets and their books. He was a prophet in himself, based on His saying, exalted is He: "Rather, he brought the truth and confirmed the messengers" [al-Ṣāffāt: 37]. He was eloquent in truthfulness, because the essence of the matter of prophethood is truthfulness, and one who confirms Allah's signs and miracles is worthy of being so. This sentence came as a parenthetical insertion between the substituted noun and its substitute, namely (Abraham).

(Idh qāla) is like your saying: "I saw Zayd, an excellent man, your brother." It is permissible for (idh) to be connected to (kāna) or to "ṣiddīqan nabiyyan", meaning: he was combining the attributes of the truthful and the prophets at the time he addressed his father with those addresses. End.

The first analysis requires that (idh) be inflected, and it has previously been established for us that it is not inflected. The second analysis is based on the premise that the defective (kāna) and its sisters govern adverbials of time and place, which is a matter of disagreement. The third analysis is not valid, because government is attributed only to a single word, and it is not attributed to a compound of two words together. It is permissible for it to be an object of "ṣiddīqan" because it is an adjective, except according to the opinion of the Kufans. It may also be an object of "nabiyyan", meaning: he was informed at the time of his saying to his father what he said, and that the informing took place at that time—which is far-fetched.

Abū al-Birr Huthaym recited (innahu kāna ṣādiqan). In His saying "yā abati" there is gentleness and an appeal through kinship. Ibn ʿĀmir, al-Aʿraj and Abū Jaʿfar recited (yā abataa) with a fatḥa on the tāʾ, and Hārūn considered this reading erroneous. The discussion of (yā abati) has preceded in Sūrat Yūsuf, peace be upon him. In the codex of ʿAbdullāh it is "wā abatī" with a waw instead of a yāʾ. Abraham, peace be upon him, inquired about the cause that moved his father to worship the idol, although it lacks hearing, sight, and the ability to avail him anything, as a warning of the monstrousness of the opinion, its ugliness and corruption in worshipping one who lacks these attributes.

Al-Zamakhsharī spoke and said: Observe when he wanted to advise his father and admonish him regarding what he was entangled in of great error and shameful commission, in which he disobeyed the command of reason and departed from the requirement of discernment; how he arranged his speech with him in the finest coherence and presented it in the most graceful manner, while employing courtesy, gentleness, kindness, softness, fine manners, and good character, following in that the counsel of his Lord, majestic and exalted is He. Abū Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, related that he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Allah revealed to Abraham, peace be upon him: You are My friend (khalīl), improve your character even with the disbelievers, you will enter the entrances of the righteous. My word has preceded for the one whose character is good: I will shade him under My Throne and settle him in the enclosure of (p-194) holiness, and bring him close to My neighborhood.'" Al-Zamakhsharī, after this, narrated much speech of the oratorical kind, which we have left out.

Regarding ﴿mā lā yasmaʿu﴾: the apparent reading is that it is a relative pronoun, though they permitted it to be an indefinite qualified noun. The object of (yasmaʿu) and (yubṣiru) is omitted and not intended, meaning: that which has no hearing or sight, because the intent is to negate these two attributes without restriction to an object. (Shayʾan) is either a verbal noun or a direct object. When he asked him about the reason for worshipping the idol and he could not find an answer, he moved with him to inform him that knowledge had come to him which had not come to him, and he did not describe his father as ignorant, since the preceding question sufficed for that. He said "min al-ʿilm" for partitive sense, meaning: some of the knowledge that is not with you. This dialogue indicates that this was after he was made a prophet, since in the expression "jāʾanī" there is the renewal of knowledge. What came to him was either the revelation brought by the angel, or knowledge of the matters of the Hereafter and its reward and punishment, or the oneness of Allah and His being singled out for divinity and worship—three opinions. "Follow me" in the affirmation of Allah's unity in worship, and abandon the idols; "I will guide you to a straight path" which is faith in Allah and singling Him out in worship. He moved from commanding him to follow him to forbidding him from worshipping Satan; his worship of Satan being his obeying him in worshipping idols. Then he made him averse to worshipping Satan by saying that he was disobedient to the Most Merciful, since he disobeyed when commanded to prostrate to Adam and refused; so he is an enemy to you and to your father Adam from before. The word "al-Raḥmān" here serves as a reminder of the vastness of His mercy, and that one with this attribute is the one who deserves to be worshipped and not disobeyed; and it informs of Satan's wretchedness in that he disobeyed one with this attribute and committed what expelled him from this mercy. Even if he was choosing for himself disobedience to his Lord, he does not choose for his offspring anyone whom he disobeys for his sake, except what he chose for himself of their disobedience.

"Yā abati innī akhāfu": al-Farrāʾ and al-Ṭabarī said "akhāfu" means "aʿlamu" (I know), as in His saying: "so We feared that it would overwhelm them" [al-Kahf: 80], meaning: We were certain. The better course is to take "akhāfu" in its original meaning, because he was not despairing of his father's faith; rather he was hopeful for it and fearful that he would not believe and would persist in disbelief so that punishment would touch him. Abraham frightened him of the evil consequence and was courteous with him, since he did not explicitly state that punishment would befall him, but expressed it in the manner of one who fears; he used the word "touch" (masss), which is gentler than "punishment," and he left "punishment" indefinite, and he ordered upon the touch of punishment what is greater than it, namely the guardianship of Satan, just as He said in contrast to that: "and the good pleasure from Allah is greater" [al-Tawbah: 72], meaning: greater than the bliss previously mentioned. He began every piece of counsel with His saying "yā abati," seeking access to him and winning his sympathy.

It was said: guardianship here means being joined with him in the Hereafter, even if they hate each other and disavow one another. It was also said: there is inversion in the speech, and the meaning is: "Indeed I fear that you will be a guardian of Satan in this world, so a punishment from the Most Merciful will touch you in the Hereafter." His saying "an yamassaka ʿadhābun min al-Raḥmān" does not specify that the punishment occurs in the Hereafter; rather it may be understood as abandonment by Allah, so that he becomes a companion of Satan; it may also be that the touch of punishment occurs in this world, by his being tested in his disbelief with a punishment in this world, and that punishment becomes a cause for his persistence in disbelief and his arriving at the guardianship of Satan until he dies upon disbelief, as He said: "And We tested them with good things and bad things, that perhaps they would return" [al-Aʿrāf: 168]. These counsels indicate the intensity of his heart's attachment to treating his father and his eagerness for his guidance, fulfilling the right of fatherhood and guiding to the right path: "that Allah guides a single man through you is better for you than red camels."

(He said), that is, his father: "Do you turn away from my gods, O Abraham?" He asked with a question of denial. Turning away from something (rughbah ʿan al-shayʾ) is abandoning it deliberately; "his gods" are his idols. He was harsh with him in this denial and called him by his name, and did not match "yā abati" with "yā bunayya." Al-Zamakhsharī said: The predicate was placed before the subject in "Do you turn away from my gods," because it was more important to him, and it is what concerns him; and in it is a kind of wonder and denial at his turning away from his gods, and that his gods are not what anyone should turn away from. In this there is consolation and cooling of the chest of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) regarding what he suffered from similar treatment from the disbelievers of his people. End.

The preferred parsing of "a-rāghibun anta" is that "rāghib" is a subject (mubtadaʾ) because it relies on the interrogative particle, and "anta" is an agent that stands in place of the predicate. This is preferred over al-Zamakhsharī's parsing that "rāghib" is the predicate and "anta" the subject, for two reasons:

First: there would be no fronting or postponement, since the rank of the predicate is to come after the subject.

Second: there would be no separation between the operator, which is "rāghib," and its complement, which is "ʿan ālihatī," by something that is not a complement of the operator; because the predicate is not an operator on the subject, unlike "anta" being the agent, which is a complement of "rāghib." So "rāghib" and "ʿan ālihatī" are not separated by an alien element; rather it is separated by a complement of it.

When he denied to him his turning away from his gods, he threatened him, swearing to carry out what he threatened him with if he did not desist. The complement of "tantahi" is omitted; it may be that it means: from addressing me with what you addressed me with and calling me to it; and it may be that "la-in lam tantahi" means from turning away from my gods. "La-arjumannaka" is the answer to the omitted oath preceding "la-in." Al-Ḥasan said: with stones. It was said: "I will surely kill you."
