Al-Hasan, Abu Hayawa, ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar, al-Aʿmash, and Ahmad ibn Musa from Abu ʿAmr read (جَنّاتُ) in the nominative, plural, meaning "they are gardens." Al-Zamakhshari said: the nominative is as the subject of a nominal sentence (ibtida'), the predicate being (الَّتِي), "which." Al-Hasan ibn Hayy and ʿAli ibn Salih read (جَنَّةَ عَدْنٍ) in the accusative, singular, and it was related from al-Aʿmash; it is so in the codex of ʿAbd Allah. Al-Yamani, al-Hasan, and Ishaq al-Azraq from Hamza read (جَنَّةُ) in the nominative, singular. If (عَدْنٍ) is a proper personal name, then (الَّتِي) is an adjective (naʿt) for what is annexed to (عَدْنٍ); if the meaning is "residence," then (الَّتِي) is an apposition (badal).

Al-Zamakhshari said: (عَدْنٍ) is definite, a proper noun for the meaning of "adn," which is residence, just as they made (فَيْنَةَ), (سَحَرَ), and (أمْسِ) proper nouns, not declined, for the meanings of "a while," "dawn," and "yesterday." So "adn" became like that. Or it is a proper name for the land of Paradise, since it is a place of residence; were it not so, the substitution would not be valid, because an indefinite noun is not substituted for a definite one except when qualified; and its qualification by (الَّتِي) would not be valid.

What he mentioned is open to objection. As for his claim that (عَدْنٌ) is a proper noun for the meaning of "adn," this requires a stipulation and hearing from the Arabs; likewise the claim of a personal proper name in it. As for his words "were it not so" up to "qualified," this is not the view of the Basrans, for their view is the permissibility of substituting an indefinite noun for a definite one even if it is not qualified; this is something said by the Baghdadis, who are refuted by the evidence of usage, as we have explained in our books on grammar. So the implication he drew is invalid. As for his words "nor would its qualification by (الَّتِي) be valid," it is not necessary that (الَّتِي) be a qualifier; we have mentioned that it may be parsed as a substitution.

(بِالغَيْبِ, "in the unseen") is a circumstantial clause (hal): that is, He promised them while it was absent from them, or they were absent from it, not witnessing it. It may also be that the (ب) indicates cause: that is, through belief in the unseen and faith in it. Abu Muslim said: the meaning is those who become servants in the unseen, that is, those who worship Him in secret. The apparent reading is that (وَعْدُهُ) is a verbal noun (masdar). It was said: (مَأْتِيًّا) means (آتِيًا), "coming." It was also said: it stays with its original meaning as a passive participle (ism al-maf'ul), "something brought." Al-Zamakhshari said: (مَأْتِيًّا) is a passive form with the meaning of an active one; the more likely view is that the promise is Paradise and they come to it; or it is from your saying "he came to him with a kindness," meaning his promise was an executed promise, fulfilled. The second view, which is his saying "the more likely view," is taken from the saying of Ibn Juraij, who said: (وَعْدُهُ) here means what was promised, which is Paradise, and (مَأْتِيًّا) means that His friends come to it.

﴿except "Peace"﴾ is a disconnected exception, and it is the saying of the angels: ﴿Peace be upon you for what you endured patiently﴾ [al-Raʿd: 24]. It was also said: God greets them with peace when they enter it. The meaning of ﴿morning and evening﴾: their food comes to them twice within the length of a day and a night. Mujahid said: there is no morning or evening there, but they are brought what they desire in this world. Qatada mentioned something similar: that it is an address in terms of what the Arabs know of comfortable living. Al-Hasan said: they were addressed according to what the Arabs knew of the finest living, because many of the Arabs would find food only once a day, and most of their living came from the trees of the desert and from animals. Al-Zamakhshari said: (اللَّغْوُ) is superfluous speech and what has no benefit in it. There is a clear indication in it of the obligation to avoid idle talk and guard against it, since God declared that abode free of it, in which there is no obligation. How excellent is His saying: ﴿When they pass by idle talk, they pass by with dignity﴾ [al-Furqan: 72]; ﴿When they hear idle talk, they turn away from it﴾ [al-Qasas: 55], and so on. That is: if the greeting of some of them to others, or the greeting of the angels to them, is (لَغْوًا, "idle talk"), then they hear nothing idle except that, and this belongs to the category of the poet's saying:

"There is no fault in them except that their swords are notched by the clashing of the battalions."

Or, ﴿they will not hear therein﴾ anything except a saying in which they are safe from fault and defect, as a disconnected exception; or because the meaning of "peace" is the supplication for safety, and the abode of peace is the abode of safety, and its people have no need of supplication for safety. So its apparent meaning would be of the category of idle talk and superfluous speech, were it not for the benefit contained in the speech. He also said: there is no night or day there, but it is by estimation. Also, because the one enjoying comfort in the eyes of the Arabs is one who finds lunch and dinner. It was also said: He meant the continuity and abundance of provision, as you say: "I am with so-and-so morning and evening, and in the morning and afternoon," and you do not mean the two specific times.

Al-Jumhur read (نُورِثُ), the present tense of (أوْرَثَ). Al-Aʿmash read (نُورِثُها) with the pronoun referring to the relative pronoun made explicit. Al-Hasan, al-Aʿraj, Qatada, Ruways, Humayd, Ibn Abi ʿAbla, Abu Hayawa, and Mahbub from Abu ʿAmr read it with a fatha on the waw and shadda on the ra'. Inheritance (التَّوْرِيثُ) is a metaphor (isti'ara): Paradise remains for them as property remains for an heir from the deceased. The righteous (الأتْقِياءُ) meet their Lord, their deeds have ended, and their fruit remains, which is Paradise; so He has given them inheritance from their piety as an heir inherits property from the deceased. It was also said: they were made to inherit from Paradise the dwellings which were for the people of Hell had they obeyed.

﴿And We do not descend except by the command of your Lord.﴾ Gabriel was delayed in coming to the Messenger once, and when he came, the Messenger (ﷺ) said: "O Gabriel, I have longed for you; will you not visit us more often than you visit us?" Then this was revealed. Mujahid and al-Dahhak said: its occasion was that Gabriel (peace be upon him) was delayed in bringing the questions mentioned earlier in surat al-Kahf, and they are like those in al-Duha. (تَنَزَّلَ, "descend") is on the pattern (تَفَعَّلَ), which is for the sense of acceptance (mutawaʿa), and it is one of the meanings of (تَفَعَّلَ). You say: "We caused it to descend (nazzalnahu), so it descended (tanazzala)," and so it indicates continuity of action over an interval. It may also be used without this nuance when it has the sense of the bare form, like their saying (taʿadda al-shayʾ, "it passed over the thing") and (ʿaddāhu), and it is not an acceptance form, so (تَنَزَّلَ) means (نَزَلَ). As the poet said:

"I am not for a human, but for an angel who descended from the air of heaven, pouring down."

Al-Zamakhshari said: (التَّنَزُّلُ) has two meanings: the meaning of descent gradually, and the meaning of descent in general, like his saying: "I am not for a human," because it is the acceptance form of (نَزَّلَ); and (نَزَّلَ) may mean (أنْزَلَ, "caused to descend") and may mean gradual progression. The fitting sense for this place is descent gradually, and the meaning is that our descent happens at times, one time after another. End.

Ibn ʿAtiyya said: this (و) in His saying ﴿and We do not descend﴾ is the conjunction joining one sentence to another, linking the two statements even if their meanings are not the same. Al-Naqqash related from some people that His saying ﴿and We do not descend﴾ is connected to His saying ﴿I am only a messenger of your Lord, to give you a pure boy﴾ [Maryam: 19]; this is a weak view. End.

What appears as the connection of this verse to what precedes it is that when God mentioned the story of Zakariyya and Maryam, and mentioned Ibrahim, Musa, Ismaʿil, and Idris, and then mentioned that He bestowed favour upon them, saying ﴿and of the offspring of Ibrahim﴾ [Maryam: 58], and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was of the offspring of Ibrahim, He mentioned that after these there succeeded a generation, namely the Jews and Christians, the people of the Books; because others are not said to have "neglected the prayer." That is said only of those who had a religious law (shariʿa) in which prayer was obligated upon them by revelation from God. The Jews were the cause of the Quraysh asking the Prophet (ﷺ) those three questions, and the revelation was delayed from him, so the Quraysh and the Jews rejoiced at that. This was part of following their desires, while they knew the prophethood of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). So God revealed ﴿and We do not descend﴾ as an alert to the story of the Quraysh and the Jews, and that the origin of that story came from those later generations who neglected the prayer and followed their desires. It also serves as a conclusion to the stories of those favoured by God, addressing their noblest, Muhammad (ﷺ), and as an excuse on behalf of Gabriel (peace be upon him) to the Messenger, that the delay was not from him, since he does not descend except by the command of God. Since the cause of the delay of revelation was the story of the question, and since the Prophet (ﷺ) had not said "God willing" when answering them, and since the question stemmed from the Jews following their desires and their hidden malice, He was content to mention the outcome, which comes after mention of what their worldly desires and malice had led them to.

[p. 204] Abu al-Aliyah said: "What is before us (ma bayna al-aydi) is the whole of this world up to the first blast (al-nafkha al-ula). What is behind us (ma khalfa dhalika) is the Hereafter from the time of resurrection (al-ba'th). What is between them (ma bayna dhalika) is what lies between the two blasts (al-nafkhatayn)." Ibn Attiyah said: "Abu al-Aliyah's statement can only be conceived with regard to the children of Adam, whereas this saying belongs to the angels, so reflect on it." Ibn Juraij said: "What is before us is the time that passed before creation (al-ijad), what is behind us is what comes after their death until the endurance of the Hereafter, and what is between them is the duration of life." In the book al-Tahrir wal-Tahbir, [it is reported that] "what is before us" is the Hereafter, and "what is behind us" is this world, transmitted by al-Awfi from Ibn Abbas, and Ibn Jubayr, Qatadah, Muqatil and Sufyan said the same. Mujahid said the reverse of this. Al-Akhfash said: "What is before us" is before we were created, "what is behind us" is after annihilation, and "what is between that" is what lies between this world and the Hereafter. Mujahid, Ikrimah and Abu al-Aliyah said: it is what lies between the two blasts. Al-Akhfash said: [it means] the time of our existence. The author of al-Ghuniyan said: "What is before us" is the descent of the angels from the heaven, "what is behind us" is [their ascent] from the earth, and "what is between that" is what lies between heaven and earth. Ibn al-Qushayri said the same as Ibn Juraij, then said: [this verse] encompasses the three times, all of which belong to God, who originates them and manages their affairs as He wills, by sending down or delaying [as He chooses]. End of quotation. There is some abridgement and rephrasing in it.

Ibn Attiyah said: "The purpose is only to convey that God, exalted is He, owns His angels, and that their little and much activity is only by His command, and their movement from place to place is only by His wisdom, since places belong to Him and they belong to Him. If one takes the verse to mean that 'what is before us and what is behind us' refers to the places in which they act, and 'what is between that' refers to themselves and their stations, it would be a valid interpretation, as if they said: 'We are bound by power; we do not move or descend except by the command of your Lord.'" End of quotation. What Ibn Attiyah said about "lahu" (to Him) and so on, al-Zamakhshari also took in a similar direction. He said: "To Him belongs what is in front of us and behind us of directions and places, and what we are in; so we cannot move from one direction to another, or from one place to another, except by the command and will of the King. The meaning is that He encompasses everything, and no hidden thing is concealed from Him. How then could we undertake an action we originate except as issuing from what His wisdom requires, and what He commands and permits us to do?" End of quotation. Al-Baghawi said: "To Him is the knowledge of what is before us."

Abu Muslim and Ibn Bahr said: "We do not descend" (wa ma natanazzalu), and the verse that follows, is not the speech of the angels, but the speech of the people of Paradise to one another when they enter it. It is connected to the first verse up to His saying "and what is between that," meaning: "We do not enter Paradise except by the command of your Lord; to Him belongs what is before us," that is, in Paradise, in the future, "and what is behind us," of what was in the world, "and what is between them," that is, between the two times. Al-Zamakhshari related this view, saying: "It is said that it is a quotation of the speech of the righteous when they enter Paradise, meaning: 'We do not enter Paradise except by permission from God upon us, for the reward of our deeds and His command for us to enter it, and He is the Owner of the affairs in their entirety, the past, the awaited and the present, the Gentle in deeds of goodness, the Granter of success in them, and the One who rewards for them.'"

Then He, exalted is He, said, affirming for them: "And your Lord was never forgetful" (wa ma kana rabbuka nasiyyan), meaning, unaware of the deeds of those who act, or heedless of what they ought to be rewarded for. How could forgetfulness or heedlessness be permitted for the Lord of the kingdom of the heavens and the earth and what is between them? End of quotation. The judge (al-Qadi) said: "This contradicts the apparent meaning in several respects:

"The first: the apparent meaning of the revelation is the descent of the angels to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, and [this is shown by] His saying 'by the command of your Lord'; the apparent sense of a command fits the context of obligation (al-taklif) better.

"The second: it is an address from a group to one person, and that is not fitting for speech among some of them to others in Paradise.

"The third: what is in its context, 'And your Lord was never forgetful, Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them,' is not fitting for the context of obligation, nor is it attributed to the Messenger." End of quotation.

The reciters (al-Jumhur) read "wa ma natanazzalu" with the nun, meaning Gabriel himself and the angels. Al-A'raj read it with the ya', as a report from God. It has been said that the pronoun in "yatanazzalu" [al-Talaq: 12] refers to Gabriel, peace be upon him. Ibn Attiyah said: "But 'lahu ma bayna aydina' refutes this, because it does not hold consistently with it. The only plausible reading is that it is a report about Gabriel: that the Qur'an does not descend except by God's command, at the times He determines." Al-Zamakhshari also said this as a quotation of Gabriel, with the pronoun referring to the revelation. End of quotation. This saying may be understood with an implied element: that is, "And Gabriel does not descend except by the command of your Lord, saying, 'To Him belongs what is before us...'" meaning he says this by way of excusing the delay on his part, that your Lord disposes of us, and we have no authority to act except by His will; and it is an announcement that He, exalted is He, does not forget you even if the revelation is delayed from you.

"Lord of the heavens and the earth" is in the nominative either as an apposition (badal) or as the predicate of an omitted subject. The majority read "hal ta'lamu" with the lam clearly pronounced before the ta'. Al-Akhawan (Hamzah and al-Kisa'i), Hisham, Ali ibn Nasr and Harun, both from Abu Amr, al-Hasan, al-A'mash, Isa and Ibn Muhaysin read both with idgham (assimilation of the lam into the ta') in both places. Abu Ubayda said: "They are two dialects." And as evidence for the assimilated form, they quoted the verse of Muzahim al-Uqayli:

"So leave that aside, but will you help one smitten [with love]
by the light of a lightning flash at the end of the night, a watcher?"

"Fasbir" (be steadfast) was transitive with the lam by way of tadmin (implicit borrowing of a meaning, where a verb is given the sense of another), meaning: "Remain firm through patience in His worship, for worship brings hardships, so remain firm in them." Its original transitivity is with "ala," as in His saying, "and be steadfast in it" [Ta-Ha: 132]. "Al-Samiyy" is the one who shares the name; you say, "This is your namesake," meaning, his name is like your name. So the meaning is that no one was ever named with the name of God, and the idolaters used to call their idols gods, and [they said] al-Uzza is a god, but they never applied the word Allah to any of their idols. It is reported from Ibn Abbas: "No one is named al-Rahman except Him." It has also been said: this may refer to His saying, "Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them," meaning: do you know anyone who is named or described by this description? That is, no one among the nations names anything by this name except God. Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr and Qatadah said "samiyyan" means "equal" (mithl) and "like" (shabih), and this was also reported from Ibn Abbas. Ibn Attiyah said: "Al-samiyy in the sense of the one who rivals and resembles comes from sumuww (loftiness), and this is a good view, though it does not fit the mention of Yahya." That is, [the meaning being] "We have not made for him before [Yahya] a samiyy." Others said: one says "So-and-so is the samiyy of So-and-so" when he shares the name with him, and "samiyyuhu" when he resembles him in his fine qualities and virtues. From this is the poet's saying:

"You are a namesake of al-Zubayr, but you are not
like al-Zubayr in that he has no equal, when he prevailed."

Al-Zajjaj said: "Do you know anyone who deserves to be called Creator and Capable except Him?" Al-Dahhak said: "[Samiyyan means] a son," in response to those who say, "God has begotten a son."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 19, verses 59–65 (part 1 of 2):

(p-201) ﴿Then there succeeded them a generation who neglected the prayer and followed their desires, so they will meet with error.﴾ ﴿Except for one who repents, believes, and does righteous deeds; those will enter Paradise and will not be wronged in the least.﴾ ﴿Gardens of perpetual residence, which the Most Merciful promised His servants in the unseen. Indeed, His promise is ever coming to pass.﴾ ﴿They will not hear therein any idle talk, but only "Peace." And they will have their provision therein morning and evening.﴾ ﴿That is the Paradise which We cause to inherit of Our servants whoever was mindful of Us.﴾ ﴿And We do not descend except by the command of your Lord. To Him belongs what is before us, what is behind us, and what is between that, and your Lord is not forgetful.﴾ ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them. So worship Him and be steadfast in His worship. Do you know of anyone worthy of His name?﴾

It was revealed (﴿فَخَلَفَ﴾) concerning the Jews, according to Ibn ʿAbbas and Muqatil; concerning them and the Christians, according to al-Suddi; and concerning a people of the Messenger's community who will come after the passing of its righteous ones, competing with one another in fornication, mounting one another in the alleys. This is related from Mujahid, Qatada, ʿAta', and Muhammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazi. From Wahb: they are drinkers of coffee (qahwa). The discussion of (خَلَفَ) has already preceded in al-Aʿraf.

The neglect of the prayer (إضاعَةُ الصَّلاةِ) means delaying it beyond its time. This was said by Ibn Masʿud, al-Nakhaʿi, al-Qasim ibn Mukhaymira, Mujahid, Ibrahim, and ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz. Al-Qurazi said, and al-Zajjaj chose this view: its neglect is failing to fulfil its conditions (shurut). It was also said: performing it outside congregations. It was also said: not believing it to be obligatory. It was also said: abandoning the mosques and being preoccupied with crafts and means of livelihood. The word (الشَّهَواتِ, "desires") is general, covering every object of desire that distracts from the prayer and the remembrance of God. From ʿAli: "One who builds lofty (shadid), rides showy (manzur), and wears conspicuous (mashhur) [things]."

ʿAbd Allah (ibn Masʿud), al-Hasan, Abu Razin al-Uqayli, al-Dahhak, and Ibn Miqsam read (الصَّلَواتِ) in the plural.

Al-ghayy (الغَيُّ), in the view of the Arabs, is every evil, and al-rashad is every good. The poet said:

"Whoever meets with good, people will praise his affair; and whoever goes astray will not lack a blamer for his error."

Al-Zajjaj said: it is by omission of a noun (مُضافٌ محذوف), meaning "the recompense of error," like His saying ﴿يَلْقَ أثامًا﴾ [al-Furqan: 68], meaning "the recompense of sins." Ibn Zayd said: al-ghayy is ruin and falling into calamities. ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr, Ibn Masʿud, and Kaʿb said: al-ghayy is a valley in Hell. Ibn Zayd said: it is misguidance. Al-Zamakhshari said: or (غَيًّا) means away from the path to Paradise. Al-Karmani related: pits in Hell into which pus and festering blood flow. It was also said: destruction. It was also said: evil.

It is reported by al-Akhfash that it was read (يُلَقَّوْنَ) with a dammah on the yaʾ, a fatha on the lam, and a shadda on the qaf.

﴿Except for one who repents﴾: this is an exception whose apparent character is connected (istithnaʾ muttasil). Al-Zajjaj said it is disconnected (munqati', i.e., exception not of the same category). (وَآمَنَ, "and believes"): this indicates that that neglect amounts to disbelief.

Al-Hasan read (يَدْخُلُونَ) in the active voice, and so is every instance of (يَدْخُلُونَ) in the Qur'an. Al-Zuhri, Humayd, Shayba, al-Aʿmash, Ibn Abi Layla, Ibn Mundhir, and Ibn Saʿdan also read it so here. Ibn Ghazwan related from Talha: (سَيَدْخُلُونَ), with the sin of the future tense, in the active voice.

The majority read (جَنّاتِ) in the accusative, plural, as a substitute (badal) for (الجَنَّةِ). ﴿and will not be wronged in the least﴾ is either a parenthetical insertion (iʿtiraḍ) or a circumstantial clause (hal). Al-Hasan, Abu Hayawa, ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar, al-Aʿmash, and Ahmad ibn Musa from Abu ʿAmr read (جَنّاتُ) in the nominative, plural, meaning "they are gardens." Al-Zamakhshari said: the nominative is as the subject of a nominal sentence (ibtida'), the predicate being (الَّتِي), "which." Al-Hasan ibn Hayy and ʿAli ibn Salih read (جَنَّةَ عَدْنٍ) in the accusative, singular, and it was related from al-Aʿmash; it is so in the codex of ʿAbd Allah. Al-Yamani, al-Hasan, and Ishaq al-Azraq from Hamza read (جَنَّةُ) in the nominative, singular. If (عَدْنٍ) is a proper personal name, then (الَّتِي) is an adjective (naʿt) for what is annexed to (عَدْنٍ); if the meaning is "residence," then (الَّتِي) is an apposition (badal).

Al-Zamakhshari said: (عَدْنٍ) is definite, a proper noun for the meaning of "adn," which is residence, just as they made (فَيْنَةَ), (سَحَرَ), and (أمْسِ) proper nouns, not declined, for the meanings of "a while," "dawn," and "yesterday." So "adn" became like that. Or it is a proper name for the land of Paradise, since it is a place of residence; were it not so, the substitution would not be valid, because an indefinite noun is not substituted for a definite one except when qualified; and its qualification by (الَّتِي) would not be valid.

What he mentioned is open to objection. As for his claim that (عَدْنٌ) is a proper noun for the meaning of "adn," this requires a stipulation and hearing from the Arabs; likewise the claim of a personal proper name in it. As for his words "were it not so" up to "qualified," this is not the view of the Basrans, for their view is the permissibility of substituting an indefinite noun for a definite one even if it is not qualified; this is something said by the Baghdadis, who are refuted by the evidence of usage, as we have explained in our books on grammar. So the implication he drew is invalid. As for his words "nor would its qualification by (الَّتِي) be valid," it is not necessary that (الَّتِي) be a qualifier; we have mentioned that it may be parsed as a substitution.

(بِالغَيْبِ, "in the unseen") is a circumstantial clause (hal): that is, He promised them while it was absent from them, or they were absent from it, not witnessing it. It may also be that the (ب) indicates cause: that is, through belief in the unseen and faith in it. Abu Muslim said: the meaning is those who become servants in the unseen, that is, those who worship Him in secret. The apparent reading is that (وَعْدُهُ) is a verbal noun (masdar). It was said: (مَأْتِيًّا) means (آتِيًا), "coming." It was also said: it stays with its original meaning as a passive participle (ism al-maf'ul), "something brought." Al-Zamakhshari said: (مَأْتِيًّا) is a passive form with the meaning of an active one; the more likely view is that the promise is Paradise and they come to it; or it is from your saying "he came to him with a kindness," meaning his promise was an executed promise, fulfilled. The second view, which is his saying "the more likely view," is taken from the saying of Ibn Juraij, who said: (وَعْدُهُ) here means what was promised, which is Paradise, and (مَأْتِيًّا) means that His friends come to it.

﴿except "Peace"﴾ is a disconnected exception, and it is the saying of the angels: ﴿Peace be upon you for what you endured patiently﴾ [al-Raʿd: 24]. It was also said: God greets them with peace when they enter it. The meaning of ﴿morning and evening﴾: their food comes to them twice within the length of a day and a night. Mujahid said: there is no morning or evening there, but they are brought what they desire in this world. Qatada mentioned something similar: that it is an address in terms of what the Arabs know of comfortable living. Al-Hasan said: they were addressed according to what the Arabs knew of the finest living, because many of the Arabs would find food only once a day, and most of their living came from the trees of the desert and from animals. Al-Zamakhshari said: (اللَّغْوُ) is superfluous speech and what has no benefit in it. There is a clear indication in it of the obligation to avoid idle talk and guard against it, since God declared that abode free of it, in which there is no obligation. How excellent is His saying: ﴿When they pass by idle talk, they pass by with dignity﴾ [al-Furqan: 72]; ﴿When they hear idle talk, they turn away from it﴾ [al-Qasas: 55], and so on. That is: if the greeting of some of them to others, or the greeting of the angels to them, is (لَغْوًا, "idle talk"), then they hear nothing idle except that, and this belongs to the category of the poet's saying:

"There is no fault in them except that their swords are notched by the clashing of the battalions."

Or, ﴿they will not hear therein﴾ anything except a saying in which they are safe from fault and defect, as a disconnected exception; or because the meaning of "peace" is the supplication for safety, and the abode of peace is the abode of safety, and its people have no need of supplication for safety. So its apparent meaning would be of the category of idle talk and superfluous speech, were it not for the benefit contained in the speech. He also said: there is no night or day there, but it is by estimation. Also, because the one enjoying comfort in the eyes of the Arabs is one who finds lunch and dinner. It was also said: He meant the continuity and abundance of provision, as you say: "I am with so-and-so morning and evening, and in the morning and afternoon," and you do not mean the two specific times.

Al-Jumhur read (نُورِثُ), the present tense of (أوْرَثَ). Al-Aʿmash read (نُورِثُها) with the pronoun referring to the relative pronoun made explicit. Al-Hasan, al-Aʿraj, Qatada, Ruways, Humayd, Ibn Abi ʿAbla, Abu Hayawa, and Mahbub from Abu ʿAmr read it with a fatha on the waw and shadda on the ra'. Inheritance (التَّوْرِيثُ) is a metaphor (isti'ara): Paradise remains for them as property remains for an heir from the deceased. The righteous (الأتْقِياءُ) meet their Lord, their deeds have ended, and their fruit remains, which is Paradise; so He has given them inheritance from their piety as an heir inherits property from the deceased. It was also said: they were made to inherit from Paradise the dwellings which were for the people of Hell had they obeyed.

﴿And We do not descend except by the command of your Lord.﴾ Gabriel was delayed in coming to the Messenger once, and when he came, the Messenger (ﷺ) said: "O Gabriel, I have longed for you; will you not visit us more often than you visit us?" Then this was revealed. Mujahid and al-Dahhak said: its occasion was that Gabriel (peace be upon him) was delayed in bringing the questions mentioned earlier in surat al-Kahf, and they are like those in al-Duha. (تَنَزَّلَ, "descend") is on the pattern (تَفَعَّلَ), which is for the sense of acceptance (mutawaʿa), and it is one of the meanings of (تَفَعَّلَ). You say: "We caused it to descend (nazzalnahu), so it descended (tanazzala)," and so it indicates continuity of action over an interval. It may also be used without this nuance when it has the sense of the bare form, like their saying (taʿadda al-shayʾ, "it passed over the thing") and (ʿaddāhu), and it is not an acceptance form, so (تَنَزَّلَ) means (نَزَلَ). As the poet said:

"I am not for a human, but for an angel who descended from the air of heaven, pouring down."

Al-Zamakhshari said: (التَّنَزُّلُ) has two meanings: the meaning of descent gradually, and the meaning of descent in general, like his saying: "I am not for a human," because it is the acceptance form of (نَزَّلَ); and (نَزَّلَ) may mean (أنْزَلَ, "caused to descend") and may mean gradual progression. The fitting sense for this place is descent gradually, and the meaning is that our descent happens at times, one time after another. End.

Ibn ʿAtiyya said: this (و) in His saying ﴿and We do not descend﴾ is the conjunction joining one sentence to another, linking the two statements even if their meanings are not the same. Al-Naqqash related from some people that His saying ﴿and We do not descend﴾ is connected to His saying ﴿I am only a messenger of your Lord, to give you a pure boy﴾ [Maryam: 19]; this is a weak view. End.

What appears as the connection of this verse to what precedes it is that when God mentioned the story of Zakariyya and Maryam, and mentioned Ibrahim, Musa, Ismaʿil, and Idris, and then mentioned that He bestowed favour upon them, saying ﴿and of the offspring of Ibrahim﴾ [Maryam: 58], and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was of the offspring of Ibrahim, He mentioned that after these there succeeded a generation, namely the Jews and Christians, the people of the Books; because others are not said to have "neglected the prayer." That is said only of those who had a religious law (shariʿa) in which prayer was obligated upon them by revelation from God. The Jews were the cause of the Quraysh asking the Prophet (ﷺ) those three questions, and the revelation was delayed from him, so the Quraysh and the Jews rejoiced at that. This was part of following their desires, while they knew the prophethood of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). So God revealed ﴿and We do not descend﴾ as an alert to the story of the Quraysh and the Jews, and that the origin of that story came from those later generations who neglected the prayer and followed their desires. It also serves as a conclusion to the stories of those favoured by God, addressing their noblest, Muhammad (ﷺ), and as an excuse on behalf of Gabriel (peace be upon him) to the Messenger, that the delay was not from him, since he does not descend except by the command of God. Since the cause of the delay of revelation was the story of the question, and since the Prophet (ﷺ) had not said "God willing" when answering them, and since the question stemmed from the Jews following their desires and their hidden malice, He was content to mention the outcome, which comes after mention of what their worldly desires and malice had led them to.

[p. 204] Abu al-Aliyah said: "What is before us (ma bayna al-aydi) is the whole of this world up to the first blast (al-nafkha al-ula). What is behind us (ma khalfa dhalika) is the Hereafter from the time of resurrection (al-ba'th). What is between them (ma bayna dhalika) is what lies between the two blasts (al-nafkhatayn)." Ibn Attiyah said: "Abu al-Aliyah's statement can only be conceived with regard to the children of Adam, whereas this saying belongs to the angels, so reflect on it." Ibn Juraij said: "What is before us is the time that passed before creation (al-ijad), what is behind us is what comes after their death until the endurance of the Hereafter, and what is between them is the duration of life." In the book al-Tahrir wal-Tahbir, [it is reported that] "what is before us" is the Hereafter, and "what is behind us" is this world, transmitted by al-Awfi from Ibn Abbas, and Ibn Jubayr, Qatadah, Muqatil and Sufyan said the same. Mujahid said the reverse of this. Al-Akhfash said: "What is before us" is before we were created, "what is behind us" is after annihilation, and "what is between that" is what lies between this world and the Hereafter. Mujahid, Ikrimah and Abu al-Aliyah said: it is what lies between the two blasts. Al-Akhfash said: [it means] the time of our existence. The author of al-Ghuniyan said: "What is before us" is the descent of the angels from the heaven, "what is behind us" is [their ascent] from the earth, and "what is between that" is what lies between heaven and earth. Ibn al-Qushayri said the same as Ibn Juraij, then said: [this verse] encompasses the three times, all of which belong to God, who originates them and manages their affairs as He wills, by sending down or delaying [as He chooses]. End of quotation. There is some abridgement and rephrasing in it.

Ibn Attiyah said: "The purpose is only to convey that God, exalted is He, owns His angels, and that their little and much activity is only by His command, and their movement from place to place is only by His wisdom, since places belong to Him and they belong to Him. If one takes the verse to mean that 'what is before us and what is behind us' refers to the places in which they act, and 'what is between that' refers to themselves and their stations, it would be a valid interpretation, as if they said: 'We are bound by power; we do not move or descend except by the command of your Lord.'" End of quotation. What Ibn Attiyah said about "lahu" (to Him) and so on, al-Zamakhshari also took in a similar direction. He said: "To Him belongs what is in front of us and behind us of directions and places, and what we are in; so we cannot move from one direction to another, or from one place to another, except by the command and will of the King. The meaning is that He encompasses everything, and no hidden thing is concealed from Him. How then could we undertake an action we originate except as issuing from what His wisdom requires, and what He commands and permits us to do?" End of quotation. Al-Baghawi said: "To Him is the knowledge of what is before us."

Abu Muslim and Ibn Bahr said: "We do not descend" (wa ma natanazzalu), and the verse that follows, is not the speech of the angels, but the speech of the people of Paradise to one another when they enter it. It is connected to the first verse up to His saying "and what is between that," meaning: "We do not enter Paradise except by the command of your Lord; to Him belongs what is before us," that is, in Paradise, in the future, "and what is behind us," of what was in the world, "and what is between them," that is, between the two times. Al-Zamakhshari related this view, saying: "It is said that it is a quotation of the speech of the righteous when they enter Paradise, meaning: 'We do not enter Paradise except by permission from God upon us, for the reward of our deeds and His command for us to enter it, and He is the Owner of the affairs in their entirety, the past, the awaited and the present, the Gentle in deeds of goodness, the Granter of success in them, and the One who rewards for them.'"

Then He, exalted is He, said, affirming for them: "And your Lord was never forgetful" (wa ma kana rabbuka nasiyyan), meaning, unaware of the deeds of those who act, or heedless of what they ought to be rewarded for. How could forgetfulness or heedlessness be permitted for the Lord of the kingdom of the heavens and the earth and what is between them? End of quotation. The judge (al-Qadi) said: "This contradicts the apparent meaning in several respects:

"The first: the apparent meaning of the revelation is the descent of the angels to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, and [this is shown by] His saying 'by the command of your Lord'; the apparent sense of a command fits the context of obligation (al-taklif) better.

"The second: it is an address from a group to one person, and that is not fitting for speech among some of them to others in Paradise.

"The third: what is in its context, 'And your Lord was never forgetful, Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them,' is not fitting for the context of obligation, nor is it attributed to the Messenger." End of quotation.

The reciters (al-Jumhur) read "wa ma natanazzalu" with the nun, meaning Gabriel himself and the angels. Al-A'raj read it with the ya', as a report from God. It has been said that the pronoun in "yatanazzalu" [al-Talaq: 12] refers to Gabriel, peace be upon him. Ibn Attiyah said: "But 'lahu ma bayna aydina' refutes this, because it does not hold consistently with it. The only plausible reading is that it is a report about Gabriel: that the Qur'an does not descend except by God's command, at the times He determines." Al-Zamakhshari also said this as a quotation of Gabriel, with the pronoun referring to the revelation. End of quotation. This saying may be understood with an implied element: that is, "And Gabriel does not descend except by the command of your Lord, saying, 'To Him belongs what is before us...'" meaning he says this by way of excusing the delay on his part, that your Lord disposes of us, and we have no authority to act except by His will; and it is an announcement that He, exalted is He, does not forget you even if the revelation is delayed from you.

"Lord of the heavens and the earth" is in the nominative either as an apposition (badal) or as the predicate of an omitted subject. The majority read "hal ta'lamu" with the lam clearly pronounced before the ta'. Al-Akhawan (Hamzah and al-Kisa'i), Hisham, Ali ibn Nasr and Harun, both from Abu Amr, al-Hasan, al-A'mash, Isa and Ibn Muhaysin read both with idgham (assimilation of the lam into the ta') in both places. Abu Ubayda said: "They are two dialects." And as evidence for the assimilated form, they quoted the verse of Muzahim al-Uqayli:

"So leave that aside, but will you help one smitten [with love]
by the light of a lightning flash at the end of the night, a watcher?"

"Fasbir" (be steadfast) was transitive with the lam by way of tadmin (implicit borrowing of a meaning, where a verb is given the sense of another), meaning: "Remain firm through patience in His worship, for worship brings hardships, so remain firm in them." Its original transitivity is with "ala," as in His saying, "and be steadfast in it" [Ta-Ha: 132]. "Al-Samiyy" is the one who shares the name; you say, "This is your namesake," meaning, his name is like your name. So the meaning is that no one was ever named with the name of God, and the idolaters used to call their idols gods, and [they said] al-Uzza is a god, but they never applied the word Allah to any of their idols. It is reported from Ibn Abbas: "No one is named al-Rahman except Him." It has also been said: this may refer to His saying, "Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them," meaning: do you know anyone who is named or described by this description? That is, no one among the nations names anything by this name except God. Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr and Qatadah said "samiyyan" means "equal" (mithl) and "like" (shabih), and this was also reported from Ibn Abbas. Ibn Attiyah said: "Al-samiyy in the sense of the one who rivals and resembles comes from sumuww (loftiness), and this is a good view, though it does not fit the mention of Yahya." That is, [the meaning being] "We have not made for him before [Yahya] a samiyy." Others said: one says "So-and-so is the samiyy of So-and-so" when he shares the name with him, and "samiyyuhu" when he resembles him in his fine qualities and virtues. From this is the poet's saying:

"You are a namesake of al-Zubayr, but you are not
like al-Zubayr in that he has no equal, when he prevailed."

Al-Zajjaj said: "Do you know anyone who deserves to be called Creator and Capable except Him?" Al-Dahhak said: "[Samiyyan means] a son," in response to those who say, "God has begotten a son."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 19, verses 59–65 (part 1 of 2):

(p-201) ﴿Then there succeeded them a generation who neglected the prayer and followed their desires, so they will meet with error.﴾ ﴿Except for one who repents, believes, and does righteous deeds; those will enter Paradise and will not be wronged in the least.﴾ ﴿Gardens of perpetual residence, which the Most Merciful promised His servants in the unseen. Indeed, His promise is ever coming to pass.﴾ ﴿They will not hear therein any idle talk, but only "Peace." And they will have their provision therein morning and evening.﴾ ﴿That is the Paradise which We cause to inherit of Our servants whoever was mindful of Us.﴾ ﴿And We do not descend except by the command of your Lord. To Him belongs what is before us, what is behind us, and what is between that, and your Lord is not forgetful.﴾ ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them. So worship Him and be steadfast in His worship. Do you know of anyone worthy of His name?﴾

It was revealed (﴿فَخَلَفَ﴾) concerning the Jews, according to Ibn ʿAbbas and Muqatil; concerning them and the Christians, according to al-Suddi; and concerning a people of the Messenger's community who will come after the passing of its righteous ones, competing with one another in fornication, mounting one another in the alleys. This is related from Mujahid, Qatada, ʿAta', and Muhammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazi. From Wahb: they are drinkers of coffee (qahwa). The discussion of (خَلَفَ) has already preceded in al-Aʿraf.

The neglect of the prayer (إضاعَةُ الصَّلاةِ) means delaying it beyond its time. This was said by Ibn Masʿud, al-Nakhaʿi, al-Qasim ibn Mukhaymira, Mujahid, Ibrahim, and ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz. Al-Qurazi said, and al-Zajjaj chose this view: its neglect is failing to fulfil its conditions (shurut). It was also said: performing it outside congregations. It was also said: not believing it to be obligatory. It was also said: abandoning the mosques and being preoccupied with crafts and means of livelihood. The word (الشَّهَواتِ, "desires") is general, covering every object of desire that distracts from the prayer and the remembrance of God. From ʿAli: "One who builds lofty (shadid), rides showy (manzur), and wears conspicuous (mashhur) [things]."

ʿAbd Allah (ibn Masʿud), al-Hasan, Abu Razin al-Uqayli, al-Dahhak, and Ibn Miqsam read (الصَّلَواتِ) in the plural.

Al-ghayy (الغَيُّ), in the view of the Arabs, is every evil, and al-rashad is every good. The poet said:

"Whoever meets with good, people will praise his affair; and whoever goes astray will not lack a blamer for his error."

Al-Zajjaj said: it is by omission of a noun (مُضافٌ محذوف), meaning "the recompense of error," like His saying ﴿يَلْقَ أثامًا﴾ [al-Furqan: 68], meaning "the recompense of sins." Ibn Zayd said: al-ghayy is ruin and falling into calamities. ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr, Ibn Masʿud, and Kaʿb said: al-ghayy is a valley in Hell. Ibn Zayd said: it is misguidance. Al-Zamakhshari said: or (غَيًّا) means away from the path to Paradise. Al-Karmani related: pits in Hell into which pus and festering blood flow. It was also said: destruction. It was also said: evil.

It is reported by al-Akhfash that it was read (يُلَقَّوْنَ) with a dammah on the yaʾ, a fatha on the lam, and a shadda on the qaf.

﴿Except for one who repents﴾: this is an exception whose apparent character is connected (istithnaʾ muttasil). Al-Zajjaj said it is disconnected (munqati', i.e., exception not of the same category). (وَآمَنَ, "and believes"): this indicates that that neglect amounts to disbelief.

Al-Hasan read (يَدْخُلُونَ) in the active voice, and so is every instance of (يَدْخُلُونَ) in the Qur'an. Al-Zuhri, Humayd, Shayba, al-Aʿmash, Ibn Abi Layla, Ibn Mundhir, and Ibn Saʿdan also read it so here. Ibn Ghazwan related from Talha: (سَيَدْخُلُونَ), with the sin of the future tense, in the active voice.

The majority read (جَنّاتِ) in the accusative, plural, as a substitute (badal) for (الجَنَّةِ). ﴿and will not be wronged in the least﴾ is either a parenthetical insertion (iʿtiraḍ) or a circumstantial clause (hal). Al-Hasan, Abu Hayawa, ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar, al-Aʿmash, and Ahmad ibn Musa from Abu ʿAmr read (جَنّاتُ) in the nominative, plural, meaning "they are gardens." Al-Zamakhshari said: the nominative is as the subject of a nominal sentence (ibtida'), the predicate being (الَّتِي), "which." Al-Hasan ibn Hayy and ʿAli ibn Salih read (جَنَّةَ عَدْنٍ) in the accusative, singular, and it was related from al-Aʿmash; it is so in the codex of ʿAbd Allah. Al-Yamani, al-Hasan, and Ishaq al-Azraq from Hamza read (جَنَّةُ) in the nominative, singular. If (عَدْنٍ) is a proper personal name, then (الَّتِي) is an adjective (naʿt) for what is annexed to (عَدْنٍ); if the meaning is "residence," then (الَّتِي) is an apposition (badal).

Al-Zamakhshari said: (عَدْنٍ) is definite, a proper noun for the meaning of "adn," which is residence, just as they made (فَيْنَةَ), (سَحَرَ), and (أمْسِ) proper nouns, not declined, for the meanings of "a while," "dawn," and "yesterday." So "adn" became like that. Or it is a proper name for the land of Paradise, since it is a place of residence; were it not so, the substitution would not be valid, because an indefinite noun is not substituted for a definite one except when qualified; and its qualification by (الَّتِي) would not be valid.

What he mentioned is open to objection. As for his claim that (عَدْنٌ) is a proper noun for the meaning of "adn," this requires a stipulation and hearing from the Arabs; likewise the claim of a personal proper name in it. As for his words "were it not so" up to "qualified," this is not the view of the Basrans, for their view is the permissibility of substituting an indefinite noun for a definite one even if it is not qualified; this is something said by the Baghdadis, who are refuted by the evidence of usage, as we have explained in our books on grammar. So the implication he drew is invalid. As for his words "nor would its qualification by (الَّتِي) be valid," it is not necessary that (الَّتِي) be a qualifier; we have mentioned that it may be parsed as a substitution.

(بِالغَيْبِ, "in the unseen") is a circumstantial clause (hal): that is, He promised them while it was absent from them, or they were absent from it, not witnessing it. It may also be that the (ب) indicates cause: that is, through belief in the unseen and faith in it. Abu Muslim said: the meaning is those who become servants in the unseen, that is, those who worship Him in secret. The apparent reading is that (وَعْدُهُ) is a verbal noun (masdar). It was said: (مَأْتِيًّا) means (آتِيًا), "coming." It was also said: it stays with its original meaning as a passive participle (ism al-maf'ul), "something brought." Al-Zamakhshari said: (مَأْتِيًّا) is a passive form with the meaning of an active one; the more likely view is that the promise is Paradise and they come to it; or it is from your saying "he came to him with a kindness," meaning his promise was an executed promise, fulfilled. The second view, which is his saying "the more likely view," is taken from the saying of Ibn Juraij, who said: (وَعْدُهُ) here means what was promised, which is Paradise, and (مَأْتِيًّا) means that His friends come to it.

﴿except "Peace"﴾ is a disconnected exception, and it is the saying of the angels: ﴿Peace be upon you for what you endured patiently﴾ [al-Raʿd: 24]. It was also said: God greets them with peace when they enter it. The meaning of ﴿morning and evening﴾: their food comes to them twice within the length of a day and a night. Mujahid said: there is no morning or evening there, but they are brought what they desire in this world. Qatada mentioned something similar: that it is an address in terms of what the Arabs know of comfortable living. Al-Hasan said: they were addressed according to what the Arabs knew of the finest living, because many of the Arabs would find food only once a day, and most of their living came from the trees of the desert and from animals. Al-Zamakhshari said: (اللَّغْوُ) is superfluous speech and what has no benefit in it. There is a clear indication in it of the obligation to avoid idle talk and guard against it, since God declared that abode free of it, in which there is no obligation. How excellent is His saying: ﴿When they pass by idle talk, they pass by with dignity﴾ [al-Furqan: 72]; ﴿When they hear idle talk, they turn away from it﴾ [al-Qasas: 55], and so on. That is: if the greeting of some of them to others, or the greeting of the angels to them, is (لَغْوًا, "idle talk"), then they hear nothing idle except that, and this belongs to the category of the poet's saying:

"There is no fault in them except that their swords are notched by the clashing of the battalions."

Or, ﴿they will not hear therein﴾ anything except a saying in which they are safe from fault and defect, as a disconnected exception; or because the meaning of "peace" is the supplication for safety, and the abode of peace is the abode of safety, and its people have no need of supplication for safety. So its apparent meaning would be of the category of idle talk and superfluous speech, were it not for the benefit contained in the speech. He also said: there is no night or day there, but it is by estimation. Also, because the one enjoying comfort in the eyes of the Arabs is one who finds lunch and dinner. It was also said: He meant the continuity and abundance of provision, as you say: "I am with so-and-so morning and evening, and in the morning and afternoon," and you do not mean the two specific times.

Al-Jumhur read (نُورِثُ), the present tense of (أوْرَثَ). Al-Aʿmash read (نُورِثُها) with the pronoun referring to the relative pronoun made explicit. Al-Hasan, al-Aʿraj, Qatada, Ruways, Humayd, Ibn Abi ʿAbla, Abu Hayawa, and Mahbub from Abu ʿAmr read it with a fatha on the waw and shadda on the ra'. Inheritance (التَّوْرِيثُ) is a metaphor (isti'ara): Paradise remains for them as property remains for an heir from the deceased. The righteous (الأتْقِياءُ) meet their Lord, their deeds have ended, and their fruit remains, which is Paradise; so He has given them inheritance from their piety as an heir inherits property from the deceased. It was also said: they were made to inherit from Paradise the dwellings which were for the people of Hell had they obeyed.

﴿And We do not descend except by the command of your Lord.﴾ Gabriel was delayed in coming to the Messenger once, and when he came, the Messenger (ﷺ) said: "O Gabriel, I have longed for you; will you not visit us more often than you visit us?" Then this was revealed. Mujahid and al-Dahhak said: its occasion was that Gabriel (peace be upon him) was delayed in bringing the questions mentioned earlier in surat al-Kahf, and they are like those in al-Duha. (تَنَزَّلَ, "descend") is on the pattern (تَفَعَّلَ), which is for the sense of acceptance (mutawaʿa), and it is one of the meanings of (تَفَعَّلَ). You say: "We caused it to descend (nazzalnahu), so it descended (tanazzala)," and so it indicates continuity of action over an interval. It may also be used without this nuance when it has the sense of the bare form, like their saying (taʿadda al-shayʾ, "it passed over the thing") and (ʿaddāhu), and it is not an acceptance form, so (تَنَزَّلَ) means (نَزَلَ). As the poet said:

"I am not for a human, but for an angel who descended from the air of heaven, pouring down."

Al-Zamakhshari said: (التَّنَزُّلُ) has two meanings: the meaning of descent gradually, and the meaning of descent in general, like his saying: "I am not for a human," because it is the acceptance form of (نَزَّلَ); and (نَزَّلَ) may mean (أنْزَلَ, "caused to descend") and may mean gradual progression. The fitting sense for this place is descent gradually, and the meaning is that our descent happens at times, one time after another. End.

Ibn ʿAtiyya said: this (و) in His saying ﴿and We do not descend﴾ is the conjunction joining one sentence to another, linking the two statements even if their meanings are not the same. Al-Naqqash related from some people that His saying ﴿and We do not descend﴾ is connected to His saying ﴿I am only a messenger of your Lord, to give you a pure boy﴾ [Maryam: 19]; this is a weak view. End.

What appears as the connection of this verse to what precedes it is that when God mentioned the story of Zakariyya and Maryam, and mentioned Ibrahim, Musa, Ismaʿil, and Idris, and then mentioned that He bestowed favour upon them, saying ﴿and of the offspring of Ibrahim﴾ [Maryam: 58], and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was of the offspring of Ibrahim, He mentioned that after these there succeeded a generation, namely the Jews and Christians, the people of the Books; because others are not said to have "neglected the prayer." That is said only of those who had a religious law (shariʿa) in which prayer was obligated upon them by revelation from God. The Jews were the cause of the Quraysh asking the Prophet (ﷺ) those three questions, and the revelation was delayed from him, so the Quraysh and the Jews rejoiced at that. This was part of following their desires, while they knew the prophethood of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). So God revealed ﴿and We do not descend﴾ as an alert to the story of the Quraysh and the Jews, and that the origin of that story came from those later generations who neglected the prayer and followed their desires. It also serves as a conclusion to the stories of those favoured by God, addressing their noblest, Muhammad (ﷺ), and as an excuse on behalf of Gabriel (peace be upon him) to the Messenger, that the delay was not from him, since he does not descend except by the command of God. Since the cause of the delay of revelation was the story of the question, and since the Prophet (ﷺ) had not said "God willing" when answering them, and since the question stemmed from the Jews following their desires and their hidden malice, He was content to mention the outcome, which comes after mention of what their worldly desires and malice had led them to.

[p. 204] Abu al-Aliyah said: "What is before us (ma bayna al-aydi) is the whole of this world up to the first blast (al-nafkha al-ula). What is behind us (ma khalfa dhalika) is the Hereafter from the time of resurrection (al-ba'th). What is between them (ma bayna dhalika) is what lies between the two blasts (al-nafkhatayn)." Ibn Attiyah said: "Abu al-Aliyah's statement can only be conceived with regard to the children of Adam, whereas this saying belongs to the angels, so reflect on it." Ibn Juraij said: "What is before us is the time that passed before creation (al-ijad), what is behind us is what comes after their death until the endurance of the Hereafter, and what is between them is the duration of life." In the book al-Tahrir wal-Tahbir, [it is reported that] "what is before us" is the Hereafter, and "what is behind us" is this world, transmitted by al-Awfi from Ibn Abbas, and Ibn Jubayr, Qatadah, Muqatil and Sufyan said the same. Mujahid said the reverse of this. Al-Akhfash said: "What is before us" is before we were created, "what is behind us" is after annihilation, and "what is between that" is what lies between this world and the Hereafter. Mujahid, Ikrimah and Abu al-Aliyah said: it is what lies between the two blasts. Al-Akhfash said: [it means] the time of our existence. The author of al-Ghuniyan said: "What is before us" is the descent of the angels from the heaven, "what is behind us" is [their ascent] from the earth, and "what is between that" is what lies between heaven and earth. Ibn al-Qushayri said the same as Ibn Juraij, then said: [this verse] encompasses the three times, all of which belong to God, who originates them and manages their affairs as He wills, by sending down or delaying [as He chooses]. End of quotation. There is some abridgement and rephrasing in it.

Ibn Attiyah said: "The purpose is only to convey that God, exalted is He, owns His angels, and that their little and much activity is only by His command, and their movement from place to place is only by His wisdom, since places belong to Him and they belong to Him. If one takes the verse to mean that 'what is before us and what is behind us' refers to the places in which they act, and 'what is between that' refers to themselves and their stations, it would be a valid interpretation, as if they said: 'We are bound by power; we do not move or descend except by the command of your Lord.'" End of quotation. What Ibn Attiyah said about "lahu" (to Him) and so on, al-Zamakhshari also took in a similar direction. He said: "To Him belongs what is in front of us and behind us of directions and places, and what we are in; so we cannot move from one direction to another, or from one place to another, except by the command and will of the King. The meaning is that He encompasses everything, and no hidden thing is concealed from Him. How then could we undertake an action we originate except as issuing from what His wisdom requires, and what He commands and permits us to do?" End of quotation. Al-Baghawi said: "To Him is the knowledge of what is before us."

Abu Muslim and Ibn Bahr said: "We do not descend" (wa ma natanazzalu), and the verse that follows, is not the speech of the angels, but the speech of the people of Paradise to one another when they enter it. It is connected to the first verse up to His saying "and what is between that," meaning: "We do not enter Paradise except by the command of your Lord; to Him belongs what is before us," that is, in Paradise, in the future, "and what is behind us," of what was in the world, "and what is between them," that is, between the two times. Al-Zamakhshari related this view, saying: "It is said that it is a quotation of the speech of the righteous when they enter Paradise, meaning: 'We do not enter Paradise except by permission from God upon us, for the reward of our deeds and His command for us to enter it, and He is the Owner of the affairs in their entirety, the past, the awaited and the present, the Gentle in deeds of goodness, the Granter of success in them, and the One who rewards for them.'"

Then He, exalted is He, said, affirming for them: "And your Lord was never forgetful" (wa ma kana rabbuka nasiyyan), meaning, unaware of the deeds of those who act, or heedless of what they ought to be rewarded for. How could forgetfulness or heedlessness be permitted for the Lord of the kingdom of the heavens and the earth and what is between them? End of quotation. The judge (al-Qadi) said: "This contradicts the apparent meaning in several respects:

"The first: the apparent meaning of the revelation is the descent of the angels to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, and [this is shown by] His saying 'by the command of your Lord'; the apparent sense of a command fits the context of obligation (al-taklif) better.

"The second: it is an address from a group to one person, and that is not fitting for speech among some of them to others in Paradise.

"The third: what is in its context, 'And your Lord was never forgetful, Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them,' is not fitting for the context of obligation, nor is it attributed to the Messenger." End of quotation.

The reciters (al-Jumhur) read "wa ma natanazzalu" with the nun, meaning Gabriel himself and the angels. Al-A'raj read it with the ya', as a report from God. It has been said that the pronoun in "yatanazzalu" [al-Talaq: 12] refers to Gabriel, peace be upon him. Ibn Attiyah said: "But 'lahu ma bayna aydina' refutes this, because it does not hold consistently with it. The only plausible reading is that it is a report about Gabriel: that the Qur'an does not descend except by God's command, at the times He determines." Al-Zamakhshari also said this as a quotation of Gabriel, with the pronoun referring to the revelation. End of quotation. This saying may be understood with an implied element: that is, "And Gabriel does not descend except by the command of your Lord, saying, 'To Him belongs what is before us...'" meaning he says this by way of excusing the delay on his part, that your Lord disposes of us, and we have no authority to act except by His will; and it is an announcement that He, exalted is He, does not forget you even if the revelation is delayed from you.

"Lord of the heavens and the earth" is in the nominative either as an apposition (badal) or as the predicate of an omitted subject. The majority read "hal ta'lamu" with the lam clearly pronounced before the ta'. Al-Akhawan (Hamzah and al-Kisa'i), Hisham, Ali ibn Nasr and Harun, both from Abu Amr, al-Hasan, al-A'mash, Isa and Ibn Muhaysin read both with idgham (assimilation of the lam into the ta') in both places. Abu Ubayda said: "They are two dialects." And as evidence for the assimilated form, they quoted the verse of Muzahim al-Uqayli:

"So leave that aside, but will you help one smitten [with love]
by the light of a lightning flash at the end of the night, a watcher?"

"Fasbir" (be steadfast) was transitive with the lam by way of tadmin (implicit borrowing of a meaning, where a verb is given the sense of another), meaning: "Remain firm through patience in His worship, for worship brings hardships, so remain firm in them." Its original transitivity is with "ala," as in His saying, "and be steadfast in it" [Ta-Ha: 132]. "Al-Samiyy" is the one who shares the name; you say, "This is your namesake," meaning, his name is like your name. So the meaning is that no one was ever named with the name of God, and the idolaters used to call their idols gods, and [they said] al-Uzza is a god, but they never applied the word Allah to any of their idols. It is reported from Ibn Abbas: "No one is named al-Rahman except Him." It has also been said: this may refer to His saying, "Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them," meaning: do you know anyone who is named or described by this description? That is, no one among the nations names anything by this name except God. Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr and Qatadah said "samiyyan" means "equal" (mithl) and "like" (shabih), and this was also reported from Ibn Abbas. Ibn Attiyah said: "Al-samiyy in the sense of the one who rivals and resembles comes from sumuww (loftiness), and this is a good view, though it does not fit the mention of Yahya." That is, [the meaning being] "We have not made for him before [Yahya] a samiyy." Others said: one says "So-and-so is the samiyy of So-and-so" when he shares the name with him, and "samiyyuhu" when he resembles him in his fine qualities and virtues. From this is the poet's saying:

"You are a namesake of al-Zubayr, but you are not
like al-Zubayr in that he has no equal, when he prevailed."

Al-Zajjaj said: "Do you know anyone who deserves to be called Creator and Capable except Him?" Al-Dahhak said: "[Samiyyan means] a son," in response to those who say, "God has begotten a son."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 19, verses 59–65 (part 1 of 2):

(p-201) ﴿Then there succeeded them a generation who neglected the prayer and followed their desires, so they will meet with error.﴾ ﴿Except for one who repents, believes, and does righteous deeds; those will enter Paradise and will not be wronged in the least.﴾ ﴿Gardens of perpetual residence, which the Most Merciful promised His servants in the unseen. Indeed, His promise is ever coming to pass.﴾ ﴿They will not hear therein any idle talk, but only "Peace." And they will have their provision therein morning and evening.﴾ ﴿That is the Paradise which We cause to inherit of Our servants whoever was mindful of Us.﴾ ﴿And We do not descend except by the command of your Lord. To Him belongs what is before us, what is behind us, and what is between that, and your Lord is not forgetful.﴾ ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them. So worship Him and be steadfast in His worship. Do you know of anyone worthy of His name?﴾

It was revealed (﴿فَخَلَفَ﴾) concerning the Jews, according to Ibn ʿAbbas and Muqatil; concerning them and the Christians, according to al-Suddi; and concerning a people of the Messenger's community who will come after the passing of its righteous ones, competing with one another in fornication, mounting one another in the alleys. This is related from Mujahid, Qatada, ʿAta', and Muhammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazi. From Wahb: they are drinkers of coffee (qahwa). The discussion of (خَلَفَ) has already preceded in al-Aʿraf.

The neglect of the prayer (إضاعَةُ الصَّلاةِ) means delaying it beyond its time. This was said by Ibn Masʿud, al-Nakhaʿi, al-Qasim ibn Mukhaymira, Mujahid, Ibrahim, and ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz. Al-Qurazi said, and al-Zajjaj chose this view: its neglect is failing to fulfil its conditions (shurut). It was also said: performing it outside congregations. It was also said: not believing it to be obligatory. It was also said: abandoning the mosques and being preoccupied with crafts and means of livelihood. The word (الشَّهَواتِ, "desires") is general, covering every object of desire that distracts from the prayer and the remembrance of God. From ʿAli: "One who builds lofty (shadid), rides showy (manzur), and wears conspicuous (mashhur) [things]."

ʿAbd Allah (ibn Masʿud), al-Hasan, Abu Razin al-Uqayli, al-Dahhak, and Ibn Miqsam read (الصَّلَواتِ) in the plural.

Al-ghayy (الغَيُّ), in the view of the Arabs, is every evil, and al-rashad is every good. The poet said:

"Whoever meets with good, people will praise his affair; and whoever goes astray will not lack a blamer for his error."

Al-Zajjaj said: it is by omission of a noun (مُضافٌ محذوف), meaning "the recompense of error," like His saying ﴿يَلْقَ أثامًا﴾ [al-Furqan: 68], meaning "the recompense of sins." Ibn Zayd said: al-ghayy is ruin and falling into calamities. ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr, Ibn Masʿud, and Kaʿb said: al-ghayy is a valley in Hell. Ibn Zayd said: it is misguidance. Al-Zamakhshari said: or (غَيًّا) means away from the path to Paradise. Al-Karmani related: pits in Hell into which pus and festering blood flow. It was also said: destruction. It was also said: evil.

It is reported by al-Akhfash that it was read (يُلَقَّوْنَ) with a dammah on the yaʾ, a fatha on the lam, and a shadda on the qaf.

﴿Except for one who repents﴾: this is an exception whose apparent character is connected (istithnaʾ muttasil). Al-Zajjaj said it is disconnected (munqati', i.e., exception not of the same category). (وَآمَنَ, "and believes"): this indicates that that neglect amounts to disbelief.

Al-Hasan read (يَدْخُلُونَ) in the active voice, and so is every instance of (يَدْخُلُونَ) in the Qur'an. Al-Zuhri, Humayd, Shayba, al-Aʿmash, Ibn Abi Layla, Ibn Mundhir, and Ibn Saʿdan also read it so here. Ibn Ghazwan related from Talha: (سَيَدْخُلُونَ), with the sin of the future tense, in the active voice.

The majority read (جَنّاتِ) in the accusative, plural, as a substitute (badal) for (الجَنَّةِ). ﴿and will not be wronged in the least﴾ is either a parenthetical insertion (iʿtiraḍ) or a circumstantial clause (hal). Al-Hasan, Abu Hayawa, ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar, al-Aʿmash, and Ahmad ibn Musa from Abu ʿAmr read (جَنّاتُ) in the nominative, plural, meaning "they are gardens." Al-Zamakhshari said: the nominative is as the subject of a nominal sentence (ibtida'), the predicate being (الَّتِي), "which." Al-Hasan ibn Hayy and ʿAli ibn Salih read (جَنَّةَ عَدْنٍ) in the accusative, singular, and it was related from al-Aʿmash; it is so in the codex of ʿAbd Allah. Al-Yamani, al-Hasan, and Ishaq al-Azraq from Hamza read (جَنَّةُ) in the nominative, singular. If (عَدْنٍ) is a proper personal name, then (الَّتِي) is an adjective (naʿt) for what is annexed to (عَدْنٍ); if the meaning is "residence," then (الَّتِي) is an apposition (badal).

Al-Zamakhshari said: (عَدْنٍ) is definite, a proper noun for the meaning of "adn," which is residence, just as they made (فَيْنَةَ), (سَحَرَ), and (أمْسِ) proper nouns, not declined, for the meanings of "a while," "dawn," and "yesterday." So "adn" became like that. Or it is a proper name for the land of Paradise, since it is a place of residence; were it not so, the substitution would not be valid, because an indefinite noun is not substituted for a definite one except when qualified; and its qualification by (الَّتِي) would not be valid.

What he mentioned is open to objection. As for his claim that (عَدْنٌ) is a proper noun for the meaning of "adn," this requires a stipulation and hearing from the Arabs; likewise the claim of a personal proper name in it. As for his words "were it not so" up to "qualified," this is not the view of the Basrans, for their view is the permissibility of substituting an indefinite noun for a definite one even if it is not qualified; this is something said by the Baghdadis, who are refuted by the evidence of usage, as we have explained in our books on grammar. So the implication he drew is invalid. As for his words "nor would its qualification by (الَّتِي) be valid," it is not necessary that (الَّتِي) be a qualifier; we have mentioned that it may be parsed as a substitution.

(بِالغَيْبِ, "in the unseen") is a circumstantial clause (hal): that is, He promised them while it was absent from them, or they were absent from it, not witnessing it. It may also be that the (ب) indicates cause: that is, through belief in the unseen and faith in it. Abu Muslim said: the meaning is those who become servants in the unseen, that is, those who worship Him in secret. The apparent reading is that (وَعْدُهُ) is a verbal noun (masdar). It was said: (مَأْتِيًّا) means (آتِيًا), "coming." It was also said: it stays with its original meaning as a passive participle (ism al-maf'ul), "something brought." Al-Zamakhshari said: (مَأْتِيًّا) is a passive form with the meaning of an active one; the more likely view is that the promise is Paradise and they come to it; or it is from your saying "he came to him with a kindness," meaning his promise was an executed promise, fulfilled. The second view, which is his saying "the more likely view," is taken from the saying of Ibn Juraij, who said: (وَعْدُهُ) here means what was promised, which is Paradise, and (مَأْتِيًّا) means that His friends come to it.

﴿except "Peace"﴾ is a disconnected exception, and it is the saying of the angels: ﴿Peace be upon you for what you endured patiently﴾ [al-Raʿd: 24]. It was also said: God greets them with peace when they enter it. The meaning of ﴿morning and evening﴾: their food comes to them twice within the length of a day and a night. Mujahid said: there is no morning or evening there, but they are brought what they desire in this world. Qatada mentioned something similar: that it is an address in terms of what the Arabs know of comfortable living. Al-Hasan said: they were addressed according to what the Arabs knew of the finest living, because many of the Arabs would find food only once a day, and most of their living came from the trees of the desert and from animals. Al-Zamakhshari said: (اللَّغْوُ) is superfluous speech and what has no benefit in it. There is a clear indication in it of the obligation to avoid idle talk and guard against it, since God declared that abode free of it, in which there is no obligation. How excellent is His saying: ﴿When they pass by idle talk, they pass by with dignity﴾ [al-Furqan: 72]; ﴿When they hear idle talk, they turn away from it﴾ [al-Qasas: 55], and so on. That is: if the greeting of some of them to others, or the greeting of the angels to them, is (لَغْوًا, "idle talk"), then they hear nothing idle except that, and this belongs to the category of the poet's saying:

"There is no fault in them except that their swords are notched by the clashing of the battalions."

Or, ﴿they will not hear therein﴾ anything except a saying in which they are safe from fault and defect, as a disconnected exception; or because the meaning of "peace" is the supplication for safety, and the abode of peace is the abode of safety, and its people have no need of supplication for safety. So its apparent meaning would be of the category of idle talk and superfluous speech, were it not for the benefit contained in the speech. He also said: there is no night or day there, but it is by estimation. Also, because the one enjoying comfort in the eyes of the Arabs is one who finds lunch and dinner. It was also said: He meant the continuity and abundance of provision, as you say: "I am with so-and-so morning and evening, and in the morning and afternoon," and you do not mean the two specific times.

Al-Jumhur read (نُورِثُ), the present tense of (أوْرَثَ). Al-Aʿmash read (نُورِثُها) with the pronoun referring to the relative pronoun made explicit. Al-Hasan, al-Aʿraj, Qatada, Ruways, Humayd, Ibn Abi ʿAbla, Abu Hayawa, and Mahbub from Abu ʿAmr read it with a fatha on the waw and shadda on the ra'. Inheritance (التَّوْرِيثُ) is a metaphor (isti'ara): Paradise remains for them as property remains for an heir from the deceased. The righteous (الأتْقِياءُ) meet their Lord, their deeds have ended, and their fruit remains, which is Paradise; so He has given them inheritance from their piety as an heir inherits property from the deceased. It was also said: they were made to inherit from Paradise the dwellings which were for the people of Hell had they obeyed.

﴿And We do not descend except by the command of your Lord.﴾ Gabriel was delayed in coming to the Messenger once, and when he came, the Messenger (ﷺ) said: "O Gabriel, I have longed for you; will you not visit us more often than you visit us?" Then this was revealed. Mujahid and al-Dahhak said: its occasion was that Gabriel (peace be upon him) was delayed in bringing the questions mentioned earlier in surat al-Kahf, and they are like those in al-Duha. (تَنَزَّلَ, "descend") is on the pattern (تَفَعَّلَ), which is for the sense of acceptance (mutawaʿa), and it is one of the meanings of (تَفَعَّلَ). You say: "We caused it to descend (nazzalnahu), so it descended (tanazzala)," and so it indicates continuity of action over an interval. It may also be used without this nuance when it has the sense of the bare form, like their saying (taʿadda al-shayʾ, "it passed over the thing") and (ʿaddāhu), and it is not an acceptance form, so (تَنَزَّلَ) means (نَزَلَ). As the poet said:

"I am not for a human, but for an angel who descended from the air of heaven, pouring down."

Al-Zamakhshari said: (التَّنَزُّلُ) has two meanings: the meaning of descent gradually, and the meaning of descent in general, like his saying: "I am not for a human," because it is the acceptance form of (نَزَّلَ); and (نَزَّلَ) may mean (أنْزَلَ, "caused to descend") and may mean gradual progression. The fitting sense for this place is descent gradually, and the meaning is that our descent happens at times, one time after another. End.

Ibn ʿAtiyya said: this (و) in His saying ﴿and We do not descend﴾ is the conjunction joining one sentence to another, linking the two statements even if their meanings are not the same. Al-Naqqash related from some people that His saying ﴿and We do not descend﴾ is connected to His saying ﴿I am only a messenger of your Lord, to give you a pure boy﴾ [Maryam: 19]; this is a weak view. End.

What appears as the connection of this verse to what precedes it is that when God mentioned the story of Zakariyya and Maryam, and mentioned Ibrahim, Musa, Ismaʿil, and Idris, and then mentioned that He bestowed favour upon them, saying ﴿and of the offspring of Ibrahim﴾ [Maryam: 58], and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was of the offspring of Ibrahim, He mentioned that after these there succeeded a generation, namely the Jews and Christians, the people of the Books; because others are not said to have "neglected the prayer." That is said only of those who had a religious law (shariʿa) in which prayer was obligated upon them by revelation from God. The Jews were the cause of the Quraysh asking the Prophet (ﷺ) those three questions, and the revelation was delayed from him, so the Quraysh and the Jews rejoiced at that. This was part of following their desires, while they knew the prophethood of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). So God revealed ﴿and We do not descend﴾ as an alert to the story of the Quraysh and the Jews, and that the origin of that story came from those later generations who neglected the prayer and followed their desires. It also serves as a conclusion to the stories of those favoured by God, addressing their noblest, Muhammad (ﷺ), and as an excuse on behalf of Gabriel (peace be upon him) to the Messenger, that the delay was not from him, since he does not descend except by the command of God. Since the cause of the delay of revelation was the story of the question, and since the Prophet (ﷺ) had not said "God willing" when answering them, and since the question stemmed from the Jews following their desires and their hidden malice, He was content to mention the outcome, which comes after mention of what their worldly desires and malice had led them to.

[p. 204] Abu al-Aliyah said: "What is before us (ma bayna al-aydi) is the whole of this world up to the first blast (al-nafkha al-ula). What is behind us (ma khalfa dhalika) is the Hereafter from the time of resurrection (al-ba'th). What is between them (ma bayna dhalika) is what lies between the two blasts (al-nafkhatayn)." Ibn Attiyah said: "Abu al-Aliyah's statement can only be conceived with regard to the children of Adam, whereas this saying belongs to the angels, so reflect on it." Ibn Juraij said: "What is before us is the time that passed before creation (al-ijad), what is behind us is what comes after their death until the endurance of the Hereafter, and what is between them is the duration of life." In the book al-Tahrir wal-Tahbir, [it is reported that] "what is before us" is the Hereafter, and "what is behind us" is this world, transmitted by al-Awfi from Ibn Abbas, and Ibn Jubayr, Qatadah, Muqatil and Sufyan said the same. Mujahid said the reverse of this.
