Al-Akhfash said: "What is before us" is before we were created, "what is behind us" is after annihilation, and "what is between that" is what lies between this world and the Hereafter. Mujahid, Ikrimah and Abu al-Aliyah said: it is what lies between the two blasts. Al-Akhfash said: [it means] the time of our existence. The author of al-Ghuniyan said: "What is before us" is the descent of the angels from the heaven, "what is behind us" is [their ascent] from the earth, and "what is between that" is what lies between heaven and earth. Ibn al-Qushayri said the same as Ibn Juraij, then said: [this verse] encompasses the three times, all of which belong to God, who originates them and manages their affairs as He wills, by sending down or delaying [as He chooses]. End of quotation. There is some abridgement and rephrasing in it.

Ibn Attiyah said: "The purpose is only to convey that God, exalted is He, owns His angels, and that their little and much activity is only by His command, and their movement from place to place is only by His wisdom, since places belong to Him and they belong to Him. If one takes the verse to mean that 'what is before us and what is behind us' refers to the places in which they act, and 'what is between that' refers to themselves and their stations, it would be a valid interpretation, as if they said: 'We are bound by power; we do not move or descend except by the command of your Lord.'" End of quotation. What Ibn Attiyah said about "lahu" (to Him) and so on, al-Zamakhshari also took in a similar direction. He said: "To Him belongs what is in front of us and behind us of directions and places, and what we are in; so we cannot move from one direction to another, or from one place to another, except by the command and will of the King. The meaning is that He encompasses everything, and no hidden thing is concealed from Him. How then could we undertake an action we originate except as issuing from what His wisdom requires, and what He commands and permits us to do?" End of quotation. Al-Baghawi said: "To Him is the knowledge of what is before us."

Abu Muslim and Ibn Bahr said: "We do not descend" (wa ma natanazzalu), and the verse that follows, is not the speech of the angels, but the speech of the people of Paradise to one another when they enter it. It is connected to the first verse up to His saying "and what is between that," meaning: "We do not enter Paradise except by the command of your Lord; to Him belongs what is before us," that is, in Paradise, in the future, "and what is behind us," of what was in the world, "and what is between them," that is, between the two times. Al-Zamakhshari related this view, saying: "It is said that it is a quotation of the speech of the righteous when they enter Paradise, meaning: 'We do not enter Paradise except by permission from God upon us, for the reward of our deeds and His command for us to enter it, and He is the Owner of the affairs in their entirety, the past, the awaited and the present, the Gentle in deeds of goodness, the Granter of success in them, and the One who rewards for them.'"

Then He, exalted is He, said, affirming for them: "And your Lord was never forgetful" (wa ma kana rabbuka nasiyyan), meaning, unaware of the deeds of those who act, or heedless of what they ought to be rewarded for. How could forgetfulness or heedlessness be permitted for the Lord of the kingdom of the heavens and the earth and what is between them? End of quotation. The judge (al-Qadi) said: "This contradicts the apparent meaning in several respects:

"The first: the apparent meaning of the revelation is the descent of the angels to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, and [this is shown by] His saying 'by the command of your Lord'; the apparent sense of a command fits the context of obligation (al-taklif) better.

"The second: it is an address from a group to one person, and that is not fitting for speech among some of them to others in Paradise.

"The third: what is in its context, 'And your Lord was never forgetful, Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them,' is not fitting for the context of obligation, nor is it attributed to the Messenger." End of quotation.

The reciters (al-Jumhur) read "wa ma natanazzalu" with the nun, meaning Gabriel himself and the angels. Al-A'raj read it with the ya', as a report from God. It has been said that the pronoun in "yatanazzalu" [al-Talaq: 12] refers to Gabriel, peace be upon him. Ibn Attiyah said: "But 'lahu ma bayna aydina' refutes this, because it does not hold consistently with it. The only plausible reading is that it is a report about Gabriel: that the Qur'an does not descend except by God's command, at the times He determines." Al-Zamakhshari also said this as a quotation of Gabriel, with the pronoun referring to the revelation. End of quotation. This saying may be understood with an implied element: that is, "And Gabriel does not descend except by the command of your Lord, saying, 'To Him belongs what is before us...'" meaning he says this by way of excusing the delay on his part, that your Lord disposes of us, and we have no authority to act except by His will; and it is an announcement that He, exalted is He, does not forget you even if the revelation is delayed from you.

"Lord of the heavens and the earth" is in the nominative either as an apposition (badal) or as the predicate of an omitted subject. The majority read "hal ta'lamu" with the lam clearly pronounced before the ta'. Al-Akhawan (Hamzah and al-Kisa'i), Hisham, Ali ibn Nasr and Harun, both from Abu Amr, al-Hasan, al-A'mash, Isa and Ibn Muhaysin read both with idgham (assimilation of the lam into the ta') in both places. Abu Ubayda said: "They are two dialects." And as evidence for the assimilated form, they quoted the verse of Muzahim al-Uqayli:

"So leave that aside, but will you help one smitten [with love]
by the light of a lightning flash at the end of the night, a watcher?"

"Fasbir" (be steadfast) was transitive with the lam by way of tadmin (implicit borrowing of a meaning, where a verb is given the sense of another), meaning: "Remain firm through patience in His worship, for worship brings hardships, so remain firm in them." Its original transitivity is with "ala," as in His saying, "and be steadfast in it" [Ta-Ha: 132]. "Al-Samiyy" is the one who shares the name; you say, "This is your namesake," meaning, his name is like your name. So the meaning is that no one was ever named with the name of God, and the idolaters used to call their idols gods, and [they said] al-Uzza is a god, but they never applied the word Allah to any of their idols. It is reported from Ibn Abbas: "No one is named al-Rahman except Him." It has also been said: this may refer to His saying, "Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them," meaning: do you know anyone who is named or described by this description? That is, no one among the nations names anything by this name except God. Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr and Qatadah said "samiyyan" means "equal" (mithl) and "like" (shabih), and this was also reported from Ibn Abbas. Ibn Attiyah said: "Al-samiyy in the sense of the one who rivals and resembles comes from sumuww (loftiness), and this is a good view, though it does not fit the mention of Yahya." That is, [the meaning being] "We have not made for him before [Yahya] a samiyy." Others said: one says "So-and-so is the samiyy of So-and-so" when he shares the name with him, and "samiyyuhu" when he resembles him in his fine qualities and virtues. From this is the poet's saying:

"You are a namesake of al-Zubayr, but you are not
like al-Zubayr in that he has no equal, when he prevailed."

Al-Zajjaj said: "Do you know anyone who deserves to be called Creator and Capable except Him?" Al-Dahhak said: "[Samiyyan means] a son," in response to those who say, "God has begotten a son."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 19, verses 59–65 (part 1 of 2):

(p-201) ﴿Then there succeeded them a generation who neglected the prayer and followed their desires, so they will meet with error.﴾ ﴿Except for one who repents, believes, and does righteous deeds; those will enter Paradise and will not be wronged in the least.﴾ ﴿Gardens of perpetual residence, which the Most Merciful promised His servants in the unseen. Indeed, His promise is ever coming to pass.﴾ ﴿They will not hear therein any idle talk, but only "Peace." And they will have their provision therein morning and evening.﴾ ﴿That is the Paradise which We cause to inherit of Our servants whoever was mindful of Us.﴾ ﴿And We do not descend except by the command of your Lord. To Him belongs what is before us, what is behind us, and what is between that, and your Lord is not forgetful.﴾ ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them. So worship Him and be steadfast in His worship. Do you know of anyone worthy of His name?﴾

It was revealed (﴿فَخَلَفَ﴾) concerning the Jews, according to Ibn ʿAbbas and Muqatil; concerning them and the Christians, according to al-Suddi; and concerning a people of the Messenger's community who will come after the passing of its righteous ones, competing with one another in fornication, mounting one another in the alleys. This is related from Mujahid, Qatada, ʿAta', and Muhammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazi. From Wahb: they are drinkers of coffee (qahwa). The discussion of (خَلَفَ) has already preceded in al-Aʿraf.

The neglect of the prayer (إضاعَةُ الصَّلاةِ) means delaying it beyond its time. This was said by Ibn Masʿud, al-Nakhaʿi, al-Qasim ibn Mukhaymira, Mujahid, Ibrahim, and ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz. Al-Qurazi said, and al-Zajjaj chose this view: its neglect is failing to fulfil its conditions (shurut). It was also said: performing it outside congregations. It was also said: not believing it to be obligatory. It was also said: abandoning the mosques and being preoccupied with crafts and means of livelihood. The word (الشَّهَواتِ, "desires") is general, covering every object of desire that distracts from the prayer and the remembrance of God. From ʿAli: "One who builds lofty (shadid), rides showy (manzur), and wears conspicuous (mashhur) [things]."

ʿAbd Allah (ibn Masʿud), al-Hasan, Abu Razin al-Uqayli, al-Dahhak, and Ibn Miqsam read (الصَّلَواتِ) in the plural.

Al-ghayy (الغَيُّ), in the view of the Arabs, is every evil, and al-rashad is every good. The poet said:

"Whoever meets with good, people will praise his affair; and whoever goes astray will not lack a blamer for his error."

Al-Zajjaj said: it is by omission of a noun (مُضافٌ محذوف), meaning "the recompense of error," like His saying ﴿يَلْقَ أثامًا﴾ [al-Furqan: 68], meaning "the recompense of sins." Ibn Zayd said: al-ghayy is ruin and falling into calamities. ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr, Ibn Masʿud, and Kaʿb said: al-ghayy is a valley in Hell. Ibn Zayd said: it is misguidance. Al-Zamakhshari said: or (غَيًّا) means away from the path to Paradise. Al-Karmani related: pits in Hell into which pus and festering blood flow. It was also said: destruction. It was also said: evil.

It is reported by al-Akhfash that it was read (يُلَقَّوْنَ) with a dammah on the yaʾ, a fatha on the lam, and a shadda on the qaf.

﴿Except for one who repents﴾: this is an exception whose apparent character is connected (istithnaʾ muttasil). Al-Zajjaj said it is disconnected (munqati', i.e., exception not of the same category). (وَآمَنَ, "and believes"): this indicates that that neglect amounts to disbelief.

Al-Hasan read (يَدْخُلُونَ) in the active voice, and so is every instance of (يَدْخُلُونَ) in the Qur'an. Al-Zuhri, Humayd, Shayba, al-Aʿmash, Ibn Abi Layla, Ibn Mundhir, and Ibn Saʿdan also read it so here. Ibn Ghazwan related from Talha: (سَيَدْخُلُونَ), with the sin of the future tense, in the active voice.

The majority read (جَنّاتِ) in the accusative, plural, as a substitute (badal) for (الجَنَّةِ). ﴿and will not be wronged in the least﴾ is either a parenthetical insertion (iʿtiraḍ) or a circumstantial clause (hal). Al-Hasan, Abu Hayawa, ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar, al-Aʿmash, and Ahmad ibn Musa from Abu ʿAmr read (جَنّاتُ) in the nominative, plural, meaning "they are gardens." Al-Zamakhshari said: the nominative is as the subject of a nominal sentence (ibtida'), the predicate being (الَّتِي), "which." Al-Hasan ibn Hayy and ʿAli ibn Salih read (جَنَّةَ عَدْنٍ) in the accusative, singular, and it was related from al-Aʿmash; it is so in the codex of ʿAbd Allah. Al-Yamani, al-Hasan, and Ishaq al-Azraq from Hamza read (جَنَّةُ) in the nominative, singular. If (عَدْنٍ) is a proper personal name, then (الَّتِي) is an adjective (naʿt) for what is annexed to (عَدْنٍ); if the meaning is "residence," then (الَّتِي) is an apposition (badal).

Al-Zamakhshari said: (عَدْنٍ) is definite, a proper noun for the meaning of "adn," which is residence, just as they made (فَيْنَةَ), (سَحَرَ), and (أمْسِ) proper nouns, not declined, for the meanings of "a while," "dawn," and "yesterday." So "adn" became like that. Or it is a proper name for the land of Paradise, since it is a place of residence; were it not so, the substitution would not be valid, because an indefinite noun is not substituted for a definite one except when qualified; and its qualification by (الَّتِي) would not be valid.

What he mentioned is open to objection. As for his claim that (عَدْنٌ) is a proper noun for the meaning of "adn," this requires a stipulation and hearing from the Arabs; likewise the claim of a personal proper name in it. As for his words "were it not so" up to "qualified," this is not the view of the Basrans, for their view is the permissibility of substituting an indefinite noun for a definite one even if it is not qualified; this is something said by the Baghdadis, who are refuted by the evidence of usage, as we have explained in our books on grammar. So the implication he drew is invalid. As for his words "nor would its qualification by (الَّتِي) be valid," it is not necessary that (الَّتِي) be a qualifier; we have mentioned that it may be parsed as a substitution.

(بِالغَيْبِ, "in the unseen") is a circumstantial clause (hal): that is, He promised them while it was absent from them, or they were absent from it, not witnessing it. It may also be that the (ب) indicates cause: that is, through belief in the unseen and faith in it. Abu Muslim said: the meaning is those who become servants in the unseen, that is, those who worship Him in secret. The apparent reading is that (وَعْدُهُ) is a verbal noun (masdar). It was said: (مَأْتِيًّا) means (آتِيًا), "coming." It was also said: it stays with its original meaning as a passive participle (ism al-maf'ul), "something brought." Al-Zamakhshari said: (مَأْتِيًّا) is a passive form with the meaning of an active one; the more likely view is that the promise is Paradise and they come to it; or it is from your saying "he came to him with a kindness," meaning his promise was an executed promise, fulfilled. The second view, which is his saying "the more likely view," is taken from the saying of Ibn Juraij, who said: (وَعْدُهُ) here means what was promised, which is Paradise, and (مَأْتِيًّا) means that His friends come to it.

﴿except "Peace"﴾ is a disconnected exception, and it is the saying of the angels: ﴿Peace be upon you for what you endured patiently﴾ [al-Raʿd: 24]. It was also said: God greets them with peace when they enter it. The meaning of ﴿morning and evening﴾: their food comes to them twice within the length of a day and a night. Mujahid said: there is no morning or evening there, but they are brought what they desire in this world. Qatada mentioned something similar: that it is an address in terms of what the Arabs know of comfortable living. Al-Hasan said: they were addressed according to what the Arabs knew of the finest living, because many of the Arabs would find food only once a day, and most of their living came from the trees of the desert and from animals. Al-Zamakhshari said: (اللَّغْوُ) is superfluous speech and what has no benefit in it. There is a clear indication in it of the obligation to avoid idle talk and guard against it, since God declared that abode free of it, in which there is no obligation. How excellent is His saying: ﴿When they pass by idle talk, they pass by with dignity﴾ [al-Furqan: 72]; ﴿When they hear idle talk, they turn away from it﴾ [al-Qasas: 55], and so on. That is: if the greeting of some of them to others, or the greeting of the angels to them, is (لَغْوًا, "idle talk"), then they hear nothing idle except that, and this belongs to the category of the poet's saying:

"There is no fault in them except that their swords are notched by the clashing of the battalions."

Or, ﴿they will not hear therein﴾ anything except a saying in which they are safe from fault and defect, as a disconnected exception; or because the meaning of "peace" is the supplication for safety, and the abode of peace is the abode of safety, and its people have no need of supplication for safety. So its apparent meaning would be of the category of idle talk and superfluous speech, were it not for the benefit contained in the speech. He also said: there is no night or day there, but it is by estimation. Also, because the one enjoying comfort in the eyes of the Arabs is one who finds lunch and dinner. It was also said: He meant the continuity and abundance of provision, as you say: "I am with so-and-so morning and evening, and in the morning and afternoon," and you do not mean the two specific times.

Al-Jumhur read (نُورِثُ), the present tense of (أوْرَثَ). Al-Aʿmash read (نُورِثُها) with the pronoun referring to the relative pronoun made explicit. Al-Hasan, al-Aʿraj, Qatada, Ruways, Humayd, Ibn Abi ʿAbla, Abu Hayawa, and Mahbub from Abu ʿAmr read it with a fatha on the waw and shadda on the ra'. Inheritance (التَّوْرِيثُ) is a metaphor (isti'ara): Paradise remains for them as property remains for an heir from the deceased. The righteous (الأتْقِياءُ) meet their Lord, their deeds have ended, and their fruit remains, which is Paradise; so He has given them inheritance from their piety as an heir inherits property from the deceased. It was also said: they were made to inherit from Paradise the dwellings which were for the people of Hell had they obeyed.

﴿And We do not descend except by the command of your Lord.﴾ Gabriel was delayed in coming to the Messenger once, and when he came, the Messenger (ﷺ) said: "O Gabriel, I have longed for you; will you not visit us more often than you visit us?" Then this was revealed. Mujahid and al-Dahhak said: its occasion was that Gabriel (peace be upon him) was delayed in bringing the questions mentioned earlier in surat al-Kahf, and they are like those in al-Duha. (تَنَزَّلَ, "descend") is on the pattern (تَفَعَّلَ), which is for the sense of acceptance (mutawaʿa), and it is one of the meanings of (تَفَعَّلَ). You say: "We caused it to descend (nazzalnahu), so it descended (tanazzala)," and so it indicates continuity of action over an interval. It may also be used without this nuance when it has the sense of the bare form, like their saying (taʿadda al-shayʾ, "it passed over the thing") and (ʿaddāhu), and it is not an acceptance form, so (تَنَزَّلَ) means (نَزَلَ). As the poet said:

"I am not for a human, but for an angel who descended from the air of heaven, pouring down."

Al-Zamakhshari said: (التَّنَزُّلُ) has two meanings: the meaning of descent gradually, and the meaning of descent in general, like his saying: "I am not for a human," because it is the acceptance form of (نَزَّلَ); and (نَزَّلَ) may mean (أنْزَلَ, "caused to descend") and may mean gradual progression. The fitting sense for this place is descent gradually, and the meaning is that our descent happens at times, one time after another. End.

Ibn ʿAtiyya said: this (و) in His saying ﴿and We do not descend﴾ is the conjunction joining one sentence to another, linking the two statements even if their meanings are not the same. Al-Naqqash related from some people that His saying ﴿and We do not descend﴾ is connected to His saying ﴿I am only a messenger of your Lord, to give you a pure boy﴾ [Maryam: 19]; this is a weak view. End.

What appears as the connection of this verse to what precedes it is that when God mentioned the story of Zakariyya and Maryam, and mentioned Ibrahim, Musa, Ismaʿil, and Idris, and then mentioned that He bestowed favour upon them, saying ﴿and of the offspring of Ibrahim﴾ [Maryam: 58], and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was of the offspring of Ibrahim, He mentioned that after these there succeeded a generation, namely the Jews and Christians, the people of the Books; because others are not said to have "neglected the prayer." That is said only of those who had a religious law (shariʿa) in which prayer was obligated upon them by revelation from God. The Jews were the cause of the Quraysh asking the Prophet (ﷺ) those three questions, and the revelation was delayed from him, so the Quraysh and the Jews rejoiced at that. This was part of following their desires, while they knew the prophethood of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). So God revealed ﴿and We do not descend﴾ as an alert to the story of the Quraysh and the Jews, and that the origin of that story came from those later generations who neglected the prayer and followed their desires. It also serves as a conclusion to the stories of those favoured by God, addressing their noblest, Muhammad (ﷺ), and as an excuse on behalf of Gabriel (peace be upon him) to the Messenger, that the delay was not from him, since he does not descend except by the command of God. Since the cause of the delay of revelation was the story of the question, and since the Prophet (ﷺ) had not said "God willing" when answering them, and since the question stemmed from the Jews following their desires and their hidden malice, He was content to mention the outcome, which comes after mention of what their worldly desires and malice had led them to.

[p. 204] Abu al-Aliyah said: "What is before us (ma bayna al-aydi) is the whole of this world up to the first blast (al-nafkha al-ula). What is behind us (ma khalfa dhalika) is the Hereafter from the time of resurrection (al-ba'th). What is between them (ma bayna dhalika) is what lies between the two blasts (al-nafkhatayn)." Ibn Attiyah said: "Abu al-Aliyah's statement can only be conceived with regard to the children of Adam, whereas this saying belongs to the angels, so reflect on it." Ibn Juraij said: "What is before us is the time that passed before creation (al-ijad), what is behind us is what comes after their death until the endurance of the Hereafter, and what is between them is the duration of life." In the book al-Tahrir wal-Tahbir, [it is reported that] "what is before us" is the Hereafter, and "what is behind us" is this world, transmitted by al-Awfi from Ibn Abbas, and Ibn Jubayr, Qatadah, Muqatil and Sufyan said the same. Mujahid said the reverse of this. Al-Akhfash said: "What is before us" is before we were created, "what is behind us" is after annihilation, and "what is between that" is what lies between this world and the Hereafter. Mujahid, Ikrimah and Abu al-Aliyah said: it is what lies between the two blasts. Al-Akhfash said: [it means] the time of our existence. The author of al-Ghuniyan said: "What is before us" is the descent of the angels from the heaven, "what is behind us" is [their ascent] from the earth, and "what is between that" is what lies between heaven and earth. Ibn al-Qushayri said the same as Ibn Juraij, then said: [this verse] encompasses the three times, all of which belong to God, who originates them and manages their affairs as He wills, by sending down or delaying [as He chooses]. End of quotation. There is some abridgement and rephrasing in it.

Ibn Attiyah said: "The purpose is only to convey that God, exalted is He, owns His angels, and that their little and much activity is only by His command, and their movement from place to place is only by His wisdom, since places belong to Him and they belong to Him. If one takes the verse to mean that 'what is before us and what is behind us' refers to the places in which they act, and 'what is between that' refers to themselves and their stations, it would be a valid interpretation, as if they said: 'We are bound by power; we do not move or descend except by the command of your Lord.'" End of quotation. What Ibn Attiyah said about "lahu" (to Him) and so on, al-Zamakhshari also took in a similar direction. He said: "To Him belongs what is in front of us and behind us of directions and places, and what we are in; so we cannot move from one direction to another, or from one place to another, except by the command and will of the King. The meaning is that He encompasses everything, and no hidden thing is concealed from Him. How then could we undertake an action we originate except as issuing from what His wisdom requires, and what He commands and permits us to do?" End of quotation. Al-Baghawi said: "To Him is the knowledge of what is before us."

Abu Muslim and Ibn Bahr said: "We do not descend" (wa ma natanazzalu), and the verse that follows, is not the speech of the angels, but the speech of the people of Paradise to one another when they enter it. It is connected to the first verse up to His saying "and what is between that," meaning: "We do not enter Paradise except by the command of your Lord; to Him belongs what is before us," that is, in Paradise, in the future, "and what is behind us," of what was in the world, "and what is between them," that is, between the two times. Al-Zamakhshari related this view, saying: "It is said that it is a quotation of the speech of the righteous when they enter Paradise, meaning: 'We do not enter Paradise except by permission from God upon us, for the reward of our deeds and His command for us to enter it, and He is the Owner of the affairs in their entirety, the past, the awaited and the present, the Gentle in deeds of goodness, the Granter of success in them, and the One who rewards for them.'"

Then He, exalted is He, said, affirming for them: "And your Lord was never forgetful" (wa ma kana rabbuka nasiyyan), meaning, unaware of the deeds of those who act, or heedless of what they ought to be rewarded for. How could forgetfulness or heedlessness be permitted for the Lord of the kingdom of the heavens and the earth and what is between them? End of quotation. The judge (al-Qadi) said: "This contradicts the apparent meaning in several respects:

"The first: the apparent meaning of the revelation is the descent of the angels to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, and [this is shown by] His saying 'by the command of your Lord'; the apparent sense of a command fits the context of obligation (al-taklif) better.

"The second: it is an address from a group to one person, and that is not fitting for speech among some of them to others in Paradise.

"The third: what is in its context, 'And your Lord was never forgetful, Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them,' is not fitting for the context of obligation, nor is it attributed to the Messenger." End of quotation.

The reciters (al-Jumhur) read "wa ma natanazzalu" with the nun, meaning Gabriel himself and the angels. Al-A'raj read it with the ya', as a report from God. It has been said that the pronoun in "yatanazzalu" [al-Talaq: 12] refers to Gabriel, peace be upon him. Ibn Attiyah said: "But 'lahu ma bayna aydina' refutes this, because it does not hold consistently with it. The only plausible reading is that it is a report about Gabriel: that the Qur'an does not descend except by God's command, at the times He determines." Al-Zamakhshari also said this as a quotation of Gabriel, with the pronoun referring to the revelation. End of quotation. This saying may be understood with an implied element: that is, "And Gabriel does not descend except by the command of your Lord, saying, 'To Him belongs what is before us...'" meaning he says this by way of excusing the delay on his part, that your Lord disposes of us, and we have no authority to act except by His will; and it is an announcement that He, exalted is He, does not forget you even if the revelation is delayed from you.

"Lord of the heavens and the earth" is in the nominative either as an apposition (badal) or as the predicate of an omitted subject. The majority read "hal ta'lamu" with the lam clearly pronounced before the ta'. Al-Akhawan (Hamzah and al-Kisa'i), Hisham, Ali ibn Nasr and Harun, both from Abu Amr, al-Hasan, al-A'mash, Isa and Ibn Muhaysin read both with idgham (assimilation of the lam into the ta') in both places. Abu Ubayda said: "They are two dialects." And as evidence for the assimilated form, they quoted the verse of Muzahim al-Uqayli:

"So leave that aside, but will you help one smitten [with love]
by the light of a lightning flash at the end of the night, a watcher?"

"Fasbir" (be steadfast) was transitive with the lam by way of tadmin (implicit borrowing of a meaning, where a verb is given the sense of another), meaning: "Remain firm through patience in His worship, for worship brings hardships, so remain firm in them." Its original transitivity is with "ala," as in His saying, "and be steadfast in it" [Ta-Ha: 132]. "Al-Samiyy" is the one who shares the name; you say, "This is your namesake," meaning, his name is like your name. So the meaning is that no one was ever named with the name of God, and the idolaters used to call their idols gods, and [they said] al-Uzza is a god, but they never applied the word Allah to any of their idols. It is reported from Ibn Abbas: "No one is named al-Rahman except Him." It has also been said: this may refer to His saying, "Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them," meaning: do you know anyone who is named or described by this description? That is, no one among the nations names anything by this name except God. Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr and Qatadah said "samiyyan" means "equal" (mithl) and "like" (shabih), and this was also reported from Ibn Abbas. Ibn Attiyah said: "Al-samiyy in the sense of the one who rivals and resembles comes from sumuww (loftiness), and this is a good view, though it does not fit the mention of Yahya." That is, [the meaning being] "We have not made for him before [Yahya] a samiyy." Others said: one says "So-and-so is the samiyy of So-and-so" when he shares the name with him, and "samiyyuhu" when he resembles him in his fine qualities and virtues. From this is the poet's saying:

"You are a namesake of al-Zubayr, but you are not
like al-Zubayr in that he has no equal, when he prevailed."

Al-Zajjaj said: "Do you know anyone who deserves to be called Creator and Capable except Him?" Al-Dahhak said: "[Samiyyan means] a son," in response to those who say, "God has begotten a son."

(p. 206) ﴿And man says, "When I have died, shall I indeed be brought forth alive?"﴾ ﴿Does not man remember that We created him before, when he was nothing?﴾ ﴿So by your Lord, We will surely gather them, and the devils too, and then We will surely bring them around Hell on their knees.﴾ ﴿Then We will surely draw out from every group whichever of them was most insolent toward the Most Merciful.﴾ ﴿Then We know best those most deserving of being burned therein.﴾ ﴿There is none of you but will come to it. That is a decree fixed by your Lord.﴾ [Maryam: 71] ﴿Then We will deliver those who were mindful of God, and leave the wrongdoers therein on their knees.﴾ [Maryam: 72] ﴿When Our clear verses are recited to them, those who disbelieved say to those who believed, "Which of the two groups is better in position and finer in assembly?"﴾ [Maryam: 73] ﴿How many generations before them have We destroyed, though they were greater in wealth and in outward show!﴾ [Maryam: 74]

It is said: the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) was that a man of Quraysh, said to be Ubayy ibn Khalaf, came with a crumbled bone, blew on it, and said to the Messenger (ﷺ): "Will this be raised up?" He denied it and mocked. The attribution of this saying to a collective (al-jins) is because it was uttered by some of them, like the words of al-Farazdaq:

"The sword of the Banu Abs, with which they struck, slipped from the two hands of Warqa' from the head of Khalid."

The striking is attributed to the Banu Abs, though what follows (slipped from the two hands of Warqa') refers to Warqa' ibn Zuhayr ibn Jadhima al-Absi. Alternatively the collective refers to the disbelieving category that denies resurrection; or the one meant is Ubayy ibn Khalaf, or al-'As ibn Wa'il, or Abu Jahl, or al-Walid ibn al-Mughira. These are the opinions.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read ﴿أئِذا﴾ with the interrogative hamza. A group including Ibn Dhakwan, according to one transmission from him, read ﴿إذا﴾ without the interrogative hamza. The majority read ﴿لَسَوْفَ﴾ with the lam. Talha ibn Musarrif read ﴿سَأُخْرَجُ﴾ without the lam and with the sin of future, in place of sawfa. On his reading, ﴿إذا﴾ is the object governed by ﴿سَأُخْرَجُ﴾, since the future particle (harf al-tanfis) does not prevent what follows it from governing what precedes it. There is an anomalous disagreement on this point, and its proponent is refuted by the attested usage. The poet said:

"When she saw him secure, her grief subsided, and she said: 'Our father, thus will he do.'"

Here ﴿هَكَذا﴾ is governed by a verb, though that verb is preceded by the future particle (sawfa). Al-Zamakhshari reports that Talha ibn Musarrif read ﴿لَسَأُخْرَجُ﴾. On the majority reading and on the reading al-Zamakhshari reports from Talha, the lam is the lam of initiation (lam al-ibtida'), so what follows it does not govern what precedes it. The governing verb is therefore taken as implied in the meaning of ﴿لَسَوْفَ أُخْرَجُ﴾, its estimated form being: "When I have died, I will be raised."

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, the lam of initiation that enters the present tense gives the meaning of the present, so how does it combine with the particle of the future? I say: it combines only as a pure emphasis, just as the hamza is purified in "ya Allah" as a compensation, and the meaning of definiteness has faded from it. End of quotation.

What is mentioned, that the lam gives the meaning of the present, is disputed. According to the view of those who do not hold this, the question falls away. As for his words "just as the hamza is purified" to the end, this holds only according to the view of those who claim that the original form is ʾilah. As for those who claim its original form is lahin, the hamza in it is not a compensation, since nothing was omitted from it. And even if we say its original is ʾilah, with the first radical of the word removed, it is not necessarily the case that the hamza in the vocative is a compensation; for if it were a compensation for something omitted, it would always remain in the vocative and elsewhere, and its omission in the vocative would not be permitted. They say "ya Allah" with its omission, and they have stated that cutting the hamza of connection (hamzat al-wasl) in the vocative is anomalous.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: The lam in His words ﴿لَسَوْفَ﴾ is brought in as a quotation of an earlier speech with this meaning, as if a speaker had said to the disbeliever: "When you die, O so-and-so, you will surely be brought forth alive." So he restated the speech in the manner of astonishment, repeating the lam as a quotation of the first saying. End of quotation. There is no need for this estimate, nor for the claim that this is a quotation of an earlier saying. Rather, this is from the disbeliever, an interrogative with the meaning of denial and rejection. As for the one who reads ﴿إذا ما﴾, the hamza may have been omitted because the meaning indicates it, or it may be a statement in the manner of mockery and derision toward the one who says it, since he did not intend that the wording correspond to the meaning.

The majority read ﴿أُخْرَجُ﴾ in the passive voice. Al-Hasan and Abu Haywa read it in the active voice.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Its placement, that is the placement of the adverbial of time (al-zarf) after the particle of denial, is because what follows death is the time when life is denied, and from this their denial arises. It is like your saying to one who does evil to a benefactor: "When the favour of so-and-so was completed upon you, did you do evil to him?"

Abu Bahriyya, al-Hasan, Shayba, Ibn Abi Layla, Ibn Munadhir, Abu Hatim, and among the Seven, ʿAsim, Ibn ʿAmir, and Nafi' read ﴿أوَلا يَذْكُرُ﴾ with a light form, as the imperfect of dhakara. The rest of the Seven read it with the dhal and the kaf vowelled with fatha and doubled, its original form being yatadhakkaru, with the ta assimilated into the dhal. Ubayy read yatadhakkaru in its original form.

Al-Zamakhshari said: The waw is conjunctive, joining ﴿لا يَذْكُرُ﴾ to ﴿يَقُولُ﴾, and the hamza of denial has been placed between the conjoined element and the conjunction. End of quotation. This is a return by him to the view of the majority, that when the interrogative hamza precedes the conjunctive particle, what follows it is conjoined to what precedes it, and the hamza is placed first because it has the front of the sentence. His own view was that between the hamza and the conjunction one should estimate something suitable to be conjoined to what follows the waw, so that the hamza remains in its place and is not a displacement from a later position. We have already refuted him on this view.

It is said: the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) was that a man of Quraysh, said to be Ubayy ibn Khalaf, came with a crumbled bone, blew on it, and said to the Messenger (ﷺ): "Will this be raised up?" He denied it and mocked. The attribution of this saying to a collective (al-jins) is because it was uttered by some of them, like the words of al-Farazdaq:

"The sword of the Banu Abs, with which they struck, slipped from the two hands of Warqa' from the head of Khalid."

The striking is attributed to the Banu Abs, though what follows (slipped from the two hands of Warqa') refers to Warqa' ibn Zuhayr ibn Jadhima al-Absi. Alternatively the collective refers to the disbelieving category that denies resurrection; or the one meant is Ubayy ibn Khalaf, or al-'As ibn Wa'il, or Abu Jahl, or al-Walid ibn al-Mughira. These are the opinions.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 19, verses 71–74 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Indeed, We created him before, when he was nothing﴾ [Maryam: 67], meaning: We brought him into being and originated him from pure non-existence into existence. So how could he deny the second creation, when this argument is extremely concise and binding upon the opponent? This type of argumentation is called the rational argument (al-ihtijaj al-nazari), and some call it the dialectical method (al-madhhab al-kalami). This argument is repeated in the Qur'an. ﴿And he was not a thing﴾ [Maryam: 67] is an allusion to pure non-existence, and the negation of thinghood from it indicates that what is non-existent is not called a thing. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: ﴿And he was not a thing﴾ [Maryam: 67] is "existent," or it is a Mu'tazili slip. The omitted noun to which (qabl, "before") is added in the sense is estimated by some as: "before his resurrection" (p-208). Al-Zamakhshari estimated it as: "before the state in which he is," which is the state of his remaining, ending quote.

When God, exalted is He, established the decisive proof for the truth of resurrection, He swore by it with His name, attributed to His Messenger, as an honouring and magnification of him. This oath is repeated in the Qur'an, as an exaltation of its truth and a raising of its status, just as He raised the status of the heaven and the earth by His saying: ﴿So by the Lord of the heaven and the earth, indeed it is the truth﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 23]. The waw in (wa-al-shayatin) is for conjunction, or it has the meaning of (ma'a, "with"): they will be gathered with their companions from the devils who misled them; each disbeliever will be coupled with a devil in a chain. This is the case when the pronoun in (la-nahshurannahum) refers to the disbelievers, and it is the view of Ibn 'Atiyya. What comes after that is informing about them, and al-Zamakhshari began with it. The apparent meaning is that it is general to all creatures, believers and disbelievers alike, and it does not distinguish between believers and disbelievers as it distinguished in the recompense. All of them are brought forth and led to the Fire so that the believers may witness the terrors from which they were saved, and thus rejoice and gloat over their disbelieving enemies. If the pronoun is general, the meaning is that they kneel down upon arriving at the edge of Hell, just as they were kneeling at the Standing-place, for it is one of the consequences of the assembly for reckoning before reaching reward and punishment. God, exalted is He, said concerning the state of the Standing-place: ﴿And you will see every nation kneeling; every nation will be called to its record﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 28]. (Jithiyyan) is a circumstantial accusative (hal muqaddarah). It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas: "sitting," and from him, by groups, (jathwah) plural, which is a gathering of dirt and stones. Mujahid, al-Hasan and al-Zajjaj said: "on their knees." Al-Suddi said: "standing on their knees," due to the narrowness of the place for them.

Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hafs read (jithiyyan), (itiyyan) and (siliyyan) with a kasra on the jim, the 'ayn and the sad, while the majority read them with a damma. ﴿Then We will surely draw out﴾ [Maryam: 69], meaning: We will surely bring out, like His saying: ﴿and he drew out his hand﴾ [al-A'raf: 108]. It is also said: We will surely throw, from "nazaʿa al-qaws" (he drew the bow), which is shooting an arrow. And (al-shi'ah) is the group bound together by one doctrine. Abu al-Ahwas said: "He begins with the greatest in sin, then the greatest." Al-Zamakhshari said: He separates from every group of the groups of error and corruption the most rebellious of them, then the most rebellious, and the most insolent, then the most insolent; when they are gathered, we throw them into the Fire in order, so the first in torment is placed first. The pronoun in (ayyuhum) refers to those gathered and brought forth. The majority read (ayyuhum) with a damma, which is a vowel of construction according to the doctrine of Sibawayh; so (ayyuhum) is an object of (la-nanza'anna) and is relative; (ashaddu) is the predicate of an omitted subject, and the clause is a relative clause of (ayyuhum). It is a vowel of inflection according to the doctrine of al-Khalil and Yunus, with differences in analysis. ﴿Which of them is most﴾ [Maryam: 69] is a subject and predicate, reported according to the doctrine of al-Khalil, meaning: those of whom it is said, "which of them is most." It is in the position of an accusative, so (la-nanza'anna) governs it as a suspended verb according to the doctrine of Yunus; the preference among these doctrines is mentioned in the science of grammar. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is possible that the drawing out falls upon ﴿from every group﴾ [Maryam: 69], like His saying: ﴿and We gave them of Our mercy﴾ [Maryam: 50], meaning: We will draw out some of ﴿every group﴾ [Maryam: 69], as if someone said: Who are they? So it was said: they are the most rebellious in insolence; end quote. Then (ayyuhum) would be relative, the predicate of an omitted subject, and this is a strained assumption and a claim of an ellipsis for which there is no necessity, and making what appears to be one clause into two clauses. Al-Khalil coupled his analysis with the verse of the poet:

"And indeed I spend the night from the young woman in a station, so I spend the night, neither blamed nor deprived."

That is, "so I spend the night" — it is said of me: "neither blamed nor deprived." Al-Zajjaj preferred the view of al-Khalil, and al-Nahhas reported from him that he considered Sibawayh to have erred in this issue. Sibawayh said: It would follow from this that one may say: "Strike the wicked thief who is called..." It was said: it does not follow, since these are single nouns and the verse is a clause, and the governance of the verb over a single noun is greater than over a clause. The doctrine of al-Kisa'i is that the meaning of (la-nanza'anna) is (la-nunadiyanna, "we will surely call out"), so it is treated as such and does not govern (ayyu) — end quote. This is reported from al-Farra'. Al-Mahdawi said: (nada) is suspended when it is followed by a clause in the accusative position, so it governs in meaning and not in wording. Al-Mubarrad said: (ayyuhum) is connected to (shi'ah), therefore it is in the nominative, and the meaning is: from those who gathered in support, "which of them is most" — as if they were competing for this; it is necessary to estimate an omitted object for (la-nanza'anna), and he also estimated in this doctrine: from those who cooperated, (ayyuhum), meaning: from those who helped one another, and they looked: "which of them is most." Al-Nahhas said: This is a good view. Al-Kisa'i reported that (tashayyu') is (ta'awun, cooperation).

Abu Bakr ibn Shuqayr related that some of the Kufans say: (ayyuhum) carries the meaning of a condition; you say: "I struck the people, whichever of them became angry," meaning: whether they became angry or did not become angry. According to this, the estimate is: whether their insolence increased or did not increase. Talhah ibn Musarrif, Mu'adh ibn Muslim al-Harra' (teacher of al-Farra'), and Za'idah from al-A'mash read (ayyahum) with a fatha as an object of (la-nanza'anna). These two readings indicate that according to the doctrine of Sibawayh, construction is not necessary in them when it is added and the first part of its relative clause is omitted; it is reported from him that construction is necessary, but it should be that in his doctrine both construction and inflection are possible. Abu 'Amr al-Jarmi said: "I left Basra and from the time I parted from the Khandaq to Makkah I did not hear anyone say: 'La-adribanna ayyuhum qa'im' with a damma, but with its fatha," end quote. Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas said: I know of no grammarian except that he has rejected Sibawayh, and I heard Abu Ishaq — meaning al-Zajjaj — say: It is not clear that Sibawayh erred in his book except in two places, and this is one of them. He said: Sibawayh inflected (ayyan), though it is singular, because it is added; so how could he build it when it is added?

﴿Upon the Most Merciful﴾ [Maryam: 69] is connected to (ashaddu). (Itiyyan) is a specifier transferred from the subject; its estimate is: "which of them, its insolence is more severe upon the Most Merciful" [Maryam: 69]. In the speech there is an omission, estimated as: "so He casts him into the most severe torment," or "so He begins with his torment, then with the one below him, down to the last of them in torment." In a hadith: "Indeed, a neck of the Fire will appear and say: I have been commanded to take every stubborn tyrant," and so it seizes them. In some reports: "They are gathered together around Hell, shackled and chained, then the most disbelieving is brought forward, then the most disbelieving." Ibn 'Abbas said: (itiyyan) means "audacity." Mujahid said: "wickedness." It was said: "slander," in the dialect of Tamim. It was said: (itiyyan) is the plural of ('at), so its accusative is as a circumstantial accusative.

﴿Then indeed We are most knowing﴾ [Maryam: 70], meaning: We, in that drawing out, do not place anything other than its place, because We have encompassed everything in knowledge, so We know who is most deserving of the burning of the Fire. Ibn Jurayj said: "most deserving of eternity." Al-Kalbi said: (siliyyan) means "entering." It was said: "remaining." It was said: it is the plural of (sali), so it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state, and (biha) is connected to (awla). The waw in His saying ﴿And there is not among you﴾ is for conjunction. Ibn 'Atiyya said: ﴿And there is not among you except that he will come to it﴾ is an oath, and the waw requires it, and the Prophet's saying explains it, ﷺ: "Whoever has three children die, the Fire will not touch him except as a passing of the oath" — end quote. He overlooked the grammarians' statement that the oath cannot be dispensed with by the answer for the meaning's indication except when the answer is with the lam or with (an); the answer here, according to his claim, came with the negating (in), so the oath may not be omitted according to what they stated. His saying "the waw requires it" indicates that it is, in his view, the waw of oath; no grammarian holds that such a waw is the waw of oath, because this would require omitting the genitive and retaining the preposition, which is not permitted except in poetry or rare speech, on condition that the description of the omitted noun stands in its place, as they interpreted in their saying: "How excellent is the journey on the wretched caravan," meaning: on a caravan which is wretched. And the poet's saying:

"By God, Zayd is not a sleeper, his companion..."

meaning: not a man who sleeps, his companion. This verse is not of this type, since the sworn-by thing was not omitted and its description did not stand in its place.

The majority read (minkum) with the second-person pronoun, and the apparent meaning is that it is general to creatures, and that "coming" is not entering for all of them. Ibn Mas'ud, al-Hasan and Qatadah said that it is the passing over the Sirat, since the Sirat is stretched over it. From Ibn 'Abbas: "It may come to a thing without entering it," like His saying: ﴿And when he came to the water of Madyan﴾ [al-Qasas: 23], and "the caravan came to the town" without entering it, but it drew near to it or reached it. The poet said:

"When they came to the water, its wells blue, they put down the staves of the one who stays, who has pitched camp."

And the Arabs say: "We came to the water of Banu Tamim and Banu Kalb," when they attended them and entered their lands, and by it is not meant the water itself. It was said: the address is to the disbelievers, that is, say to them, O Muhammad, so the coming for them is entering. According to the view of one who said that the address is general, and that believers and disbelievers both enter the Fire, but it does not harm the believers, and they mentioned the manner of the believers' entry into the Fire in a way that I do not like to transmit in this book because of the abhorrence of their saying that the believers enter the Fire (p-210) even though it does not harm them.

Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrimah and a group read (wa-in minhum) with the pronoun of absence, according to the pronouns mentioned before. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also possible that by "coming" is meant their kneeling around it; and if only the disbelievers are meant, the meaning is clear, and the subject of (kana) is a hidden pronoun returning to "coming," meaning: their coming was decreed, that is, obligatory, determined. The majority read (thumma) with the conjunctive particle, and this indicates that the coming is general. ʿAbd Allah, Ibn ʿAbbas, Ubayy, ʿAli, al-Jahdari, Ibn Abi Layla, Mu'awiyah ibn Qurrah and Ya'qub read (tharnma) with a fatha on the tha', meaning "there," and Ibn Abi Layla paused on (thammah) with the silent heh. The majority read (nunajji) with a fatha on the nun and shadda on the jim. Yahya, al-A'mash, al-Kisa'i and Ibn Muhaysin read it with a sukun on the nun and takhfif on the jim. A group read (nujji) with a single damma-vowelled nun and a shadda on the jim. ʿAli read (nunahhi), with an unpointed ha', present tense of (nahha); and the object of (ittaqaw) is omitted, meaning: the shirk and the injustice; here injustice is the injustice of disbelief.

﴿And when Our clear verses are recited to them﴾ [Maryam: 73]. It was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith and his companions. The poor among the Companions were in hardship of life and shabby clothing, while the polytheists oiled their heads, combed their hair, and wore silk and fine garments, so they said to the believers: ﴿Which of the two groups is better in station﴾ [Maryam: 73], meaning: in dwelling and abode, ﴿and better in assembly﴾ [Maryam: 73]. When He established the argument against the deniers of resurrection and followed it with what will happen on the Day of Resurrection, He informed about them that they opposed that decisive proof with the goodness of their appearance in this world, and that this, in their view, indicates their honour before God. Abu Hayyah and al-A'raj and Ibn Muhaysin read (yutla) with a ya', while the majority read it with a ta' from above. The believer used to recite the Qur'an to the disbeliever and praise the signs of the Prophet ﷺ, and the disbeliever would say: God only bestows goodness upon the most beloved of creation to Him, and bestows favour upon the people of truth, and He has favoured us over you, so we are rich and you are poor, and we have the better gathering and the more beautiful appearance.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 19, verses 71–74 (part 2 of 2):

The meaning of (bayyinat) is: with well-arranged wording, with summarized meanings, or manifestly inimitable, or proofs and evidences. (Bayyinat) is an emphatic circumstantial (hal) clause, because His signs, may He be exalted, are never anything but of this description, always.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read (maqaman) with a fatha on the mim. Ibn Kathir, Ibn Muhaysin, Humayd, al-Ju'fi and Abu Hatim, on the authority of Abu 'Amr, read it with a damma on the mim. Both the fatha and the damma allow it to be a verbal noun (masdar) or a place of standing or of establishing, and its accusative case is that of specification (tamyiz).

Then He, may He be exalted, mentioned the great number of generations He destroyed, of those who were better off than them in this world, as a warning that He destroys them and uproots their root just as He did to others, and as an admonition to them if they are among those who take admonition. The wealth and the fine appearance in which they were did not avail them. And it means the destruction of those who denied what the messengers brought. The phrase (min qarn) is a specification for "you" (lakum), and (kam) is the object of (ahlakna).

Al-Zamakhshari said: The phrase (hum ahsanu) is in a place of accusative as a qualifier of (kam). Do you not see that if you left out (hum), you would have no choice but to put (ahsana) in the accusative as a qualifier? End of quote. Abu al-Baqa' followed him in holding that (hum ahsanu) is a qualifier of (kam). Our companions (the Basran grammarians) stated explicitly that the interrogative and the informative (khabariyya) kam is neither described nor is it used as a qualifier. Accordingly, (hum ahsanu) is in the position of a qualifier for (qarn). It was made plural because the qarn comprises many individuals, so its meaning was observed; had the pronoun been made singular in accordance with the wording, it would have been correct Arabic, and it would be like the word (jami'). He said, "And all of them (jami'un) will be brought before Us" [Ya-Sin: 32], and He said, "We are a united body (jami'un) that will be victorious" [al-Qamar: 44]. So He described it with the plural and with the singular. The explanation of (athath) has already been given in Surat al-Nahl.

The majority read (wa-ri'yan) with a hamza, from the seeing of the eye (ru'yat al-'ayn), as a verbal form in the sense of a passive participle (maf'ul), like (al-tihn) and (al-siqy). Ibn 'Abbas said: al-Ri'y is the appearance (manzar). al-Hasan said: its meaning is pictures (suwaran). Al-Zuhri, Abu Ja'far, Shayba, Talha (in the narration of al-Hamdani), Ayyub, Ibn Sa'dan, Ibn Dhakwan and Qalun read (riyyan) with a doubled ya without a hamza. This may be a word originally with a hamza, from al-riwa' (fine appearance) and al-manzar, whose hamza was eased by changing it to a ya, and then the ya was assimilated into the ya. It may also be from al-rayy, the opposite of thirst, because well-watered (rayyan) water has a freshness and radiance that is desired and admired, just as it has a fine appearance from another aspect, being seen and faced. Abu Bakr, in the narration of al-A'mash from 'Asim, and Humayd read (ri'iyyan) with a ya with sukun after it followed by a hamza. This is by metathesis (qalb), and its pattern is (fil'an), and it seems to be from ra'a. The poet said:

"Every friend who saw me says, 'Because of you this is the chief of today or tomorrow.'"

It was also read (riya'an) with a ya followed by an alif and then a hamza, related by al-Yazidi, and its origin is (ri'a'an), from al-muraa'a (showing off), meaning that some of them show others their beauty. Ibn 'Abbas, as narrated from him by Talha, read (riyan) without hamza or doubling. Some people presumed to call it a solecism (lahn), but it is not so; rather it has a justification: it may be from al-riwa', and it was altered so that it became (ri'iyyan), then the vowel of the hamza was moved to the ya and the hamza was deleted; or it may be from al-rayy, with one of the two ya's deleted for lightness, as in (la siyyama), and the deleted one is the second, because it is the radical of the word, since the moving of the vowel happened to the word by its joining with the first, so it is more deserving of deletion. Ibn 'Abbas also read, as did Ibn Jubayr, Yazid al-Barbari and al-A'sam al-Makki, (wizziyyan) with a zay and a doubled ya, which is the fine garment and the assembled, admirable equipment.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 19, verses 71–74 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Indeed, We created him before, when he was nothing﴾ [Maryam: 67], meaning: We brought him into being and originated him from pure non-existence into existence. So how could he deny the second creation, when this argument is extremely concise and binding upon the opponent? This type of argumentation is called the rational argument (al-ihtijaj al-nazari), and some call it the dialectical method (al-madhhab al-kalami). This argument is repeated in the Qur'an. ﴿And he was not a thing﴾ [Maryam: 67] is an allusion to pure non-existence, and the negation of thinghood from it indicates that what is non-existent is not called a thing. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: ﴿And he was not a thing﴾ [Maryam: 67] is "existent," or it is a Mu'tazili slip. The omitted noun to which (qabl, "before") is added in the sense is estimated by some as: "before his resurrection" (p-208). Al-Zamakhshari estimated it as: "before the state in which he is," which is the state of his remaining, ending quote.

When God, exalted is He, established the decisive proof for the truth of resurrection, He swore by it with His name, attributed to His Messenger, as an honouring and magnification of him. This oath is repeated in the Qur'an, as an exaltation of its truth and a raising of its status, just as He raised the status of the heaven and the earth by His saying: ﴿So by the Lord of the heaven and the earth, indeed it is the truth﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 23]. The waw in (wa-al-shayatin) is for conjunction, or it has the meaning of (ma'a, "with"): they will be gathered with their companions from the devils who misled them; each disbeliever will be coupled with a devil in a chain. This is the case when the pronoun in (la-nahshurannahum) refers to the disbelievers, and it is the view of Ibn 'Atiyya. What comes after that is informing about them, and al-Zamakhshari began with it. The apparent meaning is that it is general to all creatures, believers and disbelievers alike, and it does not distinguish between believers and disbelievers as it distinguished in the recompense. All of them are brought forth and led to the Fire so that the believers may witness the terrors from which they were saved, and thus rejoice and gloat over their disbelieving enemies. If the pronoun is general, the meaning is that they kneel down upon arriving at the edge of Hell, just as they were kneeling at the Standing-place, for it is one of the consequences of the assembly for reckoning before reaching reward and punishment. God, exalted is He, said concerning the state of the Standing-place: ﴿And you will see every nation kneeling; every nation will be called to its record﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 28]. (Jithiyyan) is a circumstantial accusative (hal muqaddarah). It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas: "sitting," and from him, by groups, (jathwah) plural, which is a gathering of dirt and stones. Mujahid, al-Hasan and al-Zajjaj said: "on their knees." Al-Suddi said: "standing on their knees," due to the narrowness of the place for them.

Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hafs read (jithiyyan), (itiyyan) and (siliyyan) with a kasra on the jim, the 'ayn and the sad, while the majority read them with a damma. ﴿Then We will surely draw out﴾ [Maryam: 69], meaning: We will surely bring out, like His saying: ﴿and he drew out his hand﴾ [al-A'raf: 108]. It is also said: We will surely throw, from "nazaʿa al-qaws" (he drew the bow), which is shooting an arrow. And (al-shi'ah) is the group bound together by one doctrine. Abu al-Ahwas said: "He begins with the greatest in sin, then the greatest." Al-Zamakhshari said: He separates from every group of the groups of error and corruption the most rebellious of them, then the most rebellious, and the most insolent, then the most insolent; when they are gathered, we throw them into the Fire in order, so the first in torment is placed first. The pronoun in (ayyuhum) refers to those gathered and brought forth. The majority read (ayyuhum) with a damma, which is a vowel of construction according to the doctrine of Sibawayh; so (ayyuhum) is an object of (la-nanza'anna) and is relative; (ashaddu) is the predicate of an omitted subject, and the clause is a relative clause of (ayyuhum). It is a vowel of inflection according to the doctrine of al-Khalil and Yunus, with differences in analysis. ﴿Which of them is most﴾ [Maryam: 69] is a subject and predicate, reported according to the doctrine of al-Khalil, meaning: those of whom it is said, "which of them is most." It is in the position of an accusative, so (la-nanza'anna) governs it as a suspended verb according to the doctrine of Yunus; the preference among these doctrines is mentioned in the science of grammar. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is possible that the drawing out falls upon ﴿from every group﴾ [Maryam: 69], like His saying: ﴿and We gave them of Our mercy﴾ [Maryam: 50], meaning: We will draw out some of ﴿every group﴾ [Maryam: 69], as if someone said: Who are they? So it was said: they are the most rebellious in insolence; end quote. Then (ayyuhum) would be relative, the predicate of an omitted subject, and this is a strained assumption and a claim of an ellipsis for which there is no necessity, and making what appears to be one clause into two clauses. Al-Khalil coupled his analysis with the verse of the poet:

"And indeed I spend the night from the young woman in a station, so I spend the night, neither blamed nor deprived."

That is, "so I spend the night" — it is said of me: "neither blamed nor deprived." Al-Zajjaj preferred the view of al-Khalil, and al-Nahhas reported from him that he considered Sibawayh to have erred in this issue. Sibawayh said: It would follow from this that one may say: "Strike the wicked thief who is called..." It was said: it does not follow, since these are single nouns and the verse is a clause, and the governance of the verb over a single noun is greater than over a clause. The doctrine of al-Kisa'i is that the meaning of (la-nanza'anna) is (la-nunadiyanna, "we will surely call out"), so it is treated as such and does not govern (ayyu) — end quote. This is reported from al-Farra'. Al-Mahdawi said: (nada) is suspended when it is followed by a clause in the accusative position, so it governs in meaning and not in wording. Al-Mubarrad said: (ayyuhum) is connected to (shi'ah), therefore it is in the nominative, and the meaning is: from those who gathered in support, "which of them is most" — as if they were competing for this; it is necessary to estimate an omitted object for (la-nanza'anna), and he also estimated in this doctrine: from those who cooperated, (ayyuhum), meaning: from those who helped one another, and they looked: "which of them is most." Al-Nahhas said: This is a good view. Al-Kisa'i reported that (tashayyu') is (ta'awun, cooperation).

Abu Bakr ibn Shuqayr related that some of the Kufans say: (ayyuhum) carries the meaning of a condition; you say: "I struck the people, whichever of them became angry," meaning: whether they became angry or did not become angry. According to this, the estimate is: whether their insolence increased or did not increase. Talhah ibn Musarrif, Mu'adh ibn Muslim al-Harra' (teacher of al-Farra'), and Za'idah from al-A'mash read (ayyahum) with a fatha as an object of (la-nanza'anna). These two readings indicate that according to the doctrine of Sibawayh, construction is not necessary in them when it is added and the first part of its relative clause is omitted; it is reported from him that construction is necessary, but it should be that in his doctrine both construction and inflection are possible. Abu 'Amr al-Jarmi said: "I left Basra and from the time I parted from the Khandaq to Makkah I did not hear anyone say: 'La-adribanna ayyuhum qa'im' with a damma, but with its fatha," end quote. Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas said: I know of no grammarian except that he has rejected Sibawayh, and I heard Abu Ishaq — meaning al-Zajjaj — say: It is not clear that Sibawayh erred in his book except in two places, and this is one of them. He said: Sibawayh inflected (ayyan), though it is singular, because it is added; so how could he build it when it is added?

﴿Upon the Most Merciful﴾ [Maryam: 69] is connected to (ashaddu). (Itiyyan) is a specifier transferred from the subject; its estimate is: "which of them, its insolence is more severe upon the Most Merciful" [Maryam: 69]. In the speech there is an omission, estimated as: "so He casts him into the most severe torment," or "so He begins with his torment, then with the one below him, down to the last of them in torment." In a hadith: "Indeed, a neck of the Fire will appear and say: I have been commanded to take every stubborn tyrant," and so it seizes them. In some reports: "They are gathered together around Hell, shackled and chained, then the most disbelieving is brought forward, then the most disbelieving." Ibn 'Abbas said: (itiyyan) means "audacity." Mujahid said: "wickedness." It was said: "slander," in the dialect of Tamim. It was said: (itiyyan) is the plural of ('at), so its accusative is as a circumstantial accusative.

﴿Then indeed We are most knowing﴾ [Maryam: 70], meaning: We, in that drawing out, do not place anything other than its place, because We have encompassed everything in knowledge, so We know who is most deserving of the burning of the Fire. Ibn Jurayj said: "most deserving of eternity." Al-Kalbi said: (siliyyan) means "entering." It was said: "remaining." It was said: it is the plural of (sali), so it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state, and (biha) is connected to (awla). The waw in His saying ﴿And there is not among you﴾ is for conjunction. Ibn 'Atiyya said: ﴿And there is not among you except that he will come to it﴾ is an oath, and the waw requires it, and the Prophet's saying explains it, ﷺ: "Whoever has three children die, the Fire will not touch him except as a passing of the oath" — end quote. He overlooked the grammarians' statement that the oath cannot be dispensed with by the answer for the meaning's indication except when the answer is with the lam or with (an); the answer here, according to his claim, came with the negating (in), so the oath may not be omitted according to what they stated. His saying "the waw requires it" indicates that it is, in his view, the waw of oath; no grammarian holds that such a waw is the waw of oath, because this would require omitting the genitive and retaining the preposition, which is not permitted except in poetry or rare speech, on condition that the description of the omitted noun stands in its place, as they interpreted in their saying: "How excellent is the journey on the wretched caravan," meaning: on a caravan which is wretched. And the poet's saying:

"By God, Zayd is not a sleeper, his companion..."

meaning: not a man who sleeps, his companion. This verse is not of this type, since the sworn-by thing was not omitted and its description did not stand in its place.

The majority read (minkum) with the second-person pronoun, and the apparent meaning is that it is general to creatures, and that "coming" is not entering for all of them. Ibn Mas'ud, al-Hasan and Qatadah said that it is the passing over the Sirat, since the Sirat is stretched over it.
