Al-Zamakhshari estimated it as: "before the state in which he is," which is the state of his remaining, ending quote.

When God, exalted is He, established the decisive proof for the truth of resurrection, He swore by it with His name, attributed to His Messenger, as an honouring and magnification of him. This oath is repeated in the Qur'an, as an exaltation of its truth and a raising of its status, just as He raised the status of the heaven and the earth by His saying: ﴿So by the Lord of the heaven and the earth, indeed it is the truth﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 23]. The waw in (wa-al-shayatin) is for conjunction, or it has the meaning of (ma'a, "with"): they will be gathered with their companions from the devils who misled them; each disbeliever will be coupled with a devil in a chain. This is the case when the pronoun in (la-nahshurannahum) refers to the disbelievers, and it is the view of Ibn 'Atiyya. What comes after that is informing about them, and al-Zamakhshari began with it. The apparent meaning is that it is general to all creatures, believers and disbelievers alike, and it does not distinguish between believers and disbelievers as it distinguished in the recompense. All of them are brought forth and led to the Fire so that the believers may witness the terrors from which they were saved, and thus rejoice and gloat over their disbelieving enemies. If the pronoun is general, the meaning is that they kneel down upon arriving at the edge of Hell, just as they were kneeling at the Standing-place, for it is one of the consequences of the assembly for reckoning before reaching reward and punishment. God, exalted is He, said concerning the state of the Standing-place: ﴿And you will see every nation kneeling; every nation will be called to its record﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 28]. (Jithiyyan) is a circumstantial accusative (hal muqaddarah). It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas: "sitting," and from him, by groups, (jathwah) plural, which is a gathering of dirt and stones. Mujahid, al-Hasan and al-Zajjaj said: "on their knees." Al-Suddi said: "standing on their knees," due to the narrowness of the place for them.

Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hafs read (jithiyyan), (itiyyan) and (siliyyan) with a kasra on the jim, the 'ayn and the sad, while the majority read them with a damma. ﴿Then We will surely draw out﴾ [Maryam: 69], meaning: We will surely bring out, like His saying: ﴿and he drew out his hand﴾ [al-A'raf: 108]. It is also said: We will surely throw, from "nazaʿa al-qaws" (he drew the bow), which is shooting an arrow. And (al-shi'ah) is the group bound together by one doctrine. Abu al-Ahwas said: "He begins with the greatest in sin, then the greatest." Al-Zamakhshari said: He separates from every group of the groups of error and corruption the most rebellious of them, then the most rebellious, and the most insolent, then the most insolent; when they are gathered, we throw them into the Fire in order, so the first in torment is placed first. The pronoun in (ayyuhum) refers to those gathered and brought forth. The majority read (ayyuhum) with a damma, which is a vowel of construction according to the doctrine of Sibawayh; so (ayyuhum) is an object of (la-nanza'anna) and is relative; (ashaddu) is the predicate of an omitted subject, and the clause is a relative clause of (ayyuhum). It is a vowel of inflection according to the doctrine of al-Khalil and Yunus, with differences in analysis. ﴿Which of them is most﴾ [Maryam: 69] is a subject and predicate, reported according to the doctrine of al-Khalil, meaning: those of whom it is said, "which of them is most." It is in the position of an accusative, so (la-nanza'anna) governs it as a suspended verb according to the doctrine of Yunus; the preference among these doctrines is mentioned in the science of grammar. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is possible that the drawing out falls upon ﴿from every group﴾ [Maryam: 69], like His saying: ﴿and We gave them of Our mercy﴾ [Maryam: 50], meaning: We will draw out some of ﴿every group﴾ [Maryam: 69], as if someone said: Who are they? So it was said: they are the most rebellious in insolence; end quote. Then (ayyuhum) would be relative, the predicate of an omitted subject, and this is a strained assumption and a claim of an ellipsis for which there is no necessity, and making what appears to be one clause into two clauses. Al-Khalil coupled his analysis with the verse of the poet:

"And indeed I spend the night from the young woman in a station, so I spend the night, neither blamed nor deprived."

That is, "so I spend the night" — it is said of me: "neither blamed nor deprived." Al-Zajjaj preferred the view of al-Khalil, and al-Nahhas reported from him that he considered Sibawayh to have erred in this issue. Sibawayh said: It would follow from this that one may say: "Strike the wicked thief who is called..." It was said: it does not follow, since these are single nouns and the verse is a clause, and the governance of the verb over a single noun is greater than over a clause. The doctrine of al-Kisa'i is that the meaning of (la-nanza'anna) is (la-nunadiyanna, "we will surely call out"), so it is treated as such and does not govern (ayyu) — end quote. This is reported from al-Farra'. Al-Mahdawi said: (nada) is suspended when it is followed by a clause in the accusative position, so it governs in meaning and not in wording. Al-Mubarrad said: (ayyuhum) is connected to (shi'ah), therefore it is in the nominative, and the meaning is: from those who gathered in support, "which of them is most" — as if they were competing for this; it is necessary to estimate an omitted object for (la-nanza'anna), and he also estimated in this doctrine: from those who cooperated, (ayyuhum), meaning: from those who helped one another, and they looked: "which of them is most." Al-Nahhas said: This is a good view. Al-Kisa'i reported that (tashayyu') is (ta'awun, cooperation).

Abu Bakr ibn Shuqayr related that some of the Kufans say: (ayyuhum) carries the meaning of a condition; you say: "I struck the people, whichever of them became angry," meaning: whether they became angry or did not become angry. According to this, the estimate is: whether their insolence increased or did not increase. Talhah ibn Musarrif, Mu'adh ibn Muslim al-Harra' (teacher of al-Farra'), and Za'idah from al-A'mash read (ayyahum) with a fatha as an object of (la-nanza'anna). These two readings indicate that according to the doctrine of Sibawayh, construction is not necessary in them when it is added and the first part of its relative clause is omitted; it is reported from him that construction is necessary, but it should be that in his doctrine both construction and inflection are possible. Abu 'Amr al-Jarmi said: "I left Basra and from the time I parted from the Khandaq to Makkah I did not hear anyone say: 'La-adribanna ayyuhum qa'im' with a damma, but with its fatha," end quote. Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas said: I know of no grammarian except that he has rejected Sibawayh, and I heard Abu Ishaq — meaning al-Zajjaj — say: It is not clear that Sibawayh erred in his book except in two places, and this is one of them. He said: Sibawayh inflected (ayyan), though it is singular, because it is added; so how could he build it when it is added?

﴿Upon the Most Merciful﴾ [Maryam: 69] is connected to (ashaddu). (Itiyyan) is a specifier transferred from the subject; its estimate is: "which of them, its insolence is more severe upon the Most Merciful" [Maryam: 69]. In the speech there is an omission, estimated as: "so He casts him into the most severe torment," or "so He begins with his torment, then with the one below him, down to the last of them in torment." In a hadith: "Indeed, a neck of the Fire will appear and say: I have been commanded to take every stubborn tyrant," and so it seizes them. In some reports: "They are gathered together around Hell, shackled and chained, then the most disbelieving is brought forward, then the most disbelieving." Ibn 'Abbas said: (itiyyan) means "audacity." Mujahid said: "wickedness." It was said: "slander," in the dialect of Tamim. It was said: (itiyyan) is the plural of ('at), so its accusative is as a circumstantial accusative.

﴿Then indeed We are most knowing﴾ [Maryam: 70], meaning: We, in that drawing out, do not place anything other than its place, because We have encompassed everything in knowledge, so We know who is most deserving of the burning of the Fire. Ibn Jurayj said: "most deserving of eternity." Al-Kalbi said: (siliyyan) means "entering." It was said: "remaining." It was said: it is the plural of (sali), so it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state, and (biha) is connected to (awla). The waw in His saying ﴿And there is not among you﴾ is for conjunction. Ibn 'Atiyya said: ﴿And there is not among you except that he will come to it﴾ is an oath, and the waw requires it, and the Prophet's saying explains it, ﷺ: "Whoever has three children die, the Fire will not touch him except as a passing of the oath" — end quote. He overlooked the grammarians' statement that the oath cannot be dispensed with by the answer for the meaning's indication except when the answer is with the lam or with (an); the answer here, according to his claim, came with the negating (in), so the oath may not be omitted according to what they stated. His saying "the waw requires it" indicates that it is, in his view, the waw of oath; no grammarian holds that such a waw is the waw of oath, because this would require omitting the genitive and retaining the preposition, which is not permitted except in poetry or rare speech, on condition that the description of the omitted noun stands in its place, as they interpreted in their saying: "How excellent is the journey on the wretched caravan," meaning: on a caravan which is wretched. And the poet's saying:

"By God, Zayd is not a sleeper, his companion..."

meaning: not a man who sleeps, his companion. This verse is not of this type, since the sworn-by thing was not omitted and its description did not stand in its place.

The majority read (minkum) with the second-person pronoun, and the apparent meaning is that it is general to creatures, and that "coming" is not entering for all of them. Ibn Mas'ud, al-Hasan and Qatadah said that it is the passing over the Sirat, since the Sirat is stretched over it. From Ibn 'Abbas: "It may come to a thing without entering it," like His saying: ﴿And when he came to the water of Madyan﴾ [al-Qasas: 23], and "the caravan came to the town" without entering it, but it drew near to it or reached it. The poet said:

"When they came to the water, its wells blue, they put down the staves of the one who stays, who has pitched camp."

And the Arabs say: "We came to the water of Banu Tamim and Banu Kalb," when they attended them and entered their lands, and by it is not meant the water itself. It was said: the address is to the disbelievers, that is, say to them, O Muhammad, so the coming for them is entering. According to the view of one who said that the address is general, and that believers and disbelievers both enter the Fire, but it does not harm the believers, and they mentioned the manner of the believers' entry into the Fire in a way that I do not like to transmit in this book because of the abhorrence of their saying that the believers enter the Fire (p-210) even though it does not harm them.

Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrimah and a group read (wa-in minhum) with the pronoun of absence, according to the pronouns mentioned before. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also possible that by "coming" is meant their kneeling around it; and if only the disbelievers are meant, the meaning is clear, and the subject of (kana) is a hidden pronoun returning to "coming," meaning: their coming was decreed, that is, obligatory, determined. The majority read (thumma) with the conjunctive particle, and this indicates that the coming is general. ʿAbd Allah, Ibn ʿAbbas, Ubayy, ʿAli, al-Jahdari, Ibn Abi Layla, Mu'awiyah ibn Qurrah and Ya'qub read (tharnma) with a fatha on the tha', meaning "there," and Ibn Abi Layla paused on (thammah) with the silent heh. The majority read (nunajji) with a fatha on the nun and shadda on the jim. Yahya, al-A'mash, al-Kisa'i and Ibn Muhaysin read it with a sukun on the nun and takhfif on the jim. A group read (nujji) with a single damma-vowelled nun and a shadda on the jim. ʿAli read (nunahhi), with an unpointed ha', present tense of (nahha); and the object of (ittaqaw) is omitted, meaning: the shirk and the injustice; here injustice is the injustice of disbelief.

﴿And when Our clear verses are recited to them﴾ [Maryam: 73]. It was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith and his companions. The poor among the Companions were in hardship of life and shabby clothing, while the polytheists oiled their heads, combed their hair, and wore silk and fine garments, so they said to the believers: ﴿Which of the two groups is better in station﴾ [Maryam: 73], meaning: in dwelling and abode, ﴿and better in assembly﴾ [Maryam: 73]. When He established the argument against the deniers of resurrection and followed it with what will happen on the Day of Resurrection, He informed about them that they opposed that decisive proof with the goodness of their appearance in this world, and that this, in their view, indicates their honour before God. Abu Hayyah and al-A'raj and Ibn Muhaysin read (yutla) with a ya', while the majority read it with a ta' from above. The believer used to recite the Qur'an to the disbeliever and praise the signs of the Prophet ﷺ, and the disbeliever would say: God only bestows goodness upon the most beloved of creation to Him, and bestows favour upon the people of truth, and He has favoured us over you, so we are rich and you are poor, and we have the better gathering and the more beautiful appearance.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 19, verses 71–74 (part 2 of 2):

The meaning of (bayyinat) is: with well-arranged wording, with summarized meanings, or manifestly inimitable, or proofs and evidences. (Bayyinat) is an emphatic circumstantial (hal) clause, because His signs, may He be exalted, are never anything but of this description, always.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read (maqaman) with a fatha on the mim. Ibn Kathir, Ibn Muhaysin, Humayd, al-Ju'fi and Abu Hatim, on the authority of Abu 'Amr, read it with a damma on the mim. Both the fatha and the damma allow it to be a verbal noun (masdar) or a place of standing or of establishing, and its accusative case is that of specification (tamyiz).

Then He, may He be exalted, mentioned the great number of generations He destroyed, of those who were better off than them in this world, as a warning that He destroys them and uproots their root just as He did to others, and as an admonition to them if they are among those who take admonition. The wealth and the fine appearance in which they were did not avail them. And it means the destruction of those who denied what the messengers brought. The phrase (min qarn) is a specification for "you" (lakum), and (kam) is the object of (ahlakna).

Al-Zamakhshari said: The phrase (hum ahsanu) is in a place of accusative as a qualifier of (kam). Do you not see that if you left out (hum), you would have no choice but to put (ahsana) in the accusative as a qualifier? End of quote. Abu al-Baqa' followed him in holding that (hum ahsanu) is a qualifier of (kam). Our companions (the Basran grammarians) stated explicitly that the interrogative and the informative (khabariyya) kam is neither described nor is it used as a qualifier. Accordingly, (hum ahsanu) is in the position of a qualifier for (qarn). It was made plural because the qarn comprises many individuals, so its meaning was observed; had the pronoun been made singular in accordance with the wording, it would have been correct Arabic, and it would be like the word (jami'). He said, "And all of them (jami'un) will be brought before Us" [Ya-Sin: 32], and He said, "We are a united body (jami'un) that will be victorious" [al-Qamar: 44]. So He described it with the plural and with the singular. The explanation of (athath) has already been given in Surat al-Nahl.

The majority read (wa-ri'yan) with a hamza, from the seeing of the eye (ru'yat al-'ayn), as a verbal form in the sense of a passive participle (maf'ul), like (al-tihn) and (al-siqy). Ibn 'Abbas said: al-Ri'y is the appearance (manzar). al-Hasan said: its meaning is pictures (suwaran). Al-Zuhri, Abu Ja'far, Shayba, Talha (in the narration of al-Hamdani), Ayyub, Ibn Sa'dan, Ibn Dhakwan and Qalun read (riyyan) with a doubled ya without a hamza. This may be a word originally with a hamza, from al-riwa' (fine appearance) and al-manzar, whose hamza was eased by changing it to a ya, and then the ya was assimilated into the ya. It may also be from al-rayy, the opposite of thirst, because well-watered (rayyan) water has a freshness and radiance that is desired and admired, just as it has a fine appearance from another aspect, being seen and faced. Abu Bakr, in the narration of al-A'mash from 'Asim, and Humayd read (ri'iyyan) with a ya with sukun after it followed by a hamza. This is by metathesis (qalb), and its pattern is (fil'an), and it seems to be from ra'a. The poet said:

"Every friend who saw me says, 'Because of you this is the chief of today or tomorrow.'"

It was also read (riya'an) with a ya followed by an alif and then a hamza, related by al-Yazidi, and its origin is (ri'a'an), from al-muraa'a (showing off), meaning that some of them show others their beauty. Ibn 'Abbas, as narrated from him by Talha, read (riyan) without hamza or doubling. Some people presumed to call it a solecism (lahn), but it is not so; rather it has a justification: it may be from al-riwa', and it was altered so that it became (ri'iyyan), then the vowel of the hamza was moved to the ya and the hamza was deleted; or it may be from al-rayy, with one of the two ya's deleted for lightness, as in (la siyyama), and the deleted one is the second, because it is the radical of the word, since the moving of the vowel happened to the word by its joining with the first, so it is more deserving of deletion. Ibn 'Abbas also read, as did Ibn Jubayr, Yazid al-Barbari and al-A'sam al-Makki, (wizziyyan) with a zay and a doubled ya, which is the fine garment and the assembled, admirable equipment.

The waw in His saying ﴿And there is not among you﴾ is for conjunction. Ibn 'Atiyya said: ﴿And there is not among you except that he will come to it﴾ is an oath, and the waw requires it, and the Prophet's saying explains it, ﷺ: "Whoever has three children die, the Fire will not touch him except as a passing of the oath" — end quote. He overlooked the grammarians' statement that the oath cannot be dispensed with by the answer for the meaning's indication except when the answer is with the lam or with (an); the answer here, according to his claim, came with the negating (in), so the oath may not be omitted according to what they stated. His saying "the waw requires it" indicates that it is, in his view, the waw of oath; no grammarian holds that such a waw is the waw of oath, because this would require omitting the genitive and retaining the preposition, which is not permitted except in poetry or rare speech, on condition that the description of the omitted noun stands in its place, as they interpreted in their saying: "How excellent is the journey on the wretched caravan," meaning: on a caravan which is wretched. And the poet's saying:

"By God, Zayd is not a sleeper, his companion..."

meaning: not a man who sleeps, his companion. This verse is not of this type, since the sworn-by thing was not omitted and its description did not stand in its place.

The majority read (minkum) with the second-person pronoun, and the apparent meaning is that it is general to creatures, and that "coming" is not entering for all of them. Ibn Mas'ud, al-Hasan and Qatadah said that it is the passing over the Sirat, since the Sirat is stretched over it. From Ibn 'Abbas: "It may come to a thing without entering it," like His saying: ﴿And when he came to the water of Madyan﴾ [al-Qasas: 23], and "the caravan came to the town" without entering it, but it drew near to it or reached it. The poet said:

"When they came to the water, its wells blue, they put down the staves of the one who stays, who has pitched camp."

And the Arabs say: "We came to the water of Banu Tamim and Banu Kalb," when they attended them and entered their lands, and by it is not meant the water itself. It was said: the address is to the disbelievers, that is, say to them, O Muhammad, so the coming for them is entering. According to the view of one who said that the address is general, and that believers and disbelievers both enter the Fire, but it does not harm the believers, and they mentioned the manner of the believers' entry into the Fire in a way that I do not like to transmit in this book because of the abhorrence of their saying that the believers enter the Fire (p-210) even though it does not harm them.

Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrimah and a group read (wa-in minhum) with the pronoun of absence, according to the pronouns mentioned before. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also possible that by "coming" is meant their kneeling around it; and if only the disbelievers are meant, the meaning is clear, and the subject of (kana) is a hidden pronoun returning to "coming," meaning: their coming was decreed, that is, obligatory, determined. The majority read (thumma) with the conjunctive particle, and this indicates that the coming is general. ʿAbd Allah, Ibn ʿAbbas, Ubayy, ʿAli, al-Jahdari, Ibn Abi Layla, Mu'awiyah ibn Qurrah and Ya'qub read (tharnma) with a fatha on the tha', meaning "there," and Ibn Abi Layla paused on (thammah) with the silent heh. The majority read (nunajji) with a fatha on the nun and shadda on the jim. Yahya, al-A'mash, al-Kisa'i and Ibn Muhaysin read it with a sukun on the nun and takhfif on the jim. A group read (nujji) with a single damma-vowelled nun and a shadda on the jim. ʿAli read (nunahhi), with an unpointed ha', present tense of (nahha); and the object of (ittaqaw) is omitted, meaning: the shirk and the injustice; here injustice is the injustice of disbelief.

﴿And when Our clear verses are recited to them﴾ [Maryam: 73]. It was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith and his companions. The poor among the Companions were in hardship of life and shabby clothing, while the polytheists oiled their heads, combed their hair, and wore silk and fine garments, so they said to the believers: ﴿Which of the two groups is better in station﴾ [Maryam: 73], meaning: in dwelling and abode, ﴿and better in assembly﴾ [Maryam: 73]. When He established the argument against the deniers of resurrection and followed it with what will happen on the Day of Resurrection, He informed about them that they opposed that decisive proof with the goodness of their appearance in this world, and that this, in their view, indicates their honour before God. Abu Hayyah and al-A'raj and Ibn Muhaysin read (yutla) with a ya', while the majority read it with a ta' from above. The believer used to recite the Qur'an to the disbeliever and praise the signs of the Prophet ﷺ, and the disbeliever would say: God only bestows goodness upon the most beloved of creation to Him, and bestows favour upon the people of truth, and He has favoured us over you, so we are rich and you are poor, and we have the better gathering and the more beautiful appearance.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 19, verses 71–74 (part 2 of 2):

The meaning of (bayyinat) is: with well-arranged wording, with summarized meanings, or manifestly inimitable, or proofs and evidences. (Bayyinat) is an emphatic circumstantial (hal) clause, because His signs, may He be exalted, are never anything but of this description, always.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read (maqaman) with a fatha on the mim. Ibn Kathir, Ibn Muhaysin, Humayd, al-Ju'fi and Abu Hatim, on the authority of Abu 'Amr, read it with a damma on the mim. Both the fatha and the damma allow it to be a verbal noun (masdar) or a place of standing or of establishing, and its accusative case is that of specification (tamyiz).

Then He, may He be exalted, mentioned the great number of generations He destroyed, of those who were better off than them in this world, as a warning that He destroys them and uproots their root just as He did to others, and as an admonition to them if they are among those who take admonition. The wealth and the fine appearance in which they were did not avail them. And it means the destruction of those who denied what the messengers brought. The phrase (min qarn) is a specification for "you" (lakum), and (kam) is the object of (ahlakna).

Al-Zamakhshari said: The phrase (hum ahsanu) is in a place of accusative as a qualifier of (kam). Do you not see that if you left out (hum), you would have no choice but to put (ahsana) in the accusative as a qualifier? End of quote. Abu al-Baqa' followed him in holding that (hum ahsanu) is a qualifier of (kam). Our companions (the Basran grammarians) stated explicitly that the interrogative and the informative (khabariyya) kam is neither described nor is it used as a qualifier. Accordingly, (hum ahsanu) is in the position of a qualifier for (qarn). It was made plural because the qarn comprises many individuals, so its meaning was observed; had the pronoun been made singular in accordance with the wording, it would have been correct Arabic, and it would be like the word (jami'). He said, "And all of them (jami'un) will be brought before Us" [Ya-Sin: 32], and He said, "We are a united body (jami'un) that will be victorious" [al-Qamar: 44]. So He described it with the plural and with the singular. The explanation of (athath) has already been given in Surat al-Nahl.

The majority read (wa-ri'yan) with a hamza, from the seeing of the eye (ru'yat al-'ayn), as a verbal form in the sense of a passive participle (maf'ul), like (al-tihn) and (al-siqy). Ibn 'Abbas said: al-Ri'y is the appearance (manzar). al-Hasan said: its meaning is pictures (suwaran). Al-Zuhri, Abu Ja'far, Shayba, Talha (in the narration of al-Hamdani), Ayyub, Ibn Sa'dan, Ibn Dhakwan and Qalun read (riyyan) with a doubled ya without a hamza. This may be a word originally with a hamza, from al-riwa' (fine appearance) and al-manzar, whose hamza was eased by changing it to a ya, and then the ya was assimilated into the ya. It may also be from al-rayy, the opposite of thirst, because well-watered (rayyan) water has a freshness and radiance that is desired and admired, just as it has a fine appearance from another aspect, being seen and faced. Abu Bakr, in the narration of al-A'mash from 'Asim, and Humayd read (ri'iyyan) with a ya with sukun after it followed by a hamza. This is by metathesis (qalb), and its pattern is (fil'an), and it seems to be from ra'a. The poet said:

"Every friend who saw me says, 'Because of you this is the chief of today or tomorrow.'"

It was also read (riya'an) with a ya followed by an alif and then a hamza, related by al-Yazidi, and its origin is (ri'a'an), from al-muraa'a (showing off), meaning that some of them show others their beauty. Ibn 'Abbas, as narrated from him by Talha, read (riyan) without hamza or doubling. Some people presumed to call it a solecism (lahn), but it is not so; rather it has a justification: it may be from al-riwa', and it was altered so that it became (ri'iyyan), then the vowel of the hamza was moved to the ya and the hamza was deleted; or it may be from al-rayy, with one of the two ya's deleted for lightness, as in (la siyyama), and the deleted one is the second, because it is the radical of the word, since the moving of the vowel happened to the word by its joining with the first, so it is more deserving of deletion. Ibn 'Abbas also read, as did Ibn Jubayr, Yazid al-Barbari and al-A'sam al-Makki, (wizziyyan) with a zay and a doubled ya, which is the fine garment and the assembled, admirable equipment.

(p-212) "Whoever is in error, let the Most Merciful extend his term" (فَلْيَمْدُدْ) may be read as a jussive in its literal sense, as a supplication (دُعاءً). The meaning would then be: "May God extend the term of whichever of us or of you is more astray; that is, may He grant him respite until it leads him to His punishment." Supplication is expressed in the form of a command because that is the original form. It may also be a statement in meaning, with the form of a command: "Whoever among the nations is astray, God's custom toward him is to extend his term and not hasten to punish him, until that leads to his punishment in the Hereafter." Al-Zamakhshari (Zamakhshari) said: "It is expressed in the form of a command to indicate that this is binding, and that it is certain to happen, like something commanded that is carried out, in order to cut off the excuses of the one who is astray. It will be said to him on the Day of Resurrection: ﴿Did We not give you a life long enough for whoever would take heed to take heed?﴾ [Fatir: 37], or like His saying: ﴿We only give them respite so that they may increase in sin﴾ [Al 'Imran: 178]." The apparent reading is that "until" (حَتّى) is the limit of His saying "let him extend," and the meaning is: those who are in error are given respite in it until they witness the punishment, through God's support of the believers, or the Hour and its precursors.

Al-Zamakhshari also said: In this verse there are two possibilities. The first is that it connects to the verse which is its fourth, and the two verses in between are a parenthetical insertion. That is: they said ﴿Which of the two groups is better in station and finer in assembly?﴾ [Maryam: 73], ﴿until they see what they are promised﴾, meaning: they do not cease saying this statement and boasting of it, and they do not refrain from it until they see the promised thing with their own eyes, ﴿either the punishment﴾ in this world, which is the victory of the Muslims over them and their being punished by killing and captivity, and God's making His religion prevail over all religion through their hands; ﴿or the Day of Resurrection﴾ and the disgrace and torment that will befall them. Then, at the moment of witnessing, they will know that the matter is the reverse of what they had supposed, and that they are ﴿worse in station and weaker in army﴾, not ﴿better in station and finer in assembly﴾ [Maryam: 73], and that the believers are the opposite of their description. He concluded. This possibility is extremely remote because of the long separation between His saying "they said: ﴿Which of the two groups﴾" [Maryam: 73] and the limit, and it involves separation by two parenthetical clauses, which Abu 'Ali does not permit.

Al-Zamakhshari said: The second is that it connects with what follows it, so he mentioned something similar to what we have presented, and he set their saying ﴿better in station﴾ [Maryam: 73] against His saying ﴿worse in station﴾, and their saying ﴿finer in assembly﴾ [Maryam: 73] against His saying ﴿weaker in army﴾; because the nadi (نَدِيّ, the gathering) is the assembly that brings together the notables of the people, their helpers and supporters, and the jund (جُنْد, army) are the helpers and supporters. And ﴿either the punishment or the Hour﴾ is a substitute (بَدَلٌ) for "what" (مَا), the object of "they see." "Whom" (مَن) is a relative pronoun, the object of His saying "they will know" (فَسَيَعْلَمُونَ), which takes one object; and it is an interrogative, and the verb before it is suspended (مُعَلَّق), and the clause is in the position of an accusative.

When He mentioned the extension given to the one who is astray in his error, and his confusion in boasting of the blessings of this world, He followed that with an increase of guidance for the one who is guided, and with mention of "the enduring good deeds" (الباقِياتُ), which are a substitute for their enjoyment in this world, which vanishes and does not last. "Return" (مَرَدًّا) means "place of return." The explanation of ﴿the enduring good deeds﴾ [al-Kahf: 46] has already been given in Surat al-Kahf.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "He increases" (يَزِيدُ) is coordinated with the position of "let him extend" (فَلْيَمْدُدْ), because it occupies the position of a predicate; its estimated form is: "whoever is in error, the Most Merciful extends for him an extension, and increases (وَيَزِيدُ)," that is, He increases the error of the one who is astray by abandoning him, and He increases the guidance of those who are guided by granting them success. He concluded. But it is not valid for "He increases" to be coordinated with the position of "let him extend," whether it is a supplication or a statement in the form of a command, because it occupies the position of a predicate if "whoever" (مَن) is a relative pronoun, or the position of the response if "whoever" is a conditional. On both estimates, the clause ﴿God increases those who were guided in guidance﴾ lacks a pronoun referring back to "whoever," which would link the predicate clause to the subject, or the conditional clause to the response, which is "let him extend" and what is coordinated with it. This is because a coordinated item after a predicate is a predicate, and a coordinated item after the response is a response. When the conditional particle is a noun and not an adverb, it is necessary that the response clause contain a pronoun referring to it, or something that stands in its place; and likewise in the clause coordinated with it.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Better in reward" (خَيْرٌ ثَوابًا) is one of the boasts of the unbelievers, ﴿and better in return﴾, that is, better in place of return and outcome, or in benefit, from their saying: "There is no return (مَرَدٌّ) for this matter," and "Will my place return to Zayd?" If you say: How is it said "better in reward," when their boasting has a reward, so that the reward of the righteous deeds would be made better than it? I say: It is as if it were said that their reward is the Fire, following the manner of his saying: "Then they were paid back with the Sayhal," and his saying:

"A she-camel of stout build, whose gait is the walk, chewing it, its cud, when the riding camels halt and rest"

and his saying:

"Their greeting among them is a painful blow."

Then he built upon it "better in reward," and in it there is a kind of mockery, which is more enraging to the one being threatened than to be told "your punishment is the Fire." If you say: What is the sense of the comparative in the predicate, when they had partners in their boasting? I say: This is from the concise speech of their people, who say: "Summer is hotter than winter," meaning: it is more intense in its heat than winter is in its cold. He concluded.

﴿Have you seen the one who disbelieved in Our signs and said: "I will surely be given wealth and children"?﴾ It was revealed concerning al-'As ibn Wa'il. Khabbab ibn al-Aratt did work for him, and he was a qayn (قَيْن, a smith). A debt accumulated for him with him, so he demanded it, and he said: "I will not do justice to you until you disbelieve in Muhammad." Khabbab said: "I will not disbelieve in Muhammad until God causes you to die and then resurrects you." Al-'As said: "Shall I be resurrected after death?" Khabbab said: "Yes." He said: "Then, when that happens, I will have wealth and children, and at that time I will pay you your debt." Al-Hasan said: It was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, and al-Walid also had statements resembling this aim. Since seeing things is a path to comprehending them and to the soundness of reports about them, they used "have you seen" (أَرَأَيْتَ) in the sense of "inform" (أَخْبَرَ). The "fa" (فَاءُ) indicates coordination and conveys sequence, as if it were said: "Inform us also of the story of this unbeliever, following the story of those." "The signs" (الآياتُ) are the Qur'an and the proofs for resurrection.

The majority read "and children" (وَلَدًا) in all four places here and in al-Zukhruf, with a fatha on the lam and the waw, and the disagreement concerning Nuh will come. Al-A'mash, Talha, al-Kisa'i, Ibn Abi Layla, and Ibn 'Isa al-Isfahani read it with a damma on the waw and a sukun on the lam. According to the reading of the majority, the meaning is generic, not considering singularity, even though the word is singular in form. According to this reading, some said it is a plural, like asad and usud (lion and lions), and the one who held this view cited the poet's words:

"Indeed I have seen a company who have multiplied wealth and offspring."

It was also said that it is a synonym for walad (وَلَد) with two fathas, and they cited the words:

"Would that so-and-so had been in his mother's belly, and would that so-and-so had been the offspring of a donkey."

'Abd Allah and Yahya ibn Ya'mur read with a kasra on the waw and a sukun on the lam. The hamza in "has he looked into the unseen" (أطَّلَعَ) is interrogative, and for this reason "or" (أَمْ) is paired with it. It was also read with a kasra on the hamza at the beginning and its deletion in continuous speech, on the estimate that the interrogative hamza is deleted, since "or" indicates it, as in his saying: "With seven did they throw the pebbles, or with eight?" meaning: "with seven?" The construction with "have you seen" (أَرَأَيْتَ) follows the arrangement mentioned by Sibawayh, that it takes one object which it governs, and the second is an interrogative. So "has he looked into" (أطَّلَعَ) and what follows it occupy the position of the second object of "have you seen." What comes of the construction of "have you seen" in the sense of "inform me," contrary to this on the surface, should be referred back to this by interpretation.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Has he looked into the unseen" (أطَّلَعَ الغَيْبَ) comes from their saying: "He ascended the mountain" when he climbed to its top, and "he looked over the pass" (اطَّلَعَ الثَّنِيَةَ). Jarir said:

"I met the difficult summits of the mountains."

And one says: "Go, ascending (مُطَّلِعًا) to that matter," meaning: high over it and in control of it. The choice of this word has significance. You say: "Has he reached such a height of greatness that he ascended to knowledge of the unseen, which is the exclusive domain of the One, the Subduer?" The meaning is that what he claimed he would be given and swore to can only be reached by one of these two paths: either knowledge of the unseen, or a covenant from the Knower of the unseen. So by which of the two did he reach that?

"Covenant" (الْعَهْدُ): It was said it is the word of testimony. Qatada said: Does he have a righteous deed he sent ahead, so that he hopes by it for what he says? It is related from al-Kalbi: Has God made a covenant with him that He would give him that?

"No" (كَلَّا) is a rebuke and an admonition concerning the error he is in, in what he imagines for himself and wishes, so let him refrain from it. Abu Nahik read "kallan" (كَلًّا) with tanwin in both places here, and it is a verbal noun from "the sword was dulled" (كَلَّ السَّيْفُ), when it became blunt against striking. Its accusative status is due to an implied verb of the same root, and its estimate is: "Be blunt (كَلُوا) to the worship of God, or to the truth," and the like.

He used "writing" (الكِتابَةُ) as a metaphor for what results from it of recompense. Therefore the "sin" (السِّينُ), which indicates the future, entered, meaning: "We will repay him" for what he says. Al-Zamakhshari said: In it there are two possibilities:

The first: "It will become clear to him, and We will let him know that We have recorded his saying," in the manner of his saying:

"When we boast of lineage, a base woman did not bear me."

That is, he made clear and knew by the lineage that I am not the son of a base woman.

The second: that the one who threatens says to the criminal, "I will surely take revenge on you," meaning that he does not withhold from victory even if time lengthens and it is delayed. So here he used it for the sense of a threat. He concluded.

The majority read "We will write" (سَنَكْتُبُ) with a nun, and al-A'mash read it with a damma on the ya' and a fatha on the ta', in the passive voice; it is also transmitted from 'Asim. "And We will extend" (وَنَمُدُّ), that is, We will lengthen for him "of the punishment" with which the mockers are punished, or We will increase him in punishment and multiply his extension. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib read ﴿and We will extend for him﴾; it is said "madda" and "amadda" with the same meaning.

﴿And We will inherit from him what he says﴾, that is, We will strip him of wealth and children, so that We are like an heir to him. Al-Kalbi said: We will give to others what he wishes of Paradise. Abu Suhayl said: We will deprive him of what he wishes of wealth and children, and give it to others. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is possible that he desired and hoped that God would give him wealth and children in this world, and his greed reached the point that he swore against God in his saying "I will surely be given" (لَأُوتَيَنَّ), because it is the response to an implied oath, and whoever swears against God, God contradicts him. So God, Mighty and Exalted, says: Suppose We gave him what he desired; We will inherit it from him in the end, ﴿and he will come to Us alone﴾ tomorrow, without wealth and without children, like His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And you have come to Us alone, as We created you the first time﴾ [al-An'am: 94], so his desire and his oath will not benefit him. It is possible that this statement is what he says only as long as he is alive; when We take him, We will prevent him from saying it, and he will come to Us ("and he comes to Us") rejecting it, separated from it, no longer saying it. He concluded.

Al-Nahhas said: "And We will inherit from him what he says" means: We will keep it for him for the outcome; and from this comes "the scholars are the heirs of the prophets," that is, the guardians of what they said. He concluded. "Alone" (فَرْدًا) implies his humiliation and the absence of his helpers. "Says" (يَقُولُ) is the relative clause of "what" (مَا), and it is in the present form but its meaning is past, that is, what he said.

The pronoun in "they took" (وَاتَّخَذُوا) refers to the worship of idols, and what it refers to has already been mentioned: they are the wrongdoers in His saying ﴿And We leave the wrongdoers﴾ [Maryam: 72]. So every pronoun that is followed by a plural refers back to it, if it is possible for it to refer back to it. The lam in "so that they may be" (لِيَكُونُوا) is the lam of purpose, that is, "so that they may be," that is, the gods "for them a might" by which they strengthen themselves in victory, in benefit, and in rescue from punishment.

"Kallā" (by no means). Al-Zamakhsharī said: "Kallā" is a rebuke to them and a denial of their being strengthened by the gods. Ibn Nahīk recited, "Kallā sa-yakfurūna bi-ʿibādatihim" (by no means; they will deny their worship of them), meaning: they will repudiate it, like your saying, "Zayd, I passed by his servant." In Ibn Jinnī's *al-Muḥtasab*, it is "kallan" with a fatḥa on the kāf and tanwīn, and he claimed its meaning is "a lessening of this opinion and belief." One may say that if this transmission is sound, then it is the "kallā" used for rebuke, and the reader turned its alif into a nūn, as in "qawārīrā" (glass vessels). End of quote.

As for his statement, "Ibn Nahīk recited," which Ibn Khālawayh, the author of *al-Lawāmiḥ*, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, and Abū Nahīk (known by the kunya) mentioned, and who is the one from whom the irregular recitations (*shādhdh*) are transmitted, and who recited "kallan" with a fatḥa on the kāf and tanwīn, Abū al-Fatḥ also transmitted it this way from him. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said, "He means that 'kallan' is an adjective for the gods." He said: Abū ʿAmr al-Dānī transmitted from him (i.e., from Abū Nahīk) "kullan" with a ḍamma on the kāf and tanwīn, and it is in the accusative by a hidden verb indicated by "sa-yakfurūna," its estimate being: they will reject, or abandon, or deny, or the like.

As for al-Zamakhsharī's statement, "One may say..." to the end, it is not good, because he said, "It is the one for rebuke," and the particle of rebuke is a letter, and there is no basis for converting its alif into a nūn. Comparing it to "qawārīrā" is not good either, because "qawārīrā" is a noun that has been returned to its original form, so the tanwīn is not a replacement for an alif but the tanwīn of ṣarf (declension). This plural is disputed: is its prohibition from declension obligatory or permissible? There are two opinions. It is also reported that some Arabs decline what is not declined according to others, so this tanwīn is either according to the view that does not hold the prohibition to be obligatory, or according to that dialect.

Al-Ṭabarī mentioned from Abū Nahīk that he recited "kullun" with a ḍamma on the kāf and a rafʿ on the lām, its rafʿ being as the subject (mubtadaʾ), and the sentence after it being the predicate (khabar). The explicit antecedent mentioned before it is "al-ālihah" (the gods), and after it comes a pronoun in "liyakūnū." The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in "sa-yakfurūna" refers to the nearest previously mentioned noun that is spoken of. The meaning then is that the gods will deny the worship of these people of them, as He said: ﴿And when those who associated others with God see their associates﴾ [al-Naḥl: 86], and at its end: ﴿they will throw the word at them: "You are indeed liars."﴾ [al-Naḥl: 86]. "Ālihah" here may be specific to those who understand, or God may give the non-rational gods a perception by which they deny the worship of their worshippers. It is also possible that the pronoun refers to the polytheists, who deny, out of fear of the bad outcome, that they were what they said: ﴿By God, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ [al-Anʿām: 23]. But His saying "wa-yakūnūna" (and they will be) favours the first view, for the consistency of pronouns with one referent; on the other view the pronouns differ, since in "sa-yakfurūna" it refers to the polytheists and in "yakūnūna" to the gods.

The meaning of "ḍiddan" (opponents/helpers) is "helpers," as said by Ibn ʿAbbās. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: "enemies." Qatādah said: "companions." Ibn Zayd said: "a trial." Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: its meaning is that there will come to them from it the opposite of what they had hoped, so that this will lead them to a humiliation opposite to the honour they had hoped for. Thus "al-ḍidd" here is a verbal noun described by it, as the singular is described by it. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "al-ḍidd" means "the helper," used in the singular form, because they are against others as one thing, owing to the agreement of their word and their being like one thing in their extreme solidarity and conformity. The meaning of their being a helper against them is that they are the fuel of the Fire and the pebbles of Hell, and because they were punished on account of their worship.

(p-212) "Whoever is in error, let the Most Merciful extend his term" (فَلْيَمْدُدْ) may be read as a jussive in its literal sense, as a supplication (دُعاءً). The meaning would then be: "May God extend the term of whichever of us or of you is more astray; that is, may He grant him respite until it leads him to His punishment." Supplication is expressed in the form of a command because that is the original form. It may also be a statement in meaning, with the form of a command: "Whoever among the nations is astray, God's custom toward him is to extend his term and not hasten to punish him, until that leads to his punishment in the Hereafter." Al-Zamakhshari (Zamakhshari) said: "It is expressed in the form of a command to indicate that this is binding, and that it is certain to happen, like something commanded that is carried out, in order to cut off the excuses of the one who is astray. It will be said to him on the Day of Resurrection: ﴿Did We not give you a life long enough for whoever would take heed to take heed?﴾ [Fatir: 37], or like His saying: ﴿We only give them respite so that they may increase in sin﴾ [Al 'Imran: 178]." The apparent reading is that "until" (حَتّى) is the limit of His saying "let him extend," and the meaning is: those who are in error are given respite in it until they witness the punishment, through God's support of the believers, or the Hour and its precursors.

Al-Zamakhshari also said: In this verse there are two possibilities. The first is that it connects to the verse which is its fourth, and the two verses in between are a parenthetical insertion. That is: they said ﴿Which of the two groups is better in station and finer in assembly?﴾ [Maryam: 73], ﴿until they see what they are promised﴾, meaning: they do not cease saying this statement and boasting of it, and they do not refrain from it until they see the promised thing with their own eyes, ﴿either the punishment﴾ in this world, which is the victory of the Muslims over them and their being punished by killing and captivity, and God's making His religion prevail over all religion through their hands; ﴿or the Day of Resurrection﴾ and the disgrace and torment that will befall them. Then, at the moment of witnessing, they will know that the matter is the reverse of what they had supposed, and that they are ﴿worse in station and weaker in army﴾, not ﴿better in station and finer in assembly﴾ [Maryam: 73], and that the believers are the opposite of their description. He concluded. This possibility is extremely remote because of the long separation between His saying "they said: ﴿Which of the two groups﴾" [Maryam: 73] and the limit, and it involves separation by two parenthetical clauses, which Abu 'Ali does not permit.

Al-Zamakhshari said: The second is that it connects with what follows it, so he mentioned something similar to what we have presented, and he set their saying ﴿better in station﴾ [Maryam: 73] against His saying ﴿worse in station﴾, and their saying ﴿finer in assembly﴾ [Maryam: 73] against His saying ﴿weaker in army﴾; because the nadi (نَدِيّ, the gathering) is the assembly that brings together the notables of the people, their helpers and supporters, and the jund (جُنْد, army) are the helpers and supporters. And ﴿either the punishment or the Hour﴾ is a substitute (بَدَلٌ) for "what" (مَا), the object of "they see." "Whom" (مَن) is a relative pronoun, the object of His saying "they will know" (فَسَيَعْلَمُونَ), which takes one object; and it is an interrogative, and the verb before it is suspended (مُعَلَّق), and the clause is in the position of an accusative.

When He mentioned the extension given to the one who is astray in his error, and his confusion in boasting of the blessings of this world, He followed that with an increase of guidance for the one who is guided, and with mention of "the enduring good deeds" (الباقِياتُ), which are a substitute for their enjoyment in this world, which vanishes and does not last. "Return" (مَرَدًّا) means "place of return." The explanation of ﴿the enduring good deeds﴾ [al-Kahf: 46] has already been given in Surat al-Kahf.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "He increases" (يَزِيدُ) is coordinated with the position of "let him extend" (فَلْيَمْدُدْ), because it occupies the position of a predicate; its estimated form is: "whoever is in error, the Most Merciful extends for him an extension, and increases (وَيَزِيدُ)," that is, He increases the error of the one who is astray by abandoning him, and He increases the guidance of those who are guided by granting them success. He concluded. But it is not valid for "He increases" to be coordinated with the position of "let him extend," whether it is a supplication or a statement in the form of a command, because it occupies the position of a predicate if "whoever" (مَن) is a relative pronoun, or the position of the response if "whoever" is a conditional. On both estimates, the clause ﴿God increases those who were guided in guidance﴾ lacks a pronoun referring back to "whoever," which would link the predicate clause to the subject, or the conditional clause to the response, which is "let him extend" and what is coordinated with it. This is because a coordinated item after a predicate is a predicate, and a coordinated item after the response is a response. When the conditional particle is a noun and not an adverb, it is necessary that the response clause contain a pronoun referring to it, or something that stands in its place; and likewise in the clause coordinated with it.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Better in reward" (خَيْرٌ ثَوابًا) is one of the boasts of the unbelievers, ﴿and better in return﴾, that is, better in place of return and outcome, or in benefit, from their saying: "There is no return (مَرَدٌّ) for this matter," and "Will my place return to Zayd?" If you say: How is it said "better in reward," when their boasting has a reward, so that the reward of the righteous deeds would be made better than it? I say: It is as if it were said that their reward is the Fire, following the manner of his saying: "Then they were paid back with the Sayhal," and his saying:

"A she-camel of stout build, whose gait is the walk, chewing it, its cud, when the riding camels halt and rest"

and his saying:

"Their greeting among them is a painful blow."

Then he built upon it "better in reward," and in it there is a kind of mockery, which is more enraging to the one being threatened than to be told "your punishment is the Fire." If you say: What is the sense of the comparative in the predicate, when they had partners in their boasting? I say: This is from the concise speech of their people, who say: "Summer is hotter than winter," meaning: it is more intense in its heat than winter is in its cold. He concluded.

﴿Have you seen the one who disbelieved in Our signs and said: "I will surely be given wealth and children"?﴾ It was revealed concerning al-'As ibn Wa'il. Khabbab ibn al-Aratt did work for him, and he was a qayn (قَيْن, a smith). A debt accumulated for him with him, so he demanded it, and he said: "I will not do justice to you until you disbelieve in Muhammad." Khabbab said: "I will not disbelieve in Muhammad until God causes you to die and then resurrects you." Al-'As said: "Shall I be resurrected after death?" Khabbab said: "Yes." He said: "Then, when that happens, I will have wealth and children, and at that time I will pay you your debt." Al-Hasan said: It was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, and al-Walid also had statements resembling this aim. Since seeing things is a path to comprehending them and to the soundness of reports about them, they used "have you seen" (أَرَأَيْتَ) in the sense of "inform" (أَخْبَرَ). The "fa" (فَاءُ) indicates coordination and conveys sequence, as if it were said: "Inform us also of the story of this unbeliever, following the story of those." "The signs" (الآياتُ) are the Qur'an and the proofs for resurrection.

The majority read "and children" (وَلَدًا) in all four places here and in al-Zukhruf, with a fatha on the lam and the waw, and the disagreement concerning Nuh will come. Al-A'mash, Talha, al-Kisa'i, Ibn Abi Layla, and Ibn 'Isa al-Isfahani read it with a damma on the waw and a sukun on the lam. According to the reading of the majority, the meaning is generic, not considering singularity, even though the word is singular in form. According to this reading, some said it is a plural, like asad and usud (lion and lions), and the one who held this view cited the poet's words:

"Indeed I have seen a company who have multiplied wealth and offspring."

It was also said that it is a synonym for walad (وَلَد) with two fathas, and they cited the words:

"Would that so-and-so had been in his mother's belly, and would that so-and-so had been the offspring of a donkey."

'Abd Allah and Yahya ibn Ya'mur read with a kasra on the waw and a sukun on the lam. The hamza in "has he looked into the unseen" (أطَّلَعَ) is interrogative, and for this reason "or" (أَمْ) is paired with it. It was also read with a kasra on the hamza at the beginning and its deletion in continuous speech, on the estimate that the interrogative hamza is deleted, since "or" indicates it, as in his saying: "With seven did they throw the pebbles, or with eight?" meaning: "with seven?" The construction with "have you seen" (أَرَأَيْتَ) follows the arrangement mentioned by Sibawayh, that it takes one object which it governs, and the second is an interrogative. So "has he looked into" (أطَّلَعَ) and what follows it occupy the position of the second object of "have you seen." What comes of the construction of "have you seen" in the sense of "inform me," contrary to this on the surface, should be referred back to this by interpretation.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Has he looked into the unseen" (أطَّلَعَ الغَيْبَ) comes from their saying: "He ascended the mountain" when he climbed to its top, and "he looked over the pass" (اطَّلَعَ الثَّنِيَةَ). Jarir said:

"I met the difficult summits of the mountains."

And one says: "Go, ascending (مُطَّلِعًا) to that matter," meaning: high over it and in control of it. The choice of this word has significance. You say: "Has he reached such a height of greatness that he ascended to knowledge of the unseen, which is the exclusive domain of the One, the Subduer?" The meaning is that what he claimed he would be given and swore to can only be reached by one of these two paths: either knowledge of the unseen, or a covenant from the Knower of the unseen. So by which of the two did he reach that?

"Covenant" (الْعَهْدُ): It was said it is the word of testimony. Qatada said: Does he have a righteous deed he sent ahead, so that he hopes by it for what he says? It is related from al-Kalbi: Has God made a covenant with him that He would give him that?

"No" (كَلَّا) is a rebuke and an admonition concerning the error he is in, in what he imagines for himself and wishes, so let him refrain from it. Abu Nahik read "kallan" (كَلًّا) with tanwin in both places here, and it is a verbal noun from "the sword was dulled" (كَلَّ السَّيْفُ), when it became blunt against striking. Its accusative status is due to an implied verb of the same root, and its estimate is: "Be blunt (كَلُوا) to the worship of God, or to the truth," and the like.

He used "writing" (الكِتابَةُ) as a metaphor for what results from it of recompense. Therefore the "sin" (السِّينُ), which indicates the future, entered, meaning: "We will repay him" for what he says. Al-Zamakhshari said: In it there are two possibilities:

The first: "It will become clear to him, and We will let him know that We have recorded his saying," in the manner of his saying:

"When we boast of lineage, a base woman did not bear me."

That is, he made clear and knew by the lineage that I am not the son of a base woman.

The second: that the one who threatens says to the criminal, "I will surely take revenge on you," meaning that he does not withhold from victory even if time lengthens and it is delayed. So here he used it for the sense of a threat. He concluded.

The majority read "We will write" (سَنَكْتُبُ) with a nun, and al-A'mash read it with a damma on the ya' and a fatha on the ta', in the passive voice; it is also transmitted from 'Asim. "And We will extend" (وَنَمُدُّ), that is, We will lengthen for him "of the punishment" with which the mockers are punished, or We will increase him in punishment and multiply his extension. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib read ﴿and We will extend for him﴾; it is said "madda" and "amadda" with the same meaning.

﴿And We will inherit from him what he says﴾, that is, We will strip him of wealth and children, so that We are like an heir to him. Al-Kalbi said: We will give to others what he wishes of Paradise. Abu Suhayl said: We will deprive him of what he wishes of wealth and children, and give it to others. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is possible that he desired and hoped that God would give him wealth and children in this world, and his greed reached the point that he swore against God in his saying "I will surely be given" (لَأُوتَيَنَّ), because it is the response to an implied oath, and whoever swears against God, God contradicts him. So God, Mighty and Exalted, says: Suppose We gave him what he desired; We will inherit it from him in the end, ﴿and he will come to Us alone﴾ tomorrow, without wealth and without children, like His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And you have come to Us alone, as We created you the first time﴾ [al-An'am: 94], so his desire and his oath will not benefit him. It is possible that this statement is what he says only as long as he is alive; when We take him, We will prevent him from saying it, and he will come to Us ("and he comes to Us") rejecting it, separated from it, no longer saying it. He concluded.

Al-Nahhas said: "And We will inherit from him what he says" means: We will keep it for him for the outcome; and from this comes "the scholars are the heirs of the prophets," that is, the guardians of what they said. He concluded. "Alone" (فَرْدًا) implies his humiliation and the absence of his helpers. "Says" (يَقُولُ) is the relative clause of "what" (مَا), and it is in the present form but its meaning is past, that is, what he said.

The pronoun in "they took" (وَاتَّخَذُوا) refers to the worship of idols, and what it refers to has already been mentioned: they are the wrongdoers in His saying ﴿And We leave the wrongdoers﴾ [Maryam: 72]. So every pronoun that is followed by a plural refers back to it, if it is possible for it to refer back to it. The lam in "so that they may be" (لِيَكُونُوا) is the lam of purpose, that is, "so that they may be," that is, the gods "for them a might" by which they strengthen themselves in victory, in benefit, and in rescue from punishment.

"Kallā" (by no means). Al-Zamakhsharī said: "Kallā" is a rebuke to them and a denial of their being strengthened by the gods. Ibn Nahīk recited, "Kallā sa-yakfurūna bi-ʿibādatihim" (by no means; they will deny their worship of them), meaning: they will repudiate it, like your saying, "Zayd, I passed by his servant." In Ibn Jinnī's *al-Muḥtasab*, it is "kallan" with a fatḥa on the kāf and tanwīn, and he claimed its meaning is "a lessening of this opinion and belief." One may say that if this transmission is sound, then it is the "kallā" used for rebuke, and the reader turned its alif into a nūn, as in "qawārīrā" (glass vessels). End of quote.

As for his statement, "Ibn Nahīk recited," which Ibn Khālawayh, the author of *al-Lawāmiḥ*, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, and Abū Nahīk (known by the kunya) mentioned, and who is the one from whom the irregular recitations (*shādhdh*) are transmitted, and who recited "kallan" with a fatḥa on the kāf and tanwīn, Abū al-Fatḥ also transmitted it this way from him. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said, "He means that 'kallan' is an adjective for the gods." He said: Abū ʿAmr al-Dānī transmitted from him (i.e., from Abū Nahīk) "kullan" with a ḍamma on the kāf and tanwīn, and it is in the accusative by a hidden verb indicated by "sa-yakfurūna," its estimate being: they will reject, or abandon, or deny, or the like.

As for al-Zamakhsharī's statement, "One may say..." to the end, it is not good, because he said, "It is the one for rebuke," and the particle of rebuke is a letter, and there is no basis for converting its alif into a nūn. Comparing it to "qawārīrā" is not good either, because "qawārīrā" is a noun that has been returned to its original form, so the tanwīn is not a replacement for an alif but the tanwīn of ṣarf (declension). This plural is disputed: is its prohibition from declension obligatory or permissible? There are two opinions. It is also reported that some Arabs decline what is not declined according to others, so this tanwīn is either according to the view that does not hold the prohibition to be obligatory, or according to that dialect.

Al-Ṭabarī mentioned from Abū Nahīk that he recited "kullun" with a ḍamma on the kāf and a rafʿ on the lām, its rafʿ being as the subject (mubtadaʾ), and the sentence after it being the predicate (khabar). The explicit antecedent mentioned before it is "al-ālihah" (the gods), and after it comes a pronoun in "liyakūnū." The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in "sa-yakfurūna" refers to the nearest previously mentioned noun that is spoken of. The meaning then is that the gods will deny the worship of these people of them, as He said: ﴿And when those who associated others with God see their associates﴾ [al-Naḥl: 86], and at its end: ﴿they will throw the word at them: "You are indeed liars."﴾ [al-Naḥl: 86]. "Ālihah" here may be specific to those who understand, or God may give the non-rational gods a perception by which they deny the worship of their worshippers. It is also possible that the pronoun refers to the polytheists, who deny, out of fear of the bad outcome, that they were what they said: ﴿By God, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ [al-Anʿām: 23]. But His saying "wa-yakūnūna" (and they will be) favours the first view, for the consistency of pronouns with one referent; on the other view the pronouns differ, since in "sa-yakfurūna" it refers to the polytheists and in "yakūnūna" to the gods.

The meaning of "ḍiddan" (opponents/helpers) is "helpers," as said by Ibn ʿAbbās. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: "enemies." Qatādah said: "companions." Ibn Zayd said: "a trial." Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: its meaning is that there will come to them from it the opposite of what they had hoped, so that this will lead them to a humiliation opposite to the honour they had hoped for. Thus "al-ḍidd" here is a verbal noun described by it, as the singular is described by it. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "al-ḍidd" means "the helper," used in the singular form, because they are against others as one thing, owing to the agreement of their word and their being like one thing in their extreme solidarity and conformity. The meaning of their being a helper against them is that they are the fuel of the Fire and the pebbles of Hell, and because they were punished on account of their worship.

The meaning would then be: "May God extend the term of whichever of us or of you is more astray; that is, may He grant him respite until it leads him to His punishment." Supplication is expressed in the form of a command because that is the original form. It may also be a statement in meaning, with the form of a command: "Whoever among the nations is astray, God's custom toward him is to extend his term and not hasten to punish him, until that leads to his punishment in the Hereafter." Al-Zamakhshari (Zamakhshari) said: "It is expressed in the form of a command to indicate that this is binding, and that it is certain to happen, like something commanded that is carried out, in order to cut off the excuses of the one who is astray. It will be said to him on the Day of Resurrection: ﴿Did We not give you a life long enough for whoever would take heed to take heed?﴾ [Fatir: 37], or like His saying: ﴿We only give them respite so that they may increase in sin﴾ [Al 'Imran: 178]." Then, at the moment of witnessing, they will know that the matter is the reverse of what they had supposed, and that they are ﴿worse in station and weaker in army﴾, not ﴿better in station and finer in assembly﴾ [Maryam: 73], and that the believers are the opposite of their description. Al-Zamakhshari said: The second is that it connects with what follows it, so he mentioned something similar to what we have presented, and he set their saying ﴿better in station﴾ [Maryam: 73] against His saying ﴿worse in station﴾, and their saying ﴿finer in assembly﴾ [Maryam: 73] against His saying ﴿weaker in army﴾; because the nadi (نَدِيّ, the gathering) is the assembly that brings together the notables of the people, their helpers and supporters, and the jund (جُنْد, army) are the helpers and supporters. And ﴿either the punishment or the Hour﴾ is a substitute (بَدَلٌ) for "what" (مَا), the object of "they see." "Whom" (مَن) is a relative pronoun, the object of His saying "they will know" (فَسَيَعْلَمُونَ), which takes one object; and it is an interrogative, and the verb before it is suspended (مُعَلَّق), and the clause is in the position of an accusative.

When He mentioned the extension given to the one who is astray in his error, and his confusion in boasting of the blessings of this world, He followed that with an increase of guidance for the one who is guided, and with mention of "the enduring good deeds" (الباقِياتُ), which are a substitute for their enjoyment in this world, which vanishes and does not last. "Return" (مَرَدًّا) means "place of return." The explanation of ﴿the enduring good deeds﴾ [al-Kahf: 46] has already been given in Surat al-Kahf.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "He increases" (يَزِيدُ) is coordinated with the position of "let him extend" (فَلْيَمْدُدْ), because it occupies the position of a predicate; its estimated form is: "whoever is in error, the Most Merciful extends for him an extension, and increases (وَيَزِيدُ)," that is, He increases the error of the one who is astray by abandoning him, and He increases the guidance of those who are guided by granting them success. He concluded. But it is not valid for "He increases" to be coordinated with the position of "let him extend," whether it is a supplication or a statement in the form of a command, because it occupies the position of a predicate if "whoever" (مَن) is a relative pronoun, or the position of the response if "whoever" is a conditional. On both estimates, the clause ﴿God increases those who were guided in guidance﴾ lacks a pronoun referring back to "whoever," which would link the predicate clause to the subject, or the conditional clause to the response, which is "let him extend" and what is coordinated with it.
