It is possible to analogise these markers to those pronouns, but the safer course is not to say this except on the basis of hearing. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is also possible that (man) is in the accusative, by omitting a modifying noun, i.e., except the intercession of one who has taken [a covenant]."

(Al-ʿahd) here. Ibn Abbas said: "There is no god but Allah, Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah." In a hadith: "Whoever says, 'There is no god but Allah, Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah,' has a covenant with Allah." Al-Suddi said: al-ʿahd is obedience. Ibn Jurayj said: it is the righteous deed. Al-Layth said: it is one who memorised the Book of Allah. It was said: the covenant of Allah is His permission for whomever He wills in intercession, from ʿahida al-amīr ilā fulānin bikadhā (the ruler commissioned so-and-so with such-and-such), i.e., ordered him to do it; that is, none intercedes except one commanded to intercede and permitted to do so. This is supported by His saying: ﴿And intercession with Him does not benefit except for one whom He permits﴾ [Saba: 23], ﴿On that Day, intercession will not benefit except one whom the Most Merciful has permitted﴾ [Ta-Ha: 109], ﴿Their intercession will not avail them at all, except after Allah permits whom He wills and approves﴾ [al-Najm: 26].

(p-218) Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "It is possible that (al-mujrimūn) includes both disbelievers and disobedient sinners, and then He informed that they ﴿do not possess intercession﴾ except the disobedient believers, for they will be interceded for, so the exception is connected." In a hadith: "I will not cease to intercede until I say, 'O Lord, grant me intercession for whoever has said, "There is no god but Allah." ' He will say, 'O Muhammad, it is not for you, but it is for Me.'" End of quotation. Taking (al-mujrimūn) to mean disbelievers and disobedient sinners is far-fetched.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya also said: "It is possible that (man ittakhadha) refers to Muhammad, peace be upon him, and that the special intercession for Muhammad is meant as the general intercession for mankind. And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It may be that your Lord will raise you to a praiseworthy station﴾ [al-Isra': 79]. And the pronoun in (lā yamlikūna) refers to the people of the Standing (al-mawqif)." End of quotation. There is some abridgement in it.

﴿And they say, "The Most Merciful has taken a son."﴾ The pronoun in (qālū) refers to some of the Jews, when they said, "ʿUzayr is the son of Allah," and to some of the Christians, when they said, "The Messiah is the son of Allah," and to some of the Arab polytheists, when they said, "The angels are the daughters of Allah." ﴿Indeed you have produced﴾: that is, say to them, O Muhammad, ﴿Indeed you have produced﴾. Or it is an iltifāt (shift from third-person reference to direct address), moving from the absent to the second person, to add emphasis against them regarding their audacity against Allah, and their exposure to His wrath, and to alert to the enormity of what they said.

The majority read (idd[an]) with a kasra on the hamza. ʿAlī ibn Abi Talib and Abu ʿAbd al-Rahman read it with a fatḥa, meaning shayʾan iddan (a monstrous thing), where the qualified noun is omitted and the verbal noun takes its place. Nafiʿ and al-Kisa'i read (yakādu) with the ya' from below, as also in al-Shura, and this is the reading of Abu Haywa and al-A'mash. The rest of the seven read it with ta'. For (yanfaṭirna), the present tense of infaṭara, Abu ʿAmr, Hamza, Abu Bakr from ʿAsim, and Ibn ʿAmir read it here; this is the reading of Abu Bahriyya, al-Zuhri, Talha, Humayd, al-Yazidi, Ya'qub and Abu ʿUbayd. The rest of the seven read (yatafaṭṭarna), the present tense of tafaṭṭara; and the one in al-Shura was read by Abu ʿAmr and Abu Bakr from ʿAsim with ya' and nūn, while the rest of the seven read it with ya' and ta' and tashdīd. Ibn Masʿud read (yataṣadda'na), and it should be taken as an explanation, since it contradicts the consensual written text of the codex, and since reliable transmitters from him agree with the reading of the majority.

Al-Akhfash said: (takādu) means "it intends" (turīdu), and similarly His saying: ﴿I almost conceal it﴾ [Ta-Ha: 15]. He cited as evidence a line of poetry:

"And it almost was, and I almost was, and that is the best intention, if the time of passion could return with what has passed."

There is no proof in this line. The known meaning is that kaydūda is approaching something. These phrases, according to the majority, are a figure of speech (istiʿāra) to express the monstrousness of this utterance; that is, this is its due, even if the inanimate things understood its magnitude. This is a familiar style among the Arabs. Jarir said:

"When the news of al-Zubayr came, the walls of Medina humbled themselves, and the lofty mountains."

Another said:

"Did you not see a crack appearing in the sky over a son of the Banu al-Harith ibn Hisham?"

Another said:

"So the belly of Mecca became horrified, as if the earth had no Hisham in it."

Another said:

"Harith al-Jawlan wept for the loss of his lord, and Hawran, from it, was humbled and crushed."

Harith al-Jawlan is a place.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: what is the meaning of the heavens being torn apart, the earth being split, and the mountains collapsing, and how does this word affect inanimate things? I say: there are two aspects to this. The first is that Allah says: 'I almost did these things to the heavens, the earth and the mountains upon the utterance of this word, out of anger at the one who uttered it, were it not for My forbearance and My dignity, and that I do not hasten punishment,' as He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah holds the heavens and the earth lest they should cease﴾ [Fatir: 41], and so on. The second is that it is a magnification of the word and an expression of its terror, and a depiction of its effect on religion, its demolition of its pillars and foundations; and the example of that effect among tangible things is that these great bodies, which are the pillars of the world, are almost torn apart, split open, and collapse from it." End of quotation.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: "This statement made the heavens, the earth, the mountains and all creatures afraid, except the two weighty ones (humans and jinn), and they were on the verge of collapsing from it, out of glorification of God, exalted is He." It was also said: the meaning is that the Resurrection is about to occur, for these things will literally come to pass on the Day of Resurrection. It was also said: "The heavens are almost rent asunder" (تَكادُ السَّماواتُ يَتَفَطَّرْنَ), meaning they fall upon them; "and the earth is split asunder" (وتَنْشَقُّ الأرْضُ), meaning it swallows them up; "and the mountains collapse in ruin" (وتَخِرُّ الجِبالُ هَدًّا), meaning they crush them.

Abu Muslim said: "It is as if they would do that, were they to understand, because of the enormity of this utterance." Al-Nahhas held that (هَدًّا) is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), saying: "Because the meaning of (تَخِرُّ) is to be shattered (تَنْهَدُّ)." End of quote. This is on the basis that (هَدًّا) is a verbal noun of هَدَّ الحائِطُ يَهِدُّ بِالكَسْرِ هَدِيدًا وهَدًّا, which is an intransitive verb (fiʿl lāzim). It was also said that (هَدًّا) is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl), meaning "being demolished," and this is on the basis that (هَدًّا) is the verbal noun of هَدَّ الحائِطَ, meaning "he demolished the wall," which is a transitive verb (fiʿl mutaʿaddin). Al-Zamakhshari permitted that it be an object of purpose (mafʿūl lahu), meaning "because they are demolished."

Al-Zamakhshari permitted three possibilities regarding ﴿أنْ دَعَوْا﴾ (that they ascribed). He said: it may be in the genitive as a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in (مِنهُ), as in his saying:

"In a state where, if Hatim were among the people, with his generosity, Hatim would be stingy with water."

This has remoteness, because of the great separation between the substitute and what it substitutes for, by two clauses. He said: it may be in the accusative by the omission of the preposition (lām) and the transmission of the verb, meaning (هَدًّا), because (دَعَوْا) gives the reason for the collapse (الخُرُور) as "the demolition" (الهَدّ), and the demolition is by the calling of a son to the Merciful. This also has remoteness, because the apparent sense is that (هَدًّا) is not an object, but rather a verbal noun from the meaning of (وتَخِرُّ), or in the position of a circumstantial qualifier. He said: it may be in the nominative as the agent of (هَدًّا), meaning: the calling of a son to the Merciful demolished them. This has remoteness, because the apparent sense of (هَدًّا) is that it is an emphatic verbal noun (maṣdar tawkīdī), and an emphatic verbal noun does not govern. Even if we supposed it non-emphatic, it would not govern by analogy, except if it is a command or a question about it, as in ḍarban Zaydan and uḍrib Zaydan, with a difference of opinion on this. As for if it is a statement, as al-Zamakhshari estimated, meaning "the calling of the Merciful demolished them," this is not analogical; rather what comes of that is rare, as in his saying:

"Standing by them, my companions, their mounts over me."

Meaning: my companions stood.

Al-Hawfi and Abu al-Baqa said: ﴿أنْ دَعَوْا﴾ is in the accusative position as an object of purpose, and they did not specify the governing element. Abu al-Baqa also said: it is in the genitive position with the lām estimated, and in the nominative position, meaning: what necessitates that is their calling. The meaning of (دَعَوْا) is "they named," and it is transitive to two objects, the first of which is omitted, and the estimate is "they named their deity a son of the Merciful," i.e., "with a son," because دَعا in this sense is transitive to two objects, and it is permissible for the preposition (بـ) to enter the second, as you say: "I called my son with Zayd," or "I called my son Zayd." The poet said:

"The mother of ʿAmr called me her brother, though I was not her brother, nor did I suckle at her breast."

Another said:

"Many a one claims to be a sincere advisor, and if he is absent, you will find him, in his absence from you, not sincere."

Al-Zamakhshari said: he restricted it to one of them, the second, seeking generality and comprehensiveness regarding everything for which he called a son, and he said: or (دَعا) is in the sense of "ascribed," whose reflexive form is what is in his saying, peace be upon him: "Whoever claims affiliation to other than his patrons..." and the saying of the poet:

"We, the sons of Nahshal, do not claim (ascription) to a father."

Meaning, we do not attribute ourselves to him. End of quote. That (دَعَوْا) here means "named" is the view of most. It was also said: (دَعَوْا) means "made."

(يَنْبَغِي) is the reflexive form of بَغى in the sense of "sought," meaning: it is not possible for Him to take a son, because procreation is impossible, and adoption can only occur in what is of the same kind as the adopted, and He, exalted is He, has no kind. (يَنْبَغِي) is not among the verbs that lack conjugation (lā tatasarraf); rather, its past tense has been heard, they said انْبَغى. Ibn Malik had counted it in al-Tashil among the verbs that lack conjugation, and this is an error. (مَن) is a relative pronoun meaning "who/that," meaning: there is not everyone who is in the heavens and the earth. (كُلُّ) enters upon (الَّذِي) because it comes for the genus, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿والَّذِي جاءَ بِالصِّدْقِ﴾ [al-Zumar: 33], and like:

"And all that you burdened me with, I will bear."

Al-Zamakhshari said (مَن) is a descriptive (mawṣūfa), because it occurred after (كُلُّ) as an indefinite noun, as it occurred after رُبَّ in his saying:

"Many a one whose chest I have made seethe with rage."

End of quote. The better view is to make it a relative pronoun, because its being descriptive relative to the relative is rare.

ʿAbd Allah, Ibn al-Zubayr, Abu Haywa, Talha, Abu Bahriyya, Ibn Abi ʿAbla and Yaʿqub read ﴿إلّا آتٍ﴾ with tanwin, and ﴿الرَّحْمَنَ﴾ in the accusative, while the majority read it with the genitive construction. "Ati" is the predicate of "kull," and ("ʿabdan") is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier. The word ﴿الرَّحْمَنِ﴾ is repeated as an alert that no one else deserves this name, since the roots and branches of blessings come from Him. And "whoever is in the heavens and the earth" includes those whom they took as deities from among the angels, ʿIsa and ʿUzayr, by virtue of their claim of the validity of procreation, or by virtue of their assertion of that, so they associated them in worship, since serving the sons is serving the fathers. So God, exalted is He, informed that there is no deity for them in the heavens or on the earth except that it comes to the Merciful as a servant, submissive, not claiming for itself anything of what they ascribed to it.

Then God, exalted is He, mentioned that He "has counted them" and encompassed them and confined them by number, so none of them escapes Him. (فَرْدًا) is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier, meaning: alone, with no one with Him of those they made partners with Him. The predicate of ﴿كُلُّهم آتِيهِ﴾ is ﴿فَرْدًا﴾. When "kull" is attached to a definite noun that is pronounced, such as "kulluhum" and "kull al-nas," it is reported that the pronoun may return singular to the wording of "kull," so you say "kullukum dhahib" (each of you is going), and it may return plural in consideration of the meaning, so you say "kullukum dhahibun." Ibrahim ibn Asbagh, in the book Ru'us al-Masa'il, related a consensus on the permissibility of both forms. On the plural form, al-Zamakhshari's wording in his commentary on this verse in al-Kashshaf is: "wa-kulluhum mutaqallibun fi malakutihi maqhurun bi-qahrihi" (all of them are moving about in His dominion, subdued by His dominance). Abu Zayd al-Suhayli criticized this, saying: "kull," when it begins and is grammatically attached to a definite noun, it is only good to make the predicate singular, taking the meaning into account. You say "kullukum dhahib," i.e., "each one of you is going." This is the case with this issue in the Qur'an, the hadith and eloquent speech. If you say: in His saying "wa-kulluhum atihi" it is taking the wording into account, since it is a singular noun, we say: rather, it is a noun of plurality, and a noun of plurality is not predicated with a singular. You say "al-qawm dhahibun" (the people are going), and you do not say "al-qawm dhahib," even though the word "qawm" is like the singular form. The phrase "kullukum dhahib" is only good because they say "kullu wahidin minkum dhahib" (each one of you is going), so the singular was in consideration of this meaning. End of quote. Establishing "kullukum dhahibun" in the plural and similar forms requires hearing and transmission from the Arabs. As for if the defined genitive noun is omitted, then what is heard from the Arabs is both forms.

The sīn in ﴿سَيَجْعَلُ﴾ is for the future. It is possible that this making (of affection) occurs in this world, and the future particle was used because the believers were in Mecca at the time this sura was revealed, and they were hated by the disbelievers, so God promised them this when Islam becomes manifest and spreads. It is also possible that this occurs in this world in general, as in al-Tirmidhi, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When God loves a servant, He calls Jibril: 'I have loved so-and-so, so love him.' He says: Then he calls in the heaven, then love is placed for him on earth." God, mighty and majestic, said: "Indeed those who believe and do righteous deeds, the Merciful will appoint for them affection (wudd)," to the end of the hadith. He said: This is a sound hadith. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: It is possible that the verse is connected in meaning with what precedes it, meaning: when God, exalted is He, informed about the coming of everyone in the heavens and the earth in a state of servitude and solitude, He comforted the believers by telling them that He will make for them on that day "wudd," which is what appears upon them of His honor, because God's love for the servant is nothing but what appears upon him of His blessings and the signs of His forgiveness. End of quote.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Or it may be that on the Day of Resurrection He makes them beloved to His creatures by what good deeds of theirs He displays and what He spreads from the register of their deeds. He also said: The meaning is that He will create in the hearts affection for them and cultivate it for them therein, without any solicitation from them and without their resorting to the means by which people acquire affection of hearts, such as kinship, friendship, performing kindness, or other things; rather, it is an innovation from Him, initiated as a special favor to His allies with a particular honor, just as He casts terror and awe into the hearts of their enemies, magnifying and exalting their station. End of quote. It was also said: there is an ellipsis in the speech, and the estimate is: He will admit them to the abode of His honor (p-221) and make for them "wudd" by means of the removal of rancor from their breasts, unlike the disbelievers, for on the Day of Resurrection some of them disbelieve in others, curse one another, and in the Fire too some of them disown others.

The majority read "wuddan" with a dhamma on the waw. Abu al-Harith al-Hanafi read it with a fatha on it. Jinah ibn Hubaysh read "widdan" with a kasra on the waw. It was said: this verse was revealed concerning ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn ʿAwf; the Jews, Christians and hypocrites used to love him, and when he migrated from Mecca he felt lonely in Medina, so he complained of that to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and this verse was revealed. It was also said: it was revealed concerning the emigrants to Abyssinia with Jaʿfar ibn Abi Talib; God cast affection for them into the heart of the Negus. Al-Naqqash mentioned that it was revealed concerning ʿAli ibn Abi Talib. Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya said: You will not find a believer except that he loves ʿAli and his household. End of quote. Among the strange things is what our teacher, the linguist Radi al-Din Abu ʿAbd Allah Muhammad ibn ʿAli ibn Yusuf al-Ansari al-Shatibi, may God have mercy on him, recited to us, for Zaynab, daughter of Ishaq the Christian al-Rasʿani:

"ʿAdi and Taym, I do not seek to mention them with evil, but I love Hashim."

"And nothing reproaches me concerning ʿAli and his kinsfolk, when they are mentioned for God, the blame of a blamer."

"They say: why is it that the Christians love them, while the people of understanding, among Arabs and non-Arabs, do not?"

"So I said to them: I truly think their love has spread in the hearts of creation, even to the beasts."

Abu Muhammad ibn Hazm mentioned that hatred of ʿAli is among the major sins.

The pronoun in ﴿يَسَّرْناهُ﴾ refers to the Qur'an, meaning: We sent it down to you, made easy and simple "in your tongue," i.e., in your language, which is the clear Arabic tongue. ﴿لِتُبَشِّرَ بِهِ المُتَّقِينَ﴾ means: that you may inform them of what will please them and of the reward they will have for their piety. "Lud" is a plural. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "lud" means in darkness; Mujahid: wicked; al-Hasan: deaf; Abu Salih: crooked from the truth; Qatada: people of disputation with falsehood, taking up every contentious matter with argument, i.e., on every side, because of their extreme obstinacy. He means the people of Mecca.

﴿وكَمْ أهْلَكْنا﴾ is a warning to them and a threat of destruction by punishment. The pronoun in His saying "qablahum" (before them) refers to "qawman ludda" (a contentious people). ﴿هَلْ تُحِسُّ﴾ is an interrogative with the meaning of negation, i.e., you do not perceive. The majority read ﴿هَلْ تُحِسُّ﴾ as the present tense of aḥassa. Abu Haywa, Abu Bahriyya, Ibn Abi ʿAbla and Abu Jaʿfar al-Madani read "taḥussu" with a fatha on the ta and a dhamma on the ha. It was also read "taḥissu," from ḥassahu, meaning "he sensed it," and from it come "al-ḥawass" (the senses) and "al-mahsusat" (the perceptible things). Hanzala read "aw tusmaʿu," the present tense of "usmiʿat," in the passive voice. Ibn ʿAbbas said: al-rikz is a faint sound. Ibn Zayd said: it is al-ḥiss (sensation). Al-Hasan said: when Our punishment came to them, none of them remained who could be seen, nor any sound heard. It was also said: the meaning is that they died and their mention was forgotten, so no informant reports about them.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 19, verses 83–98 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Have you not seen that We have sent the devils upon the disbelievers, inciting them with strong incitement?﴾ ﴿So do not be hasty against them; We are only counting for them a count.﴾ ﴿On the Day We will gather the God-fearing to the Most Merciful as a delegation.﴾ ﴿And We will drive the criminals to Hell as a thirsty herd.﴾ ﴿They will not possess intercession, except one who has taken a covenant with the Most Merciful.﴾ ﴿And they say, "The Most Merciful has taken a son."﴾ ﴿Indeed you have produced something monstrous.﴾ ﴿The heavens are about to be torn apart from it, and the earth split open, and the mountains collapse in ruin.﴾ ﴿That they attribute to the Most Merciful a son.﴾ ﴿And it is not befitting for the Most Merciful to take a son.﴾ ﴿There is none in the heavens and the earth but that he comes to the Most Merciful as a servant.﴾ ﴿He has enumerated them and counted them with a [precise] counting.﴾ ﴿And each of them will come to Him on the Day of Resurrection alone.﴾ ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, the Most Merciful will bestow on them affection.﴾ ﴿So We have only made it easy in your tongue that you may give glad tidings thereby to the God-fearing and warn thereby a contentious people.﴾ ﴿And how many generations have We destroyed before them? Do you perceive any of them or hear from them a whisper?﴾

(p-216) (Arsalnā) means: We empowered them (salaṭnā), or: We did not stand between them and them. Its semantic parallel is His saying: ﴿We appoint for him a devil﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 36]. Its construction with ʿalā (upon) is evidence that it means empowerment. (Tawuzzuhum) means: they stir them toward disbelief. Qatada said: "They provoke them." Ibn Zayd said: "They incite them." Al-Zamakhshari said: "They spur them on to acts of disobedience and stir them to it through whisperings and enticements. The meaning is: We left them between them and them, and We did not prevent them; had He willed, He would have prevented them. The intended purpose is to express astonishment at the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), following the verses in which the arrogant among the disbelievers and their sayings were mentioned."

Ajilta ʿalayhi bikadhā (I hastened against him with such-and-such) means: I sought to hasten it from him. That is: do not be hasty against them, that they should be destroyed; for between you and what you seek of their destruction there are only limited days and counted breaths, as if in their swiftness the hour in which they are counted is spent, were it counted. Similar to it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So do not seek to hasten [the punishment] for them. It is as if, on the day they see what they are promised, they had not remained but an hour of a day.﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 35]. End of quotation.

It was said: (Naʿuddu) means their deeds, so that We may recompense them. It was said: their terms, so that when it comes We will bring punishment upon them. It was said: their days, which Our decree has preceded that We would grant them respite until. It was said: their breaths.

(Yawma) is in the accusative, governed by an implied verb: udhkur (remember) or uḥdhar (beware), or [it is governed] by [the sense of] "that will be" as an answer to an implied question whose meaning is "when will that be?" Or [it is governed by] "they will disbelieve in their worship," or by "they will be [an enemy] to them" (yakūnūna ʿalayhim ḍiddan), or by the meaning "distance" (buʿdan). The notion of counting and enumeration includes the meaning of recompense. Or [(yawma)] is governed by ﴿yawma naḥshuru﴾ [the Day We gather] and ﴿nasūqu﴾ [We drive]: We will treat both groups in a way that description cannot encompass; or it is governed by ﴿lā yamlikūna﴾ [they will not possess]. All of these are cited as possibilities for the accusative of (yawma), and the most likely is the last.

(Naḥshuru) is transitive with ﴿ilā al-Raḥmān﴾ [to the Most Merciful], to honour and exalt them. He mentioned the attribute of mercy (al-Raḥmāniyya), with which He singled them out as a mark of honour, since the word ḥashr (gathering) carries the sense of assembling from scattered places and distant regions by way of compulsion. Thus the word "al-Raḥmān" comes to indicate that they are gathered to One who shows them mercy. The word sawq (driving) carries a sense of urging on. If it is followed by ﴿ilā Jahannam﴾ [to Hell], it is to shame them and to make the state of their abode appear dreadful. The word wafd (delegation) suggests honour and reverence, just as delegations come to kings, awaiting honour from them.

It is related from Ali: "On camels whose saddles are of gold, and on swift mounts whose saddles are of ruby." And also from him: that they will come riding on camels adorned with the adornment of Paradise, whose nose-rings are of ruby and chrysolite. Amr ibn Qays al-Mala'i narrated: that they will ride upon images of their righteous deeds in the utmost beauty. It is narrated that each of them will ride whatever he loves of camels, horses or ships, which will come floating with them.

The apparent meaning is that this delegation is after the reckoning has ended, and that it is the rising towards Paradise, as He said: ﴿In a seat of truth, in the presence of a Sovereign Omnipotent﴾ [al-Qamar: 55]. They are likened to delegations because they are the nobles of mankind and the finest in appearance, though it is not a true delegation, since a delegation involves departing from the one to whom the delegation is sent, whereas these remain forever in the reward of their Lord, which is Paradise.

(Al-Warid) means the thirsty, as said by Ibn Abbas, Abu Hurayra and al-Hasan. Al-Warid is a verbal noun of warada, meaning to proceed to water. The rajaz poet said:

Come on, come on, to the watering of a dove, dumb, of the grey-brown kind, which the coolness of water has pleased.

Since one who comes to water comes only out of thirst, the term (al-warid) was applied to the thirsty, as a naming of a thing by its cause.

Al-Hasan and al-Jahdari read: "yuḥsharu al-muttaqūna, wa-yusāqu al-mujrimūna" (the God-fearing are gathered, and the criminals are driven), in the passive voice. The pronoun in (lā yamlikūna) refers to the creatures indicated by the mention of the God-fearing and the criminals, since they are its two divisions. The exception is connected (muttaṣil), and (man) is a substitute (badal) for that pronoun, or it is in the accusative as an exception. (Lā yamlikūna) is a resumptive statement of information (istiʾnāf). It was said: its position is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of the pronoun in (lā yamlikūna), and it refers to the criminals. The meaning is: not possessing [the power] that intercession be made for them, and on this view the exception is disconnected (munqaṭiʿ). It was said: the pronoun in (lā yamlikūna) refers to the God-fearing and the criminals, and the exception is connected. It was said: it refers to the God-fearing, and taking a covenant (ittikhādh al-ʿahd) is the righteous deed by which one comes to be within the scope of one who intercedes.

Traditions are consistent that the people of knowledge and righteousness will intercede, and they will be granted intercession. In a hadith: "There is among my community a man through whose intercession Allah will admit more than the tribe of Banu Tamim." Qatada said: "We used to be told that a martyr intercedes for seventy [people]." Some who made the pronoun refer to the God-fearing said: the meaning is that the God-fearing do not possess intercession (al-shafāʿa) except for this category; on this view, (man ittakhadha) refers to those for whom intercession is made. On the first interpretation, (man ittakhadha) refers to the intercessors. So the implied construction on the second interpretation is: "they do not possess intercession for anyone except one who has taken [a covenant]," and it occupies an accusative position, as in the line:

"He was not saved except [in] the sheath of a sword and a loincloth."

That is: nothing was saved except the sheath of a sword. On these views, the waw is a pronoun.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is also possible that the waw in (lā yamlikūna), i.e., the ʿ[plural] marker, is like the one in akalūnī al-barāghīthu (the fleas ate me), and the subject is (man ittakhadha), since it has the sense of a plural." End of quotation. It is not proper to construe the Qur'an according to this rare dialect, especially when making the waw a pronoun is clearly sound. Ibn ʿUṣfūr, the Ustadh Abu al-Hasan, mentioned that it is a weak dialect. Also, they said: the alif and nūn that serve as markers and not as pronouns are not known to be followed by a subject except with explicit plurality or explicit duality or coordination; either a singular word is used that applies to a plural or to a dual, and establishing that requires transmission, or pronouns in the dual and plural refer to a singular form in wording that is meant as dual or plural, which is a known and attested usage in the speech of the Arabs. It is possible to analogise these markers to those pronouns, but the safer course is not to say this except on the basis of hearing. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is also possible that (man) is in the accusative, by omitting a modifying noun, i.e., except the intercession of one who has taken [a covenant]."

(Al-ʿahd) here. Ibn Abbas said: "There is no god but Allah, Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah." In a hadith: "Whoever says, 'There is no god but Allah, Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah,' has a covenant with Allah." Al-Suddi said: al-ʿahd is obedience. Ibn Jurayj said: it is the righteous deed. Al-Layth said: it is one who memorised the Book of Allah. It was said: the covenant of Allah is His permission for whomever He wills in intercession, from ʿahida al-amīr ilā fulānin bikadhā (the ruler commissioned so-and-so with such-and-such), i.e., ordered him to do it; that is, none intercedes except one commanded to intercede and permitted to do so. This is supported by His saying: ﴿And intercession with Him does not benefit except for one whom He permits﴾ [Saba: 23], ﴿On that Day, intercession will not benefit except one whom the Most Merciful has permitted﴾ [Ta-Ha: 109], ﴿Their intercession will not avail them at all, except after Allah permits whom He wills and approves﴾ [al-Najm: 26].

(p-218) Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "It is possible that (al-mujrimūn) includes both disbelievers and disobedient sinners, and then He informed that they ﴿do not possess intercession﴾ except the disobedient believers, for they will be interceded for, so the exception is connected." In a hadith: "I will not cease to intercede until I say, 'O Lord, grant me intercession for whoever has said, "There is no god but Allah." ' He will say, 'O Muhammad, it is not for you, but it is for Me.'" End of quotation. Taking (al-mujrimūn) to mean disbelievers and disobedient sinners is far-fetched.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya also said: "It is possible that (man ittakhadha) refers to Muhammad, peace be upon him, and that the special intercession for Muhammad is meant as the general intercession for mankind. And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It may be that your Lord will raise you to a praiseworthy station﴾ [al-Isra': 79]. And the pronoun in (lā yamlikūna) refers to the people of the Standing (al-mawqif)." End of quotation. There is some abridgement in it.

﴿And they say, "The Most Merciful has taken a son."﴾ The pronoun in (qālū) refers to some of the Jews, when they said, "ʿUzayr is the son of Allah," and to some of the Christians, when they said, "The Messiah is the son of Allah," and to some of the Arab polytheists, when they said, "The angels are the daughters of Allah." ﴿Indeed you have produced﴾: that is, say to them, O Muhammad, ﴿Indeed you have produced﴾. Or it is an iltifāt (shift from third-person reference to direct address), moving from the absent to the second person, to add emphasis against them regarding their audacity against Allah, and their exposure to His wrath, and to alert to the enormity of what they said.

The majority read (idd[an]) with a kasra on the hamza. ʿAlī ibn Abi Talib and Abu ʿAbd al-Rahman read it with a fatḥa, meaning shayʾan iddan (a monstrous thing), where the qualified noun is omitted and the verbal noun takes its place. Nafiʿ and al-Kisa'i read (yakādu) with the ya' from below, as also in al-Shura, and this is the reading of Abu Haywa and al-A'mash. The rest of the seven read it with ta'. For (yanfaṭirna), the present tense of infaṭara, Abu ʿAmr, Hamza, Abu Bakr from ʿAsim, and Ibn ʿAmir read it here; this is the reading of Abu Bahriyya, al-Zuhri, Talha, Humayd, al-Yazidi, Ya'qub and Abu ʿUbayd. The rest of the seven read (yatafaṭṭarna), the present tense of tafaṭṭara; and the one in al-Shura was read by Abu ʿAmr and Abu Bakr from ʿAsim with ya' and nūn, while the rest of the seven read it with ya' and ta' and tashdīd. Ibn Masʿud read (yataṣadda'na), and it should be taken as an explanation, since it contradicts the consensual written text of the codex, and since reliable transmitters from him agree with the reading of the majority.

Al-Akhfash said: (takādu) means "it intends" (turīdu), and similarly His saying: ﴿I almost conceal it﴾ [Ta-Ha: 15]. He cited as evidence a line of poetry:

"And it almost was, and I almost was, and that is the best intention, if the time of passion could return with what has passed."

There is no proof in this line. The known meaning is that kaydūda is approaching something. These phrases, according to the majority, are a figure of speech (istiʿāra) to express the monstrousness of this utterance; that is, this is its due, even if the inanimate things understood its magnitude. This is a familiar style among the Arabs. Jarir said:

"When the news of al-Zubayr came, the walls of Medina humbled themselves, and the lofty mountains."

Another said:

"Did you not see a crack appearing in the sky over a son of the Banu al-Harith ibn Hisham?"

Another said:

"So the belly of Mecca became horrified, as if the earth had no Hisham in it."

Another said:

"Harith al-Jawlan wept for the loss of his lord, and Hawran, from it, was humbled and crushed."

Harith al-Jawlan is a place.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: what is the meaning of the heavens being torn apart, the earth being split, and the mountains collapsing, and how does this word affect inanimate things? I say: there are two aspects to this. The first is that Allah says: 'I almost did these things to the heavens, the earth and the mountains upon the utterance of this word, out of anger at the one who uttered it, were it not for My forbearance and My dignity, and that I do not hasten punishment,' as He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah holds the heavens and the earth lest they should cease﴾ [Fatir: 41], and so on. The second is that it is a magnification of the word and an expression of its terror, and a depiction of its effect on religion, its demolition of its pillars and foundations; and the example of that effect among tangible things is that these great bodies, which are the pillars of the world, are almost torn apart, split open, and collapse from it." End of quotation.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: "This statement made the heavens, the earth, the mountains and all creatures afraid, except the two weighty ones (humans and jinn), and they were on the verge of collapsing from it, out of glorification of God, exalted is He." It was also said: the meaning is that the Resurrection is about to occur, for these things will literally come to pass on the Day of Resurrection. It was also said: "The heavens are almost rent asunder" (تَكادُ السَّماواتُ يَتَفَطَّرْنَ), meaning they fall upon them; "and the earth is split asunder" (وتَنْشَقُّ الأرْضُ), meaning it swallows them up; "and the mountains collapse in ruin" (وتَخِرُّ الجِبالُ هَدًّا), meaning they crush them.

Abu Muslim said: "It is as if they would do that, were they to understand, because of the enormity of this utterance." Al-Nahhas held that (هَدًّا) is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), saying: "Because the meaning of (تَخِرُّ) is to be shattered (تَنْهَدُّ)." End of quote. This is on the basis that (هَدًّا) is a verbal noun of هَدَّ الحائِطُ يَهِدُّ بِالكَسْرِ هَدِيدًا وهَدًّا, which is an intransitive verb (fiʿl lāzim). It was also said that (هَدًّا) is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl), meaning "being demolished," and this is on the basis that (هَدًّا) is the verbal noun of هَدَّ الحائِطَ, meaning "he demolished the wall," which is a transitive verb (fiʿl mutaʿaddin). Al-Zamakhshari permitted that it be an object of purpose (mafʿūl lahu), meaning "because they are demolished."

Al-Zamakhshari permitted three possibilities regarding ﴿أنْ دَعَوْا﴾ (that they ascribed). He said: it may be in the genitive as a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in (مِنهُ), as in his saying:

"In a state where, if Hatim were among the people, with his generosity, Hatim would be stingy with water."

This has remoteness, because of the great separation between the substitute and what it substitutes for, by two clauses. He said: it may be in the accusative by the omission of the preposition (lām) and the transmission of the verb, meaning (هَدًّا), because (دَعَوْا) gives the reason for the collapse (الخُرُور) as "the demolition" (الهَدّ), and the demolition is by the calling of a son to the Merciful. This also has remoteness, because the apparent sense is that (هَدًّا) is not an object, but rather a verbal noun from the meaning of (وتَخِرُّ), or in the position of a circumstantial qualifier. He said: it may be in the nominative as the agent of (هَدًّا), meaning: the calling of a son to the Merciful demolished them. This has remoteness, because the apparent sense of (هَدًّا) is that it is an emphatic verbal noun (maṣdar tawkīdī), and an emphatic verbal noun does not govern. Even if we supposed it non-emphatic, it would not govern by analogy, except if it is a command or a question about it, as in ḍarban Zaydan and uḍrib Zaydan, with a difference of opinion on this. As for if it is a statement, as al-Zamakhshari estimated, meaning "the calling of the Merciful demolished them," this is not analogical; rather what comes of that is rare, as in his saying:

"Standing by them, my companions, their mounts over me."

Meaning: my companions stood.

Al-Hawfi and Abu al-Baqa said: ﴿أنْ دَعَوْا﴾ is in the accusative position as an object of purpose, and they did not specify the governing element. Abu al-Baqa also said: it is in the genitive position with the lām estimated, and in the nominative position, meaning: what necessitates that is their calling. The meaning of (دَعَوْا) is "they named," and it is transitive to two objects, the first of which is omitted, and the estimate is "they named their deity a son of the Merciful," i.e., "with a son," because دَعا in this sense is transitive to two objects, and it is permissible for the preposition (بـ) to enter the second, as you say: "I called my son with Zayd," or "I called my son Zayd." The poet said:

"The mother of ʿAmr called me her brother, though I was not her brother, nor did I suckle at her breast."

Another said:

"Many a one claims to be a sincere advisor, and if he is absent, you will find him, in his absence from you, not sincere."

Al-Zamakhshari said: he restricted it to one of them, the second, seeking generality and comprehensiveness regarding everything for which he called a son, and he said: or (دَعا) is in the sense of "ascribed," whose reflexive form is what is in his saying, peace be upon him: "Whoever claims affiliation to other than his patrons..." and the saying of the poet:

"We, the sons of Nahshal, do not claim (ascription) to a father."

Meaning, we do not attribute ourselves to him. End of quote. That (دَعَوْا) here means "named" is the view of most. It was also said: (دَعَوْا) means "made."

(يَنْبَغِي) is the reflexive form of بَغى in the sense of "sought," meaning: it is not possible for Him to take a son, because procreation is impossible, and adoption can only occur in what is of the same kind as the adopted, and He, exalted is He, has no kind. (يَنْبَغِي) is not among the verbs that lack conjugation (lā tatasarraf); rather, its past tense has been heard, they said انْبَغى. Ibn Malik had counted it in al-Tashil among the verbs that lack conjugation, and this is an error. (مَن) is a relative pronoun meaning "who/that," meaning: there is not everyone who is in the heavens and the earth. (كُلُّ) enters upon (الَّذِي) because it comes for the genus, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿والَّذِي جاءَ بِالصِّدْقِ﴾ [al-Zumar: 33], and like:

"And all that you burdened me with, I will bear."

Al-Zamakhshari said (مَن) is a descriptive (mawṣūfa), because it occurred after (كُلُّ) as an indefinite noun, as it occurred after رُبَّ in his saying:

"Many a one whose chest I have made seethe with rage."

End of quote. The better view is to make it a relative pronoun, because its being descriptive relative to the relative is rare.

ʿAbd Allah, Ibn al-Zubayr, Abu Haywa, Talha, Abu Bahriyya, Ibn Abi ʿAbla and Yaʿqub read ﴿إلّا آتٍ﴾ with tanwin, and ﴿الرَّحْمَنَ﴾ in the accusative, while the majority read it with the genitive construction. "Ati" is the predicate of "kull," and ("ʿabdan") is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier. The word ﴿الرَّحْمَنِ﴾ is repeated as an alert that no one else deserves this name, since the roots and branches of blessings come from Him. And "whoever is in the heavens and the earth" includes those whom they took as deities from among the angels, ʿIsa and ʿUzayr, by virtue of their claim of the validity of procreation, or by virtue of their assertion of that, so they associated them in worship, since serving the sons is serving the fathers. So God, exalted is He, informed that there is no deity for them in the heavens or on the earth except that it comes to the Merciful as a servant, submissive, not claiming for itself anything of what they ascribed to it.

Then God, exalted is He, mentioned that He "has counted them" and encompassed them and confined them by number, so none of them escapes Him. (فَرْدًا) is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier, meaning: alone, with no one with Him of those they made partners with Him. The predicate of ﴿كُلُّهم آتِيهِ﴾ is ﴿فَرْدًا﴾. When "kull" is attached to a definite noun that is pronounced, such as "kulluhum" and "kull al-nas," it is reported that the pronoun may return singular to the wording of "kull," so you say "kullukum dhahib" (each of you is going), and it may return plural in consideration of the meaning, so you say "kullukum dhahibun." Ibrahim ibn Asbagh, in the book Ru'us al-Masa'il, related a consensus on the permissibility of both forms. On the plural form, al-Zamakhshari's wording in his commentary on this verse in al-Kashshaf is: "wa-kulluhum mutaqallibun fi malakutihi maqhurun bi-qahrihi" (all of them are moving about in His dominion, subdued by His dominance). Abu Zayd al-Suhayli criticized this, saying: "kull," when it begins and is grammatically attached to a definite noun, it is only good to make the predicate singular, taking the meaning into account. You say "kullukum dhahib," i.e., "each one of you is going." This is the case with this issue in the Qur'an, the hadith and eloquent speech. If you say: in His saying "wa-kulluhum atihi" it is taking the wording into account, since it is a singular noun, we say: rather, it is a noun of plurality, and a noun of plurality is not predicated with a singular. You say "al-qawm dhahibun" (the people are going), and you do not say "al-qawm dhahib," even though the word "qawm" is like the singular form. The phrase "kullukum dhahib" is only good because they say "kullu wahidin minkum dhahib" (each one of you is going), so the singular was in consideration of this meaning. End of quote. Establishing "kullukum dhahibun" in the plural and similar forms requires hearing and transmission from the Arabs. As for if the defined genitive noun is omitted, then what is heard from the Arabs is both forms.

The sīn in ﴿سَيَجْعَلُ﴾ is for the future. It is possible that this making (of affection) occurs in this world, and the future particle was used because the believers were in Mecca at the time this sura was revealed, and they were hated by the disbelievers, so God promised them this when Islam becomes manifest and spreads. It is also possible that this occurs in this world in general, as in al-Tirmidhi, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When God loves a servant, He calls Jibril: 'I have loved so-and-so, so love him.' He says: Then he calls in the heaven, then love is placed for him on earth." God, mighty and majestic, said: "Indeed those who believe and do righteous deeds, the Merciful will appoint for them affection (wudd)," to the end of the hadith. He said: This is a sound hadith. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: It is possible that the verse is connected in meaning with what precedes it, meaning: when God, exalted is He, informed about the coming of everyone in the heavens and the earth in a state of servitude and solitude, He comforted the believers by telling them that He will make for them on that day "wudd," which is what appears upon them of His honor, because God's love for the servant is nothing but what appears upon him of His blessings and the signs of His forgiveness. End of quote.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Or it may be that on the Day of Resurrection He makes them beloved to His creatures by what good deeds of theirs He displays and what He spreads from the register of their deeds. He also said: The meaning is that He will create in the hearts affection for them and cultivate it for them therein, without any solicitation from them and without their resorting to the means by which people acquire affection of hearts, such as kinship, friendship, performing kindness, or other things; rather, it is an innovation from Him, initiated as a special favor to His allies with a particular honor, just as He casts terror and awe into the hearts of their enemies, magnifying and exalting their station. End of quote. It was also said: there is an ellipsis in the speech, and the estimate is: He will admit them to the abode of His honor (p-221) and make for them "wudd" by means of the removal of rancor from their breasts, unlike the disbelievers, for on the Day of Resurrection some of them disbelieve in others, curse one another, and in the Fire too some of them disown others.

The majority read "wuddan" with a dhamma on the waw. Abu al-Harith al-Hanafi read it with a fatha on it. Jinah ibn Hubaysh read "widdan" with a kasra on the waw. It was said: this verse was revealed concerning ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn ʿAwf; the Jews, Christians and hypocrites used to love him, and when he migrated from Mecca he felt lonely in Medina, so he complained of that to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and this verse was revealed. It was also said: it was revealed concerning the emigrants to Abyssinia with Jaʿfar ibn Abi Talib; God cast affection for them into the heart of the Negus. Al-Naqqash mentioned that it was revealed concerning ʿAli ibn Abi Talib. Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya said: You will not find a believer except that he loves ʿAli and his household. End of quote. Among the strange things is what our teacher, the linguist Radi al-Din Abu ʿAbd Allah Muhammad ibn ʿAli ibn Yusuf al-Ansari al-Shatibi, may God have mercy on him, recited to us, for Zaynab, daughter of Ishaq the Christian al-Rasʿani:

"ʿAdi and Taym, I do not seek to mention them with evil, but I love Hashim."

"And nothing reproaches me concerning ʿAli and his kinsfolk, when they are mentioned for God, the blame of a blamer."

"They say: why is it that the Christians love them, while the people of understanding, among Arabs and non-Arabs, do not?"

"So I said to them: I truly think their love has spread in the hearts of creation, even to the beasts."

Abu Muhammad ibn Hazm mentioned that hatred of ʿAli is among the major sins.

The pronoun in ﴿يَسَّرْناهُ﴾ refers to the Qur'an, meaning: We sent it down to you, made easy and simple "in your tongue," i.e., in your language, which is the clear Arabic tongue. ﴿لِتُبَشِّرَ بِهِ المُتَّقِينَ﴾ means: that you may inform them of what will please them and of the reward they will have for their piety. "Lud" is a plural. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "lud" means in darkness; Mujahid: wicked; al-Hasan: deaf; Abu Salih: crooked from the truth; Qatada: people of disputation with falsehood, taking up every contentious matter with argument, i.e., on every side, because of their extreme obstinacy. He means the people of Mecca.

﴿وكَمْ أهْلَكْنا﴾ is a warning to them and a threat of destruction by punishment. The pronoun in His saying "qablahum" (before them) refers to "qawman ludda" (a contentious people). ﴿هَلْ تُحِسُّ﴾ is an interrogative with the meaning of negation, i.e., you do not perceive. The majority read ﴿هَلْ تُحِسُّ﴾ as the present tense of aḥassa. Abu Haywa, Abu Bahriyya, Ibn Abi ʿAbla and Abu Jaʿfar al-Madani read "taḥussu" with a fatha on the ta and a dhamma on the ha. It was also read "taḥissu," from ḥassahu, meaning "he sensed it," and from it come "al-ḥawass" (the senses) and "al-mahsusat" (the perceptible things). Hanzala read "aw tusmaʿu," the present tense of "usmiʿat," in the passive voice. Ibn ʿAbbas said: al-rikz is a faint sound. Ibn Zayd said: it is al-ḥiss (sensation). Al-Hasan said: when Our punishment came to them, none of them remained who could be seen, nor any sound heard. It was also said: the meaning is that they died and their mention was forgotten, so no informant reports about them.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 19, verses 83–98 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Have you not seen that We have sent the devils upon the disbelievers, inciting them with strong incitement?﴾ ﴿So do not be hasty against them; We are only counting for them a count.﴾ ﴿On the Day We will gather the God-fearing to the Most Merciful as a delegation.﴾ ﴿And We will drive the criminals to Hell as a thirsty herd.﴾ ﴿They will not possess intercession, except one who has taken a covenant with the Most Merciful.﴾ ﴿And they say, "The Most Merciful has taken a son."﴾ ﴿Indeed you have produced something monstrous.﴾ ﴿The heavens are about to be torn apart from it, and the earth split open, and the mountains collapse in ruin.﴾ ﴿That they attribute to the Most Merciful a son.﴾ ﴿And it is not befitting for the Most Merciful to take a son.﴾ ﴿There is none in the heavens and the earth but that he comes to the Most Merciful as a servant.﴾ ﴿He has enumerated them and counted them with a [precise] counting.﴾ ﴿And each of them will come to Him on the Day of Resurrection alone.﴾ ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, the Most Merciful will bestow on them affection.﴾ ﴿So We have only made it easy in your tongue that you may give glad tidings thereby to the God-fearing and warn thereby a contentious people.﴾ ﴿And how many generations have We destroyed before them? Do you perceive any of them or hear from them a whisper?﴾

(p-216) (Arsalnā) means: We empowered them (salaṭnā), or: We did not stand between them and them. Its semantic parallel is His saying: ﴿We appoint for him a devil﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 36]. Its construction with ʿalā (upon) is evidence that it means empowerment. (Tawuzzuhum) means: they stir them toward disbelief. Qatada said: "They provoke them." Ibn Zayd said: "They incite them." Al-Zamakhshari said: "They spur them on to acts of disobedience and stir them to it through whisperings and enticements. The meaning is: We left them between them and them, and We did not prevent them; had He willed, He would have prevented them. The intended purpose is to express astonishment at the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), following the verses in which the arrogant among the disbelievers and their sayings were mentioned."

Ajilta ʿalayhi bikadhā (I hastened against him with such-and-such) means: I sought to hasten it from him. That is: do not be hasty against them, that they should be destroyed; for between you and what you seek of their destruction there are only limited days and counted breaths, as if in their swiftness the hour in which they are counted is spent, were it counted. Similar to it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So do not seek to hasten [the punishment] for them. It is as if, on the day they see what they are promised, they had not remained but an hour of a day.﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 35]. End of quotation.

It was said: (Naʿuddu) means their deeds, so that We may recompense them. It was said: their terms, so that when it comes We will bring punishment upon them. It was said: their days, which Our decree has preceded that We would grant them respite until. It was said: their breaths.

(Yawma) is in the accusative, governed by an implied verb: udhkur (remember) or uḥdhar (beware), or [it is governed] by [the sense of] "that will be" as an answer to an implied question whose meaning is "when will that be?" Or [it is governed by] "they will disbelieve in their worship," or by "they will be [an enemy] to them" (yakūnūna ʿalayhim ḍiddan), or by the meaning "distance" (buʿdan). The notion of counting and enumeration includes the meaning of recompense. Or [(yawma)] is governed by ﴿yawma naḥshuru﴾ [the Day We gather] and ﴿nasūqu﴾ [We drive]: We will treat both groups in a way that description cannot encompass; or it is governed by ﴿lā yamlikūna﴾ [they will not possess]. All of these are cited as possibilities for the accusative of (yawma), and the most likely is the last.

(Naḥshuru) is transitive with ﴿ilā al-Raḥmān﴾ [to the Most Merciful], to honour and exalt them. He mentioned the attribute of mercy (al-Raḥmāniyya), with which He singled them out as a mark of honour, since the word ḥashr (gathering) carries the sense of assembling from scattered places and distant regions by way of compulsion. Thus the word "al-Raḥmān" comes to indicate that they are gathered to One who shows them mercy. The word sawq (driving) carries a sense of urging on. If it is followed by ﴿ilā Jahannam﴾ [to Hell], it is to shame them and to make the state of their abode appear dreadful. The word wafd (delegation) suggests honour and reverence, just as delegations come to kings, awaiting honour from them.

It is related from Ali: "On camels whose saddles are of gold, and on swift mounts whose saddles are of ruby." And also from him: that they will come riding on camels adorned with the adornment of Paradise, whose nose-rings are of ruby and chrysolite. Amr ibn Qays al-Mala'i narrated: that they will ride upon images of their righteous deeds in the utmost beauty. It is narrated that each of them will ride whatever he loves of camels, horses or ships, which will come floating with them.

The apparent meaning is that this delegation is after the reckoning has ended, and that it is the rising towards Paradise, as He said: ﴿In a seat of truth, in the presence of a Sovereign Omnipotent﴾ [al-Qamar: 55]. They are likened to delegations because they are the nobles of mankind and the finest in appearance, though it is not a true delegation, since a delegation involves departing from the one to whom the delegation is sent, whereas these remain forever in the reward of their Lord, which is Paradise.

(Al-Warid) means the thirsty, as said by Ibn Abbas, Abu Hurayra and al-Hasan. Al-Warid is a verbal noun of warada, meaning to proceed to water. The rajaz poet said:

Come on, come on, to the watering of a dove, dumb, of the grey-brown kind, which the coolness of water has pleased.

Since one who comes to water comes only out of thirst, the term (al-warid) was applied to the thirsty, as a naming of a thing by its cause.

Al-Hasan and al-Jahdari read: "yuḥsharu al-muttaqūna, wa-yusāqu al-mujrimūna" (the God-fearing are gathered, and the criminals are driven), in the passive voice. The pronoun in (lā yamlikūna) refers to the creatures indicated by the mention of the God-fearing and the criminals, since they are its two divisions. The exception is connected (muttaṣil), and (man) is a substitute (badal) for that pronoun, or it is in the accusative as an exception. (Lā yamlikūna) is a resumptive statement of information (istiʾnāf). It was said: its position is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of the pronoun in (lā yamlikūna), and it refers to the criminals. The meaning is: not possessing [the power] that intercession be made for them, and on this view the exception is disconnected (munqaṭiʿ). It was said: the pronoun in (lā yamlikūna) refers to the God-fearing and the criminals, and the exception is connected. It was said: it refers to the God-fearing, and taking a covenant (ittikhādh al-ʿahd) is the righteous deed by which one comes to be within the scope of one who intercedes.

Traditions are consistent that the people of knowledge and righteousness will intercede, and they will be granted intercession. In a hadith: "There is among my community a man through whose intercession Allah will admit more than the tribe of Banu Tamim." Qatada said: "We used to be told that a martyr intercedes for seventy [people]." Some who made the pronoun refer to the God-fearing said: the meaning is that the God-fearing do not possess intercession (al-shafāʿa) except for this category; on this view, (man ittakhadha) refers to those for whom intercession is made. On the first interpretation, (man ittakhadha) refers to the intercessors. So the implied construction on the second interpretation is: "they do not possess intercession for anyone except one who has taken [a covenant]," and it occupies an accusative position, as in the line:

"He was not saved except [in] the sheath of a sword and a loincloth."

That is: nothing was saved except the sheath of a sword. On these views, the waw is a pronoun.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is also possible that the waw in (lā yamlikūna), i.e., the ʿ[plural] marker, is like the one in akalūnī al-barāghīthu (the fleas ate me), and the subject is (man ittakhadha), since it has the sense of a plural." End of quotation. It is not proper to construe the Qur'an according to this rare dialect, especially when making the waw a pronoun is clearly sound. Ibn ʿUṣfūr, the Ustadh Abu al-Hasan, mentioned that it is a weak dialect. Also, they said: the alif and nūn that serve as markers and not as pronouns are not known to be followed by a subject except with explicit plurality or explicit duality or coordination; either a singular word is used that applies to a plural or to a dual, and establishing that requires transmission, or pronouns in the dual and plural refer to a singular form in wording that is meant as dual or plural, which is a known and attested usage in the speech of the Arabs. It is possible to analogise these markers to those pronouns, but the safer course is not to say this except on the basis of hearing. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is also possible that (man) is in the accusative, by omitting a modifying noun, i.e., except the intercession of one who has taken [a covenant]."

(Al-ʿahd) here. Ibn Abbas said: "There is no god but Allah, Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah." In a hadith: "Whoever says, 'There is no god but Allah, Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah,' has a covenant with Allah." Al-Suddi said: al-ʿahd is obedience. Ibn Jurayj said: it is the righteous deed. Al-Layth said: it is one who memorised the Book of Allah. It was said: the covenant of Allah is His permission for whomever He wills in intercession, from ʿahida al-amīr ilā fulānin bikadhā (the ruler commissioned so-and-so with such-and-such), i.e., ordered him to do it; that is, none intercedes except one commanded to intercede and permitted to do so. This is supported by His saying: ﴿And intercession with Him does not benefit except for one whom He permits﴾ [Saba: 23], ﴿On that Day, intercession will not benefit except one whom the Most Merciful has permitted﴾ [Ta-Ha: 109], ﴿Their intercession will not avail them at all, except after Allah permits whom He wills and approves﴾ [al-Najm: 26].

(p-218) Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "It is possible that (al-mujrimūn) includes both disbelievers and disobedient sinners, and then He informed that they ﴿do not possess intercession﴾ except the disobedient believers, for they will be interceded for, so the exception is connected." In a hadith: "I will not cease to intercede until I say, 'O Lord, grant me intercession for whoever has said, "There is no god but Allah." ' He will say, 'O Muhammad, it is not for you, but it is for Me.'" End of quotation. Taking (al-mujrimūn) to mean disbelievers and disobedient sinners is far-fetched.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya also said: "It is possible that (man ittakhadha) refers to Muhammad, peace be upon him, and that the special intercession for Muhammad is meant as the general intercession for mankind. And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It may be that your Lord will raise you to a praiseworthy station﴾ [al-Isra': 79]. And the pronoun in (lā yamlikūna) refers to the people of the Standing (al-mawqif)." End of quotation. There is some abridgement in it.

﴿And they say, "The Most Merciful has taken a son."﴾ The pronoun in (qālū) refers to some of the Jews, when they said, "ʿUzayr is the son of Allah," and to some of the Christians, when they said, "The Messiah is the son of Allah," and to some of the Arab polytheists, when they said, "The angels are the daughters of Allah." ﴿Indeed you have produced﴾: that is, say to them, O Muhammad, ﴿Indeed you have produced﴾. Or it is an iltifāt (shift from third-person reference to direct address), moving from the absent to the second person, to add emphasis against them regarding their audacity against Allah, and their exposure to His wrath, and to alert to the enormity of what they said.

The majority read (idd[an]) with a kasra on the hamza. ʿAlī ibn Abi Talib and Abu ʿAbd al-Rahman read it with a fatḥa, meaning shayʾan iddan (a monstrous thing), where the qualified noun is omitted and the verbal noun takes its place. Nafiʿ and al-Kisa'i read (yakādu) with the ya' from below, as also in al-Shura, and this is the reading of Abu Haywa and al-A'mash. The rest of the seven read it with ta'. For (yanfaṭirna), the present tense of infaṭara, Abu ʿAmr, Hamza, Abu Bakr from ʿAsim, and Ibn ʿAmir read it here; this is the reading of Abu Bahriyya, al-Zuhri, Talha, Humayd, al-Yazidi, Ya'qub and Abu ʿUbayd. The rest of the seven read (yatafaṭṭarna), the present tense of tafaṭṭara; and the one in al-Shura was read by Abu ʿAmr and Abu Bakr from ʿAsim with ya' and nūn, while the rest of the seven read it with ya' and ta' and tashdīd. Ibn Masʿud read (yataṣadda'na), and it should be taken as an explanation, since it contradicts the consensual written text of the codex, and since reliable transmitters from him agree with the reading of the majority.

Al-Akhfash said: (takādu) means "it intends" (turīdu), and similarly His saying: ﴿I almost conceal it﴾ [Ta-Ha: 15]. He cited as evidence a line of poetry:

"And it almost was, and I almost was, and that is the best intention, if the time of passion could return with what has passed."

There is no proof in this line. The known meaning is that kaydūda is approaching something. These phrases, according to the majority, are a figure of speech (istiʿāra) to express the monstrousness of this utterance; that is, this is its due, even if the inanimate things understood its magnitude. This is a familiar style among the Arabs. Jarir said:

"When the news of al-Zubayr came, the walls of Medina humbled themselves, and the lofty mountains."

Another said:

"Did you not see a crack appearing in the sky over a son of the Banu al-Harith ibn Hisham?"

Another said:

"So the belly of Mecca became horrified, as if the earth had no Hisham in it."

Another said:

"Harith al-Jawlan wept for the loss of his lord, and Hawran, from it, was humbled and crushed."

Harith al-Jawlan is a place.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: what is the meaning of the heavens being torn apart, the earth being split, and the mountains collapsing, and how does this word affect inanimate things? I say: there are two aspects to this. The first is that Allah says: 'I almost did these things to the heavens, the earth and the mountains upon the utterance of this word, out of anger at the one who uttered it, were it not for My forbearance and My dignity, and that I do not hasten punishment,' as He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah holds the heavens and the earth lest they should cease﴾ [Fatir: 41], and so on. The second is that it is a magnification of the word and an expression of its terror, and a depiction of its effect on religion, its demolition of its pillars and foundations; and the example of that effect among tangible things is that these great bodies, which are the pillars of the world, are almost torn apart, split open, and collapse from it." End of quotation.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: "This statement made the heavens, the earth, the mountains and all creatures afraid, except the two weighty ones (humans and jinn), and they were on the verge of collapsing from it, out of glorification of God, exalted is He." It was also said: the meaning is that the Resurrection is about to occur, for these things will literally come to pass on the Day of Resurrection. It was also said: "The heavens are almost rent asunder" (تَكادُ السَّماواتُ يَتَفَطَّرْنَ), meaning they fall upon them; "and the earth is split asunder" (وتَنْشَقُّ الأرْضُ), meaning it swallows them up; "and the mountains collapse in ruin" (وتَخِرُّ الجِبالُ هَدًّا), meaning they crush them.

Abu Muslim said: "It is as if they would do that, were they to understand, because of the enormity of this utterance." Al-Nahhas held that (هَدًّا) is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), saying: "Because the meaning of (تَخِرُّ) is to be shattered (تَنْهَدُّ)." End of quote. This is on the basis that (هَدًّا) is a verbal noun of هَدَّ الحائِطُ يَهِدُّ بِالكَسْرِ هَدِيدًا وهَدًّا, which is an intransitive verb (fiʿl lāzim). It was also said that (هَدًّا) is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl), meaning "being demolished," and this is on the basis that (هَدًّا) is the verbal noun of هَدَّ الحائِطَ, meaning "he demolished the wall," which is a transitive verb (fiʿl mutaʿaddin). Al-Zamakhshari permitted that it be an object of purpose (mafʿūl lahu), meaning "because they are demolished."

Al-Zamakhshari permitted three possibilities regarding ﴿أنْ دَعَوْا﴾ (that they ascribed). He said: it may be in the genitive as a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in (مِنهُ), as in his saying:

"In a state where, if Hatim were among the people, with his generosity, Hatim would be stingy with water."

This has remoteness, because of the great separation between the substitute and what it substitutes for, by two clauses. He said: it may be in the accusative by the omission of the preposition (lām) and the transmission of the verb, meaning (هَدًّا), because (دَعَوْا) gives the reason for the collapse (الخُرُور) as "the demolition" (الهَدّ), and the demolition is by the calling of a son to the Merciful. This also has remoteness, because the apparent sense is that (هَدًّا) is not an object, but rather a verbal noun from the meaning of (وتَخِرُّ), or in the position of a circumstantial qualifier. He said: it may be in the nominative as the agent of (هَدًّا), meaning: the calling of a son to the Merciful demolished them. This has remoteness, because the apparent sense of (هَدًّا) is that it is an emphatic verbal noun (maṣdar tawkīdī), and an emphatic verbal noun does not govern. Even if we supposed it non-emphatic, it would not govern by analogy, except if it is a command or a question about it, as in ḍarban Zaydan and uḍrib Zaydan, with a difference of opinion on this. As for if it is a statement, as al-Zamakhshari estimated, meaning "the calling of the Merciful demolished them," this is not analogical; rather what comes of that is rare, as in his saying:

"Standing by them, my companions, their mounts over me."

Meaning: my companions stood.

Al-Hawfi and Abu al-Baqa said: ﴿أنْ دَعَوْا﴾ is in the accusative position as an object of purpose, and they did not specify the governing element. Abu al-Baqa also said: it is in the genitive position with the lām estimated, and in the nominative position, meaning: what necessitates that is their calling. The meaning of (دَعَوْا) is "they named," and it is transitive to two objects, the first of which is omitted, and the estimate is "they named their deity a son of the Merciful," i.e., "with a son," because دَعا in this sense is transitive to two objects, and it is permissible for the preposition (بـ) to enter the second, as you say: "I called my son with Zayd," or "I called my son Zayd." The poet said:

"The mother of ʿAmr called me her brother, though I was not her brother, nor did I suckle at her breast."

Another said:

"Many a one claims to be a sincere advisor, and if he is absent, you will find him, in his absence from you, not sincere."

Al-Zamakhshari said: he restricted it to one of them, the second, seeking generality and comprehensiveness regarding everything for which he called a son, and he said: or (دَعا) is in the sense of "ascribed," whose reflexive form is what is in his saying, peace be upon him: "Whoever claims affiliation to other than his patrons..." and the saying of the poet:

"We, the sons of Nahshal, do not claim (ascription) to a father."

Meaning, we do not attribute ourselves to him. End of quote. That (دَعَوْا) here means "named" is the view of most. It was also said: (دَعَوْا) means "made."

(يَنْبَغِي) is the reflexive form of بَغى in the sense of "sought," meaning: it is not possible for Him to take a son, because procreation is impossible, and adoption can only occur in what is of the same kind as the adopted, and He, exalted is He, has no kind. (يَنْبَغِي) is not among the verbs that lack conjugation (lā tatasarraf); rather, its past tense has been heard, they said انْبَغى. Ibn Malik had counted it in al-Tashil among the verbs that lack conjugation, and this is an error. (مَن) is a relative pronoun meaning "who/that," meaning: there is not everyone who is in the heavens and the earth. (كُلُّ) enters upon (الَّذِي) because it comes for the genus, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿والَّذِي جاءَ بِالصِّدْقِ﴾ [al-Zumar: 33], and like:

"And all that you burdened me with, I will bear."

Al-Zamakhshari said (مَن) is a descriptive (mawṣūfa), because it occurred after (كُلُّ) as an indefinite noun, as it occurred after رُبَّ in his saying:

"Many a one whose chest I have made seethe with rage."

End of quote. The better view is to make it a relative pronoun, because its being descriptive relative to the relative is rare.

ʿAbd Allah, Ibn al-Zubayr, Abu Haywa, Talha, Abu Bahriyya, Ibn Abi ʿAbla and Yaʿqub read ﴿إلّا آتٍ﴾ with tanwin, and ﴿الرَّحْمَنَ﴾ in the accusative, while the majority read it with the genitive construction. "Ati" is the predicate of "kull," and ("ʿabdan") is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier. The word ﴿الرَّحْمَنِ﴾ is repeated as an alert that no one else deserves this name, since the roots and branches of blessings come from Him. And "whoever is in the heavens and the earth" includes those whom they took as deities from among the angels, ʿIsa and ʿUzayr, by virtue of their claim of the validity of procreation, or by virtue of their assertion of that, so they associated them in worship, since serving the sons is serving the fathers. So God, exalted is He, informed that there is no deity for them in the heavens or on the earth except that it comes to the Merciful as a servant, submissive, not claiming for itself anything of what they ascribed to it.

Then God, exalted is He, mentioned that He "has counted them" and encompassed them and confined them by number, so none of them escapes Him. (فَرْدًا) is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier, meaning: alone, with no one with Him of those they made partners with Him. The predicate of ﴿كُلُّهم آتِيهِ﴾ is ﴿فَرْدًا﴾. When "kull" is attached to a definite noun that is pronounced, such as "kulluhum" and "kull al-nas," it is reported that the pronoun may return singular to the wording of "kull," so you say "kullukum dhahib" (each of you is going), and it may return plural in consideration of the meaning, so you say "kullukum dhahibun." Ibrahim ibn Asbagh, in the book Ru'us al-Masa'il, related a consensus on the permissibility of both forms. On the plural form, al-Zamakhshari's wording in his commentary on this verse in al-Kashshaf is: "wa-kulluhum mutaqallibun fi malakutihi maqhurun bi-qahrihi" (all of them are moving about in His dominion, subdued by His dominance). Abu Zayd al-Suhayli criticized this, saying: "kull," when it begins and is grammatically attached to a definite noun, it is only good to make the predicate singular, taking the meaning into account. You say "kullukum dhahib," i.e., "each one of you is going." This is the case with this issue in the Qur'an, the hadith and eloquent speech. If you say: in His saying "wa-kulluhum atihi" it is taking the wording into account, since it is a singular noun, we say: rather, it is a noun of plurality, and a noun of plurality is not predicated with a singular. You say "al-qawm dhahibun" (the people are going), and you do not say "al-qawm dhahib," even though the word "qawm" is like the singular form. The phrase "kullukum dhahib" is only good because they say "kullu wahidin minkum dhahib" (each one of you is going), so the singular was in consideration of this meaning. End of quote. Establishing "kullukum dhahibun" in the plural and similar forms requires hearing and transmission from the Arabs. As for if the defined genitive noun is omitted, then what is heard from the Arabs is both forms.

The sīn in ﴿سَيَجْعَلُ﴾ is for the future. It is possible that this making (of affection) occurs in this world, and the future particle was used because the believers were in Mecca at the time this sura was revealed, and they were hated by the disbelievers, so God promised them this when Islam becomes manifest and spreads. It is also possible that this occurs in this world in general, as in al-Tirmidhi, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When God loves a servant, He calls Jibril: 'I have loved so-and-so, so love him.' He says: Then he calls in the heaven, then love is placed for him on earth." God, mighty and majestic, said: "Indeed those who believe and do righteous deeds, the Merciful will appoint for them affection (wudd)," to the end of the hadith. He said: This is a sound hadith. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: It is possible that the verse is connected in meaning with what precedes it, meaning: when God, exalted is He, informed about the coming of everyone in the heavens and the earth in a state of servitude and solitude, He comforted the believers by telling them that He will make for them on that day "wudd," which is what appears upon them of His honor, because God's love for the servant is nothing but what appears upon him of His blessings and the signs of His forgiveness. End of quote.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Or it may be that on the Day of Resurrection He makes them beloved to His creatures by what good deeds of theirs He displays and what He spreads from the register of their deeds. He also said: The meaning is that He will create in the hearts affection for them and cultivate it for them therein, without any solicitation from them and without their resorting to the means by which people acquire affection of hearts, such as kinship, friendship, performing kindness, or other things; rather, it is an innovation from Him, initiated as a special favor to His allies with a particular honor, just as He casts terror and awe into the hearts of their enemies, magnifying and exalting their station. End of quote. It was also said: there is an ellipsis in the speech, and the estimate is: He will admit them to the abode of His honor (p-221) and make for them "wudd" by means of the removal of rancor from their breasts, unlike the disbelievers, for on the Day of Resurrection some of them disbelieve in others, curse one another, and in the Fire too some of them disown others.

The majority read "wuddan" with a dhamma on the waw. Abu al-Harith al-Hanafi read it with a fatha on it. Jinah ibn Hubaysh read "widdan" with a kasra on the waw. It was said: this verse was revealed concerning ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn ʿAwf; the Jews, Christians and hypocrites used to love him, and when he migrated from Mecca he felt lonely in Medina, so he complained of that to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and this verse was revealed. It was also said: it was revealed concerning the emigrants to Abyssinia with Jaʿfar ibn Abi Talib; God cast affection for them into the heart of the Negus. Al-Naqqash mentioned that it was revealed concerning ʿAli ibn Abi Talib. Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya said: You will not find a believer except that he loves ʿAli and his household. End of quote. Among the strange things is what our teacher, the linguist Radi al-Din Abu ʿAbd Allah Muhammad ibn ʿAli ibn Yusuf al-Ansari al-Shatibi, may God have mercy on him, recited to us, for Zaynab, daughter of Ishaq the Christian al-Rasʿani:

"ʿAdi and Taym, I do not seek to mention them with evil, but I love Hashim."

"And nothing reproaches me concerning ʿAli and his kinsfolk, when they are mentioned for God, the blame of a blamer."

"They say: why is it that the Christians love them, while the people of understanding, among Arabs and non-Arabs, do not?"

"So I said to them: I truly think their love has spread in the hearts of creation, even to the beasts."

Abu Muhammad ibn Hazm mentioned that hatred of ʿAli is among the major sins.

The pronoun in ﴿يَسَّرْناهُ﴾ refers to the Qur'an, meaning: We sent it down to you, made easy and simple "in your tongue," i.e., in your language, which is the clear Arabic tongue. ﴿لِتُبَشِّرَ بِهِ المُتَّقِينَ﴾ means: that you may inform them of what will please them and of the reward they will have for their piety. "Lud" is a plural. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "lud" means in darkness; Mujahid: wicked; al-Hasan: deaf; Abu Salih: crooked from the truth; Qatada: people of disputation with falsehood, taking up every contentious matter with argument, i.e., on every side, because of their extreme obstinacy. He means the people of Mecca.

﴿وكَمْ أهْلَكْنا﴾ is a warning to them and a threat of destruction by punishment. The pronoun in His saying "qablahum" (before them) refers to "qawman ludda" (a contentious people). ﴿هَلْ تُحِسُّ﴾ is an interrogative with the meaning of negation, i.e., you do not perceive. The majority read ﴿هَلْ تُحِسُّ﴾ as the present tense of aḥassa. Abu Haywa, Abu Bahriyya, Ibn Abi ʿAbla and Abu Jaʿfar al-Madani read "taḥussu" with a fatha on the ta and a dhamma on the ha. It was also read "taḥissu," from ḥassahu, meaning "he sensed it," and from it come "al-ḥawass" (the senses) and "al-mahsusat" (the perceptible things). Hanzala read "aw tusmaʿu," the present tense of "usmiʿat," in the passive voice. Ibn ʿAbbas said: al-rikz is a faint sound. Ibn Zayd said: it is al-ḥiss (sensation).
